A cryptographic proof that a statement is true without revealing the underlying information.

explainers.title: Admin keys, upgradeability and who really controls a protocol
explainers.summary: How control over DeFi protocols is exercised in practice through admin keys, upgrades, multisigs, governance tokens and front-ends, and why it matters for risk and regulation.
explainers.bodyHtml:
DeFi protocols are often described as decentralised, but in practice many are controlled, at least in part, by identifiable people. Understanding who controls a protocol is essential for assessing its risks and how regulation applies.

Admin keys

An admin key is a privileged key that can call special functions in a protocol's smart contracts, such as:

  • upgrading the code;
  • changing parameters, such as interest rates, collateral limits or fees;
  • pausing the protocol;
  • minting tokens or moving funds held by the contract.

Whoever holds the admin key can change how the protocol works, and in some designs can take users' funds.

Upgradeability

Many protocols use upgradeable contracts, often through a proxy that points to code that can be replaced. Upgrades let developers fix bugs and add features, but they also mean the code users trusted can be changed.

Safeguards include:

  • multisig control, so several people must approve an upgrade;
  • timelocks, which delay changes so users can review them and exit;
  • governance votes before upgrades;
  • renouncing admin rights entirely once a protocol is mature, making the code immutable.

Governance tokens and DAOs

Many protocols hand control to holders of governance tokens, who vote on proposals, sometimes through a DAO. In practice:

  • token holdings are often concentrated among founders, early investors and large holders;
  • voter turnout is often low;
  • votes can be bought or borrowed, enabling governance attacks;
  • a foundation or core team may still drive proposals and execute them.

Other points of control

  • Front-ends: the website most users use to access the protocol, usually run by a company that can block users or tokens.
  • Oracles: whoever controls the price feeds influences the protocol.
  • Treasury and token supply: control over the protocol's funds and new tokens.
  • Off-chain infrastructure, such as relayers, sequencers on layer 2 networks, and bridges.

Why it matters

  • Risk: concentrated control creates the risk of misuse, coercion, error or key compromise.
  • Regulation: regulators look for people with control or sufficient influence. If they exist, they may be treated as service providers needing authorisation, as under FATF guidance and in the debate on DeFi under MiCA.
  • Accountability: users and counterparties need to know who to hold responsible if something goes wrong.

Questions to ask

  • Who holds admin keys, how many signatures are needed, and is there a timelock?
  • How concentrated is voting power?
  • Who runs the front-end, oracles and other infrastructure?
  • Could anyone change the rules or move user funds, and how would users know?
explainers.sortKey: admin keys, upgradeability and who really controls a protocol

explainers.title: Agentic AI in financial services
explainers.summary: What agentic AI is, how AI agents that act on their own are starting to be used in finance and payments, the new risks they bring and the controls firms need.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Agentic AI refers to AI systems that do not just answer questions but take actions: planning tasks, using tools, calling other systems and carrying out steps on their own to reach a goal. An AI agent might research a topic, draft and send emails, update records, execute trades or make payments.

Emerging uses

  • Operations: agents that process documents, reconcile accounts and resolve exceptions end to end.
  • Compliance: agents that gather customer due diligence information, run checks and draft reports.
  • Customer service: agents that resolve requests rather than just answering questions.
  • Investment and trading: agents that monitor markets and act within set limits.
  • Software development: agents that write, test and deploy code.
  • Payments and commerce: agents that buy goods and services on a customer's behalf, sometimes called agentic commerce. Card schemes, payment firms and crypto platforms are building ways for agents to pay, including with stablecoins and programmable wallets.

Why it is different

Traditional AI produces outputs that humans act on. Agentic AI acts directly, so errors and misuse can have immediate effects:

  • an agent can take wrong actions at speed and scale;
  • agents can be manipulated through malicious instructions hidden in emails, documents or web pages (prompt injection);
  • chains of agents interacting with each other can produce unexpected outcomes;
  • it can be unclear who authorised an action, and who is liable.

Controls

  • Least privilege: give agents only the permissions they need, with hard limits on amounts, counterparties and actions.
  • Human approval for significant or irreversible actions, such as payments above a threshold.
  • Identity and authentication for agents, so systems know when an agent is acting and on whose behalf.
  • Logging and audit trails of every action and the reasoning behind it.
  • Monitoring and kill switches to stop an agent quickly.
  • Testing in sandboxes before deployment, including against adversarial inputs.
  • Clear accountability: a named owner for each agent.

Regulation

There is no agent-specific financial regulation yet, but existing rules apply: conduct and consumer protection, payment authorisation and liability, AML/CFT, operational resilience, outsourcing and senior management accountability. The EU AI Act applies according to the use case. Regulators, including in the UK's consultation on payments regulation, are considering how rules on consent, authentication and liability should apply when an AI agent makes a payment.

Questions for boards

  • Where are agents already in use, including in third-party tools?
  • What can each agent do without human approval?
  • How would we detect and stop an agent acting wrongly?

explainers.title: Agents and distributors
explainers.summary: How payment and e-money institutions use agents and distributors to reach customers, the regulatory requirements, and the risks firms must manage.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Payment and e-money institutions often reach customers through third parties: agents that provide payment services on their behalf, and distributors that distribute or redeem e-money. Embedded finance and banking-as-a-service models also depend on partners.

Agents

  • Provide payment services in the name of the authorised institution, for example a shop offering money remittance.
  • Must be registered with the institution's regulator before they start, with information on their management and AML controls.
  • The institution is fully responsible for their acts.
  • Agents in other member states can be used under the passport.

Distributors

  • Distribute or redeem e-money for an e-money institution, such as retailers selling prepaid cards.
  • Cannot issue e-money themselves.
  • Must be notified to the regulator in some cases, such as when used in another member state.

Other partners

  • Programme managers that design and market card or account programmes using the institution's licence.
  • Embedded finance partners that offer payments within their own platforms.
  • Technical service providers, which are not regulated themselves but support the service.

Requirements and risks

  • Due diligence before appointment on fitness, AML controls and financial standing.
  • Training and monitoring, including AML/CFT and conduct.
  • Safeguarding: funds received by agents and distributors must be safeguarded from receipt.
  • Customer clarity: customers must know which institution provides the service.
  • Financial crime risk: agents can be exploited by criminals or complicit in laundering.
  • Concentration and growth risk: rapid expansion through partners can outpace controls.

What boards should ask

  • How many agents, distributors and partners do we have, and how do we monitor them?
  • How quickly do we detect and act on misconduct?
  • Are customer funds safeguarded from the moment partners receive them?

explainers.title: AI in financial services: uses and risks
explainers.summary: How financial firms use artificial intelligence, from fraud detection to investment research and customer service, the main risks, and how regulation and governance are responding.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is used across financial services. The arrival of generative AI, which can produce text, code and analysis, has widened its use from specialist models to everyday tools.

Main uses

  • Fraud detection and AML: spotting unusual transactions, detecting mule accounts, reducing false alerts, analysing networks.
  • Credit and underwriting: assessing creditworthiness and pricing risk.
  • Investment: research, signal generation, portfolio construction, trading execution.
  • Customer service: chatbots, call summarisation, personalised communications.
  • Operations: document processing, reconciliations, reporting, code generation.
  • Compliance and risk: regulatory change tracking, surveillance, policy drafting, horizon scanning.
  • Board and management information: summarising papers and data.

Main risks

  • Accuracy and hallucination: generative AI can produce confident but wrong answers.
  • Bias and unfair outcomes, especially in credit, insurance and customer treatment.
  • Explainability: difficulty explaining how a model reached a decision to customers, auditors or regulators.
  • Data protection and confidentiality: client data entering external tools, or models revealing training data.
  • Model risk: poor design, drift over time, misuse outside intended purpose.
  • Third-party and concentration risk: dependence on a few AI providers.
  • Cyber risk: AI-enabled attacks, and attacks on AI systems such as prompt injection.
  • Market risk: herding if many firms use similar models.
  • Accountability: unclear ownership when AI contributes to decisions.

Regulation

  • EU AI Act: high-risk obligations for creditworthiness assessments of individuals and life and health insurance pricing apply from December 2027. AI literacy duties apply now.
  • Financial regulation applies regardless of technology: conduct rules, the Consumer Duty in the UK, model risk management, outsourcing, operational resilience and senior management accountability.
  • Data protection law on automated decision-making and personal data.
  • Supervisors increasingly ask firms about their AI use and governance.

Good governance

  • An inventory of AI systems, classified by risk.
  • A board-approved AI policy and clear accountability.
  • Testing, validation and monitoring proportionate to risk.
  • Human oversight for significant decisions.
  • Controls on data entering AI tools.
  • Training for staff and the board.
explainers.sortKey: ai in financial services: uses and risks

explainers.title: Authorised push payment fraud and reimbursement
explainers.summary: What authorised push payment (APP) fraud is, the common scams, how reimbursement rules work in the UK and EU, and what payment firms can do to prevent it.
explainers.bodyHtml:
In authorised push payment (APP) fraud, a criminal tricks a victim into sending money themselves, for example by bank transfer. Because the victim authorised the payment, traditional rules on unauthorised transactions did not protect them.

Common scams

  • Impersonation: criminals pose as the victim's bank, the police, a utility or a government body, often warning of a problem that needs an urgent transfer to a "safe account".
  • Purchase scams: goods advertised online that never arrive.
  • Investment scams, increasingly involving crypto-assets and fake trading platforms.
  • Romance scams that build trust over time before asking for money.
  • Invoice and mandate fraud: criminals intercept or fake invoices, changing the bank details.
  • CEO fraud: impersonating a senior executive to order an urgent transfer.

Fraud is now one of the largest sources of criminal proceeds, and the money is quickly moved through mule accounts, often crossing borders and converting into crypto-assets.

Reimbursement

UK. Since October 2024, payment service providers in the Faster Payments system must reimburse most victims of APP fraud, with the cost split equally between the sending and receiving firms, up to a maximum amount. Exceptions apply where the customer acted with gross negligence or was complicit. The rules were set by the Payment Systems Regulator.

EU. The forthcoming Payment Services Regulation will require providers to refund customers who are tricked into payments by criminals impersonating their provider's staff, in some circumstances. It also introduces payee name verification for all credit transfers and obligations on online platforms.

Prevention

  • Confirmation or verification of payee: checking the payee name matches the account before a transfer.
  • Transaction monitoring and friction: spotting unusual payments and intervening with warnings, delays or calls.
  • Data sharing between banks, payment firms, telecoms and online platforms.
  • Mule account detection: monitoring incoming payments and account behaviour.
  • Customer education about common scams.

Questions for boards

  • What are our fraud losses and reimbursement costs, and how are they trending?
  • How effective are our warnings and interventions?
  • How quickly do we detect and close mule accounts?
  • Do we share intelligence with others in the payment chain?
explainers.sortKey: authorised push payment fraud and reimbursement

explainers.title: Automated market makers and liquidity pools (including impermanent loss)
explainers.summary: How automated market makers price trades using liquidity pools, how liquidity providers earn fees, what impermanent loss is, and the risks for traders and providers.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Most decentralised exchanges do not match buyers and sellers in an order book. Instead, they use automated market makers (AMMs): smart contracts that hold pools of tokens and quote prices using a formula.

Liquidity pools

A liquidity pool holds two (or more) tokens, for example ETH and a dollar stablecoin. Liquidity providers (LPs) deposit both tokens into the pool and receive LP tokens representing their share. Traders swap one token for the other against the pool, paying a fee that goes to the LPs.

The pricing formula

The simplest and best-known formula is the constant product: the quantity of token A multiplied by the quantity of token B must stay constant (x × y = k). When a trader buys ETH from the pool, the pool's ETH falls and its stablecoins rise, so the price of ETH in the pool goes up. The bigger the trade relative to the pool, the more the price moves. This is price impact or slippage.

Other designs include:

  • Stable swap curves for assets that should trade near each other, such as two stablecoins, giving low slippage near the peg.
  • Concentrated liquidity, where LPs choose a price range for their liquidity, using capital more efficiently but needing active management.

How prices stay in line with the market

The pool does not know the market price. Arbitrage traders buy from the pool when it is cheaper than other markets and sell when it is dearer, bringing the pool price back in line and earning the difference.

Impermanent loss

Because arbitrageurs trade against the pool when prices move, LPs end up holding more of the token that has fallen in value and less of the one that has risen. Compared with simply holding the two tokens, the LP is worse off. This shortfall is impermanent loss (also called divergence loss). It is "impermanent" only in that it disappears if prices return to where they started. If the LP withdraws after prices have moved, the loss is real.

Trading fees can offset impermanent loss, but in volatile markets they often do not.

Risks

For traders: - Slippage on large trades or thin pools. - Front-running and sandwich attacks, where others place transactions before and after a trade to profit from its price impact. - Scam tokens and manipulated pools.

For liquidity providers: - Impermanent loss. - Smart-contract exploits. - Loss if one token in the pool collapses or de-pegs. - Rug pulls, where a token's creators withdraw liquidity.

Why it matters

AMMs let anyone create a market in any token and are a core building block of DeFi. But their prices can be manipulated, and they are often used as price sources by other protocols, so weaknesses can spread.

explainers.title: Becoming a CASP under MiCA
explainers.summary: A practical outline of how a firm becomes an authorised crypto-asset service provider under MiCA: what the application covers, what regulators look for and the obligations that follow.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Since the end of the transitional period on 1 July 2026, firms providing crypto-asset services to clients in the EU need MiCA authorisation (or must be an authorised financial firm that has notified its regulator). Authorisation in one member state gives a passport across the EU.

Before applying

  • Define the services. Which of the MiCA services will the firm provide, for which crypto-assets, to which clients and in which member states?
  • Choose the home member state. Firms consider the regulator's approach and timelines, the local talent pool, and where substance can realistically be built. Regulators expect real presence: management and key staff in the EU, and a registered office in the home member state.
  • Pre-application engagement. Most regulators expect, and benefit from, early discussions.

What the application covers

Regulators assess the application against MiCA and technical standards that set out the required information, including:

  • programme of operations and business plan for at least three years;
  • legal entity, ownership structure and qualifying holders, with evidence of their good repute;
  • management body members' good repute, knowledge, skills and experience, and time commitment;
  • governance arrangements, internal control mechanisms, risk management and compliance;
  • prudential safeguards, showing capital and how it will be maintained;
  • ICT systems and security arrangements meeting DORA;
  • business continuity and wind-down plans;
  • procedures for client asset segregation and custody;
  • complaints handling, conflicts of interest and outsourcing policies;
  • AML/CFT policies and procedures;
  • service-specific policies, such as trading platform operating rules or execution policies;
  • marketing and client information.

What regulators look for

  • A credible business plan and enough capital and resources to deliver it.
  • A management body with real crypto and regulatory expertise, able to challenge.
  • Substance in the EU, not reliance on group staff elsewhere.
  • Well-controlled outsourcing, especially to group entities outside the EU.
  • Strong AML/CFT, including blockchain analytics and travel rule compliance.
  • Robust custody and key management.

Supervisors have stressed that they expect a consistent approach across the EU and will not accept forum-shopping for an easier regulator.

After authorisation

  • Ongoing compliance with conduct, prudential, governance and reporting requirements.
  • Notifications before changes of control, services or key personnel.
  • Passport notifications for other member states.
  • Market abuse surveillance and reporting.
  • Supervisory reviews, which may be more intensive in the first years.

Looking ahead

The Commission has proposed moving authorisation and supervision of CASPs to ESMA. Whatever the outcome, firms should expect increasingly convergent supervision across the EU.

explainers.title: Blockchain attacks: 51%, Sybil, reorgs and finality
explainers.summary: The main attacks on blockchain consensus and networks, what finality means, and how firms that accept crypto deposits or build on blockchains manage the risks.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Blockchains are designed to be secure without a central operator, but their security depends on assumptions that can fail, particularly for smaller networks.

51% attacks

If one party controls most of the mining power (proof of work) or stake (proof of stake), it can:

  • reorganise recent blocks and reverse its own transactions, enabling double spending;
  • censor transactions;
  • prevent other blocks being added.

These attacks are expensive on large networks but have happened several times on smaller proof-of-work chains, where hash power can be rented.

Chain reorganisations

A reorg replaces recent blocks with an alternative chain. Short reorgs happen naturally; deep reorgs indicate an attack or a serious fault. Transactions in replaced blocks may disappear or change.

Sybil and eclipse attacks

  • Sybil attack: creating many fake identities to gain influence over a network, a vote or an airdrop.
  • Eclipse attack: isolating a node so it sees only attacker-controlled peers and a false version of the chain.

Other risks

  • Long-range attacks on proof-of-stake chains using old validator keys.
  • Validator concentration: a few staking providers or exchanges controlling a large share of stake.
  • Client bugs: if most validators use the same software, a bug can halt or split the chain.

Finality

  • Probabilistic finality (Bitcoin): a transaction becomes safer as more blocks follow it.
  • Deterministic finality (many proof-of-stake chains): after a checkpoint, reversal would require destroying a large amount of stake.

Controls for firms

  • Set confirmation thresholds for deposits based on each network's security, value and history.
  • Monitor for reorgs and halt deposits during incidents.
  • Assess network concentration and client diversity before supporting a new chain.
  • Include consensus risk in token listing due diligence.
explainers.sortKey: blockchain attacks: 51%, sybil, reorgs and finality

explainers.title: Bridges and cross-chain risk
explainers.summary: How blockchain bridges move tokens between networks, the main bridge designs, why bridges have been hacked so often, and the wider risks of cross-chain activity.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Blockchains cannot natively read each other's data or move assets between them. Bridges connect them, letting users move tokens or messages from one chain to another.

How bridges work

The most common model is lock and mint:

  1. A user sends tokens to a bridge contract on chain A, which locks them.
  2. The bridge confirms the deposit.
  3. A corresponding wrapped token is minted on chain B.
  4. To go back, the wrapped token is burned on chain B and the original released on chain A.

Other models use liquidity networks, where the bridge holds pools of tokens on each chain and swaps between them, or native burn and mint by the token's issuer across chains.

Who confirms the transfer?

The key question is how the bridge verifies that a deposit really happened on the other chain:

  • Trusted or federated bridges rely on a group of operators or validators who sign off transfers. If enough of them are compromised, they can mint tokens or release locked funds.
  • Light-client and zero-knowledge bridges verify the other chain's state cryptographically, reducing trust in operators but adding complexity.
  • Optimistic bridges assume transfers are valid unless challenged within a time window.

Why bridges are risky

Bridges hold large pools of locked assets, making them attractive targets. Major bridge hacks have exploited:

  • compromised validator or operator keys;
  • smart-contract bugs, such as failing to verify messages properly;
  • weak upgrade controls.

If a bridge is drained, the wrapped tokens on the other chain may lose their backing and value.

Wider cross-chain risks

  • Wrapped token risk: a wrapped token is only as good as the bridge and custodian behind it.
  • Fragmentation: the same asset may exist in several wrapped versions on one chain, with different risks.
  • Contagion: a bridge failure can spread to protocols that accept its wrapped tokens as collateral.
  • Financial crime: bridges are used to hop between chains and obscure the trail of stolen or illicit funds.

Questions to ask

  • Who or what verifies transfers, and how many keys are needed to approve them?
  • How is the bridge's code audited and upgraded?
  • How much value is locked, and what happens to wrapped tokens if the bridge fails?
  • Does our exposure to wrapped tokens reflect the risks of the bridges behind them?

explainers.title: Buy now pay later and consumer credit
explainers.summary: How buy now pay later works, why it was outside credit regulation, and how the UK and EU are bringing it in, with what it means for lenders, merchants and payment firms.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Buy now pay later (BNPL) lets customers split a purchase into instalments, usually interest-free, with the provider paying the merchant up front. It has grown rapidly, especially online.

How it works

  • At checkout, the customer chooses BNPL and the provider makes a quick credit decision.
  • The provider pays the merchant, less a fee, which is the provider's main income.
  • The customer repays in instalments, often four payments over six weeks or monthly over a few months.
  • Late fees may apply if payments are missed.

Why it was unregulated

Interest-free credit repaid in a small number of instalments within a short period fell within exemptions from consumer credit rules in the UK and EU, which were designed for trade credit from merchants.

UK: deferred payment credit

Since 15 July 2026, third-party lenders offering interest-free credit repayable in 12 or fewer instalments within 12 months (deferred payment credit) must be authorised by the FCA. Requirements include:

  • creditworthiness assessments;
  • clear pre-contract information;
  • fair treatment of customers in financial difficulty;
  • access to the Financial Ombudsman Service;
  • the Consumer Duty.

Merchants offering their own credit and the broking of DPC remain exempt. Existing lenders could continue under a temporary permissions regime while applying.

EU: the revised Consumer Credit Directive

The revised Consumer Credit Directive, applying from 20 November 2026, brings BNPL and small loans into scope, with creditworthiness checks, information requirements and caps on costs set nationally. Some exemptions remain for merchants' own deferred payment terms.

Issues for firms

  • Affordability data: BNPL use has not always appeared on credit files.
  • Partnerships with merchants and payment firms: who is the lender, and who is responsible for the customer?
  • Embedded finance: lenders operating through other firms' checkouts must oversee how products are presented.
explainers.sortKey: buy now pay later and consumer credit

explainers.title: Central bank digital currencies and the digital euro
explainers.summary: What central bank digital currencies are, the difference between retail and wholesale CBDCs, how the digital euro would work and the debates around it.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A central bank digital currency (CBDC) is a digital form of central bank money: a direct claim on the central bank, like banknotes, but electronic.

Today, the public holds central bank money only as cash. Most money people use is commercial bank money, a claim on a private bank, protected by deposit insurance up to a limit.

Retail and wholesale CBDCs

  • Retail CBDC: available to the public for everyday payments.
  • Wholesale CBDC: available only to banks and other financial institutions, for settling large-value payments and securities transactions, including tokenised assets.

Why central banks are interested

  • To keep central bank money relevant as cash use declines.
  • To provide a public, risk-free digital means of payment alongside private options.
  • To strengthen monetary sovereignty, reducing dependence on foreign card schemes, big tech and foreign-currency stablecoins.
  • To support innovation and the settlement of tokenised assets (wholesale).

The digital euro

The Eurosystem has been preparing a possible digital euro since 2021.

  • Use: online and offline payments across the euro area, in shops, online and between people.
  • Distribution: through banks and other payment service providers, which would offer digital euro wallets to customers.
  • Holding limits: individuals would be limited in how much they can hold, to avoid draining bank deposits.
  • No interest would be paid.
  • Privacy: offline payments would offer cash-like privacy, and the ECB would not see individuals' identities for online payments.
  • Legal tender: it would have legal tender status, with merchants generally required to accept it.

The digital euro requires an EU regulation, which is being negotiated by the Parliament and Council. The ECB has said it could be ready for issuance in a few years, after the law is adopted.

The debates

  • Bank funding: whether deposits would move to the digital euro, especially in a crisis.
  • Need: whether private solutions, such as instant payments and stablecoins, are enough.
  • Privacy and state control: how to protect privacy while preventing financial crime.
  • Costs for banks and merchants.

Elsewhere

The Bank of England and HM Treasury have explored a digital pound, while focusing more recently on wholesale and tokenised settlement. Several central banks have launched retail CBDCs, and many are working on wholesale projects.
explainers.sortKey: central bank digital currencies and the digital euro

explainers.title: Change in control and qualifying holdings
explainers.summary: When acquiring or increasing a stake in a regulated firm needs regulatory approval, how the assessment works, typical timelines and common pitfalls.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Regulators want to know who owns and controls the firms they supervise. Anyone acquiring a significant stake in a regulated firm usually needs the regulator's prior approval.

Thresholds

In the EU and UK, approval is needed when a person acquires a qualifying holding (generally 10% or more of capital or voting rights, or significant influence) or increases it past thresholds such as 20%, 30% or 50%. Indirect holdings, through parent companies, count. Some regimes use different thresholds for certain firms.

The regime applies to banks, investment firms, insurers, fund managers, payment and e-money institutions and crypto-asset service providers.

What regulators assess

  • The reputation and integrity of the acquirer and its controllers.
  • The financial soundness of the acquirer and how the acquisition is funded.
  • Whether the firm will still meet its regulatory requirements, including under a new group structure.
  • Whether the acquirer's structure allows effective supervision, including close links.
  • Money laundering and terrorist financing risks, including source of funds.
  • The fitness of any new directors or senior managers.

Timeline

Regulators have a set period to assess a complete notification, often 60 working days in the EU, which can be paused for requests for further information. Pre-notification discussions are common for complex transactions.

Common pitfalls

  • Missing indirect changes, such as restructurings higher in a group or investment funds acquiring stakes.
  • Completing before approval, which is a criminal offence or breach in many jurisdictions.
  • Incomplete information on ultimate beneficial owners and funding.
  • Underestimating the time for multi-jurisdiction approvals.

Ongoing obligations

Firms must notify regulators of changes in controllers and usually report their controllers annually. Boards should know their ownership structure and monitor changes.
explainers.sortKey: change in control and qualifying holdings

explainers.title: Consensus: proof of work and proof of stake
explainers.summary: How blockchains agree on the state of the ledger without a central authority, how proof of work and proof of stake differ, and what each means for security, energy use and risk.
explainers.bodyHtml:
In a blockchain with no central operator, nodes need a way to agree which transactions are valid and in what order. This is the consensus mechanism. It must work even if some participants are dishonest.

Proof of work

Used by Bitcoin and some other networks.

  • Miners compete to solve a computational puzzle: finding a number that makes the block's hash meet a target. It takes enormous computing power to find, but is easy for others to check.
  • The winner adds the next block and receives newly created coins and transaction fees.
  • The chain with the most accumulated work is treated as the valid one.

Security: to rewrite history, an attacker would need more computing power than the rest of the network combined (a 51% attack), which is very expensive for large networks.

Drawbacks: high energy use, specialised hardware (ASICs), and concentration of mining in large pools.

Proof of stake

Used by Ethereum since 2022 and most newer networks.

  • Validators lock up (stake) the network's native token as collateral.
  • Validators are chosen to propose blocks, often in proportion to their stake, and others attest to them.
  • Validators earn rewards for honest behaviour and can lose stake (slashing) for misbehaviour.

Security: an attacker would need to control a large share of the staked tokens, and would risk losing them.

Advantages: far lower energy use than proof of work, and faster finality on some designs.

Drawbacks: wealth concentration, the influence of large staking providers and exchanges, and complexity.

Other mechanisms

  • Byzantine fault tolerant (BFT) protocols, often used in permissioned ledgers and some public networks, where a known set of validators agree in rounds and can tolerate up to a third being faulty.
  • Proof of authority, where approved, identified validators produce blocks.

Why it matters

  • Security and finality: how hard it is to reverse a transaction, and how long to wait before treating it as final.
  • Environmental disclosure: MiCA requires information on the environmental impact of a crypto-asset's consensus mechanism.
  • Concentration risk: who controls mining or staking power.
  • Staking: proof of stake creates staking products and their risks.
explainers.sortKey: consensus: proof of work and proof of stake

explainers.title: Cross-border payments and correspondent banking
explainers.summary: How cross-border payments work through correspondent banking, why they are slow and costly, the G20 roadmap to improve them, and the role of new technologies.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Sending money across borders is still slower, more expensive and less transparent than domestic payments. Most cross-border payments rely on correspondent banking.

How correspondent banking works

  • Banks hold accounts with each other in different currencies: a nostro account (our money held at your bank) and a vostro account (your money held at our bank).
  • A payment from one country to another passes through one or more correspondent banks, each debiting and crediting accounts and passing on messages, usually via SWIFT.
  • Each bank in the chain may charge fees, apply its own checks and hold the payment for reviews.

Why it is slow and costly

  • Multiple intermediaries and time zones.
  • Different messaging standards and data quality.
  • Sanctions and AML screening at each step.
  • Foreign exchange conversion and limited liquidity in some currency pairs.
  • De-risking: banks have reduced correspondent relationships with smaller or higher-risk countries, reducing access.

AML considerations

Correspondent relationships carry higher money laundering risk because the correspondent relies on the respondent's controls. Rules require enhanced due diligence, understanding the respondent's business and controls, and restrictions on nested relationships and shell banks. Payment messages must carry payer and payee information under the FATF travel rule, which the FATF strengthened in 2025.

Improving cross-border payments

The G20 roadmap, coordinated by the FSB and CPMI, has targets for 2027 on cost, speed, access and transparency. Measures include:

  • ISO 20022 messaging with richer data;
  • linking instant payment systems across countries;
  • extending operating hours of payment systems;
  • better access for non-banks;
  • harmonising data and AML requirements.

New technologies

  • Payment firms and fintechs using local accounts in many countries to avoid correspondent chains.
  • Stablecoins for faster, cheaper transfers, with their own risks.
  • Tokenised deposits and wholesale CBDC projects for interbank settlement.

explainers.title: Crypto AML: blockchain analytics and tracing
explainers.summary: How firms use blockchain analytics to manage financial crime risk in crypto: tracing funds, screening addresses, typologies of misuse, and the limits of the tools.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Public blockchains record every transaction permanently and openly. That makes crypto very different from cash: funds can be traced from address to address. Blockchain analytics tools turn this raw data into intelligence that firms and authorities use to fight financial crime.

What blockchain analytics does

  • Clustering: grouping addresses likely to be controlled by the same person or service, using patterns in how they transact.
  • Attribution: labelling clusters with real-world entities, such as exchanges, mixers, darknet markets, scams, ransomware groups and sanctioned persons.
  • Exposure analysis: showing how much of a deposit or withdrawal comes from, or goes to, risky sources, directly or indirectly.
  • Tracing: following funds through many hops, across tokens and, increasingly, across blockchains through bridges.

How firms use it

  • Screening deposits and withdrawals against risk categories and sanctions lists before crediting or sending funds.
  • Customer risk assessment, using on-chain activity alongside traditional due diligence.
  • Transaction monitoring and investigations, with alerts reviewed by analysts.
  • Travel rule counterparty checks, identifying whether an address belongs to another VASP.
  • Responding to authorities, including freezing assets linked to crime where possible.

Common typologies

  • Scams and fraud, including investment and romance scams, now among the largest sources of illicit crypto flows.
  • Hacks and theft, including by state-linked groups, laundered through mixers, bridges and many hops.
  • Ransomware payments.
  • Sanctions evasion, including use of stablecoins and exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions.
  • Darknet markets and illicit goods.
  • Money mule networks and cash-out services, including crypto ATMs and peer-to-peer trading.

Obfuscation techniques

Criminals try to break the trail using mixers, privacy coins with hidden transactions, chain-hopping through bridges and swaps, peel chains of many small transactions, and unhosted wallets. Under the EU AML Regulation, CASPs may not handle anonymity-enhancing coins from July 2027.

Limits of the tools

  • Attribution is probabilistic and can be wrong; analytics is intelligence, not proof.
  • Coverage varies by blockchain and token.
  • Privacy technologies and cross-chain activity reduce visibility.
  • Over-reliance on risk scores without human judgment leads to poor decisions.

Good practice

  • Set clear risk appetite and thresholds for exposure to high-risk categories.
  • Combine analytics with customer due diligence and behavioural monitoring.
  • Document decisions on alerts.
  • Assess analytics providers for coverage, accuracy and data quality.
  • Report suspicious activity promptly and freeze assets where required.
explainers.sortKey: crypto aml: blockchain analytics and tracing

explainers.title: Crypto custody models: hot, cold, multisig and MPC
explainers.summary: How regulated firms hold crypto-assets for clients: wallet structures, key management technologies, segregation, reconciliation and the protections clients should expect.
explainers.bodyHtml:
For a crypto-asset service provider, custody means controlling the private keys to clients' crypto-assets. It is the activity where failures have caused the largest losses to clients, through hacks, theft, lost keys and misuse of client assets.

Wallet architecture

Custodians usually spread assets across tiers:

  • Cold storage for most assets, with keys generated and kept offline in secure facilities. Moving assets out takes time and several people.
  • Warm wallets for moderate amounts, with automated controls and approvals.
  • Hot wallets for the small share needed to process withdrawals quickly, with limits and frequent top-ups from cold storage.

The split is set by policy, reflecting withdrawal patterns and risk appetite.

Key management technologies

  • Hardware security modules (HSMs): tamper-resistant devices that generate and store keys and sign transactions without exposing them.
  • Multisig: transactions need signatures from several keys, held by different people or systems, so no single person can move assets.
  • Multi-party computation (MPC): a key is split into shares, held separately, that sign together without the full key ever existing in one place. MPC works across blockchains, including those without native multisig.

Whatever the technology, the controls around it matter most: who holds key shares, how they are vetted, how many are needed, how they are rotated when people leave, and how the system is recovered if something fails.

Segregation and records

  • Client assets must be kept separate from the firm's own, on-chain and in the books.
  • Omnibus wallets pool many clients' assets, with the firm's records showing each client's entitlement. Segregated wallets hold each client's assets separately.
  • Reconciliation of internal records with on-chain balances should be frequent, ideally daily or continuous, with differences investigated immediately.

Legal protection

Clients need assurance that their assets are protected if the custodian fails. That depends on the legal analysis of ownership in the relevant jurisdiction, the custody agreement and the quality of records. MiCA requires segregation and makes custodians liable for loss of crypto-assets caused by incidents attributable to them.

Third parties

Many firms use technology providers or sub-custodians. The firm remains responsible and needs due diligence, contractual rights and an exit plan.

Assurance

  • Independent audits of controls, such as SOC 2 reports.
  • Proof of reserves, showing on-chain holdings, is useful only if it also covers liabilities to clients and is independently verified.
  • Insurance, with attention to what is actually covered and the limits relative to assets held.

Red flags

  • Client and firm assets mixed in the same wallets.
  • Infrequent or manual reconciliations.
  • A few individuals able to move large amounts alone.
  • Using client assets for lending, staking or trading without clear consent and controls.
explainers.sortKey: crypto custody models: hot, cold, multisig and mpc

explainers.title: Crypto derivatives and leverage: perpetuals, margin and liquidations
explainers.summary: How perpetual futures and margin trading work on crypto platforms, how liquidations and insurance funds operate, the risks to customers, and how regulators restrict leveraged products.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Most crypto trading volume is in derivatives, especially perpetual futures, many offered with high leverage on platforms outside the main regulated markets.

Perpetual futures

A perpetual future is a contract that tracks the price of a crypto-asset and has no expiry date. To keep it close to the spot price, traders on one side periodically pay the other a funding rate: when the perpetual trades above spot, longs pay shorts, and vice versa.

Margin and leverage

Traders post margin as collateral and can take positions many times larger than their margin. With 10x leverage, a 10% price move against the trader wipes out the margin.

  • Isolated margin: each position has its own margin.
  • Cross margin: all positions share the account balance, so one losing position can drain the whole account.

Liquidations

When margin falls below the maintenance level, the platform's liquidation engine closes the position. In fast markets, liquidations can cascade: forced selling pushes prices down, triggering more liquidations.

If a position cannot be closed at a price that covers its losses, the platform uses its insurance fund. If that is not enough, auto-deleveraging may close profitable opposing positions.

Risks to customers

  • Rapid total loss.
  • Liquidations at poor prices during volatility or outages.
  • Conflicts where the platform is also a market maker or counterparty.
  • Opaque insurance funds and liquidation practices.
  • Platforms operating without authorisation in the customer's country.

Regulatory approach

  • In the EU, crypto derivatives are generally financial instruments under MiFID, not MiCA, and retail CFDs face leverage limits and negative balance protection.
  • The UK bans the sale of crypto derivatives to retail consumers.
  • In the US, crypto futures are regulated by the CFTC.
  • Decentralised perpetual exchanges raise similar risks, often with no investor protections.
explainers.sortKey: crypto derivatives and leverage: perpetuals, margin and liquidations

explainers.title: Crypto ETPs and ETFs
explainers.summary: How exchange-traded products give investors exposure to crypto-assets, the differences between ETFs, ETNs and ETCs, how they are regulated in the EU, UK and US, and the risks.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Crypto exchange-traded products (ETPs) let investors gain exposure to crypto-assets through a regulated security traded on a stock exchange, without holding the crypto-assets directly.

Types

  • Exchange-traded funds (ETFs): funds that hold crypto-assets, such as spot bitcoin and ether ETFs in the US and Hong Kong.
  • Exchange-traded notes (ETNs) or certificates: debt securities issued by a special purpose vehicle, typically backed by crypto-assets held with a custodian. Common in Europe.
  • Futures-based products that track crypto futures rather than holding the asset.

How they work

  • The issuer buys and holds crypto-assets with a custodian, often in cold storage.
  • Authorised participants create and redeem units, in cash or in kind, keeping the market price close to the value of the holdings.
  • Investors trade units through brokers and platforms like any listed security.

Regulation

  • EU: crypto-assets are not eligible assets for UCITS, so EU crypto ETPs are usually notes, not funds. They are covered by the Prospectus Regulation and MiFID II rules for complex products.
  • UK: retail access to crypto ETNs listed on UK exchanges was allowed from October 2025, subject to financial promotion and Consumer Duty rules.
  • US: spot bitcoin ETFs were approved in January 2024 and spot ether ETFs in 2024; in 2025 the SEC approved generic listing standards for crypto ETPs.

Benefits

  • Familiar, regulated wrapper and access through existing accounts.
  • No need to manage keys.
  • Some products can be held in tax-advantaged accounts.

Risks

  • Price volatility of the underlying crypto-assets.
  • Custody risk and dependence on a few custodians.
  • Counterparty risk for notes, which are debt of the issuer.
  • Tracking differences and fees.
  • Premiums or discounts to NAV in stressed markets.
  • Some products stake the underlying assets, adding staking risks.

explainers.title: Crypto lending and earn products
explainers.summary: How centralised crypto lending and 'earn' products work, where the yield comes from, why several large lenders failed, and how regulation treats them.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Crypto lending and earn products offer clients a return on their crypto-assets. They take several forms.

Types

  • Centralised lending platforms: clients deposit crypto-assets, which the platform lends to borrowers such as trading firms or uses in its own strategies, paying clients interest.
  • Exchange earn products: exchanges offer fixed or flexible yields on deposited assets, sourced from lending, staking or DeFi.
  • Staking services: returns come from proof-of-stake rewards.
  • DeFi lending: clients lend through smart contracts directly, usually over-collateralised.

Where the yield comes from

  • Interest from borrowers, often trading firms using leverage.
  • Staking rewards.
  • DeFi yields, including liquidity provision and incentives.
  • In some failed platforms, risky or undisclosed strategies, or new deposits used to pay existing clients.

Why lenders failed

In 2022 several large centralised crypto lenders failed. Common features included:

  • Maturity and liquidity mismatch: clients could withdraw at any time, while assets were lent or locked up.
  • Concentrated, under-collateralised loans to a few borrowers.
  • Commingling of client and firm assets, and clients' legal position as unsecured creditors under the terms of use.
  • Opaque risk-taking and poor disclosure.

Clients faced frozen withdrawals and lengthy insolvencies.

How regulation treats them

  • In the EU, MiCA does not cover crypto lending and borrowing as a service, though custody does apply, and the Commission is reviewing this gap.
  • Some regulators have banned or restricted retail crypto lending, and many treat certain earn products as investment products or collective investment schemes.
  • In the UK, the FCA has consulted on how cryptoasset lending and borrowing should be treated under the new regime, and arranging staking will be a regulated activity from October 2027.

Questions for clients and boards

  • Who owns the assets once deposited, and what happens if the platform fails?
  • Where exactly does the yield come from, and how is it collateralised?
  • Can clients withdraw at any time, and what if many do?

explainers.title: Crypto scams and fraud typologies
explainers.summary: The main crypto-related scams, from investment and relationship scams to rug pulls and address poisoning, how the money moves, and how firms can protect customers.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Crypto-assets are attractive to fraudsters because transfers are fast, global and irreversible. Many scams combine traditional manipulation techniques with crypto payments.

Main typologies

  • Investment scams: fake trading platforms, often promoted through social media, adverts using fake celebrity endorsements or cold calls. Victims see fake profits and are pressed to invest more, then cannot withdraw.
  • Relationship investment scams (sometimes called pig butchering): the fraudster builds a friendship or romance over weeks before introducing an investment opportunity.
  • Impersonation: posing as an exchange, bank, police or tax authority to persuade victims to move funds to a "safe" wallet.
  • Rug pulls: developers launch a token or DeFi project, attract funds and then disappear with them.
  • Pump and dump: promoting a thinly traded token to inflate its price, then selling.
  • Phishing and wallet drainers: fake websites or approvals that give attackers control of victims' wallets.
  • Address poisoning: tricking victims into copying a look-alike address.
  • Recovery scams: targeting previous victims with offers to recover lost funds for a fee.

How the money moves

Victims typically buy crypto-assets at a legitimate exchange or crypto ATM and send them to the scammer's wallet. Funds are then moved through many addresses, swapped, bridged and cashed out through exchanges, often using money mules.

Protecting customers

  • Warnings at the point of withdrawal to new addresses, tailored to scam patterns.
  • Address screening against known scam addresses using blockchain analytics.
  • Behavioural signals: first-time large withdrawals, older customers, sudden changes in activity, remote access software.
  • Delays and friction for high-risk transfers, with conversations to check the customer's understanding.
  • Information sharing with other firms and law enforcement.

Regulatory context

Banks and payment firms increasingly block or delay payments to crypto exchanges because of fraud. In the UK, mandatory reimbursement for authorised push payment fraud applies to Faster Payments and CHAPS, but not to transfers of crypto-assets themselves.

explainers.title: Culture and conduct risk
explainers.summary: What conduct risk and culture mean in financial services, how regulators assess them, the drivers of good and poor culture, and how firms can measure and improve it.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Conduct risk is the risk that a firm's behaviour leads to poor outcomes for customers or harms market integrity. Culture is the set of shared values and behaviours that shape how people in the firm act, especially when no rule tells them what to do.

Many of the biggest scandals in financial services, from mis-selling to market manipulation, were failures of culture as much as of rules.

Drivers of culture

  • Purpose and strategy: what the firm is trying to achieve, and whether it values customers' interests.
  • Leadership: what senior people say, do and tolerate.
  • Incentives: how people are paid, promoted and recognised.
  • Governance and controls: whether challenge is welcome and controls are respected.
  • Speaking up: whether people raise concerns, and what happens when they do.
  • Capability: whether people have the skills and support to do the right thing.

How regulators assess it

Regulators look for evidence, not statements of values:

  • outcomes for customers, complaints and redress;
  • breaches, incidents and how they are handled;
  • remuneration and how it reflects conduct;
  • the board's understanding of culture and actions taken;
  • whistleblowing volumes and handling;
  • how management responds to challenge.

Measuring culture

No single metric works. Firms combine:

  • staff surveys and focus groups;
  • conduct indicators, such as breaches, complaints, attestation failures and training completion;
  • HR data, such as turnover, grievances and disciplinary cases;
  • control function and internal audit findings;
  • observation of meetings and decision-making.

Improving culture

  • Leaders model the behaviours they expect.
  • Incentives reward how results are achieved, not just results.
  • Consequences apply to everyone, regardless of seniority or performance.
  • Speaking up is encouraged and protected, and leads to visible action.
  • The board receives culture information regularly and acts on it.

explainers.title: Customer due diligence and beneficial ownership
explainers.summary: What customer due diligence involves, how firms identify the beneficial owners behind companies and trusts, and when simplified or enhanced measures apply.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Customer due diligence (CDD) means knowing who your customers are, understanding what they are doing and keeping that knowledge up to date. It is the core preventive measure in AML/CFT rules.

The elements of CDD

  1. Identify and verify the customer, using reliable, independent documents, data or information, including electronic identification.
  2. Identify the beneficial owner and take reasonable measures to verify their identity.
  3. Understand the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship.
  4. Conduct ongoing monitoring of the relationship and transactions, keeping information up to date.

CDD applies when establishing a relationship, for occasional transactions above set thresholds, when there is a suspicion of money laundering, and when there are doubts about previously obtained information.

Beneficial ownership

A beneficial owner is the natural person who ultimately owns or controls a customer that is a legal entity or arrangement.

  • Companies: usually any person owning or controlling more than 25% of the shares or voting rights, directly or indirectly, or exercising control by other means. Under the EU AML Regulation, the threshold is 25% or more, and lower thresholds may be set for higher-risk sectors. If no one qualifies, a senior managing official is recorded, after exhausting other means.
  • Trusts: the settlor, trustees, protector, beneficiaries and anyone else exercising effective control.

Firms must understand the ownership and control structure, especially where there are layers of companies, nominees or trusts across jurisdictions. Central beneficial ownership registers help, but firms cannot rely on them alone.

Simplified and enhanced measures

  • Simplified due diligence may apply where risk is demonstrably low, such as some regulated entities or public bodies, but monitoring continues.
  • Enhanced due diligence is required for higher risk, including PEPs, customers linked to high-risk third countries, complex or unusual transactions and certain correspondent relationships. It involves more information on the source of funds and wealth, senior management approval and closer monitoring.

Reliance and outsourcing

Firms can rely on CDD done by other regulated firms, or outsource it, but remain responsible.

Common failures

  • Not understanding complex ownership structures.
  • Out-of-date customer information and review backlogs.
  • Weak source of funds and wealth checks for high-risk customers.
  • Treating CDD as a one-off onboarding exercise.
explainers.sortKey: customer due diligence and beneficial ownership

explainers.title: Cyber resilience testing: from penetration tests to TLPT
explainers.summary: How financial firms test their cyber resilience, from vulnerability scans and penetration tests to intelligence-led red teaming under DORA, TIBER-EU and CBEST.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Firms need evidence that their defences work. Testing ranges from routine scans to sophisticated simulated attacks.

Types of testing

  • Vulnerability scanning: automated tools find known weaknesses in systems and software.
  • Penetration testing: specialists try to exploit vulnerabilities in a defined scope, such as a web application or network.
  • Red teaming: a team simulates a real attacker, using any methods within agreed rules, to test detection and response as well as prevention. The defending team (blue team) is not told in advance.
  • Purple teaming: red and blue teams work together to improve detection.
  • Scenario-based and tabletop exercises: testing decision-making and communications during a simulated incident.

Threat-led penetration testing (TLPT)

Under DORA, financial entities designated by their authorities, usually larger and systemically important firms, must carry out threat-led penetration testing at least every three years. It:

  • covers critical or important functions on live production systems;
  • is based on threat intelligence about actors likely to target the firm;
  • uses external testers, or internal testers under conditions;
  • involves critical ICT providers where relevant;
  • is overseen by the authority and results in a remediation plan.

TIBER-EU, the European framework for intelligence-led red teaming, has been aligned with DORA's requirements. The UK's equivalent is CBEST.

For all firms

DORA requires all in-scope firms, proportionately, to run a digital operational resilience testing programme, including vulnerability assessments, network security assessments, scenario-based tests and penetration tests, with tests by independent parties.

Making testing useful

  • Test what matters most, based on important business services and threats.
  • Track findings to remediation, with owners and deadlines.
  • Report themes and trends to the board, not just numbers of tests.
  • Retest to confirm fixes.
explainers.sortKey: cyber resilience testing: from penetration tests to tlpt

explainers.title: DAOs and governance tokens
explainers.summary: How decentralised autonomous organisations and governance tokens work, the governance problems they face, their legal status, and why they matter to regulators.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A decentralised autonomous organisation (DAO) is a group that coordinates through rules encoded in smart contracts and votes by token holders, rather than a traditional management structure. Many DeFi protocols are governed by DAOs.

How DAOs work

  • Holders of governance tokens propose and vote on changes, such as protocol parameters, upgrades, fee levels and use of the treasury.
  • Votes are often weighted by the number of tokens held, and may be on-chain (binding, executed by smart contracts) or off-chain (signalling, executed by a trusted group).
  • Token holders can often delegate their votes to others.
  • A treasury controlled by the DAO holds the protocol's funds.

Problems in practice

  • Concentration: founders, early investors and large holders often control most votes.
  • Low participation: many token holders never vote.
  • Governance attacks: votes can be bought, borrowed (sometimes with flash loans) or captured to drain the treasury.
  • Accountability: it can be unclear who is responsible for decisions and their consequences.
  • Speed: governance can be too slow to respond to emergencies, so many DAOs give special powers to a small security council or multisig.

Legal status

Many DAOs operate without a legal entity. Depending on the jurisdiction, members may be treated as partners with unlimited liability. Increasingly, DAOs use legal wrappers, such as foundations, limited liability companies or special DAO entities available in some jurisdictions.

Why it matters to regulators

  • If a DAO or identifiable group controls a protocol, regulators may treat them as responsible for regulated activities, such as operating a trading platform or providing custody.
  • Governance tokens may be securities or other regulated instruments, depending on their features.
  • The FATF and IOSCO look for persons with control or sufficient influence over DeFi arrangements.

Questions to ask

  • Who really controls the protocol, and how concentrated is voting power?
  • What emergency powers exist, and who holds them?
  • What legal entity, if any, stands behind the DAO?

explainers.title: DeFi lending, collateral and liquidations
explainers.summary: How DeFi lending protocols work: over-collateralised loans, interest rates set by algorithms, health factors, automatic liquidations and the risks of cascades.
explainers.bodyHtml:
DeFi lending protocols let users lend crypto-assets to earn interest, or borrow by posting collateral, without a bank in the middle. Smart contracts manage the loans.

How it works

  • Lenders (suppliers) deposit tokens into a pool and receive interest-bearing tokens representing their claim.
  • Borrowers deposit collateral and borrow other tokens from the pool, up to a limit.
  • Interest rates are set by an algorithm based on utilisation: the more of the pool that is borrowed, the higher the rate, to attract lenders and discourage borrowing.

Over-collateralisation

Because borrowers are anonymous and there is no credit assessment, loans are over-collateralised: a borrower must post collateral worth more than the loan. Each collateral type has a loan-to-value limit, for example 75%, and a liquidation threshold.

A borrower's health factor compares the value of their collateral, adjusted for these thresholds, with their debt. If it falls below 1, the position can be liquidated.

Liquidations

When collateral prices fall, or the borrowed asset rises, a position may become under-collateralised. Liquidators, usually automated bots, repay part of the borrower's debt and receive the borrower's collateral at a discount (the liquidation bonus). This protects lenders but costs the borrower.

Oracles

Protocols rely on oracles to provide prices for collateral and debt. If an oracle is manipulated or fails, healthy positions can be liquidated or bad loans left in place.

Risks

  • Liquidation cascades: a sharp price fall triggers liquidations, which push prices down further, triggering more.
  • Bad debt: if collateral cannot be sold fast enough, the protocol is left with losses, which may be spread across lenders.
  • Oracle manipulation, often combined with flash loans.
  • Smart-contract exploits and governance attacks.
  • Collateral risk: using volatile or illiquid tokens, or liquid staking tokens that can de-peg, as collateral.
  • Leverage loops: borrowing against collateral to buy more of the same asset and repeat, which magnifies losses.

Flash loans

A flash loan lets a user borrow any amount with no collateral, provided it is repaid within the same transaction. If not repaid, the whole transaction is reversed. Flash loans are used for arbitrage and refinancing, and also in many exploits.

Regulatory angle

Lending and borrowing of crypto-assets is not a specific service under MiCA, and the Commission is reviewing it. Centralised crypto lending, where a firm takes customers' assets and lends them on, has led to major failures and is regulated or restricted in many jurisdictions.

explainers.title: Delegation and substance
explainers.summary: Why fund managers delegate functions, what EU rules require when they do, and how regulators judge whether a manager has enough substance.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Fund managers often delegate functions to other firms, most commonly portfolio management. Delegation can bring expertise and efficiency, but regulators worry that it can leave the authorised firm as an empty shell. Two concepts govern this: delegation rules and substance.

What can be delegated

Under UCITS and AIFMD, a management company or AIFM can delegate functions such as:

  • portfolio management;
  • risk management;
  • administration, including valuation and transfer agency;
  • marketing and distribution.

Delegation of portfolio or risk management under AIFMD must be to an entity authorised for asset management and subject to supervision; delegation to a firm outside the EU needs cooperation between regulators.

Conditions for delegation

The manager must:

  • be able to justify the whole delegation structure on objective reasons;
  • carry out due diligence on the delegate's qualifications, resources and good repute;
  • keep the ability to monitor the delegate effectively, give instructions at any time and withdraw the delegation immediately if that is in investors' interests;
  • manage conflicts of interest, for example where the delegate is in the same group;
  • remain liable to the fund and investors.

Sub-delegation needs the manager's consent.

The letter-box test

A manager is a letter-box entity if it no longer has the expertise and resources to supervise its delegates, no longer has the power to take decisions in key areas, or delegates investment management functions to an extent that substantially exceeds those it keeps.

Substance

Regulators expect a manager to have real presence. Common expectations include:

  • enough senior staff with the right skills, employed or committed to the firm, living close enough to manage it;
  • managerial functions allocated to named individuals who spend meaningful time on them;
  • decision-making, board meetings and records in the home jurisdiction;
  • adequate systems, data and management information on every fund and delegate.

AIFMD II added a requirement that at least two people resident in the EU conduct the business of the AIFM or management company, and more information on delegation in authorisation applications and reporting.

Making delegation work

  • Clear contracts with service levels, reporting, audit rights and termination rights.
  • Risk-based oversight: closer monitoring of critical delegates, regular reviews and on-site visits.
  • Independent challenge of delegates' reports, not just receiving them.
  • Board reporting that highlights issues and their resolution.

Supervisors across Europe have focused on delegation and substance in their reviews, particularly for third-party management companies and managers that delegate portfolio management outside the EU.

explainers.title: Derivatives in UCITS: global exposure, the commitment approach and VaR
explainers.summary: How UCITS may use derivatives, how their exposure is measured using the commitment approach or value at risk, and the limits and controls that apply.
explainers.bodyHtml:
UCITS can use financial derivatives for investment purposes, hedging and efficient portfolio management, but within strict limits designed to keep risk under control.

Eligible derivatives

Derivatives must be on eligible underlying assets (such as transferable securities, indices, interest rates and currencies), traded on regulated markets or over the counter (OTC) with approved counterparties, and valued reliably every day. Exposure to a single OTC counterparty is limited to 10% of net assets for banks and 5% for others.

Measuring global exposure

A UCITS must measure its global exposure from derivatives every day, using one of two methods, chosen according to its strategy.

Commitment approach. Each derivative is converted into the market value of an equivalent position in the underlying asset. Netting and hedging arrangements may reduce the total. Global exposure must not exceed 100% of net assets, so total exposure cannot exceed 200%. Suitable for funds using derivatives simply.

Value at risk (VaR). A statistical estimate of the maximum loss over a set period at a given confidence level (for UCITS, typically 20 days at 99%). Two versions: - Relative VaR: the fund's VaR must not exceed twice the VaR of an unleveraged reference portfolio. - Absolute VaR: the fund's VaR must not exceed 20% of net assets.

Funds using VaR must also disclose their expected level of leverage, calculated as the sum of the notionals of derivatives, which can be much higher than the VaR suggests.

Other controls

  • Risk management process approved by the board, with stress testing and back-testing of VaR models.
  • Cover rules: the fund must be able to meet its obligations under derivatives, holding liquid assets or the underlying.
  • Collateral received must meet quality, liquidity and diversification criteria.
  • Disclosure in the prospectus and reports.

Questions to ask

  • Which method does each fund use, and why?
  • How high is gross leverage for VaR funds, and how does it behave in stress?
  • How are VaR models validated and back-tested?
  • How is counterparty and collateral risk monitored?
explainers.sortKey: derivatives in ucits: global exposure, the commitment approach and var

explainers.title: DLT in capital markets: settlement and the DLT Pilot Regime
explainers.summary: How distributed ledger technology is being used to issue, trade and settle securities, what the EU DLT Pilot Regime allows, and the obstacles to wider adoption.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Capital markets rely on chains of intermediaries: issuers, central securities depositories (CSDs), custodians, brokers, trading venues and clearing houses, each keeping its own records. DLT offers a shared record that could simplify this chain.

What DLT could change

  • Issuance: securities issued directly on a ledger, with the ledger as the register.
  • Settlement: faster settlement, potentially atomic delivery versus payment, where the securities and cash move together.
  • Fewer reconciliations: participants share the same record.
  • Collateral mobility: moving collateral between parties and markets quickly, around the clock.
  • Programmability: automatic coupon payments and corporate actions.

Obstacles

  • Legal frameworks built for traditional registers and intermediaries.
  • The cash leg: settlement needs a reliable digital form of money on or linked to the ledger, ideally central bank money.
  • Interoperability between ledgers and with existing systems.
  • Liquidity fragmentation across many platforms.
  • Operational and cyber risks of new technology.

The EU DLT Pilot Regime

Regulation (EU) 2022/858 has applied since March 2023. It creates a legal sandbox for market infrastructures using DLT:

  • DLT multilateral trading facilities (trading only);
  • DLT settlement systems (settlement only);
  • DLT trading and settlement systems (both combined in one entity, which is normally not allowed).

Operators can request exemptions from some requirements of MiFID II and CSDR, subject to conditions and limits on the size of eligible instruments (such as shares of companies with market capitalisation below a threshold, and bonds and fund units below set limits) and on the total value recorded.

Take-up has been modest. The Commission has proposed, through its Market Integration and Supervision Package, to make the regime more flexible and raise thresholds, and ESMA has reported on its experience.

Central bank money settlement

The Eurosystem has run trials of settling DLT transactions in central bank money and is developing permanent solutions. Other central banks are running similar projects. Wholesale settlement in central bank money is seen as key to scaling tokenised markets safely.

Questions to ask

  • What problem does DLT solve for this market, compared with improving existing systems?
  • What is the settlement asset, and how is finality achieved?
  • How does the platform connect to the rest of the market?
explainers.sortKey: dlt in capital markets: settlement and the dlt pilot regime

explainers.title: DORA's register of information
explainers.summary: What DORA's register of information is, what it must contain, who must keep it, how it is used by supervisors and how to keep it accurate.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Under the EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), every financial entity must keep a register of information on all its contractual arrangements for ICT services provided by third parties.

Purpose

  • Gives the firm a complete view of its dependence on ICT providers.
  • Lets supervisors assess concentration risk across the financial sector.
  • Helps the European Supervisory Authorities identify critical ICT third-party providers for direct oversight.

What it covers

All contractual arrangements for ICT services, not only outsourcing and not only critical services, including those provided by group companies. For each arrangement it records, among other things:

  • the provider, identified by its legal entity identifier where available;
  • the ICT services provided;
  • the business functions they support, and whether those functions are critical or important;
  • the contract dates, governing law and termination notice;
  • data storage and processing locations;
  • the supply chain of subcontractors supporting critical or important functions;
  • substitutability and exit plans.

The register is kept at entity, sub-consolidated and consolidated levels, using templates set out in EU implementing technical standards.

Reporting

Firms submit their registers to their national competent authority annually, and on request. The first submissions took place in 2025.

Keeping it accurate

  • Make one owner responsible, with input from procurement, IT, legal and business owners.
  • Link it to the contract management system so new contracts and changes flow through.
  • Validate data, especially legal entity identifiers and function classifications.
  • Reconcile it with outsourcing registers kept under other rules.
  • Review it at least annually and after significant changes.

Why boards should care

The register shows where the firm depends on a few providers, where critical functions rely on long subcontracting chains, and where exit would be hard. It is a source of insight, not just a reporting obligation.

explainers.title: E-money tokens: where e-money meets crypto
explainers.summary: What an e-money token is under MiCA, who can issue one, how it differs from traditional e-money and other stablecoins, and the overlap with payments law.
explainers.bodyHtml:
An e-money token (EMT) is a crypto-asset that aims to keep a stable value by referencing one official currency, such as the euro or US dollar. Under MiCA, EMTs are treated as electronic money, bringing together crypto and payments regulation.

Who can issue an EMT

Only:

  • credit institutions (banks); and
  • e-money institutions.

They must notify their regulator and publish a crypto-asset white paper before offering the token to the public or seeking its admission to trading.

Key rules

  • Issuance at par: EMTs must be issued at par value on receipt of funds.
  • Redemption: holders have a claim against the issuer and can redeem at any time, at par, free of charge.
  • No interest: neither the issuer nor CASPs may pay interest on EMTs.
  • Safeguarding and investment of funds: funds received are safeguarded under the e-money rules, with at least 30% in bank deposits (60% for significant EMTs) and the rest in high-quality liquid assets, matched to the currency of the token.
  • Recovery and redemption plans.
  • Significant EMTs: where the EBA classifies an EMT as significant, additional requirements apply and, for e-money institution issuers, the EBA supervises.

How EMTs differ from traditional e-money

  • They circulate on blockchains and can be transferred between holders without the issuer's involvement, including to self-hosted wallets.
  • Holders may not be the issuer's customers. The issuer may not know who holds its tokens at any time.
  • They can be traded on crypto-asset platforms, where the price may deviate from par.

How EMTs differ from other stablecoins

  • Asset-referenced tokens (ARTs) reference a basket or non-currency assets and have different reserve and redemption rules.
  • Stablecoins issued by firms not authorised in the EU cannot be offered to the public there, and CASPs must check what they list.

The overlap with payments law

Because EMTs are e-money, using them for payments can involve payment services. The EBA has addressed the overlap, and PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation will clarify how firms that provide both crypto and payment services should be authorised.

Multi-issuance

Some stablecoins are issued by an EU entity and a non-EU entity in the same group, as fully interchangeable tokens. This raises questions about whether EU holders are protected if redemptions are concentrated in the EU. The Commission is examining this as part of its MiCA review.
explainers.sortKey: e-money tokens: where e-money meets crypto

explainers.title: ESG funds: SFDR Article 6, 8 and 9 products
explainers.summary: How the EU classifies funds by their sustainability characteristics under SFDR, what Article 6, 8 and 9 mean, the rules on fund names, and how the proposed SFDR 2.0 would change things.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The EU's Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) requires asset managers to explain how their funds take sustainability into account. It was designed as a disclosure regime, but in practice the market has used its articles as labels.

The three types of fund

Article 6 funds. All funds must disclose how sustainability risks (environmental, social or governance events that could hurt the value of investments) are integrated into investment decisions, or why they are not relevant. A fund that does nothing more is often called an Article 6 fund.

Article 8 funds. Funds that promote environmental or social characteristics among other characteristics, provided the companies they invest in follow good governance practices.
