Examples include funds that exclude certain sectors, favour companies with better ESG ratings, or commit to a minimum share of sustainable investments. They must disclose, in prescribed templates, which characteristics they promote, how they meet them and, if relevant, the share of sustainable investments.

Article 9 funds. Funds with sustainable investment as their objective, such as a reduction in carbon emissions. With limited exceptions for hedging and liquidity, all their investments must be sustainable investments: contributing to an environmental or social objective, doing no significant harm to other objectives and following good governance.

Related rules

  • Principal adverse impacts (PAIs): how investment decisions affect sustainability factors, such as greenhouse gas emissions, biodiversity, and human rights. Larger managers must report them at entity level; funds may consider them at product level.
  • EU Taxonomy: funds must disclose the share of their investments aligned with the EU's classification of environmentally sustainable activities.
  • Fund names: under ESMA guidelines, funds using ESG, sustainability, environmental, social, impact or transition-related terms in their names must invest at least 80% to meet those characteristics and apply exclusions.

Why it has been difficult

  • The concept of "sustainable investment" was loosely defined, so managers applied it differently.
  • Article 8 covered everything from light exclusions to ambitious strategies.
  • Investors treated the articles as quality labels.
  • Data on companies was incomplete.

Many funds changed category, especially from Article 9 to Article 8, as supervisors clarified expectations.

SFDR 2.0

The Commission's proposal of November 2025 would replace Articles 8 and 9 with three voluntary categories: Sustainable, Transition and ESG Basics. Each would require at least 70% of investments to meet the category's objective and apply exclusions. Products outside the categories would face limits on using sustainability-related terms. The Council and Parliament have agreed their positions and are negotiating, with the new rules unlikely to apply before about 2029.

Questions to ask

  • Is each fund's classification supported by its investment process and portfolio?
  • Do marketing materials say more than the legal documents?
  • How reliable is the ESG data we use?
  • Which category would each fund fit under SFDR 2.0?
explainers.sortKey: esg funds: sfdr article 6, 8 and 9 products

explainers.title: Exchange-traded funds, including active ETFs
explainers.summary: How exchange-traded funds work, the role of authorised participants and market makers, physical and synthetic replication, active ETFs and the risks to watch.
explainers.bodyHtml:
An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is an open-ended fund whose shares are listed and traded on a stock exchange throughout the day. Most ETFs track an index, but active ETFs, where a manager selects investments, are growing quickly.

How ETFs work

Primary market. Large financial institutions called authorised participants (APs) create new ETF shares by delivering a basket of securities or cash to the fund, and redeem shares by returning them for securities or cash. This happens in large blocks (creation units).

Secondary market. Most investors buy and sell ETF shares on an exchange, from other investors and market makers.

Arbitrage. If the ETF price moves above the value of its holdings, APs create shares and sell them; if below, they buy shares and redeem them. This keeps the market price close to the NAV. An indicative NAV published during the day helps investors judge fair value.

Replication

  • Physical replication: the ETF holds the securities in the index, either fully or a representative sample.
  • Synthetic replication: the ETF uses a swap with a counterparty to deliver the index return, creating counterparty risk managed through collateral.

Active ETFs

Active ETFs give investors active management in an ETF wrapper. Some disclose their portfolios daily, others less often, to protect the manager's strategy, which can make arbitrage harder. Active ETF share classes of existing mutual funds are also becoming available in some markets.

Risks

  • Liquidity mismatch: an ETF can trade more easily than its underlying assets, for example in bond ETFs, and prices can move to large discounts in stress.
  • AP and market maker withdrawal in stressed markets.
  • Tracking error between the ETF and its index.
  • Counterparty risk for synthetic ETFs and securities lending.
  • Concentration in popular indices.

Regulation

In the EU, most ETFs are UCITS, subject to ESMA guidelines on ETFs. They must be identified as ETFs in their names and documents, and disclose how they track their index.

explainers.title: Financial promotions
explainers.summary: What counts as a financial promotion, who can make or approve one, the standards it must meet, and the specific rules for high-risk investments and crypto-assets.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A financial promotion is an invitation or inducement to engage in investment activity, communicated in the course of business. Most countries restrict who can make them and set standards for content.

The UK regime

  • Under section 21 of FSMA, only authorised firms may communicate financial promotions, or approve them for unauthorised persons, unless an exemption applies.
  • Since February 2024, firms must have FCA permission (the section 21 gateway) to approve promotions for unauthorised persons.
  • Promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading, with balanced information about risks and benefits.
  • Exemptions include promotions to investment professionals, certified high net worth individuals and certified sophisticated investors.

High-risk investments and crypto-assets

Since October 2023, promotions of crypto-assets to UK consumers must be made or approved by an authorised firm, or by a registered crypto firm. Rules for high-risk investments include:

  • prescribed risk warnings;
  • a ban on incentives to invest, such as refer-a-friend bonuses;
  • a 24-hour cooling-off period for first-time investors;
  • client categorisation and appropriateness assessments.

The EU

  • MiFID requires marketing communications to be fair, clear and not misleading and clearly identifiable.
  • ESMA's guidelines on fund marketing communications set detailed standards, including on sustainability claims.
  • MiCA requires crypto marketing communications to be consistent with the white paper and to carry warnings.

Social media and finfluencers

Regulators apply the same rules to social media posts and influencers paid to promote financial products. Unauthorised influencers promoting regulated products can commit criminal offences, and firms are responsible for promotions made on their behalf.

Good practice

  • A clear approval process, with compliance sign-off and records.
  • Monitoring of affiliates, introducers and influencers.
  • Testing of customer understanding, especially for complex products.

explainers.title: Fund administration and how the NAV is calculated
explainers.summary: What a fund administrator does and how the net asset value is calculated, step by step, including accruals, pricing and checks.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The fund administrator keeps the fund's books and calculates its net asset value (NAV), the figure that determines the price at which every investor buys and sells. Accuracy and timeliness are critical.

What the administrator does

  • Records all the fund's transactions: trades, income, expenses, subscriptions and redemptions.
  • Reconciles cash and positions with the depositary, custodians and brokers.
  • Values the portfolio using prices from independent sources.
  • Accrues income and expenses.
  • Calculates the NAV and NAV per share for each share class.
  • Prepares financial statements and regulatory and tax reports.

How the NAV is calculated

1. Value the assets. Each holding is valued at the valuation point using the fund's valuation policy: market prices for listed securities, prices from data vendors or brokers for bonds, models for derivatives and some private assets, and the latest NAV for other funds held.

2. Add other assets. Cash, income receivable (accrued interest and declared dividends), amounts due from brokers for sales and subscriptions receivable.

3. Deduct liabilities. Amounts owed for purchases, redemptions payable, borrowings and accrued expenses such as management fees, depositary and administration fees, audit fees and performance fees.

4. Arrive at the NAV. Total assets minus total liabilities.

5. Calculate NAV per share. The NAV attributable to each share class is divided by the number of shares in issue in that class. Share classes can differ in currency, fees, hedging and income treatment, so each has its own NAV per share.

Checks and controls

  • Tolerance checks on price movements, with stale or unusual prices investigated.
  • Reconciliations of cash and positions.
  • Review of large or unusual movements in the NAV.
  • Independent review of the NAV before it is released.
  • Depositary oversight of the NAV calculation.

NAV errors

When the NAV is wrong, investors may have dealt at the wrong price. Funds set a materiality threshold (often a fraction of a percent, depending on the type of fund). Above it, the error must be corrected and affected investors, or the fund, compensated. Errors below the threshold are recorded and the causes fixed.

Oversight

The management company or AIFM remains responsible for the NAV even when administration is delegated. Boards should receive reports on NAV errors, pricing exceptions, stale prices and the timeliness of the NAV.
explainers.sortKey: fund administration and how the nav is calculated

explainers.title: Fund distribution and cross-border marketing: passports, NPPR and reverse solicitation
explainers.summary: How funds are sold across borders in the EU: the marketing passports for UCITS and AIFs, national private placement regimes, pre-marketing and reverse solicitation.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A fund is useful only if it reaches investors. In the EU, the rules on marketing funds across borders depend on the type of fund, the type of investor and where the manager is based.

What counts as marketing

Under AIFMD, marketing is a direct or indirect offering or placement, at the initiative of the manager or on its behalf, of units or shares of a fund to investors in the EU. Each member state may interpret this differently, and local rules on what activities are permitted before notification vary.

UCITS: the retail passport

A UCITS authorised in one member state can be marketed to all investors, including retail, in any other member state. The home regulator sends a notification file to the host regulator, after which marketing can start. The host member state's rules on marketing communications and investor facilities apply.

EU AIFs: the professional passport

An authorised EU AIFM can market EU AIFs to professional investors across the EU through a notification. Marketing to retail investors depends on each member state's rules, except for European long-term investment funds (ELTIFs), which have their own retail passport.

Non-EU managers and funds: national private placement regimes

Managers or funds from outside the EU cannot use the AIFMD passport. Instead, they rely on each member state's national private placement regime (NPPR), under Article 42 of AIFMD. Conditions vary: some countries require only a notification and AIFMD-style disclosure and reporting, some require a depositary-like arrangement, and some do not allow private placement at all. Cooperation arrangements between the regulators are required, and the third country must not be on the FATF's list of high-risk jurisdictions.

Pre-marketing

Since 2021, EU AIFMs can pre-market: test investor interest in a strategy or fund not yet established or notified, without offering subscriptions. The AIFM must notify its home regulator within two weeks, and subscriptions by pre-marketed investors within 18 months are treated as resulting from marketing.

Reverse solicitation

Where a professional investor approaches the manager on its own initiative, without any prior marketing, the marketing rules do not apply. Regulators read this narrowly. It must be documented and cannot be used as a business model. MiCA has similarly narrow rules for crypto-assets.

Distribution chains

Funds are mostly sold through intermediaries: banks, platforms, wealth managers and advisers. Product governance rules require the manufacturer to define the target market and the distributor to check that the fund reaches it. Managers need data from distributors on where and to whom their funds are sold.

The direction of travel

The EU's Market Integration and Supervision Package, proposed in December 2025, aims to simplify cross-border marketing further, for example by allowing notification at authorisation and reducing national additions to EU rules.
explainers.sortKey: fund distribution and cross-border marketing: passports, nppr and reverse solicitation

explainers.title: Fund domicile: Ireland
explainers.summary: An overview of Ireland as a fund domicile: the main fund types and legal structures, the Central Bank of Ireland's approach, and what managers should know.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Ireland is one of Europe's two largest centres for cross-border investment funds, with a particular strength in UCITS, exchange-traded funds and money market funds, and a large number of non-Irish managers using Irish fund structures.

Fund types

  • UCITS, authorised under the Irish UCITS Regulations.
  • Qualifying investor AIF (QIAIF): for professional and qualifying investors, with flexible investment rules and a fast-track authorisation process, often 24 hours for a fully compliant application.
  • Retail investor AIF (RIAIF): for retail investors, with more restrictions.
  • Loan-originating QIAIFs, subject to AIFMD II rules.

Legal structures

  • Irish collective asset-management vehicle (ICAV): a corporate vehicle designed for funds, with the option to elect US "check the box" tax treatment. The most popular structure for new funds.
  • Investment company (plc).
  • Unit trust.
  • Common contractual fund (CCF): tax transparent, used for pooling pension assets.
  • Investment limited partnership (ILP): for private markets.

Management companies

Funds appoint an Irish or EU management company or AIFM, or are self-managed. Irish fund management companies are subject to the Central Bank's guidance on governance and delegate oversight (known as CP86), including designated persons and location rules.

The regulator

The Central Bank of Ireland authorises and supervises funds, their managers and service providers. It sets rules through the Central Bank UCITS Regulations and the AIF Rulebook. In 2026 it reviewed delegation practices and is reviewing fund management company governance.

Tax

Irish funds are generally exempt from Irish tax on income and gains. Irish-resident investors may be subject to exit tax. Ireland has an extensive tax treaty network.

Points to consider

  • Strong service provider and ETF ecosystem.
  • Speed of authorisation for QIAIFs.
  • Substance and governance expectations for Irish management companies.

explainers.title: Fund domicile: Luxembourg
explainers.summary: An overview of Luxembourg as a fund domicile: the main fund regimes and legal structures, the CSSF's role, the RAIF and what managers should know.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Luxembourg is Europe's largest fund domicile and a leading centre for cross-border UCITS distribution and for alternative funds, especially private equity, real estate and private debt.

Fund regimes

  • UCITS (Part I funds) under the 2010 Law on undertakings for collective investment.
  • Part II UCIs: other regulated funds that can be sold to retail investors, with an AIFM.
  • Specialised investment fund (SIF): regulated AIF for well-informed investors, supervised by the CSSF.
  • Reserved alternative investment fund (RAIF): an AIF that is not approved or supervised directly by the CSSF, but must be managed by an authorised AIFM, which is supervised. It can be launched quickly.
  • Unregulated partnerships managed by an AIFM.
  • EU labels such as ELTIFs, EuVECAs and money market funds.

Legal structures

  • SICAV / SICAF: investment companies with variable or fixed capital.
  • Fonds commun de placement (FCP): a contractual fund managed by a management company.
  • Special limited partnership (SCSp) and limited partnership (SCS): widely used for private markets.
  • Umbrella structures with segregated sub-funds.

Management companies

Luxembourg has many management companies and AIFMs, including large third-party management companies used by non-EU managers.

The regulator

The Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF) authorises and supervises funds (except RAIFs and unregulated vehicles), management companies, AIFMs and service providers. It has issued detailed circulars on governance, delegation, valuation and liquidity.

Tax

Funds are generally exempt from income tax but subject to an annual subscription tax (taxe d'abonnement) on net assets, at reduced rates or exempt for some fund types. Luxembourg has a broad tax treaty network.

Points to consider

  • Range of regimes for every type of strategy and investor.
  • Deep pool of service providers and cross-border distribution expertise.
  • Substance and governance expectations for Luxembourg managers.

explainers.title: Fund errors and breaches: NAV errors, investment breaches and compensation
explainers.summary: How fund managers should identify, correct and compensate for NAV errors and breaches of investment restrictions, the role of materiality thresholds, and what boards should expect to see.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Errors happen in any fund. What matters is how quickly they are found, how fairly they are corrected and what is learned from them.

NAV errors

A NAV error occurs when a fund's net asset value is wrong, for example because of a pricing mistake, a missed corporate action or an accrual error. Investors who subscribed or redeemed at the wrong price may have gained or lost.

Typical approach:

  • Materiality thresholds define which errors need correction and compensation, often expressed as a percentage of NAV and set by asset class (such as 0.5% for equity funds, lower for money market funds). Some jurisdictions set thresholds; others leave them to fund policy.
  • Below the threshold: the error is corrected going forward and recorded.
  • Above the threshold: affected investors and the fund are compensated, usually by the party responsible, such as the manager or administrator.
  • Notifications to the depositary, board and, where required, the regulator.

Investment breaches

  • Active breach: caused by the manager's own decision, such as buying beyond a limit. It must be corrected immediately and any loss compensated to the fund.
  • Passive breach: caused by market movements, redemptions or other events outside the manager's control. It must be corrected within a reasonable time, taking investors' interests into account.

A good process

  1. Detect: independent checks by the administrator, depositary and risk function.
  2. Escalate promptly, with clear responsibilities.
  3. Quantify impact on the fund and individual investors.
  4. Correct and compensate fairly, including former investors where feasible.
  5. Report to the board, depositary and regulator as required.
  6. Find the root cause and fix it.

What boards should ask

  • How many errors and breaches were there, and are they increasing?
  • Were any near misses identified?
  • Who paid compensation, and were all affected investors reached?
  • What has changed to prevent recurrence?
explainers.sortKey: fund errors and breaches: nav errors, investment breaches and compensation

explainers.title: Fund fees and costs: OCF, performance fees and value for money
explainers.summary: The different fees and costs investors pay in a fund, how they are disclosed, how performance fees work and how regulators assess whether funds offer value for money.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Costs reduce investors' returns every year, and their effect compounds over time. A difference of one percentage point a year can make a large difference over 20 years.

Types of cost

One-off charges - Entry (initial) charge: taken when investing, often paid to the distributor. - Exit charge or redemption fee: taken when selling.

Ongoing charges - Management fee: paid to the manager, usually a percentage of assets per year. - Fees of other service providers: depositary, administrator, transfer agent, auditor, legal and regulatory fees. - Costs of underlying funds where the fund invests in other funds.

The ongoing charges figure (OCF) expresses these as a single percentage of average assets.

Transaction costs - Brokerage commissions, taxes and bid-ask spreads when the fund buys and sells assets. These are not in the OCF but are disclosed separately in the key information document.

Incidental costs - Performance fees: paid to the manager when performance exceeds a benchmark or hurdle.

Performance fees

A performance fee can align the manager's interests with investors', but poorly designed fees can reward luck, encourage excess risk or charge investors for performance they did not receive. Good practice, reflected in ESMA guidelines for UCITS, includes:

  • a performance reference consistent with the fund's objective;
  • a high-water mark or similar, so fees are paid only on new gains after losses are recovered;
  • a reference period of at least five years for recovering past underperformance;
  • calculation frequency and crystallisation no more than once a year;
  • clear disclosure, with examples.

How costs are disclosed

  • The key information document shows total costs over different holding periods and their breakdown.
  • MiFID costs and charges disclosures show the combined costs of the product and the advice or service, before and after.
  • Annual reports show the expenses actually charged.

Value for money

Regulators increasingly expect managers to show that costs are justified by what investors receive. Under the EU's undue costs rule, funds must not charge costs that are not justified. The Retail Investment Strategy, politically agreed in December 2025, will require manufacturers and distributors of retail investment products to assess value for money against peer group benchmarks. In the UK, managers of authorised funds publish annual assessments of value, and the Consumer Duty requires fair value.

A value assessment typically considers:

  • the quality of service;
  • performance after costs, against objectives and comparable funds;
  • the costs themselves and economies of scale;
  • comparable market rates and the manager's other products;
  • whether investors are in the most appropriate share class.

What boards should ask

  • How do our funds' costs compare with similar funds, and what justifies any difference?
  • Is every cost charged to the fund justified and disclosed?
  • How are performance fees designed, and have they rewarded real outperformance?
explainers.sortKey: fund fees and costs: ocf, performance fees and value for money

explainers.title: Fund legal forms: corporate, contractual, trust and partnership
explainers.summary: The main legal structures used for investment funds, how they differ in ownership, governance and tax, and why managers choose one over another.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A fund's legal form determines who legally owns the assets, who governs the fund, how investors' rights are set out and often how it is taxed. Regulation such as UCITS or AIFMD applies regardless of the form, but the form shapes how the fund works in practice.

Corporate funds

The fund is a company, and investors are shareholders. It has its own board of directors, which is responsible for the fund. Most corporate funds have variable capital, so shares can be issued and cancelled freely as investors come and go.

Examples include investment companies with variable capital (often called SICAVs in continental Europe, OEICs or ICVCs in the UK) and similar corporate vehicles in other domiciles.

Features: a board that can hold service providers to account; shareholder meetings for major changes; familiar to investors worldwide.

Contractual funds

The fund has no legal personality. It is a pool of assets owned jointly by investors under a contract with the management company, which manages the fund on their behalf. Examples are the French and Luxembourg fonds commun de placement (FCP) and common contractual funds.

Features: no board of its own, as the management company's board is responsible; often tax transparent, which can help certain investors claim treaty benefits.

Unit trusts

The assets are held by a trustee on trust for the unitholders, under a trust deed. A manager runs the fund. Unit trusts are common in the UK, Ireland and other common-law jurisdictions.

Features: the trustee has a fiduciary duty to unitholders and oversees the manager; investors are beneficiaries rather than shareholders.

Limited partnerships

Investors are limited partners whose liability is limited to what they commit. A general partner manages the partnership and has unlimited liability, usually through a special-purpose company. Partnerships are the standard form for private equity, venture capital, infrastructure and private credit funds.

Features: flexible terms set in a limited partnership agreement; commitments called over time; usually tax transparent.

Choosing a form

Managers consider:

  • investor expectations, as institutional private markets investors expect partnerships, and retail investors are used to corporate funds;
  • tax, especially whether the vehicle is transparent or opaque, and treaty access;
  • governance, such as whether a separate board is wanted;
  • flexibility, such as umbrella structures with segregated sub-funds and multiple share classes;
  • cost and speed of set-up.

Many domiciles offer umbrella funds with legally segregated sub-funds, so that the liabilities of one sub-fund cannot be met from the assets of another.
explainers.sortKey: fund legal forms: corporate, contractual, trust and partnership

explainers.title: Fund tax basics: transparency, treaties, FATCA and CRS
explainers.summary: The tax concepts every fund director and manager should understand: tax-neutral funds, transparency, withholding tax and treaties, investor tax reporting regimes and international reporting under FATCA and CRS.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Funds aim to be tax-neutral, so investors are taxed broadly as if they had invested directly, without an extra layer of tax at fund level. How this is achieved depends on the fund's domicile, legal form and investors. This explainer gives general concepts, not tax advice.

Tax at fund level

  • Most fund domiciles, such as Ireland, Luxembourg and the Cayman Islands, do not tax funds on their income and gains, though some charge a small annual tax, such as Luxembourg's subscription tax.
  • Tax transparent funds, such as partnerships and some contractual funds, are ignored for tax purposes; investors are taxed on their share of income and gains.
  • Opaque funds, usually companies, are treated as separate taxpayers even if exempt.

Withholding tax and treaties

When funds receive dividends or interest from other countries, those countries may withhold tax. Tax treaties can reduce this, but whether a fund can benefit depends on whether it is treated as resident and as the beneficial owner. Transparent funds may let investors claim treaty benefits themselves. Managing reclaims is part of fund administration.

Investor tax regimes

Investors' home countries have their own rules for taxing fund investments, for example:

  • the UK reporting fund regime for offshore funds;
  • the US PFIC rules for non-US funds;
  • national rules distinguishing distributing and accumulating share classes.

Funds marketed widely may need to provide data to meet several regimes.

International reporting

  • FATCA: funds must identify US investors and report them, usually through their local tax authority.
  • Common Reporting Standard (CRS): funds must identify the tax residence of investors and report accounts of residents of other participating countries.
  • These obligations make due diligence on investors, including self-certifications, essential, and are linked to AML onboarding.

Governance

Boards should understand the fund's tax status, the risks to it (such as substance requirements and changes in law), and how FATCA and CRS compliance is overseen.

explainers.title: How a blockchain works
explainers.summary: A plain-English explanation of how a blockchain records transactions: blocks, hashes, nodes, consensus and why the record is hard to change.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A blockchain is a type of distributed ledger: a record of transactions shared across many computers (nodes), with no single party in charge of the master copy. Transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block is linked to the one before it, forming a chain.

Step by step

  1. A transaction is created. A user signs a transaction with their private key, for example to send tokens to another address, and broadcasts it to the network.
  2. It waits in the mempool. Pending transactions are held by nodes until they are included in a block.
  3. A block is proposed. A miner (in proof of work) or validator (in proof of stake) collects transactions into a block.
  4. Consensus. The network agrees, using its consensus mechanism, that the block is valid and is the next one in the chain.
  5. The block is added. Every node updates its copy of the ledger.
  6. Finality. As more blocks are added on top, the transaction becomes harder to reverse. Some blockchains offer explicit finality after a set point.

Hashes and the chain

Each block contains a hash (a unique digital fingerprint) of the previous block. Changing any data in an earlier block would change its hash and break the link with every later block. To rewrite history, an attacker would need to redo the work or win the agreement of a majority of the network, which is designed to be impractical.

Nodes

  • Full nodes keep a complete copy of the ledger and check every transaction against the rules.
  • Light nodes keep less data and rely on full nodes.
  • Miners or validators also propose and confirm blocks.

What is stored

Blockchains record balances and transactions between addresses, and the state of smart contracts. They do not usually record real-world identities, which is why blockchains are described as pseudonymous rather than anonymous.

Strengths

  • No single point of failure or control.
  • A tamper-evident, shared record.
  • Transactions can be verified by anyone.
  • Programmability through smart contracts.

Limits

  • Scalability: public blockchains can process only a limited number of transactions, which is why layer 2 networks exist.
  • Fees can rise sharply when the network is busy.
  • Irreversibility: mistakes and thefts usually cannot be undone.
  • Privacy: all transactions are visible on public chains.
  • Governance: changing the rules needs broad agreement and can split the network (a fork).
  • Energy use, for proof-of-work networks.

explainers.title: How a card payment works
explainers.summary: The steps and parties in a card payment, from tapping a card to the merchant getting paid: authorisation, clearing and settlement, and the fees involved.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A card payment takes seconds at the till, but involves several parties and steps that continue for days afterwards.

The parties

  • Cardholder: the customer paying.
  • Issuer: the bank or e-money institution that issued the card and holds the cardholder's account.
  • Merchant: the business being paid.
  • Acquirer: the bank or payment institution that provides the merchant with card acceptance and receives funds on its behalf.
  • Card scheme: the network, such as Visa or Mastercard, that sets the rules and routes messages between issuers and acquirers.
  • Payment service providers and processors that provide terminals, gateways and processing for merchants and issuers.

The steps

1. Authorisation (seconds) - The cardholder taps, inserts or enters card details online. - The merchant's terminal or gateway sends the request to the acquirer, which forwards it through the card scheme to the issuer. - The issuer checks the card, available funds and fraud risk, and may require strong customer authentication (for example, a one-time code or biometric check in the banking app). - The issuer approves or declines, and the response travels back. Funds are reserved on the cardholder's account.

2. Clearing (usually end of day) - The merchant submits the batch of approved transactions to the acquirer. - The scheme exchanges the transaction details between acquirers and issuers and calculates what each owes.

3. Settlement (usually one to two days) - Issuers pay the scheme, which pays acquirers. - The acquirer pays the merchant, after deducting its fees.

Who pays what

  • Interchange fee: paid by the acquirer to the issuer on each transaction. In the EU, interchange on consumer cards is capped at 0.2% for debit and 0.3% for credit.
  • Scheme fees: paid by issuers and acquirers to the card scheme.
  • Merchant service charge: paid by the merchant to the acquirer, covering interchange, scheme fees and the acquirer's margin.

Chargebacks

If a cardholder disputes a transaction, for example for fraud or goods not received, the issuer can raise a chargeback through the scheme. The acquirer may recover the amount from the merchant.

Risks

  • Fraud, including card-not-present fraud online.
  • Merchant failure before delivering goods, leaving acquirers exposed to chargebacks.
  • Operational outages at processors or schemes.

explainers.title: How crypto exchanges work: centralised and decentralised
explainers.summary: How centralised crypto exchanges and decentralised exchanges work, how they differ in custody, trading and regulation, and the risks of each.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Crypto-assets are traded in two very different ways: through centralised exchanges (CEXs), run by companies, and through decentralised exchanges (DEXs), run by smart contracts on a blockchain.

Centralised exchanges

A centralised exchange is a business that matches buyers and sellers. Typically:

  • Custody. Customers deposit crypto-assets or cash with the exchange, which holds them, usually in omnibus wallets. Trades between customers are recorded in the exchange's internal ledger, not on the blockchain. Only deposits and withdrawals go on-chain.
  • Order book. Buy and sell orders are matched in a central limit order book, much like a stock exchange.
  • Other services. Many exchanges combine several roles: broker, market maker, custodian, lender, staking provider and even issuer of their own token.

Risks: - Customers rely on the exchange to hold their assets safely and keep accurate records. If the exchange is hacked, misuses customer assets or fails, customers may lose their assets. - Conflicts of interest where the exchange trades against its customers or lists its own tokens. - Market manipulation, wash trading and opaque pricing.

Under MiCA, operating a trading platform and providing custody are regulated services, with rules on segregation of client assets, conflicts of interest, operating rules, transparency and market abuse.

Decentralised exchanges

A decentralised exchange is a set of smart contracts that lets users trade directly from their own wallets.

  • Self-custody. Users keep control of their assets until the moment of the trade, which settles on-chain.
  • Automated market makers (AMMs). Most DEXs do not use order books. Instead, users trade against liquidity pools, and prices are set by a formula based on the pool's balances.
  • Access. Anyone with a wallet can trade, usually without identity checks. Many DEXs are accessed through a website (the front-end) run by a developer or company.

Risks: - Smart-contract bugs and exploits. - Front-running and other forms of extracting value from users' transactions. - Price manipulation of thinly traded tokens and scam tokens. - Financial crime, as there are usually no AML checks at protocol level. - Unclear legal responsibility.

Hybrids

Some platforms combine features, such as centralised order books with on-chain settlement, or DEX aggregators that route orders across many venues.

How they connect

Prices on CEXs and DEXs are kept close by arbitrage traders. Stablecoins are the main bridge between them and between crypto and traditional money.

Questions to ask

  • Who holds the assets, and are customers' assets segregated and protected if the platform fails?
  • Who controls the platform or smart contracts, and can they change or pause them?
  • How are prices formed, and how is manipulation prevented and detected?
explainers.sortKey: how crypto exchanges work: centralised and decentralised

explainers.title: How EU financial regulation is made (Level 1, 2 and 3)
explainers.summary: How EU financial services law is made: the roles of the Commission, Parliament and Council, the ordinary legislative procedure, trilogues, and the Level 2 and Level 3 rules that fill in the detail.
explainers.bodyHtml:
EU financial regulation is built in layers. Understanding how it is made helps firms anticipate change and engage at the right moment.

The institutions

  • European Commission: proposes legislation and adopts detailed rules. Its Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union (DG FISMA) leads on financial services.
  • European Parliament: directly elected; one of the two co-legislators. Its Economic and Monetary Affairs Committee (ECON) handles financial services files.
  • Council of the EU: member state governments; the other co-legislator. Finance ministers meet in ECOFIN; officials negotiate in working parties.
  • European Supervisory Authorities (ESAs): ESMA, the EBA and EIOPA draft technical standards and issue guidelines.

Level 1: the legislation

  1. The Commission consults and publishes a proposal for a regulation (directly applicable) or a directive (transposed into national law).
  2. The Parliament and Council each agree their positions.
  3. They negotiate in trilogues, facilitated by the Commission, to reach a provisional agreement.
  4. Both formally adopt the text, which is published in the Official Journal and enters into force, usually 20 days later.
  5. Directives must be transposed into national law by a deadline. Application dates are often later still.

The process typically takes two to four years from proposal to application.

Level 2: the detail

Level 1 texts empower the Commission to adopt more detailed rules:

  • Delegated acts, which supplement or amend non-essential elements of the law.
  • Regulatory technical standards (RTS) and implementing technical standards (ITS), drafted by the ESAs and adopted by the Commission.

The Parliament and Council can object to delegated acts and RTS within a set period.

Level 3: supervisory convergence

The ESAs issue guidelines and recommendations, which national supervisors must comply with or explain why not, and Q&As on how the rules apply. They also run peer reviews and supervisory briefings.

National implementation

National authorities transpose directives, supervise firms and may add their own guidance. Differences in transposition ("gold-plating") are a recurring concern, which is one reason recent EU laws use regulations more often than directives.

Review clauses

Most EU laws include review clauses requiring the Commission to assess them after a few years, often leading to the next round of amendments, such as UCITS VI, AIFMD II and the MiCA review.

When to engage

  • Commission consultations and calls for evidence, before a proposal.
  • Parliament and Council negotiations, often through trade associations.
  • ESA consultations on technical standards and guidelines.
explainers.sortKey: how eu financial regulation is made (level 1, 2 and 3)

explainers.title: Instant payments and SEPA
explainers.summary: How the Single Euro Payments Area works, the shift to instant euro payments under the Instant Payments Regulation, and what it means for banks, payment firms and fraud.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) lets people and businesses make euro payments across Europe as easily as domestic ones, using common schemes and standards.

The SEPA schemes

  • SEPA Credit Transfer: standard euro transfers, usually settled within one business day.
  • SEPA Instant Credit Transfer: euro transfers that reach the payee within ten seconds, at any time.
  • SEPA Direct Debit: core and business-to-business schemes for collections.

The schemes are managed by the European Payments Council and use the ISO 20022 messaging standard. Payments are settled through clearing systems, including the Eurosystem's TIPS for instant payments.

The Instant Payments Regulation

The EU's Instant Payments Regulation (2024) aims to make instant payments the norm:

  • providers that offer euro credit transfers must offer instant ones too;
  • instant transfers must cost no more than standard ones;
  • payers must be offered verification of payee, checking the name matches the account before paying;
  • sanctions screening of customers is done daily rather than transaction by transaction;
  • payment and e-money institutions can join payment systems directly.

Euro area providers had to send instant payments from October 2025; non-euro member states and payment institutions have deadlines in 2027.

Benefits

  • Money available immediately, around the clock.
  • Lower working capital needs for businesses.
  • A base for account-to-account payments at the point of sale and online, competing with cards.

Risks

  • Fraud: money moves instantly and is hard to recall, making instant payments attractive for scams and mules.
  • Liquidity: banks need to manage liquidity 24/7.
  • Operational resilience: systems must run continuously.

The wider picture

Instant payments are a foundation for European payment initiatives, including bank-led schemes for retail payments and the proposed digital euro.

explainers.title: Investor categories: retail, professional and qualifying investors
explainers.summary: How regulators classify investors, the categories used in the EU, UK and US, what each allows firms to offer, and the protections that change with classification.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Regulators set different levels of protection depending on who the investor is. The classification determines which products can be sold, what information must be given and which checks apply.

EU and UK: MiFID client categories

  • Retail clients: the highest protection. Most product and conduct rules apply in full.
  • Professional clients: per se professionals (such as banks, insurers, funds and large companies) and elective professional clients, retail clients who ask to be treated as professional and meet tests of experience, portfolio size and trading frequency.
  • Eligible counterparties: the most sophisticated institutions, for certain business only, with the fewest protections.

Fund-specific categories

  • Professional investors under AIFMD: alternative investment funds can be marketed to them under the AIFMD passport.
  • Semi-professional or well-informed investors: national categories that allow funds for experienced investors meeting minimum investment thresholds, such as Luxembourg's well-informed investor.
  • Qualifying investors: Irish qualifying investor AIFs require a minimum subscription and certification.
  • Retail access to AIFs depends on national rules, or EU products such as ELTIFs.

UK financial promotions

Certain exemptions allow promotions to certified high net worth and sophisticated investors. Stricter rules apply to high-risk investments, including crypto-assets, with risk warnings, cooling-off periods and appropriateness checks.

US categories

  • Accredited investors: meeting income or wealth tests, they may invest in private offerings.
  • Qualified purchasers: a higher threshold allowing investment in funds relying on section 3(c)(7).
  • Qualified clients: allowed to be charged performance fees.

Why it matters

  • Misclassifying retail investors as professional is a common enforcement finding.
  • Firms must have clear procedures, evidence of tests and periodic review.
  • Investors who opt up lose protections and should be told so clearly.
explainers.sortKey: investor categories: retail, professional and qualifying investors

explainers.title: Launching a fund: from idea to authorisation
explainers.summary: The main steps in launching a regulated investment fund: product design, choosing the domicile, structure and service providers, documentation, authorisation and launch.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Launching a regulated fund is a project with many parties and decisions. Typical timeframes range from a few weeks for a new sub-fund on an existing platform to several months for a new structure.

1. Design the product

  • Investment objective, strategy and risk profile.
  • Target investors and distribution channels.
  • Liquidity and dealing terms that match the assets.
  • Fees and share classes, and whether they offer value.
  • Sustainability features and how they will be described.

2. Choose the regime and domicile

  • UCITS for broad retail distribution; an AIF for strategies outside UCITS limits or for professional investors.
  • Domicile, based on distribution reach, tax, regulator approach, speed, service provider capability and cost. Ireland and Luxembourg are the largest EU cross-border centres.

3. Choose the structure

  • Standalone fund or sub-fund of an umbrella.
  • Legal form: investment company, contractual fund, unit trust or partnership.
  • Own management company or a third-party management company.

4. Appoint service providers

Investment manager, depositary, administrator, transfer agent, auditor, legal advisers, distributors and, if needed, a third-party management company.

5. Prepare documentation

  • Prospectus or offering memorandum and supplements.
  • Constitutional documents.
  • Key information document for retail investors.
  • Service agreements.
  • Policies, such as valuation, liquidity and conflicts.

6. Authorisation

  • Submit the application to the regulator. Regulators review the documents, the manager and service providers, and raise comments.
  • Many regulators offer fast-track processes for certain fund types, for example for funds for professional investors.

7. Launch and distribution

  • Seed capital and initial offer period.
  • Register for marketing in other countries.
  • Set up dealing, reporting and data feeds.

Governance from day one

The board should approve the launch, understand the risks, and set up oversight of delegates and reporting before the first investor subscribes.
explainers.sortKey: launching a fund: from idea to authorisation

explainers.title: Layer 2 networks and rollups
explainers.summary: Why layer 2 networks exist, how rollups work, the difference between optimistic and zero-knowledge rollups, and the risks they introduce.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Public blockchains such as Ethereum can process only a limited number of transactions, so fees rise when demand is high. Layer 2 (L2) networks process transactions away from the main blockchain (layer 1) and settle back to it, increasing capacity and cutting costs while relying on layer 1 for security.

Rollups

The most common L2 design is the rollup:

  1. Users send transactions to the rollup.
  2. An operator called the sequencer orders and executes them off-chain.
  3. The rollup posts compressed transaction data and the resulting state to layer 1.
  4. Layer 1 provides a way to check that the state is correct.

Two types

Optimistic rollups assume transactions are valid unless challenged. Anyone can submit a fraud proof during a challenge period, often about seven days. Withdrawals to layer 1 must wait out this period, unless users use a third-party bridge.

Zero-knowledge (ZK) rollups submit a validity proof with each batch, a cryptographic proof that the transactions were executed correctly. Withdrawals can be faster, but the proofs are complex to generate.

Other designs

  • Sidechains: separate blockchains with their own security, connected by bridges.
  • Validiums: like ZK rollups but storing data off-chain.
  • Layer 3s: networks built on layer 2s, often for one application.

Risks

  • Centralised sequencers: many rollups rely on a single sequencer, which could censor transactions or go offline.
  • Upgradeability: many rollups can be upgraded by a small group, sometimes without a delay.
  • Immature fraud or validity proofs.
  • Bridge risk for assets moving between layers.
  • Fragmentation of liquidity across many networks.

Why it matters

Many stablecoin payments, DeFi activity and tokenisation projects now run on layer 2 networks. Firms should assess the security model of the specific network, not just the layer 1 it settles to.

explainers.title: Liquidity management tools: swing pricing, levies, gates, suspensions and side pockets
explainers.summary: The tools open-ended funds use to manage redemptions and protect remaining investors, how each works, when it is used and what EU rules now require.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Liquidity management tools (LMTs) help open-ended funds deal with large or sudden redemptions without harming investors who stay. Some pass the cost of trading on to the investors who cause it; others limit or delay redemptions.

Since April 2026, EU managers of UCITS and open-ended AIFs must choose at least two tools from a harmonised list (money market funds need only one), set them out in the fund documents and have policies for using them. Suspension and side pockets are available in addition.

Tools that pass on costs

Swing pricing. The NAV per share is adjusted up on days of net subscriptions and down on days of net redemptions, by a swing factor reflecting the cost of trading. The investors whose dealing causes the trading bear its cost. With partial swing pricing, the adjustment applies only when net flows exceed a threshold.

Dual pricing. The fund quotes separate prices for buying and selling, reflecting the bid and offer prices of the underlying assets.

Anti-dilution levy. A charge on investors who subscribe or redeem, paid into the fund to cover trading costs. It does not change the NAV.

Redemption fee. A fee on redemptions, paid to the fund, often reducing over time.

Tools that limit or delay redemptions

Notice periods. Investors must give advance notice before redeeming, giving the manager time to sell assets in an orderly way.

Redemption gates. When redemption requests on a dealing day exceed a threshold, for example 10% of the NAV, the fund pays only a portion of each request and carries the rest forward. Gates spread large outflows over time.

Extension of the notice period. Lengthening the notice period temporarily in exceptional circumstances.

Redemptions in kind. Paying redeeming investors with a slice of the portfolio instead of cash, usually only for large professional investors and with their agreement.

Tools for exceptional circumstances

Side pockets. Separating hard-to-value or illiquid assets from the rest of the portfolio. Existing investors keep their share of the side pocket, which is wound down over time, while the main fund continues dealing.

Suspension. Halting subscriptions and redemptions altogether, for example when assets cannot be valued or when dealing would harm investors. It is a last resort, must be in investors' interests, and must be notified to the regulator and investors promptly.

Using the tools well

  • Tools must be suitable for the fund's investment strategy, liquidity profile and investor base.
  • The criteria for activation should be clear, with governance over who decides, and operational readiness tested in advance.
  • Investors need clear disclosure in the prospectus of which tools may be used and how.
  • Regulators expect the anti-dilution tools to be calibrated to reflect real trading costs, including in stressed markets.
explainers.sortKey: liquidity management tools: swing pricing, levies, gates, suspensions and side pockets

explainers.title: Management companies and AIFMs, including third-party management companies
explainers.summary: What a UCITS management company or AIFM does, why funds need one, how third-party (host) management companies work and what regulators expect.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Under EU law, every UCITS and every AIF must have a single entity responsible for its management: a UCITS management company for a UCITS or an AIFM for an AIF. A fund can be self-managed, in which case the fund itself takes on these responsibilities, but most funds appoint an external manager.

What the manager is responsible for

The core functions are portfolio management and risk management. The manager is also responsible for administration, marketing and, for AIFs, activities related to the fund's assets. In practice, the manager:

  • sets and monitors the investment strategy within the fund's documents;
  • runs an independent risk management function, separate from portfolio management;
  • manages liquidity and, where relevant, leverage;
  • approves and oversees valuation;
  • manages conflicts of interest;
  • selects, appoints and oversees delegates and service providers;
  • reports to investors and regulators.

Authorisation and substance

Management companies and AIFMs must be authorised by their home regulator. They need minimum capital, fit and proper directors and senior managers, sound organisation and policies on risk, liquidity, valuation, conflicts and remuneration.

Regulators insist on substance: the manager must have enough experienced people, located appropriately, who actually perform or oversee its functions. Many regulators allocate these functions to named senior people, often called designated persons or conducting officers, and set expectations for the time they commit.

Delegation

Managers can delegate functions, most often portfolio management to an investment manager in the same group or a third party. They remain fully responsible, must justify the delegation, carry out due diligence and monitor the delegate, and must not delegate so much that they become a letter-box entity.

Third-party (host) management companies

Many asset managers, especially those based outside the EU, use a third-party management company (also called a host ManCo or super ManCo). It provides the regulated management company, and often risk management and compliance, while the asset manager's own firm acts as investment manager under delegation.

Benefits: speed to market, no need to build and maintain an authorised EU firm, and access to experienced governance.

Points to watch:

  • Conflicts of interest, as the third-party ManCo depends on fees from the asset manager it must oversee.
  • Whether the ManCo has enough resources and expertise for each strategy it hosts.
  • Regulators have increased their scrutiny of these models, including the quality of oversight of delegates and the costs charged to funds.

The board's role

The board of the management company is responsible for running the firm soundly. The fund board, where there is one, oversees the management company on behalf of investors.
explainers.sortKey: management companies and aifms, including third-party management companies

explainers.title: Market abuse in crypto markets
explainers.summary: The main forms of market abuse in crypto markets, such as pump-and-dumps, wash trading, spoofing and insider dealing on listings, and how MiCA and surveillance address them.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Crypto markets are particularly exposed to market abuse: many tokens are thinly traded, information is uneven, trading is fragmented across platforms, and some platforms both operate markets and trade on them.

Common forms

  • Pump-and-dump: promoters, often coordinating on social media, drive up a token's price and sell to latecomers.
  • Wash trading: trading with oneself or with colluding parties to create false volume, making a token or platform look more active.
  • Spoofing and layering: placing orders with no intention of executing them to move prices.
  • Insider dealing: trading ahead of announcements such as exchange listings, token unlocks or partnerships.
  • Front-running: trading ahead of known client orders, or, on-chain, extracting value from pending transactions.
  • Manipulating price oracles that DeFi protocols rely on.
  • Rug pulls: creators abandon a project and take investors' funds.
  • Misleading information, including undisclosed paid promotion.

Regulation in the EU

Title VI of MiCA prohibits insider dealing, unlawful disclosure of inside information and market manipulation for crypto-assets admitted to trading on EU platforms. It requires:

  • issuers and offerors to disclose inside information;
  • persons professionally arranging or executing transactions, including trading platforms, to have systems to detect and report suspicious orders and transactions;
  • national regulators to cooperate across borders, coordinated by ESMA.

The UK's new regime includes a market abuse regime for cryptoassets, and the US relies on securities and commodities anti-fraud laws.

Surveillance

Effective surveillance combines order book data, on-chain data, cross-platform monitoring and social media analysis. Many abusive schemes span several venues and chains, which makes detection and enforcement difficult.

Questions for boards

  • Does our surveillance cover all the markets and tokens we offer?
  • How do we manage conflicts where we list tokens and also trade them?
  • How do we control staff and insiders around listing decisions?

explainers.title: Maximal extractable value (MEV)
explainers.summary: What maximal extractable value is, how block producers and searchers profit from ordering transactions, the harms to users, and the mitigations.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Maximal extractable value (MEV) is the profit that can be made by including, excluding or re-ordering transactions in a block, beyond normal fees and rewards.

How it arises

Pending transactions on public blockchains wait in a public mempool before they are included in a block. Anyone can see them. Whoever decides the order of transactions in a block (the block producer, or specialised builders they work with) can profit by placing their own transactions before or after others.

Searchers run software that scans the mempool for opportunities and pays block producers to include their transactions in a particular order.

Common forms

  • Arbitrage: buying a token where it is cheap and selling where it is dear, across decentralised exchanges. Generally benign; it keeps prices aligned.
  • Liquidations: being first to liquidate an under-collateralised loan to earn the bonus.
  • Front-running: copying a profitable pending transaction and placing it first.
  • Sandwich attacks: placing a buy before a user's large trade and a sell after it, profiting from the price movement the user causes, at the user's expense.
  • Back-running: placing a transaction immediately after a known event.

Harms

  • Worse prices for ordinary users.
  • Higher fees as searchers compete.
  • Pressure towards centralisation of block building.
  • Possible risks to consensus if rewards from re-ordering blocks become very large.

Mitigations

  • Private transaction relays that send transactions directly to builders, hiding them from the public mempool.
  • Slippage limits set by users.
  • Batch auctions and other designs that remove ordering advantages.
  • Proposer-builder separation and auctions that redistribute MEV.
  • Encrypted mempools, under development.

Regulatory angle

Some MEV practices resemble front-running and market manipulation in traditional markets. Regulators are considering how market abuse rules apply when the actors are anonymous searchers and validators.

explainers.title: MiCA crypto-asset services explained
explainers.summary: The ten crypto-asset services regulated under MiCA, what each covers, which capital tier applies, and how they compare to MiFID investment services.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Under MiCA, a crypto-asset service provider (CASP) is authorised for one or more defined services. Each has its own conduct requirements, and the services provided determine the minimum capital.

The services

  1. Custody and administration of crypto-assets on behalf of clients: holding crypto-assets or the keys that control them. Must segregate client assets and is liable for losses from incidents attributable to the provider.
  2. Operation of a trading platform for crypto-assets: running a multilateral system matching third-party interests. Cannot deal on own account on its own platform.
  3. Exchange of crypto-assets for funds: buying or selling crypto-assets against fiat currency using the provider's own capital.
  4. Exchange of crypto-assets for other crypto-assets.
  5. Execution of orders on behalf of clients: with a best execution obligation.
  6. Placing of crypto-assets: marketing them on behalf of the offeror.
  7. Reception and transmission of orders: passing clients' orders to another provider.
  8. Advice on crypto-assets: personalised recommendations, with a suitability assessment.
  9. Portfolio management of crypto-assets: discretionary management under a mandate, also with suitability.
  10. Transfer services for crypto-assets: moving crypto-assets between addresses on behalf of clients.

Capital tiers

MiCA sets three minimum capital levels, or a quarter of fixed overheads if higher:

  • €50,000: reception and transmission, execution, placing, advice, portfolio management and transfer services.
  • €125,000: also custody or exchange services.
  • €150,000: also operating a trading platform.

Relationship with MiFID

Crypto-assets that are financial instruments, such as tokenised shares, fall under MiFID instead. Firms authorised under MiFID, and certain other financial institutions, can provide equivalent crypto-asset services after notifying their regulator rather than obtaining full CASP authorisation.

Common requirements

All CASPs must meet requirements on governance, fit and proper management, conflicts, complaints, outsourcing, safeguarding of client funds, wind-down plans, and AML/CFT and the Travel Rule.

explainers.title: Model risk, explainability and AI governance
explainers.summary: How financial firms govern models and AI: model inventories, validation, explainability, monitoring and accountability, and how regulatory expectations are evolving.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Financial firms rely on models for pricing, valuation, risk measurement, credit decisions, fraud detection, trading and, increasingly, AI tools. Model risk is the risk of loss or poor decisions from models that are wrong or misused.

Sources of model risk

  • Errors in design, code or data.
  • Use outside the purpose or conditions for which the model was built.
  • Changes in the world that make the model's assumptions invalid (drift).
  • Over-reliance on outputs without judgment.
  • For AI, opacity, bias and unpredictable behaviour.

A model risk framework

  • Inventory: a complete list of models and AI tools, with owners, uses and risk ratings.
  • Development standards: documentation of purpose, data, methods, assumptions and limitations.
  • Independent validation before use and periodically, proportionate to risk.
  • Monitoring: performance, stability and drift, with thresholds for action.
  • Change control for updates.
  • Use controls: limits on where and how models can be used, and human oversight.
  • Governance: clear accountability, from model owners to a senior manager and the board.

Explainability

Explainability is being able to explain how a model reached its output in terms people understand. It matters for:

  • customers affected by decisions, such as credit refusals;
  • validators and auditors;
  • supervisors;
  • the firm's own confidence in using the model.

Techniques range from simple, interpretable models to methods that explain the drivers of complex models' outputs. Where a model cannot be explained adequately, its use should be limited.

AI governance

AI brings additional challenges: models supplied by third parties, generative outputs that can be wrong, rapid change, and agents that act autonomously. Good AI governance builds on model risk management and adds:

  • an AI policy and acceptable uses;
  • controls on data and confidentiality;
  • testing for bias and robustness;
  • staff training (AI literacy);
  • specific controls for agents.

Regulatory expectations

Banking supervisors have long set model risk standards. The EU AI Act sets requirements for high-risk AI systems, including credit scoring, from December 2027. Financial regulators increasingly ask firms to show how they govern AI under existing rules on governance, risk management and senior accountability.

explainers.title: Money market funds
explainers.summary: What money market funds are, why investors use them, the EU types (VNAV, LVNAV, CNAV), how they are regulated and the lessons from stress episodes.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A money market fund (MMF) invests in short-term, high-quality debt such as treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, bank deposits and reverse repos. Investors use MMFs to manage cash: they offer daily liquidity, diversification and returns close to short-term interest rates.

Who uses them

Corporate treasurers, pension funds, insurers, asset managers, local authorities and, increasingly, as collateral and on-chain cash in tokenised form.

The three EU types

  • Variable NAV (VNAV): the share price moves with the market value of the assets. Short-term and standard versions.
  • Low volatility NAV (LVNAV): can keep a stable price as long as it stays within 0.2% of the market-value NAV, investing in short-term assets.
  • Public debt constant NAV (CNAV): keeps a stable price, investing almost entirely in public debt.

Main rules

The EU Money Market Funds Regulation sets:

  • eligible assets and diversification limits;
  • maximum weighted average maturity and life;
  • minimum daily and weekly liquid assets;
  • liquidity fees and redemption gates for stable-NAV funds when liquidity falls;
  • regular stress tests and reporting;
  • a ban on external support from sponsors;
  • know-your-customer and concentration monitoring.

Stress episodes

MMFs have faced heavy redemptions in market stress, for example in March 2020, when investors rushed for cash and some markets dried up. Concerns centred on stable-NAV funds, where investors might rush to redeem before a fund breaks its stable price, and on thresholds that could trigger fees or gates, creating an incentive to redeem early.

Regulators have responded in different ways. In the EU, the Commission concluded in 2026 that the framework works well overall and issued guidance on maintaining and using liquidity buffers. The UK plans to replace its rules with FCA rules that raise liquidity requirements. The US raised liquidity requirements and introduced mandatory liquidity fees for some funds.

Questions to ask

  • How concentrated is the investor base, and how quickly could the largest investors redeem?
  • How do liquidity buffers compare with stress test results?
  • How would the fund handle a breach of liquidity thresholds?

explainers.title: Money mules and payment fraud typologies
explainers.summary: How criminals use money mules to launder the proceeds of fraud, the main payment fraud typologies, and how payment firms detect and prevent them.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A money mule is a person whose account is used to receive and move criminal proceeds. Mules are the backbone of payment fraud: without them, criminals cannot get stolen money out of the system.

Types of mule

  • Complicit mules: knowingly sell or rent their accounts.
  • Recruited mules: lured by fake job adverts ("payment processing agent"), social media offers or romance, often young people or students.
  • Unwitting mules: victims of scams whose accounts are used without their understanding.
  • Synthetic or account-takeover mules: accounts opened with false or stolen identities, or taken over.

How the money moves

  1. The victim is tricked into paying, or their account is compromised.
  2. Funds go to a first-layer mule account.
  3. They are rapidly split and moved through further mule accounts, often across banks and borders.
  4. They are cashed out, converted to crypto-assets, or used to buy goods.

Instant payments mean this can happen in minutes.

Common fraud typologies

  • Authorised push payment scams (impersonation, investment, romance, purchase, invoice).
  • Account takeover via phishing or SIM swapping.
  • Card-not-present fraud.
  • First-party fraud, where customers falsely claim to have been defrauded.
  • Synthetic identities and fake businesses.

Detection and prevention

  • Onboarding controls: robust identity verification and checks for synthetic identities.
  • Behavioural monitoring: new accounts receiving and quickly forwarding funds, unusual device or location patterns, many inbound payments from different payers.
  • Network analytics: linking accounts through shared devices, addresses or counterparties.
  • Inbound payment monitoring, not just outbound.
  • Data sharing between banks, payment firms, telecoms and platforms.
  • Verification of payee and warnings for payers.
  • Rapid freezing and repatriation of funds.

Accountability

Reimbursement rules in the UK, and forthcoming rules in the EU, make receiving firms share the cost of fraud, increasing the incentive to stop mules.
