explainers.title: Open banking: account information and payment initiation services
explainers.summary: How open banking lets licensed third parties access customers' payment accounts with consent, the two types of service, how security works and where open finance is heading.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Open banking gives customers the right to let licensed third parties access their payment accounts at banks and other providers. It was created in the EU by PSD2 and in the UK through PSD2 and the CMA's open banking remedy.

The two services

Account information services (AIS). A provider, with the customer's consent, retrieves information from one or more of the customer's payment accounts. Uses include: - showing all accounts in one app; - budgeting and financial management tools; - affordability and credit checks; - accounting software that reads business bank transactions.

Payment initiation services (PIS). A provider, with the customer's consent, initiates a payment directly from the customer's account. Uses include: - paying online merchants by bank transfer instead of card; - topping up wallets or investment accounts; - paying bills.

Firms providing these services are third-party providers (TPPs): account information service providers (AISPs) and payment initiation service providers (PISPs). The bank or provider holding the account is the account servicing payment service provider (ASPSP).

How it works

  • The customer gives explicit consent to the TPP.
  • The TPP connects to the account provider through a dedicated interface, usually an API, identifying itself securely.
  • The customer authenticates with their own provider, using strong customer authentication.
  • The TPP receives the data or the payment is initiated. It never sees the customer's banking credentials.

Benefits and risks

Benefits: competition, innovation, cheaper payments for merchants, better financial management and credit decisions.

Risks: data protection and misuse, fraud (for example, criminals using payment initiation to move stolen funds quickly), unclear liability when things go wrong, and uneven API quality.

What is changing

  • EU: the Payment Services Regulation will require better-performing interfaces, ban obstacles that account providers put in TPPs' way, and give customers a permissions dashboard to see and withdraw access.
  • Open finance: the EU's proposed Financial Data Access regulation would extend data sharing to savings, investments, pensions and insurance.
  • UK: the government and FCA are developing a long-term framework for open banking, including commercial variable recurring payments, and the HM Treasury consultation on payments regulation addresses its future.
explainers.sortKey: open banking: account information and payment initiation services

explainers.title: Open-ended and closed-ended funds
explainers.summary: How open-ended and closed-ended funds differ in how investors get in and out, what that means for the price they pay, and why it matters for the assets a fund can hold.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The most basic way to classify funds is by how investors get their money back.

Open-ended funds

An open-ended fund issues new shares when investors subscribe and cancels them when investors redeem. The size of the fund grows and shrinks with investor demand. Investors deal with the fund itself, at a price based on the net asset value (NAV) per share.

Dealing frequency varies: most UCITS and money market funds deal daily, some funds weekly or monthly, and some semi-liquid funds quarterly with notice periods.

Strengths: investors can usually exit at a price close to the value of the underlying assets, and there is no need for a buyer in the market.

Challenges: the fund must be able to sell assets to meet redemptions. If many investors leave at once, the fund may have to sell assets quickly and at a discount, which harms those who stay. This is why open-ended funds need liquidity risk management and tools such as swing pricing, redemption gates and suspension.

Closed-ended funds

A closed-ended fund raises a fixed amount of capital, usually at launch, and does not redeem investors on demand. Investors exit by selling their shares to someone else, for example on a stock exchange (as with an investment trust or listed investment company), or by waiting until the fund returns capital at the end of its life (as with many private equity and infrastructure funds).

Strengths: the manager does not have to sell assets to meet redemptions, so the fund can hold illiquid, long-term investments such as private companies, infrastructure or property.

Challenges: the price an investor gets depends on the market. A listed closed-ended fund can trade at a discount or premium to its NAV. Investors in unlisted closed-ended funds may have to wait years for their money.

In between

Some funds sit between the two:

  • Interval or semi-liquid funds allow redemptions at set intervals, often with notice periods and limits on how much can be redeemed.
  • Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are open-ended, but most investors buy and sell shares on an exchange. Authorised participants create and redeem shares with the fund in large blocks, which keeps the market price close to the NAV.
  • Evergreen private markets funds are open-ended in principle but have long notice periods, gates and other limits.

Why it matters

Under EU rules, the difference has legal consequences. AIFMD treats an AIF as open-ended if investors can redeem before liquidation or the wind-down phase. Loan-originating AIFs must generally be closed-ended. UCITS must be open-ended.

For boards and investors, the key test is whether the fund's dealing terms match the liquidity of what it holds.

explainers.title: Operational resilience
explainers.summary: What operational resilience means for financial firms, how it differs from business continuity, the key steps of identifying important services and setting tolerances, and how regulators approach it.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Operational resilience is the ability of a firm to prevent, adapt to, respond to, recover from and learn from operational disruptions. The underlying assumption is that disruption will happen: the question is whether the firm can keep delivering what matters most.

How it differs from business continuity

Traditional business continuity focuses on recovering systems and premises after an incident. Operational resilience starts from the services the firm provides to clients and markets, and asks how much disruption to each could be tolerated.

The key steps

1. Identify important business services. Services whose disruption could cause intolerable harm to clients, threaten market integrity or the firm's viability. Examples: making payments, processing redemptions, providing access to client assets.

2. Set impact tolerances. The maximum tolerable level of disruption for each service, such as a maximum outage time or volume of failed transactions.

3. Map the service. Identify the people, processes, technology, facilities, information and third parties that support each service, and where they are vulnerable.

4. Test against severe but plausible scenarios. For example, a cyber attack, loss of a key supplier, failure of a data centre or a pandemic. Can the firm stay within its tolerances?

5. Fix vulnerabilities. Invest to remove single points of failure, improve recovery and strengthen third-party arrangements.

6. Communicate and learn. Plan how to communicate with clients and regulators during disruption, and learn from incidents and tests.

The regulatory frameworks

  • EU: DORA sets detailed requirements for ICT risk, incident reporting, testing and third-party risk for most financial firms.
  • UK: FCA and PRA rules require firms to identify important business services, set impact tolerances, map and test, and be able to remain within tolerances.
  • International: the Basel Committee's principles for operational resilience and the FSB's work on third-party risk.

The board's role

  • Approve important business services and impact tolerances.
  • Receive the results of mapping and testing and track remediation.
  • Understand the firm's dependence on third parties and concentration risk.
  • Lead during incidents and learn from them.

Common weaknesses

  • Treating resilience as an IT project.
  • Tolerances set to match current capability rather than what clients can bear.
  • Untested assumptions about third parties.
  • Testing only mild scenarios.

explainers.title: Oracles and price manipulation
explainers.summary: What blockchain oracles are, why DeFi depends on them, how attackers manipulate them, and how protocols defend against it.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Smart contracts cannot see information outside their blockchain. Oracles bring it in: asset prices, interest rates, weather, sports results or the state of another blockchain. In DeFi, price oracles decide when loans are liquidated, how much can be borrowed and what derivatives pay.

Types of oracle

  • On-chain price oracles: read prices from decentralised exchange pools, sometimes as a time-weighted average.
  • Decentralised oracle networks: many independent node operators fetch prices from several sources and aggregate them, publishing the result on-chain.
  • Centralised oracles: a single provider publishes data.
  • Cross-chain oracles relay information between blockchains.

How manipulation works

The classic attack:

  1. The attacker takes a flash loan of a large amount.
  2. Uses it to trade heavily in a thin liquidity pool that a protocol uses as its price source, temporarily distorting the price.
  3. Uses the distorted price on the target protocol, for example to borrow far more than the collateral is worth, or to liquidate others.
  4. Repays the flash loan in the same transaction and keeps the profit.

Other attacks include corrupting a small set of oracle operators, exploiting stale prices during volatility, and manipulating thinly traded tokens accepted as collateral.

Defences

  • Using time-weighted average prices rather than spot prices.
  • Aggregating multiple independent sources and operators.
  • Setting conservative limits for illiquid collateral.
  • Circuit breakers that pause activity when prices move abnormally.
  • Monitoring and rapid response.

Why it matters

Oracle failures have caused some of the largest DeFi losses. For firms using DeFi or accepting tokens as collateral, understanding the price source is as important as understanding the smart contract. Oracle manipulation can also amount to market manipulation under market abuse rules.

explainers.title: Outsourcing and delegation
explainers.summary: How regulated firms outsource functions, the rules that apply (including critical or important functions and DORA), and how to oversee providers and plan for exit.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Almost every regulated firm relies on others: group companies, administrators, technology and cloud providers, data vendors, custodians and specialist consultants. Regulators allow outsourcing, but the firm keeps full responsibility.

Outsourcing and delegation

  • Outsourcing: an arrangement where a service provider performs a process, service or activity that the firm would otherwise do itself.
  • Delegation: the term used in fund regulation for passing functions such as portfolio or risk management to another firm.
  • Third-party arrangements more broadly include any supplier, whether or not it counts as outsourcing.

Critical or important functions

Stricter rules apply when the function is critical or important: one whose failure would materially impair the firm's performance, the continuity of its services, or its compliance with its authorisation. For these, firms usually must:

  • carry out thorough due diligence;
  • assess risks, including concentration and substitutability;
  • include specific contract terms on service levels, data, audit and access rights, subcontracting, incident reporting and termination;
  • notify or seek approval from their regulator, where required;
  • have tested exit strategies.

The rules

  • EBA and ESMA guidelines on outsourcing and cloud outsourcing for banks, investment firms, payment firms, fund managers and others.
  • DORA for ICT third-party risk, with mandatory contract terms, a register of all ICT arrangements and oversight of critical ICT providers.
  • Fund rules on delegation, including the letter-box test.
  • MiCA for crypto-asset service providers.
  • UK rules on outsourcing and operational resilience.

Overseeing providers

  • A named owner for each relationship, with enough expertise to challenge.
  • Regular performance reports, incident reports and audit findings.
  • Periodic reviews and site visits for the most important providers.
  • Monitoring of the provider's financial health and control environment.
  • Clear escalation when service fails.

Group arrangements

Using group companies does not remove the requirements. Firms must still assess, contract, monitor and plan exit, and manage conflicts of interest.

Exit planning

For each critical arrangement, the firm needs a documented, realistic plan for moving the service to another provider or bringing it in-house, including how long it would take and what it would cost.

Questions for boards

  • Do we have a complete register of outsourcing and ICT arrangements?
  • Where are we concentrated on one provider?
  • Could we exit our most critical arrangements without disruption?

explainers.title: Payment institutions, e-money institutions and banks: what's the difference?
explainers.summary: How payment institutions, e-money institutions and banks differ in what they can do, how they hold customers' money and what protection customers get.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Many firms offer accounts, cards and transfers. Their legal status determines what they can do and how customers' money is protected.

Banks (credit institutions)

  • Take deposits and lend them out, using customers' money in their business.
  • Must meet strict prudential rules on capital and liquidity.
  • Deposits are protected by a deposit guarantee scheme up to a limit (in the EU, €100,000 per depositor per bank).
  • Can provide payment services and issue e-money.

Payment institutions

  • Provide payment services, such as payment accounts, transfers, card issuing and acquiring, money remittance, payment initiation and account information services.
  • Cannot take deposits or lend customers' funds (beyond limited credit linked to payments).
  • Must safeguard customers' funds, keeping them separate from the firm's own money or covered by insurance.
  • Customers' money is not covered by deposit guarantee schemes. If the firm fails, customers rely on safeguarding to get their money back, which can take time.

E-money institutions

  • Issue electronic money: stored value that can be used for payments, such as prepaid cards and wallets.
  • Can also provide payment services.
  • Must safeguard funds received for e-money and redeem e-money at par on request.
  • Cannot pay interest on e-money.
  • Not covered by deposit guarantee schemes.
  • Under MiCA, can issue e-money tokens.

Under the EU's forthcoming PSD3, e-money institutions will become a category of payment institution.

Side by side

Bank Payment institution E-money institution
Take deposits Yes No No
Lend Yes Limited Limited
Issue e-money Yes No Yes
Customer money Used in the business Safeguarded Safeguarded
Deposit guarantee Yes No No
Capital requirements High Lower Lower

Why it matters

Customers often assume an app with a sort code or IBAN is a bank. When a payment or e-money firm fails, weak safeguarding can leave customers waiting months for their money or suffering losses. Regulators have tightened safeguarding rules, for example the UK's new rules from May 2026 and the EU's PSD3.

Firms should be clear with customers about their status and how their money is protected.
explainers.sortKey: payment institutions, e-money institutions and banks: what's the difference?

explainers.title: Payment system access and settlement
explainers.summary: How payment firms connect to payment systems, the difference between direct and indirect access, settlement and finality, and the dependence on sponsor banks.
explainers.bodyHtml:
To move money, payment and e-money institutions need access to payment systems, such as instant payment and clearing systems, and to accounts where funds settle.

Payment systems and schemes

  • A payment scheme sets the rules for a type of payment, such as SEPA Instant.
  • A payment system clears and settles transactions between participants. Some settle each payment individually in central bank money (real-time gross settlement); others net payments and settle periodically (deferred net settlement).

Direct and indirect access

  • Direct participants connect to the system and settle in it, usually through an account at the central bank.
  • Indirect participants access the system through a direct participant, typically a bank acting as sponsor.

Historically, non-bank payment firms could rarely be direct participants. The EU's 2024 amendments to the Settlement Finality Directive and PSD2, introduced with the Instant Payments Regulation, allow payment and e-money institutions to participate in designated systems, subject to risk requirements. In the UK, the Bank of England has opened settlement accounts to non-bank payment firms.

Settlement finality

Settlement finality means a completed transfer cannot be unwound, even if a participant becomes insolvent. It is protected by law for designated systems. This is a key consideration for blockchain-based settlement too.

Dependence on sponsor banks

Most payment firms rely on one or a few banks for safeguarding accounts, settlement and access. Losing a sponsor, whether through the bank's de-risking, its failure or a dispute, can stop a payment firm overnight. Firms should:

  • have more than one banking relationship where feasible;
  • understand the sponsor's risk appetite and contract terms;
  • include loss of a sponsor bank in wind-down planning and scenario testing.

In the UK

Responsibility for payment systems regulation is moving from the Payment Systems Regulator to the FCA, following the government's decision to abolish the PSR, subject to legislation.

explainers.title: Private fund terms: commitments, waterfalls and carried interest
explainers.summary: How closed-ended private funds work commercially: commitments and capital calls, fees, the distribution waterfall, carried interest, and the key investor protections in the partnership agreement.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Private equity, private credit, infrastructure and venture capital funds are usually closed-ended limited partnerships. Their economics are set out in the limited partnership agreement (LPA) and differ significantly from open-ended funds.

Commitments and capital calls

Investors (limited partners) make a capital commitment. The manager (through the general partner) calls capital as it finds investments, typically over an investment period of four to six years. Investors that fail to meet a call face penalties, such as losing part of their interest.

Many funds use subscription line facilities to bridge capital calls. These are convenient but can flatter the internal rate of return by shortening the period investors' money is at work.

Fees

  • Management fee: often 1.5% to 2% a year, charged on commitments during the investment period and on invested capital afterwards.
  • Fee offsets: transaction and monitoring fees received from portfolio companies are often offset against the management fee.
  • Fund expenses: legal, audit, administration and other costs charged to the fund, which investors scrutinise closely.

The distribution waterfall

Proceeds are typically distributed in this order:

  1. Return of capital contributed by investors.
  2. Preferred return (hurdle), often 8% a year.
  3. Catch-up, giving the manager its share of profits so far.
  4. Carried interest split, commonly 80% to investors and 20% to the manager.

In a European (whole-fund) waterfall, the manager receives carried interest only after investors have received all their capital and the preferred return across the fund. In an American (deal-by-deal) waterfall, carry can be paid on individual deals earlier, protected by a clawback.

Investor protections

  • Key person clause: suspends investing if key individuals leave.
  • No-fault removal of the manager by a qualified majority.
  • LP advisory committee to review conflicts.
  • Most favoured nation rights for side letter terms.
  • Reporting rights and valuation policies.

Liquidity before the end

Investors can sell interests through secondaries. Managers increasingly use continuation funds to hold assets longer, and NAV facilities to borrow against the portfolio. Both create conflicts that boards and advisory committees should examine closely.
explainers.sortKey: private fund terms: commitments, waterfalls and carried interest

explainers.title: Private markets funds: ELTIFs, LTAFs and semi-liquid funds
explainers.summary: How private markets funds are being opened to wealthier individual investors through semi-liquid structures, ELTIFs and LTAFs, and the trade-offs between access and liquidity.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Private markets (private equity, private credit, infrastructure and real estate) have traditionally been reserved for institutions through closed-ended limited partnerships with ten-year lives. Asset managers are now offering them to wealthier individuals through new structures.

The structures

Semi-liquid (evergreen) funds. Open-ended funds that invest mainly in private assets, with periodic dealing, such as monthly or quarterly. They typically use: - notice periods; - redemption limits (gates), often around 5% of NAV per quarter; - a liquidity sleeve of cash and liquid credit; - credit facilities.

ELTIFs. The EU's European long-term investment fund, revised in 2024, offers a retail passport across the EU, with rules on eligible assets, diversification, borrowing and limited redemptions.

LTAFs. The UK's long-term asset fund, with dealing no more often than monthly and at least 90 days' notice, aimed at defined contribution pensions and wealthier investors.

Listed closed-ended funds, such as investment trusts, remain an alternative, with a market price that can trade at a discount to NAV.

Benefits

  • Access to returns and diversification not available in public markets.
  • No need to manage capital calls and distributions, as with traditional funds.

Trade-offs and risks

  • Liquidity: investors may not get their money when they want it, especially if many redeem at once.
  • Valuation: private assets are valued by models and appraisals, infrequently. Investors dealing at stale or optimistic valuations can be advantaged or disadvantaged.
  • Costs: fees are usually higher than for public market funds.
  • Leverage at fund and asset level.
  • Conflicts, such as assets transferred from other funds of the manager.
  • Suitability for individual investors and the clarity of disclosure.

Questions to ask

  • Do the dealing terms match the liquidity of the assets in a downturn?
  • How independent and frequent are valuations?
  • What happens if redemption requests exceed the gate for several quarters?
explainers.sortKey: private markets funds: eltifs, ltafs and semi-liquid funds

explainers.title: Proof of reserves: what it shows and what it doesn't
explainers.summary: What proof of reserves is, how it is done, what it can and cannot tell clients about a crypto platform's solvency, and what good assurance looks like.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Proof of reserves is a way for a crypto platform to show that it holds the crypto-assets it owes to clients. It became popular after platform failures in which client assets turned out to be missing.

How it works

  • Assets: the platform shows control of on-chain addresses holding crypto-assets, for example by signing messages with the private keys or moving funds in a pre-announced way.
  • Liabilities: the platform publishes a cryptographic summary of client balances, often using a Merkle tree, so that each client can check their balance is included without revealing others' balances.
  • Comparison: total assets are compared with total client liabilities for each asset.

Some platforms engage auditors or specialist firms to perform agreed procedures, and some use zero-knowledge proofs to prove solvency while keeping balances private.

What it can show

  • That, at a point in time, the platform controlled addresses holding a certain amount of each crypto-asset.
  • That a client's balance was included in the liability total.

What it cannot show

  • Other liabilities: loans, debts and obligations not included in the client liability figure. A platform can hold client assets but still be insolvent.
  • Encumbrance: whether the assets are pledged, lent or borrowed temporarily for the snapshot.
  • Ownership: whether the assets belong to the platform or to someone else.
  • Ongoing position: it is a snapshot, and the position can change the next day.
  • Fiat and off-chain assets, unless separately verified.
  • Control quality: whether keys are secure and controls effective.

Good practice

  • Regular, frequent attestations, not one-off events.
  • Independent assurance under recognised standards, covering liabilities as well as assets.
  • Coverage of all client assets, including fiat.
  • Disclosure of methodology and limitations.
  • Combined with segregation, regulatory supervision and audited financial statements.

Proof of reserves is useful evidence, but it is not a substitute for regulation, audit and segregation of client assets.
explainers.sortKey: proof of reserves: what it shows and what it doesn't

explainers.title: Prudential capital for investment firms: own funds, K-factors and the ICARA
explainers.summary: How investment firms and asset managers calculate their capital and liquidity requirements under the EU IFR/IFD and the UK MIFIDPRU regime, and the role of the ICARA in the UK.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Investment firms, including many asset managers and crypto firms, must hold enough capital and liquidity to absorb losses and wind down in an orderly way. Since 2021 the EU and UK have had dedicated regimes: the Investment Firms Regulation and Directive (IFR/IFD) in the EU and MIFIDPRU in the UK.

Classes of firm

  • Large or systemic firms remain subject to bank-style rules.
  • Non-small and non-interconnected firms apply the full regime.
  • Small and non-interconnected firms have simpler requirements.

Own funds requirement

A firm must hold own funds at least equal to the highest of:

  1. its permanent minimum capital requirement, set by its activities (for example €75,000, €150,000 or €750,000 in the EU);
  2. its fixed overheads requirement, a quarter of the previous year's fixed expenses;
  3. its K-factor requirement, for non-small firms.

K-factors

K-factors measure the risks a firm poses to:

  • clients, such as assets under management, client money held, assets safeguarded and client orders handled;
  • markets, such as net position risk and clearing margin;
  • the firm itself, such as trading counterparty default and concentration risk.

Liquidity

Firms must hold liquid assets equal to at least one third of the fixed overheads requirement.

The ICARA (UK)

UK MIFIDPRU firms must carry out an internal capital adequacy and risk assessment (ICARA), which:

  • identifies material potential harms from ongoing operations and from winding down;
  • assesses whether own funds and liquid assets are adequate;
  • sets out recovery actions and wind-down planning;
  • is reviewed at least annually and approved by the governing body.

EU firms carry out a similar internal assessment under the IFD.

Fund managers

UCITS management companies and AIFMs have their own capital rules, but those also authorised for MiFID top-up services fall partly under the investment firm regime. Crypto-asset service providers have separate MiCA requirements, while the UK is consulting on a dedicated prudential regime for crypto firms modelled on MIFIDPRU.
explainers.sortKey: prudential capital for investment firms: own funds, k-factors and the icara

explainers.title: Public, private and permissioned ledgers
explainers.summary: The differences between public and private, permissionless and permissioned distributed ledgers, and why financial institutions choose one model over another.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Distributed ledgers differ in who can use them and who can validate transactions.

Two questions

  • Who can read and submit transactions? On a public ledger, anyone. On a private ledger, only approved participants.
  • Who can validate and add blocks? On a permissionless ledger, anyone who meets the protocol's rules (for example, by staking). On a permissioned ledger, only approved, usually identified, validators.

The main models

Public permissionless (such as Bitcoin and Ethereum) - Open to all, global, with large networks of users and developers. - No one can block participation, and the record is highly resistant to change. - Transactions are visible to everyone, and identities are pseudonymous. - Governance is diffuse, and the firm using it cannot control upgrades or outages.

Private permissioned (such as enterprise ledgers run by a consortium) - Participants and validators are known and approved. - Privacy and access controls are easier, and performance can be higher. - Rules can be changed by the operators. - Fewer participants and less independence, so the benefits over a shared database must be justified.

Public permissioned (hybrid) - Anyone can read or use the network, but validators are approved.

Permissioned applications on public chains - Many tokenised assets are issued on public blockchains but with permissioned tokens: smart contracts that let only approved, identified wallets hold or transfer them (allow-lists).

How financial institutions choose

Consideration Public Private or permissioned
Reach and liquidity High Limited to participants
Control over upgrades and outages Low High
Privacy Low by default High
AML/CFT control Via permissioned tokens and screening Built in
Legal certainty and accountability Harder Easier
Regulatory comfort Growing for tokenised assets with controls Generally higher

Regulators' main concerns with public networks include operational resilience, governance, finality, cyber risk and financial crime. With private networks, the question is often whether DLT adds real value.

Prudential treatment

The Basel Committee's cryptoasset standard for banks originally placed stricter treatment on tokenised assets on permissionless blockchains, and the Committee has been reviewing this in light of market developments.

explainers.title: Quantum computing and blockchain security
explainers.summary: Why large quantum computers could threaten the cryptography that secures blockchains and financial systems, the timeline debate, and how to prepare.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Blockchains, payment systems and most internet security rely on public-key cryptography. Large, error-corrected quantum computers could break the most widely used schemes, such as elliptic curve signatures (ECDSA) used by Bitcoin and Ethereum, and RSA.

The threat

  • Signatures: a quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could derive a private key from a public key, allowing an attacker to forge transactions and steal assets.
  • Exposed public keys: on many blockchains, public keys are revealed when an address first sends a transaction, or permanently for some older address types. Assets at these addresses would be the first at risk.
  • Harvest now, decrypt later: attackers can store encrypted data today and decrypt it once quantum computers are available, a risk for confidential financial data.
  • Hash functions are much less affected; their security is reduced but not broken.

Timeline

No quantum computer today can break these schemes. Estimates of when one might exist vary widely, from the early 2030s to much later. Because migrating systems takes many years, governments and standard setters urge organisations to start now.

Post-quantum cryptography

New algorithms believed to resist quantum attacks have been standardised. In 2024 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology published its first post-quantum standards for key establishment and digital signatures. Authorities in the EU and UK have published migration roadmaps with targets in the late 2020s and early 2030s for critical systems.

For blockchains

  • Networks need to agree upgrades to post-quantum signatures, a difficult governance process.
  • Users will need to move assets to new, quantum-safe addresses.
  • Assets in lost or abandoned wallets with exposed public keys raise hard questions.
  • Proposals to add quantum-resistant address types are under discussion for major networks.

For financial firms

  • Make an inventory of where cryptography is used, including in custody, payments and data.
  • Build crypto-agility: the ability to swap algorithms without redesigning systems.
  • Follow regulatory roadmaps and vendor plans.
  • Consider quantum risk in custody and key management strategies.

explainers.title: Regulating DeFi: decentralisation tests and the front end
explainers.summary: How regulators approach decentralised finance: tests of decentralisation, identifying responsible persons, the role of front ends and interfaces, and the current debate in the EU, UK and internationally.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Financial regulation is built around intermediaries that can be authorised, supervised and held accountable. DeFi aims to remove intermediaries, which raises the question: who, if anyone, should be regulated?

The approaches

Look through the label. Regulators generally do not accept that a protocol is decentralised simply because it says so. They look at who controls or significantly influences it.

Identify responsible persons. IOSCO's 2023 DeFi recommendations and FATF guidance focus on people with control or sufficient influence: developers, admin key holders, foundations, large token holders, front-end operators and those who profit from the arrangement.

Regulate access points. Even where a protocol is truly decentralised, firms that provide access to it, such as front ends, wallets, exchanges and brokers, can be regulated.

Tests of decentralisation

Factors regulators and commentators consider include:

  • Can anyone change, pause or upgrade the smart contracts? Who holds admin keys?
  • How concentrated are governance tokens and voting?
  • Who runs the front end, and can it block users or tokens?
  • Who controls the treasury and receives fees?
  • Who controls oracles and other critical infrastructure?
  • Could the protocol continue if the original team disappeared?

The front end

Most users interact with DeFi through a website or app run by an identifiable company. Front ends can screen users, block sanctioned addresses and give information, so they are a natural focus for regulation.

Where things stand (as at November 2026)

  • EU: MiCA excludes services provided in a fully decentralised manner. The Commission's review is considering how to treat DeFi, and ESMA has favoured a clear definition with a narrow exemption.
  • UK: the FCA's perimeter guidance for the new cryptoasset regime explains when DeFi activities need authorisation.
  • US: treatment depends on securities and commodities laws, with legislation on market structure stalled.
  • International: IOSCO and the FATF continue to monitor implementation.

For firms

Firms offering access to DeFi should analyse whether they are carrying on a regulated activity, and apply investor protection, AML and sanctions controls at the access point.
