explainers.title: Remuneration: deferral, malus and clawback
explainers.summary: Why financial regulators regulate pay, the main remuneration requirements for funds, investment firms and banks, and how deferral, malus and clawback link pay to risk.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Pay structures that reward short-term revenue without regard to risk contributed to past crises and mis-selling scandals. Regulators therefore require firms to align remuneration with sound risk management and good conduct.

Who is covered

Rules apply most strictly to material risk takers (or identified staff in funds): senior management, risk takers, control functions and others whose activities materially affect the firm's risk profile.

Core requirements

  • A remuneration policy approved by the board, consistent with risk appetite, strategy and investors' or customers' interests.
  • A remuneration committee in significant firms.
  • An appropriate balance between fixed and variable remuneration.
  • Performance assessed on financial and non-financial criteria, including conduct and risk.
  • Control functions paid independently of the business they oversee.
  • Guaranteed bonuses only in exceptional cases.

Deferral, malus and clawback

  • Deferral: a portion of variable pay, often 40% to 60%, is paid over several years.
  • Payment in instruments: part of variable pay in shares, fund units or equivalent instruments.
  • Malus: unvested deferred pay can be reduced or cancelled if misconduct, losses or risk failures come to light.
  • Clawback: pay already received can be recovered for a set period.

Regimes

  • UCITS and AIFMD remuneration rules, applied proportionately.
  • Investment Firms Directive (EU) and MIFIDPRU (UK) for investment firms.
  • CRD for banks, including the bonus cap in the EU; the UK removed its bonus cap in 2023.
  • MiCA and payment rules require sound remuneration policies but are less prescriptive.

Disclosure

Firms must disclose remuneration information in annual reports or public disclosures, depending on their regime.

Board questions

  • Does the remuneration framework reward the behaviours we want?
  • Have we applied malus or clawback when needed, or have adjustments been rare?
  • Are risk and compliance views reflected in individual awards?

explainers.title: Risk appetite frameworks
explainers.summary: What a risk appetite framework is, how to write a useful risk appetite statement, how limits and metrics cascade through the business, and how boards use it.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A risk appetite framework sets out how much risk a firm is willing to take to achieve its objectives, and how that is controlled. It is the board's main tool for steering risk.

The components

  • Risk capacity: the maximum risk the firm can bear before breaching capital, liquidity or regulatory requirements, or its obligations to clients.
  • Risk appetite: the amount and type of risk the firm is willing to take, within its capacity.
  • Risk appetite statement: the written expression of the appetite, approved by the board.
  • Risk limits and tolerances: quantitative measures for specific risks, business lines or legal entities.
  • Roles and responsibilities for setting, monitoring and reporting.

A useful risk appetite statement

  • Covers all material risks: strategic, financial, operational, conduct, compliance, financial crime, reputational.
  • Combines qualitative statements (for example, "no appetite for breaches of sanctions") with quantitative metrics (for example, capital ratio above X%, operational losses below Y).
  • Uses thresholds, such as green, amber and red, with clear escalation at each level.
  • Is linked to the strategy and business plan.
  • Is short enough to be understood and used.

Cascading it

The appetite should flow into:

  • limits for business lines and products;
  • delegated authorities;
  • new product approval;
  • outsourcing and third-party decisions;
  • remuneration, so that pay does not reward excessive risk-taking.

Monitoring and breaches

  • Management reports against the metrics regularly, highlighting trends and breaches.
  • Breaches are escalated promptly, with a plan to return within appetite or a decision by the right level to accept or change the limit.
  • The board reviews the framework at least annually, and when strategy or conditions change.

Common weaknesses

  • Statements too vague to act on.
  • Metrics that never breach, set far from reality.
  • No link to decisions, so the appetite sits on a shelf.
  • Limits raised after breaches without challenge.
  • Conduct and non-financial risks left unmeasured.

explainers.title: Safeguarding client funds
explainers.summary: How payment and e-money institutions protect customers' money: what must be safeguarded, the methods allowed, reconciliation, and what happens if the firm fails.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Payment and e-money institutions do not take deposits, and their customers are not protected by deposit guarantee schemes. Instead, they must safeguard customers' money so that it can be returned if the firm fails.

What must be safeguarded

Relevant funds: money received from customers, or for their benefit, for payment transactions, and money received in exchange for e-money. Safeguarding usually starts as soon as the firm receives the funds.

Methods

Segregation. The firm keeps relevant funds separate from its own money and deposits them in a designated safeguarding account with a bank (or central bank), or invests them in secure, liquid, low-risk assets held in a separate account. The account must be named and acknowledged so that it is protected from the firm's other creditors.

Insurance or guarantee. The firm arranges an insurance policy or comparable guarantee from an insurer or bank that pays out the amount of relevant funds if the firm becomes insolvent.

Many firms combine methods.

Reconciliation and records

The firm must be able to show, at all times, which funds belong to which customers and that the safeguarded amount matches what it owes. This requires:

  • accurate records of customer balances;
  • regular reconciliations, internal (records against records) and external (records against bank statements);
  • prompt correction of shortfalls from the firm's own money;
  • clear identification of funds in transit.

What goes wrong

  • Customer money mixed with the firm's own operating funds.
  • Safeguarding accounts not properly designated or acknowledged.
  • Reconciliations not done, or differences left unexplained.
  • Funds held at a single bank that closes the account.
  • Delays in safeguarding money received through agents or partners.

When firms with weak safeguarding have failed, customers have waited a long time for their money, and some have suffered losses because of shortfalls and administrators' costs.

Recent reforms

  • UK: the FCA's new safeguarding rules took effect in May 2026, requiring daily reconciliations, monthly reporting, a resolution pack, annual audits above a threshold and a named senior manager responsible.
  • EU: PSD3 will strengthen safeguarding and align it for payment and e-money institutions, including measures against concentration on one bank.

What boards should ask

  • How quickly could customer funds be identified and returned if we failed?
  • Have reconciliations shown any unexplained differences?
  • What did the latest safeguarding audit find?
  • How concentrated are we on a single safeguarding bank?

explainers.title: Sanctions and crypto
explainers.summary: How sanctions apply to crypto-assets, how sanctioned actors use crypto, what the main regimes require of firms, and the tools for compliance.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Sanctions apply to crypto-assets in the same way as to other funds and economic resources. Firms dealing in crypto must not make assets available to sanctioned persons and must freeze assets they hold for them.

How sanctioned actors use crypto

  • State-linked hacking groups steal crypto-assets and launder them through mixers, bridges and over-the-counter brokers.
  • Sanctioned states and their banks use crypto, including stablecoins and dedicated tokens, to settle trade and move value outside the banking system.
  • Ransomware groups, some designated, demand payment in crypto.
  • Exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions can serve sanctioned clients.

What regimes require

  • Screening customers, counterparties and wallet addresses against sanctions lists. The US OFAC lists include specific crypto addresses, and EU and UK lists name persons and entities whose addresses must be identified.
  • Ownership and control: blocking assets of entities owned or controlled by sanctioned persons.
  • Freezing and reporting to the relevant authority.
  • Sector-specific bans: for example, EU rules ban providing crypto wallet, account or custody services to Russian nationals and residents, ban transactions in specific Russian tokens such as the A7A5 rouble stablecoin, and, from May 2026, ban transactions with Russian crypto-asset service providers.

Compliance tools

  • Blockchain analytics to identify exposure to sanctioned addresses and services, directly and indirectly.
  • Geolocation and IP controls to detect access from sanctioned jurisdictions, including through VPNs.
  • Travel rule data to know counterparties.
  • Token issuer controls: some stablecoin issuers can freeze tokens held at sanctioned addresses.

Challenges

  • Indirect exposure through many hops and chains.
  • Decentralised protocols with no one to apply controls.
  • Speed of new designations and evasion techniques.
  • Conflicting regimes for global firms.

Questions for boards

  • How quickly do we screen against new designations, including addresses?
  • What indirect exposure do we accept?
  • How do we detect circumvention, such as nested exchanges and VPN use?

explainers.title: Sanctions screening
explainers.summary: How sanctions screening works in financial firms: what is screened, against which lists, name matching and false positives, ownership and control, and how to test effectiveness.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Sanctions screening checks customers, counterparties, payments and other data against sanctions lists, so that firms do not deal with designated persons or breach sanctions.

What is screened

  • Customers and related parties (directors, beneficial owners, authorised signatories) at onboarding and on an ongoing basis.
  • Payments, including payer, payee, banks, addresses and free-text fields.
  • Trade finance documents, vessels and ports.
  • Investments and counterparties, including fund investors and issuers.
  • Crypto wallet addresses, using blockchain analytics.

The lists

Firms screen against all regimes that apply to them, typically UN, EU, UK (OFSI) and US (OFAC) lists, and sometimes others, plus internal lists. Lists change often, so updates must be applied promptly, ideally the same day.

Name matching

Names vary in spelling, order and transliteration. Screening systems use fuzzy matching to catch variations, which produces false positives that analysts must review. Calibration balances catching true matches against workload. Additional identifiers, such as dates of birth and nationalities, help resolve alerts.

Ownership and control

Sanctions extend to entities owned or controlled by designated persons, generally where they own 50% or more (rules differ between regimes). Screening names alone is not enough; firms need beneficial ownership information and analysis.

Handling alerts

  • Clear procedures, timelines and escalation.
  • Documented decisions.
  • Freezing and reporting of true matches.
  • Quality assurance of analysts' decisions.

Testing effectiveness

  • Regular testing with known sanctioned names and variations.
  • Checking that list updates are loaded on time.
  • Reviewing data quality, as missing or incomplete fields reduce effectiveness.
  • Independent review or audit.

Common weaknesses

  • Lists updated late.
  • Poor data in customer records and payment messages.
  • Overly loose or tight matching thresholds.
  • No ownership and control analysis.

explainers.title: Share classes: hedged, accumulating and distributing
explainers.summary: Why funds offer different share classes, the main types (accumulating, distributing, currency-hedged, fee-based), and the rules and risks involved.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A single fund can issue several share classes that invest in the same portfolio but differ in features such as fees, currency, minimum investment or income treatment. Each class has its own net asset value per share.

Common types

By income treatment - Accumulating (Acc): income is retained and reinvested, raising the share price. - Distributing (Dist or Inc): income is paid out to investors, typically monthly, quarterly or annually.

By currency - Unhedged currency classes: priced in another currency but exposed to exchange-rate moves between that currency and the portfolio's assets. - Currency-hedged classes: use forward contracts to reduce the effect of exchange-rate movements between the fund's base currency and the class currency. The hedging costs and gains belong to that class alone.

By investor and fees - Retail, clean or institutional classes with different management fees, minimum investments and distribution payments. - Founder or seed classes with lower fees for early investors.

Rules and risks

  • Fair treatment: differences between classes must be justified and disclosed. Costs specific to a class should be borne only by that class.
  • Hedging contagion: in UCITS, ESMA's opinion limits hedged share classes to currency hedging and requires measures so that hedging in one class does not spill over to others, with over- and under-hedging kept within limits.
  • Cost of hedging: depends on interest rate differentials between the currencies.
  • Legacy classes: investors left in older, more expensive classes after cheaper ones are introduced is a value-for-money concern.

Questions to ask

  • Are investors in the most appropriate class for them?
  • How are hedged classes managed and monitored?
  • Are fee differences between classes justified?
explainers.sortKey: share classes: hedged, accumulating and distributing

explainers.title: Smart contracts
explainers.summary: What smart contracts are, how they work, what they are used for in finance, their legal status and the risks they bring.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A smart contract is a program stored on a blockchain that runs automatically when certain conditions are met. Despite the name, it is not necessarily a legal contract. It is code.

How smart contracts work

  • A developer writes the code (for example in Solidity for Ethereum) and deploys it to the blockchain, where it gets its own address.
  • Users and other contracts call its functions by sending transactions.
  • Every node runs the code and agrees on the result, so the outcome does not depend on trusting any one party.
  • The contract can hold and move tokens according to its rules.
  • Running code costs fees (gas), paid in the network's native token.

What they are used for

  • Creating and managing tokens, including stablecoins and tokenised securities.
  • Decentralised exchanges, lending and derivatives.
  • Escrow and conditional payments.
  • Automated distributions and corporate actions for tokenised assets.
  • Enforcing transfer restrictions, such as allow-lists of approved holders.
  • Delivery versus payment, where an asset and payment move together or not at all.

Oracles

Smart contracts cannot see data outside the blockchain. Oracles feed in external information, such as prices, interest rates or events. The contract is only as reliable as its oracles.

Legal status

Whether a smart contract creates legally binding obligations depends on the circumstances and applicable law. Many arrangements combine a legal agreement with code that performs it. Questions arise about:

  • what happens when code and legal terms conflict;
  • liability for bugs;
  • how to reverse or remedy transactions when the law requires it.

MiCA and the EU Data Act include requirements for smart contracts in some contexts, such as the ability to stop or interrupt them.

Risks

  • Bugs and exploits, which can cause irreversible losses.
  • Upgradeability, which allows fixes but also changes by whoever controls the contract.
  • Oracle failure or manipulation.
  • Dependencies on other contracts, which can spread failures.
  • Key management for privileged functions.

Audits, testing, formal verification, monitoring and careful governance reduce, but do not eliminate, these risks.

explainers.title: Smart-contract risk and audits
explainers.summary: Why smart contracts can fail, the main vulnerability types, what a smart-contract audit does and does not cover, and other controls that reduce risk.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A smart contract is code deployed on a blockchain that runs automatically when called. Once deployed, it may be hard or impossible to change. If it contains a flaw, attackers can exploit it to drain funds, often within minutes, and the transactions cannot be reversed.

Common vulnerabilities

  • Re-entrancy: a contract calls an external contract before updating its own records, letting the attacker call back in and withdraw repeatedly.
  • Access control errors: functions that should be restricted to administrators are left open.
  • Oracle manipulation: the contract relies on a price that can be manipulated, often using a flash loan.
  • Logic and arithmetic errors: mistakes in calculations, rounding or assumptions.
  • Upgrade and initialisation flaws: errors in how upgradeable contracts are set up or changed.
  • Economic design flaws: the code works as written, but the incentives can be gamed.
  • Signature and message verification errors, especially in bridges.

What an audit does

A smart-contract audit is a review by specialists of a protocol's code and design, looking for vulnerabilities. It typically includes:

  • manual line-by-line review;
  • automated analysis tools;
  • testing, including simulated attacks;
  • sometimes formal verification, mathematically proving that the code meets specified properties.

The output is a report of findings by severity, and the developer's responses.

What an audit does not do

  • It covers a specific version of the code at a point in time. Later changes may not be audited.
  • It cannot guarantee there are no vulnerabilities.
  • It usually does not cover off-chain components, key management or governance.
  • Quality varies widely between auditors.

Many exploited protocols had been audited.

Other controls

  • Multiple independent audits, especially for high-value protocols.
  • Bug bounties that reward people who find and report vulnerabilities.
  • Gradual launch with limits on the value at risk.
  • Monitoring and automated alerts for unusual activity.
  • Pause mechanisms and circuit breakers, balanced against the centralisation they introduce.
  • Time delays on upgrades so users can react.
  • Secure key management for admin functions.

Questions to ask

  • Who audited the code, which version, and were the findings fixed?
  • How much value is at risk, and how has the code performed over time?
  • Who can upgrade or pause the contracts, and with what safeguards?

explainers.title: Stablecoin runs and depegs
explainers.summary: Why stablecoins lose their peg, how runs unfold, what reserve and redemption design does to the risk, and what holders and regulators can learn.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A stablecoin depegs when its market price moves materially away from its reference value, such as one US dollar. A depeg can be brief and minor, or the start of a collapse.

Why depegs happen

  • Doubts about reserves: holders question whether the assets backing the coin are enough, liquid enough or really there.
  • Reserve losses or frozen reserves: for example, if a bank holding reserves fails, or reserve assets lose value.
  • Redemption frictions: if only a few large firms can redeem directly, or redemptions are slow, the market price can fall below par when selling pressure rises.
  • Design failures: algorithmic stablecoins without real reserves depend on confidence and can collapse in a spiral.
  • Collateral crashes: crypto-collateralised stablecoins can depeg if collateral falls faster than it can be liquidated.
  • Market stress: sudden demand for dollars or exits from crypto.

How a run unfolds

  1. A trigger raises doubts.
  2. Holders who can redeem do so; others sell on exchanges.
  3. The issuer sells reserve assets to meet redemptions. If they are not liquid, it may sell at a loss, worsening the doubts.
  4. The price falls further, spreading to platforms and protocols that hold the coin or use it as collateral.

The first to leave get par; those who wait may not, so there is an incentive to run early, as with bank runs or money market funds.

What reduces the risk

  • High-quality, short-term reserves, mostly cash and government bills.
  • Segregation of reserves from the issuer's own assets.
  • Frequent, independent verification of reserves.
  • Clear, broad and fast redemption rights at par.
  • Diversification across banks and custodians.
  • Tested recovery and redemption plans.

These are the core of regulatory regimes such as MiCA in the EU and the GENIUS Act in the US.

For firms that use stablecoins

  • Limit exposure to any one stablecoin.
  • Know whether you can redeem directly and how quickly.
  • Monitor reserve reports and market prices.
  • Have a plan for a depeg, including client communications.

explainers.title: Stablecoins as a means of payment
explainers.summary: How stablecoins are being used for payments, cross-border transfers and settlement, the benefits and risks, and how payments and crypto regulation apply.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Stablecoins started as a tool for crypto trading. They are now increasingly used for payments: cross-border transfers, business payments, payroll, merchant payments and settlement between platforms.

Why use stablecoins for payments?

  • Speed: transfers settle in minutes or seconds, around the clock.
  • Cost: potentially cheaper than correspondent banking for cross-border payments.
  • Reach: anyone with a wallet can receive them, including in countries with weak banking systems.
  • Programmability: payments can be automated through smart contracts.
  • Access to dollars: for people and businesses in countries with unstable currencies.

How a stablecoin payment works

  1. The payer converts money into stablecoins through an issuer, exchange or payment provider, or already holds them.
  2. The stablecoins are sent on a blockchain to the payee's wallet address.
  3. The payee keeps the stablecoins or converts them to local currency through an off-ramp provider.

Payment firms can hide the stablecoin leg so that payer and payee deal only in their own currencies.

Risks

  • Stability and redemption: the coin is only as good as its reserves and the holder's ability to redeem.
  • Operational risk: wrong addresses, lost keys and irreversible transfers.
  • Financial crime: stablecoins, especially US dollar coins on low-cost networks, are widely used in scams, sanctions evasion and illicit finance.
  • Consumer protection: limited rights compared with traditional payments, such as no chargebacks.
  • Monetary sovereignty: widespread use of foreign-currency stablecoins could weaken control over domestic money, a concern for the euro area and emerging markets.

Regulation

  • EU: e-money tokens are electronic money and may only be issued by banks and e-money institutions under MiCA. Using them in payments can be a payment service, and PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation will clarify the overlap. MiCA limits the use as a means of exchange of asset-referenced tokens and of e-money tokens in non-EU currencies.
  • UK: stablecoin issuance in the UK will be regulated from October 2027, with systemic payment stablecoins supervised by the Bank of England, and HM Treasury has consulted on how payments regulation should apply.
  • US: the GENIUS Act sets federal rules for payment stablecoins.
  • AML: the travel rule applies to transfers.

Questions for firms

  • Which stablecoins do we accept or use, and are they authorised where we and our customers are?
  • How do we redeem them, and how quickly?
  • How do we screen wallets and transactions for financial crime?
explainers.sortKey: stablecoins as a means of payment

explainers.title: Stablecoins: design, reserves and redemption
explainers.summary: How stablecoins try to hold a stable value, the different designs, what makes a reserve sound, how redemption works and the risks of a run.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A stablecoin is a crypto-asset designed to keep a stable value relative to a reference, usually a currency such as the US dollar or euro. Stablecoins are used for trading, settlement and increasingly for payments.

Designs

Fiat-backed. The issuer holds reserve assets, such as bank deposits, short-term government bonds and money market fund units, equal to or greater than the stablecoins in issue, and promises to redeem at par. Most large stablecoins work this way.

Crypto-collateralised. Users lock crypto-assets worth more than the stablecoins they create in smart contracts. If the collateral's value falls too far, it is automatically sold. The over-collateralisation absorbs price swings.

Commodity-backed. Backed by gold or other commodities held in custody.

Synthetic or hedged. Kept stable through derivatives strategies, for example holding crypto-assets and short-selling futures. These carry market, funding and counterparty risks.

Algorithmic. Rely on algorithms and incentives, often involving a second token, to keep the peg, with little or no reserve. Several have collapsed, and they cannot qualify as compliant stablecoins under MiCA.

What makes a reserve sound

  • Quality: cash and very short-term, high-quality government securities.
  • Liquidity: enough can be turned into cash immediately to meet redemptions in a run.
  • Segregation: reserve assets are legally separate from the issuer's own assets and protected from its creditors.
  • Custody: held with reliable custodians and banks, without concentration on one bank.
  • Transparency: regular, independent verification of reserve composition and value.

Redemption

Holders should be able to redeem at par, promptly and without excessive fees. In practice, many holders cannot redeem directly with the issuer and rely on selling on exchanges, where the price can fall below par in stress.

Runs and de-pegging

If holders doubt the reserve or the issuer, they rush to redeem or sell. If the issuer has to sell reserve assets quickly, or cannot get cash from its bank, the price can break from its peg. Stablecoins have de-pegged when a bank holding reserves failed and when reserves turned out to be smaller or less liquid than claimed.

Regulation

  • EU: MiCA regulates e-money tokens and asset-referenced tokens, with reserve, redemption, no-interest and governance rules, and EBA supervision of significant tokens.
  • UK: stablecoin issuance in the UK is becoming a regulated activity, with systemic stablecoins supervised by the Bank of England.
  • US: the GENIUS Act of 2025 sets federal rules for payment stablecoins.

Questions to ask

  • What exactly backs the stablecoin, where is it held, and who verifies it?
  • Can holders redeem directly, at par, and how quickly?
  • How would the issuer cope with a large share of holders redeeming at once?

explainers.title: Staking, liquid staking and restaking
explainers.summary: How staking secures proof-of-stake blockchains, how investors earn rewards, what liquid staking and restaking add, and the risks involved.
explainers.bodyHtml:
What staking is

In a proof-of-stake blockchain, validators propose and confirm new blocks. To become a validator, a participant must lock up (stake) the network's native token as collateral. Validators earn rewards for doing the work correctly and can lose part of their stake (slashing) for misbehaviour, such as signing conflicting blocks or long downtime.

Token holders who do not run a validator themselves can delegate their tokens to a validator, or use a staking service provided by an exchange or custodian.

Why investors stake

Staking rewards provide a yield on holdings, paid in the native token. The rate depends on the network's rules, the amount staked across the network and the validator's fees.

Liquid staking

Staked tokens are usually locked and cannot be withdrawn immediately. Liquid staking protocols solve this: users deposit tokens, the protocol stakes them, and users receive a liquid staking token representing their staked position and its rewards. The liquid staking token can be traded or used in DeFi, for example as collateral.

Restaking

Restaking lets already-staked tokens, or liquid staking tokens, be used to secure additional services, such as oracles, bridges or data availability layers, in return for extra rewards. Liquid restaking tokens represent these positions.

The risks

  • Slashing: losing part of the stake for validator faults. Restaking adds further slashing conditions.
  • Lock-up and liquidity risk: unstaking can take days or weeks; liquid staking tokens can trade below the value of the underlying stake in stress.
  • Smart-contract risk in liquid staking and restaking protocols.
  • Concentration: large liquid staking protocols or exchanges controlling a big share of staked tokens can create risks for the network.
  • Counterparty risk where a staking service provider holds the tokens.
  • Layered risk: using liquid staking or restaking tokens as collateral to borrow and stake again creates leverage and can unwind quickly.

Regulation

  • Custody of staked assets by a CASP falls under MiCA custody rules. Staking itself is not a specific MiCA service, and the Commission is reviewing how it should be treated.
  • In the UK, arranging cryptoasset staking will become a regulated activity from October 2027.
  • For investment funds and products, staking raises questions about eligible assets, liquidity and the depositary's role.
  • Tax treatment of rewards varies.

Questions to ask

  • Who runs the validators, and what controls prevent slashing?
  • How long would it take to unstake, and what happens to liquidity in stress?
  • Are clients' staked assets segregated and protected?
  • What extra risks does restaking or using liquid staking tokens add?

explainers.title: Strong customer authentication
explainers.summary: What strong customer authentication requires, when it applies, the exemptions, how it works for cards and online banking, and how it is evolving.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Strong customer authentication (SCA) is the requirement, introduced by PSD2 in the EU and retained in the UK, that payment service providers verify a customer's identity using at least two independent elements before certain actions.

The three categories

  • Knowledge: something only the customer knows, such as a password or PIN.
  • Possession: something only the customer has, such as a phone or card.
  • Inherence: something the customer is, such as a fingerprint or face.

Two different categories must be used, and the compromise of one must not compromise the other.

When SCA applies

When a payer:

  • accesses a payment account online;
  • initiates an electronic payment;
  • carries out any action through a remote channel that may imply a risk of fraud.

For remote electronic payments, authentication must be dynamically linked to the amount and payee.

Exemptions

Providers may choose not to apply SCA in defined cases, such as:

  • low-value contactless payments, within cumulative limits;
  • low-value remote payments;
  • trusted beneficiaries the customer has listed;
  • recurring payments of the same amount to the same payee, after the first;
  • transactions assessed as low risk by real-time transaction risk analysis, within fraud rate thresholds;
  • secure corporate payment processes.

How it works in practice

  • Cards online: issuers use protocols such as 3-D Secure, often asking for approval in the banking app.
  • Online banking: login and payment approval via app biometrics or one-time codes.
  • Open banking: customers authenticate with their own provider, not the third party.

How it is evolving

  • The EU Payment Services Regulation will clarify responsibilities, improve accessibility for people without smartphones and address new fraud patterns.
  • Authentication is increasingly combined with behavioural analysis and device signals.
  • AI agents making payments on customers' behalf raise new questions about how consent and authentication should work.

explainers.title: The depositary: safekeeping, oversight and cash monitoring
explainers.summary: What a fund depositary does: holding assets safely, monitoring the fund's cash, overseeing the manager, and when it is liable for losses.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Every UCITS and every EU AIF must appoint a single depositary. The depositary is an independent check on the fund manager and the guardian of the fund's assets. Depositaries are usually banks or specialist depositary firms.

The three core duties

1. Safekeeping

  • Financial instruments that can be held in custody, such as shares and bonds, must be held in segregated accounts in the name of the fund, either directly or through sub-custodians.
  • Other assets, such as derivatives, property or private company interests, cannot be held in custody. For these, the depositary verifies the fund's ownership and keeps an up-to-date record.

2. Cash monitoring

The depositary must make sure that all the fund's cash flows are properly monitored, that all subscriptions are received, and that the fund's cash is booked in accounts in the fund's name. It reconciles cash movements and investigates unusual items.

3. Oversight

The depositary checks that:

  • subscriptions, redemptions and cancellations are carried out in line with the rules and fund documents;
  • the value of shares is calculated correctly;
  • the manager's instructions comply with the rules and fund documents, including investment restrictions;
  • transactions are settled within usual time limits;
  • income is applied correctly.

When the depositary finds problems, it escalates them to the manager and, if not resolved, to the board and the regulator.

Liability

The depositary is liable for the loss of financial instruments held in custody, including by a sub-custodian. It must return an identical instrument or the corresponding amount without delay, unless the loss was caused by an external event beyond its reasonable control. For UCITS this liability cannot be contracted out. Some AIF depositaries can discharge liability to a sub-custodian in limited circumstances.

For other losses, the depositary is liable if they result from its negligent or intentional failure to perform its duties.

Independence

The depositary must act independently and in the interests of investors. It may not be the manager, and conflicts must be managed where it is in the same group as the manager or a service provider.

What boards should ask

  • What exceptions did the depositary report this period, and how were they resolved?
  • How does the depositary oversee sub-custodians, particularly in emerging markets?
  • How are assets that cannot be held in custody, such as private assets, verified?
  • How independent is the depositary from the manager's group?
explainers.sortKey: the depositary: safekeeping, oversight and cash monitoring

explainers.title: The economics of card payments: interchange, scheme fees and chargebacks
explainers.summary: Who the parties to a card payment are, who pays what, how interchange and scheme fees are regulated, and how chargebacks and disputes work.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Every card payment involves four main parties and several layers of fees. Understanding them explains much of how payment businesses make money and where their risks lie.

The parties

  • Cardholder and card issuer (the cardholder's bank or e-money institution).
  • Merchant and acquirer (the firm that contracts with the merchant to accept cards).
  • Card scheme, which sets the rules and runs the network.
  • Processors, payment facilitators and gateways that provide technical services.

Who pays what

  • The merchant pays the acquirer a merchant service charge.
  • Out of this, the acquirer pays interchange to the issuer and scheme fees to the scheme, keeping the rest as margin.
  • Issuers use interchange to fund card programmes, rewards and fraud costs.

Regulation of fees

  • The EU Interchange Fee Regulation caps consumer interchange at 0.2% for debit and 0.3% for credit cards. The UK retained it.
  • Commercial cards and cards issued outside the region are not capped in the same way, and cross-border interchange between the UK and EU has been a focus of regulators.
  • Scheme fees are not capped but are under scrutiny for transparency.
  • Merchants may not surcharge consumer cards covered by the caps in the EU and UK.

Chargebacks

A chargeback reverses a card payment through the scheme's dispute process, for example for fraud, goods not received or not as described.

  1. The cardholder disputes the payment with the issuer.
  2. The issuer raises a chargeback to the acquirer.
  3. The merchant can respond with evidence (representment).
  4. Unresolved disputes may go to scheme arbitration.

Merchants with high chargeback rates face fees, monitoring programmes and possible termination. Acquirers bear the loss if a merchant fails and cannot cover chargebacks, so they hold reserves for higher-risk merchants.

Liability shift

When a transaction is authenticated with 3-D Secure, fraud liability generally shifts from the merchant to the issuer.
explainers.sortKey: the economics of card payments: interchange, scheme fees and chargebacks

explainers.title: The fund board: role, composition and effectiveness
explainers.summary: What a fund board does, how it differs from a trading company board, how it should be composed, and how it oversees delegates and assesses its own effectiveness.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Corporate funds, such as SICAVs, ICAVs and investment companies, have their own boards. Management companies and AIFMs also have boards. Although most activities are delegated, the board remains responsible for the fund and for overseeing those who run it.

What a fund board does

  • Sets or approves the fund's strategy and investment policy.
  • Appoints and oversees the management company or AIFM and other service providers, such as the depositary, administrator, auditor and distributors.
  • Oversees risk management, valuation, liquidity and conflicts of interest.
  • Approves financial statements and key documents.
  • Makes decisions reserved to it, such as suspending dealing, launching or closing sub-funds and approving material changes.
  • Ensures investors are treated fairly.

How it differs from a trading company board

A fund usually has no employees. The board's work is mostly oversight of delegates through reports, meetings and challenge, rather than directing an internal management team. Investors' interests are central; the board must be able to act independently of the manager when interests conflict.

Composition

  • A mix of independent directors and directors connected with the manager or promoter.
  • Relevant skills: investment, risk, legal and regulatory, operations, accounting.
  • Sufficient time commitment; regulators watch for directors with too many appointments.
  • In some jurisdictions, local residence or substance requirements.
  • Diversity of background and perspective.

Effective oversight

  • A clear matters reserved for the board document.
  • Good board packs, with management information focused on risks and outcomes.
  • Regular meetings with delegates, including on-site or deep-dive reviews.
  • Challenge recorded in minutes.
  • An annual board evaluation, periodically facilitated externally.

Warning signs

  • Board packs that are long but uninformative.
  • Little evidence of challenge.
  • Directors relying entirely on the manager's views.
  • Persistent problems with delegates that are never escalated.
explainers.sortKey: the fund board: role, composition and effectiveness

explainers.title: The risk-based approach to AML/CFT
explainers.summary: What the risk-based approach to anti-money laundering means in practice: assessing risk at business and customer level, applying proportionate measures and documenting decisions.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The risk-based approach (RBA) is the foundation of modern anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing rules. Firms must understand their exposure to financial crime and focus their efforts where the risks are greatest, rather than applying the same checks to everyone.

Business-wide risk assessment

Each firm must assess the money laundering and terrorist financing risks it faces, considering:

  • customers: types, including corporate structures, PEPs and high-net-worth individuals;
  • products and services: for example, anonymity, cross-border transfers, cash, crypto-assets;
  • delivery channels: face-to-face, online, through intermediaries;
  • geographies: where customers are, where money comes from and goes;
  • transactions: size, complexity and patterns.

The assessment should reflect national and supranational risk assessments and typologies, be approved by senior management and be updated when the business or risks change.

Customer risk assessment

Each customer is assessed and given a risk rating, which determines:

  • simplified due diligence for demonstrably lower-risk situations;
  • standard due diligence for most customers;
  • enhanced due diligence for higher-risk customers, including PEPs, customers from high-risk third countries and complex structures.

Proportionate controls

The RBA shapes:

  • the depth of identification and verification;
  • how often customer information is reviewed;
  • transaction monitoring thresholds and scenarios;
  • the level of senior approval for onboarding;
  • training and resources.

Risk appetite

Firms should decide which risks they are willing to accept and which they will not, for example certain countries or business types, and apply that consistently.

Pitfalls

  • Tick-box compliance: using a generic risk assessment that does not reflect the actual business.
  • De-risking: refusing whole categories of customers rather than managing risk, which can exclude legitimate customers and push activity into less transparent channels. The FATF has emphasised that measures should be proportionate and support financial inclusion.
  • Static ratings that are never updated.
  • Poor documentation of decisions.

What supervisors look for

  • A risk assessment that matches the business.
  • Controls that clearly follow from the risks identified.
  • Evidence that the approach works, such as effective monitoring and reporting.
  • Senior management ownership.

explainers.title: The three lines of defence
explainers.summary: How the three lines of defence model divides responsibility for risk management between the business, risk and compliance functions, and internal audit, and the model's strengths and limits.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The three lines of defence is the most widely used way of organising risk management and control in financial firms. It clarifies who owns risk, who oversees it and who provides independent assurance.

The three lines

First line: the business. Front-office and operational teams own and manage the risks in their activities. They design and operate controls day to day, identify issues and fix them.

Second line: risk management and compliance. Independent functions that set the framework, policies and risk appetite, monitor and challenge the first line, and report to senior management and the board. They include risk management, compliance, and often the MLRO's function.

Third line: internal audit. Provides independent and objective assurance to the board, usually through the audit committee, on whether risk management and controls work, including those of the second line.

External auditors and regulators are sometimes described as additional lines outside the firm.

The board's role

The board sets the risk appetite and the tone, and oversees all three lines. It needs direct access to the heads of risk, compliance and internal audit, who should be able to escalate concerns to it without going through management.

Making it work

  • Clear ownership: each risk has an owner in the first line.
  • Independence: second and third lines must be independent of the activities they oversee, with appropriate reporting lines, resources and pay not tied to business results.
  • Coordination: the lines share information and avoid gaps or duplication.
  • Challenge: the second line must be willing and able to say no.

Limits and criticisms

  • Blurred lines: in small firms, one person may sit in several lines; in large firms, "1.5 lines" of business-side control teams are common.
  • Diffused responsibility: the first line may treat risk as the second line's job.
  • Bureaucracy: too much focus on structure and documents rather than outcomes.
  • The Institute of Internal Auditors updated the model in 2020 as the Three Lines Model, emphasising collaboration and the role of governing bodies, rather than "defence".

Questions for boards

  • Does the first line genuinely own its risks?
  • Are the second-line functions adequately resourced and independent?
  • Does internal audit cover the highest risks, and are its findings closed on time?
  • When did the second or third line last stop something?

explainers.title: The Travel Rule in practice
explainers.summary: How the travel rule works day to day for crypto-asset service providers: what data travels, how it is sent, how counterparties are identified, and what to do with missing information and self-hosted wallets.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The travel rule requires information about the originator and beneficiary to accompany a transfer, so that each firm in the chain knows who is sending and receiving funds. It has long applied to bank wire transfers. Since 30 December 2024, the EU has applied it to crypto-asset transfers between CASPs, with no minimum threshold.

What has to travel

For a crypto-asset transfer, the originator's CASP must send:

  • the originator's name;
  • the originator's distributed ledger address or account number;
  • the originator's address, official document number, customer number or date and place of birth;
  • the beneficiary's name and address or account number.

The beneficiary's CASP must check that this information is received and complete.

How the information is sent

Blockchains do not carry this data, so it is sent separately, using travel rule solutions and messaging standards that allow CASPs to exchange data securely. Different solutions must interoperate, and the information must be sent before or at the same time as the transfer.

Identifying the counterparty

Before sending data, a CASP must know whether the destination address belongs to another CASP or to a self-hosted wallet, and if a CASP, which one. Firms use:

  • address ownership proofs and counterparty directories;
  • blockchain analytics to attribute addresses;
  • counterparty due diligence, assessing whether the other CASP is legitimate, licensed and has adequate AML controls and data protection, especially outside the EU.

Missing or incomplete information

The beneficiary's CASP must have risk-based procedures to decide whether to:

  • reject or return the transfer;
  • suspend it while requesting the missing information;
  • execute it and request the information afterwards.

Repeated failures by a counterparty should lead to warnings, restrictions or ending the relationship, and reporting to the regulator.

Self-hosted wallets

Transfers to or from self-hosted wallets do not involve a counterparty CASP, so there is no one to exchange data with. CASPs must still collect originator and beneficiary information from their customers, and for transfers above €1,000 must assess whether the self-hosted wallet is owned or controlled by their customer, using methods such as a signed message or a small test transaction.

The sunrise problem

Not all countries apply the travel rule yet. EU CASPs still have to comply when dealing with counterparties in countries that have not implemented it, which may mean extra checks or declining transfers.

What good looks like

  • High data completeness rates, monitored and reported to management.
  • Clear procedures for missing information and self-hosted wallets.
  • Documented counterparty due diligence.
  • Integration with sanctions screening and transaction monitoring.

explainers.title: Tokenisation and real-world assets
explainers.summary: What tokenisation of real-world assets means, which assets are being tokenised, the legal and operational models, and the benefits and risks.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Tokenisation is the process of representing rights in an asset as a token on a distributed ledger. Real-world assets (RWAs) are traditional assets, such as government bonds, money market funds, private credit, property and commodities, that are represented this way.

What is being tokenised

  • Government bonds and money market funds: the largest category, used as on-chain cash equivalents and collateral.
  • Private credit: loans originated off-chain and represented on-chain.
  • Fund units: tokenised versions of conventional funds.
  • Commodities: especially gold.
  • Property and private equity: often in fractional form.
  • Deposits: tokenised bank deposits issued by banks.

How it is done

Direct (native) issuance. The asset is issued on the ledger from the start, and the token is the legal record of ownership. This needs legal recognition of DLT records, as with digital securities laws in several countries.

Indirect (wrapped or mirrored). A traditional asset is held by a custodian or special purpose vehicle, which issues tokens representing claims on it. The token holder's rights depend on the legal structure and the custodian.

Why tokenise?

  • Faster, potentially round-the-clock settlement, and delivery versus payment on-chain.
  • Fewer reconciliations and intermediaries.
  • Fractional ownership and wider access.
  • Use as collateral in DeFi and in institutional markets.
  • Programmable features, such as automatic income payments or transfer restrictions.

Risks and questions

  • Legal rights: what exactly does the token holder own, and is it enforceable on the issuer's or custodian's insolvency?
  • Link to the asset: how is the on-chain token kept in line with the off-chain asset, and who checks?
  • Liquidity: tokenising an illiquid asset does not make it liquid.
  • Smart contract and network risk.
  • AML and sanctions: controlling who can hold tokens, usually through permissioned tokens and allow-lists.
  • Settlement asset: the need for reliable on-chain money, such as stablecoins, tokenised deposits or central bank money.
  • Interoperability between different ledgers and with traditional systems.

Regulation

A tokenised financial instrument is still a financial instrument. In the EU, MiFID II, the Prospectus Regulation, CSDR and fund rules apply. The DLT Pilot Regime allows market infrastructures to trade and settle tokenised securities with some exemptions. Tokens that are not financial instruments may fall under MiCA.

Central banks and regulators are also exploring settlement of tokenised assets in central bank money, through projects such as the Eurosystem's work on DLT settlement.

explainers.title: Tokenised deposits and wholesale CBDC
explainers.summary: What tokenised deposits are, how they differ from stablecoins, the role of wholesale central bank digital currency in settling tokenised assets, and current projects.
explainers.bodyHtml:
As assets are increasingly tokenised, markets need a form of money on the same ledgers to settle transactions. Three main options are emerging: stablecoins, tokenised deposits and wholesale central bank digital currency.

Tokenised deposits

A tokenised deposit is a commercial bank deposit recorded as a token on a distributed ledger. It is still a deposit, a liability of the bank:

  • covered by bank regulation, capital and liquidity rules;
  • covered by deposit insurance, where applicable;
  • usually limited to the bank's own customers or a network of banks.

How they differ from stablecoins

Tokenised deposit Stablecoin
Issuer Bank Bank, e-money institution or specialist issuer
Backing The bank's balance sheet A segregated reserve of assets
Interest Can pay interest Generally cannot (EU, US)
Transferability Usually within permissioned networks Often freely transferable, including to self-hosted wallets
Deposit insurance Usually yes No

Wholesale CBDC

A wholesale central bank digital currency is central bank money available only to banks and other financial institutions, on or connected to a distributed ledger, for settling large-value and securities transactions. It provides the safest settlement asset.

Projects and status (as at November 2026)

  • The Eurosystem has trialled settling DLT transactions in central bank money and is developing permanent services, linking DLT platforms to its existing settlement systems.
  • The Bank of England and other central banks are running similar experiments and synchronisation projects.
  • International projects coordinated by the BIS explore cross-border settlement with tokenised deposits and wholesale central bank money.
  • Several banks offer tokenised deposit services for corporate clients, for example for treasury and cross-border payments.

Why it matters

The choice of settlement asset affects safety, interoperability and who captures value. Regulators generally prefer settlement in central bank money for systemically important activity, while allowing regulated private money for other uses.

explainers.title: Tokenised funds: native and mirrored registers
explainers.summary: How investment funds are being tokenised: what a tokenised fund is, the difference between native and mirrored registers, the benefits, the risks and the regulatory questions.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A tokenised fund is a fund whose units or shares are represented as tokens on a distributed ledger. The fund itself is usually a conventional regulated fund, such as a money market fund or UCITS. What changes is how ownership is recorded and transferred.

Two models

Mirrored (or digital twin) register. The official register of investors is still kept in the traditional way by the transfer agent. Tokens on a blockchain mirror the register, and the two are reconciled. The token is a representation of the holding, not the legal record. This is the most common model today because it fits existing law and operations.

Native register. The distributed ledger is the official register. Ownership is legally recorded on-chain, and transferring the token transfers the shares. This requires legal recognition of the ledger as the register, which several jurisdictions now provide, and a transfer agent able to operate it.

Hybrid approaches also exist, for example where the on-chain record is authoritative for some investors and the traditional register for others.

Why tokenise?

  • Faster settlement, potentially near-instant and around the clock.
  • Lower costs through fewer reconciliations and intermediaries.
  • New uses, such as using tokenised money market fund shares as collateral or as an on-chain cash equivalent.
  • Programmability, such as automated distributions or transfer restrictions built into the token.
  • Wider distribution, including to digital asset platforms and their clients.

Risks and challenges

  • Legal certainty: whether the ledger is legally recognised and how ownership is protected on insolvency.
  • Operational and technology risk: smart-contract bugs, key management, outages and the resilience of the network.
  • Public vs permissioned networks: public blockchains bring reach and liquidity but raise questions about control, privacy and who validates transactions.
  • AML/CFT: identifying investors who hold tokens in wallets, and controlling transfers to unknown wallets, usually through allow-lists.
  • Interoperability with traditional systems and between ledgers.
  • Settlement asset: whether there is a reliable on-chain cash leg, such as a tokenised deposit, stablecoin or wholesale central bank money.
  • Liquidity mismatch: faster dealing for a token does not make the underlying assets more liquid.

Regulation

In the EU, tokenised fund shares are still fund shares and financial instruments: UCITS or AIFMD, MiFID II, depositary and AML rules all apply. The DLT Pilot Regime allows market infrastructures to trade and settle tokenised instruments under certain exemptions. Supervisors expect the depositary to understand and control the risks of holding or recording assets on DLT.

Questions to ask

  • Which register is the legal record, and what happens if the ledger and the register disagree?
  • Who controls the smart contract, and how can it be upgraded or paused?
  • How are investors identified and transfers restricted?
  • What does the depositary do differently?
explainers.sortKey: tokenised funds: native and mirrored registers

explainers.title: Tokenomics: supply, vesting and unlocks
explainers.summary: How crypto-asset supply, allocation, vesting schedules, issuance and burns affect value and risk, and what to look for in a token's design.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Tokenomics is the economic design of a crypto-asset. It affects price, governance and the risk that early holders sell to later buyers.

Supply

  • Circulating supply: tokens available to trade now.
  • Total supply: tokens issued, including locked ones.
  • Maximum supply: the cap, if any. Some tokens, like bitcoin, are capped; others are inflationary.
  • Fully diluted valuation: price multiplied by maximum supply, showing the value if all tokens existed today.

A token with a small circulating supply and a large locked supply can look cheaper than it is.

Allocation

Typical categories include the team, early investors, a foundation or treasury, ecosystem incentives, community airdrops and public sale. High allocations to insiders increase the risk of selling pressure and concentrated governance.

Vesting and unlocks

Insider allocations are usually vested: released gradually, often after an initial cliff. Large unlocks can lead to price falls as holders sell. Investors should check the schedule and how much is due to unlock in the coming months.

Issuance and burning

  • New tokens may be issued as staking rewards or incentives, diluting holders.
  • Some protocols burn tokens from fees or buy back tokens with revenue, reducing supply.
  • The net effect determines whether supply grows or shrinks.

Utility and value capture

Ask what the token is used for and whether the protocol's success flows to token holders: through fees, staking rewards, governance rights or burns. Many tokens have weak links between protocol usage and token value.

Regulatory angle

  • Under MiCA, white papers must describe the rights attached to tokens, supply and allocation.
  • Misleading statements about tokenomics can amount to market manipulation or misrepresentation.
  • Concentrated insider holdings and coordinated selling around unlocks raise market abuse concerns.

explainers.title: Transfer agency and the register of investors
explainers.summary: What a fund's transfer agent does: keeping the register of investors, processing dealing, carrying out investor due diligence and handling investor communications.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The transfer agent (TA), sometimes called the registrar, is the fund's link with its investors. It keeps the official record of who owns the fund and processes every subscription, redemption and transfer.

Main functions

Maintaining the register. The register is the legal record of ownership of the fund's shares or units. The TA records each investor's holdings and updates them after every transaction.

Processing dealing. - Receiving orders by the dealing cut-off and checking they are complete. - Applying the correct dealing price, usually the NAV per share calculated after the cut-off (forward pricing). - Issuing contract notes and confirmations. - Arranging settlement of subscription monies and payment of redemption proceeds. - Applying fees, such as entry or exit charges, and any anti-dilution measures.

Investor due diligence. The TA usually carries out AML/CFT checks on investors for the fund: identifying and verifying investors and beneficial owners, screening against sanctions and PEP lists, monitoring transactions and reporting suspicions. In practice it often relies on distributors for underlying investors held through nominee accounts, which needs careful oversight.

Income and corporate actions. Paying distributions and processing reinvestments.

Investor servicing and reporting. Answering queries, sending statements, handling complaints, and producing tax reporting.

Distribution chains

Many investors do not appear on the register directly. They invest through platforms, banks and wealth managers that hold shares in nominee names. The fund then sees only the nominee, which makes it harder to know who the end investors are, to monitor where the fund is sold and to apply investor protections. Distributor due diligence and data sharing are important controls.

Risks to watch

  • Dealing errors, such as orders processed at the wrong price or after the cut-off. Late trading and market timing are prohibited.
  • AML/CFT failures, including backlogs in investor reviews.
  • Unclaimed money and dormant accounts.
  • Fraud, such as false redemption requests or changes to bank details.
  • Data protection and cyber security.

What boards should ask

  • Are dealing errors and their correction reported, with investor compensation where due?
  • What is the backlog of investor due diligence reviews?
  • How are nominee and distributor relationships assessed for AML/CFT?
  • What are the main complaints, and what do they tell us?
explainers.sortKey: transfer agency and the register of investors

explainers.title: UCITS and AIFs: what's the difference?
explainers.summary: The two main EU fund regimes explained: what a UCITS is, what an AIF is, who can invest in each and how the rules differ.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Every fund in the EU falls into one of two categories. It is either a UCITS (undertaking for collective investment in transferable securities) or an AIF (alternative investment fund).

UCITS

UCITS are funds authorised under the UCITS Directive. They are designed for retail investors and are regulated at product level:

  • Eligible assets only: transferable securities, money market instruments, units of other funds, deposits and derivatives.
  • Diversification limits, such as no more than 10% in a single issuer.
  • Limits on leverage, through global exposure rules and a 10% cap on temporary borrowing.
  • Liquidity: investors must be able to redeem at least twice a month, and in practice most UCITS deal daily.
  • A single depositary with strict liability.
  • Investor disclosure: prospectus, reports and a key information document.

A UCITS authorised in one member state can be marketed to retail investors across the EU. The brand is also widely recognised outside Europe, particularly in Asia and Latin America.

AIFs

An AIF is any collective investment undertaking that is not a UCITS. The category is very broad: hedge funds, private equity, venture capital, real estate, infrastructure, private credit, funds of funds and many retail funds that are not UCITS.

AIFMD regulates the manager (the AIFM) rather than the fund. There are no EU-wide limits on what an AIF can invest in or how much leverage it can use, although AIFMs must manage risk, liquidity and leverage and report on them. Loan-originating AIFs have specific limits.

Under AIFMD, AIFs can be marketed across the EU to professional investors using the AIFM's passport. Marketing to retail investors depends on national rules, unless the fund is an EU product such as an ELTIF.

Many member states have their own regulated AIF types, often with investment rules of their own, such as qualifying investor funds and reserved alternative investment funds.

Side by side

UCITS AIF
Regulated through The fund and its management company The manager (AIFM)
Typical investors Retail and institutional Mainly professional; retail where national rules allow
Assets Liquid, eligible assets only Any
Leverage Strictly limited Managed and reported; limits for loan origination
Dealing At least twice a month Any, including closed-ended
EU marketing passport To all investors To professional investors
Depositary Required Required

Choosing between them

Managers choose UCITS for broad distribution to retail investors and a recognised brand. They choose an AIF for strategies that do not fit UCITS limits, such as illiquid assets, high leverage or concentrated positions, or where the investor base is professional.

explainers.title: Valuation and fair value
explainers.summary: How fund assets are valued, what fair value means, the hierarchy of valuation inputs and how to deal with assets that are hard to value.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Every subscription and redemption in an open-ended fund happens at a price based on the value of the fund's assets. If those values are wrong, money moves unfairly between investors, performance is misreported and fees are miscalculated.

Fair value

Most funds value their assets at fair value: the price that would be received to sell an asset in an orderly transaction between market participants at the valuation date. Accounting standards set out a hierarchy of inputs:

  • Level 1: quoted prices in active markets for identical assets, such as most listed shares.
  • Level 2: other observable inputs, such as quoted prices for similar assets, broker quotes or yield curves, as used for many bonds and over-the-counter derivatives.
  • Level 3: unobservable inputs, using the manager's own assumptions and models, as for private companies, private loans, property and complex instruments.

The higher the share of Level 3 assets, the more judgment and the greater the valuation risk.

The valuation framework

Regulation requires managers to have:

  • a written valuation policy covering each asset type, approved by the board;
  • a valuation function that is functionally independent of portfolio management, or an external valuer;
  • procedures for pricing sources, price challenges, overrides, stale prices and suspended securities;
  • regular review of methods and back-testing.

Many managers set up a valuation committee to oversee the process and take decisions on difficult assets.

Hard-to-value assets

Common approaches:

  • Private equity: comparable company multiples, discounted cash flows, recent transactions, often following industry valuation guidelines.
  • Private credit: discounted cash flows using appropriate market spreads, with adjustments for credit deterioration.
  • Property: independent valuers' appraisals, usually quarterly or more often in volatile markets.
  • Suspended or illiquid securities: last price adjusted for events, or a model, reviewed frequently.

Signs of weak valuation include valuations that rarely move, heavy reliance on the manager's own estimates, and sale prices that differ significantly from recent valuations.

Fair value pricing for dealing

Funds that deal at a time when markets in their underlying assets are closed, for example a European fund holding Asian shares, may apply fair value adjustments to reflect events since those markets closed. This protects existing investors from opportunistic trading.

What boards should ask

  • What share of assets is Level 3, and how is it trending?
  • How many price overrides and stale prices were there, and why?
  • How do valuations compare with eventual sale prices?
  • Is the valuation function genuinely independent of the portfolio managers?

explainers.title: Wallets and keys
explainers.summary: How crypto wallets and keys work: public and private keys, addresses, seed phrases, custodial and self-hosted wallets, and how to keep them safe.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A crypto wallet does not store crypto-assets. The assets are recorded on the blockchain. What a wallet holds is the keys that prove ownership and authorise transfers.

Keys and addresses

  • Private key. A secret number that allows its holder to sign transactions and move assets. Anyone who has it controls the assets. If it is lost, the assets usually cannot be recovered.
  • Public key. Derived from the private key. It lets others verify signatures without revealing the private key.
  • Address. A shorter identifier, derived from the public key, to which others send assets. Like an account number, it can be shared.

The security of the whole system rests on keeping private keys secret and available.

Seed phrases

Most wallets generate keys from a seed phrase (or recovery phrase) of 12 or 24 words. The seed phrase can regenerate all the wallet's keys, so it must be protected as carefully as the keys themselves. Scammers frequently try to trick users into revealing it.

Types of wallet

By who controls the keys - Custodial wallets. A third party, such as an exchange or custodian, holds the keys for the customer. The customer relies on the provider. - Self-hosted (non-custodial or unhosted) wallets. The user holds their own keys. They have full control and full responsibility.

By connection to the internet - Hot wallets are connected to the internet, convenient for frequent transactions but more exposed to hacking. - Cold wallets keep keys offline, for example on hardware devices or in air-gapped systems, and are used for larger holdings. - Warm wallets sit in between, with additional controls.

By how signing works - Single-signature wallets need one key. - Multi-signature (multisig) wallets need several keys, for example three of five, to approve a transaction. - Multi-party computation (MPC) splits a key into shares held by different parties, which sign together without ever reassembling the key.

Smart-contract wallets use code to set rules, such as spending limits, recovery options or approvals.

Keeping keys safe

  • Generate keys securely and keep backups in separate, protected places.
  • Use hardware wallets or hardware security modules for significant holdings.
  • Require more than one person to approve large transfers.
  • Protect against phishing and social engineering, the most common causes of loss.
  • Test recovery procedures.

Regulatory angle

Custodial wallet providers are regulated in many jurisdictions. Transfers to and from self-hosted wallets attract extra AML/CFT checks under the EU's Transfer of Funds Regulation, including checks on ownership for transfers above €1,000.

explainers.title: What is a crypto-asset? Token types explained
explainers.summary: What crypto-assets are, how they differ from traditional assets, and the main types of token: payment tokens, stablecoins, utility tokens, security tokens, governance tokens and NFTs.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A crypto-asset is a digital representation of value or rights that can be transferred and stored electronically using distributed ledger technology (DLT) or similar technology. Ownership is recorded on a ledger shared across many computers, and control is exercised through cryptographic keys.

What makes crypto-assets different

  • No central record-keeper. On a public blockchain, the ledger is maintained by a network of participants following agreed rules, rather than by a bank or registrar.
  • Bearer-like control. Whoever controls the private key can move the asset. Lost keys usually mean lost assets.
  • Programmability. Tokens can be created and controlled by smart contracts, which can enforce rules automatically.
  • Global and always on. Transfers can happen at any time, across borders, often within minutes.

Native coins and tokens

  • Native coins are built into a blockchain and pay for its use, such as bitcoin on Bitcoin and ether on Ethereum.
  • Tokens are created on top of an existing blockchain using smart contracts, such as the many ERC-20 tokens on Ethereum.

Main types by function

Payment or exchange tokens. Intended as a means of payment or store of value, such as bitcoin. Their price can be very volatile.

Stablecoins. Designed to keep a stable value by reference to an official currency, a basket of assets or a commodity. Under MiCA, those referencing a single currency are e-money tokens and others are asset-referenced tokens.

Utility tokens. Give access to a good or service provided by the issuer, such as storage on a network.

Governance tokens. Give holders votes on changes to a protocol, often in DeFi.

Security or investment tokens. Represent rights similar to shares, bonds or fund units. These are financial instruments and fall under securities law (in the EU, MiFID II), not crypto-specific rules.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs). Unique tokens representing a specific item, such as digital art or a collectible. Genuinely unique NFTs are generally outside MiCA, but large series of supposedly unique tokens may be treated as fungible.

Tokenised real-world assets. Tokens representing claims on traditional assets such as bonds, fund units, property or commodities.

Why classification matters

The type of token determines which rules apply. The same token can have features of several types, and its classification can change as the project develops. Regulators look at the substance of the rights and expectations a token creates, not its label.

The risks

  • Price volatility and the possibility of total loss.
  • Hacks, scams, lost keys and failures of intermediaries.
  • Limited investor protection outside regulated regimes.
  • Financial crime, sanctions evasion and market manipulation.
