explainers.title: What is an investment fund?
explainers.summary: A plain-English introduction to investment funds: what they are, why investors use them, how they are structured and who protects investors' interests.
explainers.bodyHtml:
An investment fund pools money from many investors and invests it according to a stated objective and policy. Each investor owns a share of the pool, so they share in its gains and losses in proportion to what they put in.

Why investors use funds

  • Diversification. A single fund can hold dozens or hundreds of investments, spreading risk in a way most individual investors could not achieve on their own.
  • Professional management. A professional investment manager selects and monitors the investments.
  • Access. Funds give access to markets and assets that are hard to reach directly, such as overseas bonds, private companies or property.
  • Economies of scale. Trading, custody and research costs are shared across many investors.
  • Liquidity. Many funds let investors buy and sell on a regular basis, often daily.
  • Regulation. Regulated funds must follow rules on how they invest, how their assets are held and what they tell investors.

How a fund works

Investors buy units or shares in the fund. Their money is added to the pool and invested. The value of each unit or share, the net asset value (NAV) per share, is calculated regularly by taking the value of everything the fund owns, deducting what it owes, and dividing by the number of shares in issue.

When investors want their money back, they sell their shares. In an open-ended fund, the fund itself buys back (redeems) the shares at the NAV. In a closed-ended fund, investors usually sell to other investors, for example on a stock exchange.

Who is involved

A fund relies on several specialist parties:

  • a board or trustee, which oversees the fund in investors' interests;
  • a management company or AIFM, which is responsible for managing the fund;
  • an investment manager, which picks the investments;
  • a depositary or custodian, which holds the assets safely and checks the fund is run properly;
  • an administrator, which keeps the accounts and calculates the NAV;
  • a transfer agent, which keeps the register of investors and processes their dealings;
  • an auditor and distributors.

Separating these roles is a key protection: the people who decide what to buy do not hold the assets or calculate their value.

Types of fund

Funds vary by what they invest in (equities, bonds, money market instruments, property, private assets, other funds), how investors deal (open-ended or closed-ended), their legal form (company, trust, contract or partnership) and their regulatory regime. In the EU, the two main regimes are UCITS, for retail funds investing in liquid assets, and AIFs, which cover everything else.

The risks

Investors can lose money. The value of the fund depends on the value of its investments. Other risks include liquidity risk (not being able to sell assets quickly enough), leverage, the costs charged, and operational failures. The fund's documents, and for retail investors its key information document, set out its objective, risks and costs.

explainers.title: What is DeFi?
explainers.summary: An introduction to decentralised finance: what it is, how it works, the main types of protocol, why people use it, the risks, and how regulators approach it.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Decentralised finance (DeFi) is financial services built from smart contracts on public blockchains. Instead of a bank or broker, code executes trades, loans and other transactions, and users interact directly from their own wallets.

How it works

  • Smart contracts hold assets and apply rules automatically: for example, lending tokens to anyone who posts enough collateral, or exchanging one token for another at a price set by a formula.
  • Self-custody: users keep control of their keys and assets until they interact with a protocol.
  • Composability: protocols can be combined like building blocks. A token from one protocol can be used as collateral in another, and so on.
  • Open access: anyone with a wallet can use most DeFi protocols, usually without identity checks.
  • Governance: many protocols are governed by holders of governance tokens, who vote on changes, sometimes through a decentralised autonomous organisation (DAO).

Main types of protocol

  • Decentralised exchanges, often using automated market makers and liquidity pools.
  • Lending and borrowing protocols, with over-collateralised loans and automatic liquidations.
  • Stablecoins, including crypto-collateralised ones.
  • Derivatives, such as perpetual futures and options.
  • Liquid staking and restaking.
  • Yield aggregators that move funds between protocols to optimise returns.
  • Bridges between blockchains.

Why people use it

  • Access to financial services without intermediaries or accounts.
  • Transparency: transactions and positions are visible on-chain.
  • Speed and availability around the clock.
  • New forms of yield and financial products.

The risks

  • Smart-contract bugs and exploits, which have led to large losses.
  • Governance attacks and control by insiders through admin keys.
  • Oracle manipulation, where price feeds are distorted.
  • Liquidation cascades in volatile markets.
  • Bridge hacks.
  • Financial crime: open access makes DeFi attractive for laundering and sanctions evasion.
  • Lack of recourse: there is often no one to complain to and no compensation scheme.

How regulators approach it

DeFi challenges regulation built around intermediaries. Regulators generally look through the label: where a person or group controls or has significant influence over a protocol, its front-end, its funds or its governance, they may be treated as service providers and need authorisation.

  • EU: MiCA excludes services provided in a fully decentralised manner, but the Commission is reviewing DeFi, and ESMA favours a clear definition and a narrow exemption.
  • FATF: owners and operators of DeFi arrangements may be VASPs.
  • UK: the FCA's perimeter guidance explains when DeFi activities need authorisation.

The degree of decentralisation is a question of fact, assessed case by case.

explainers.title: What is leverage? Leverage in funds
explainers.summary: A plain-English explanation of leverage, how funds create it through borrowing and derivatives, how it is measured under EU rules and the risks it brings.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Leverage means increasing a fund's exposure to markets beyond what its own capital would allow. It magnifies gains when markets move in the fund's favour, and magnifies losses when they do not.

A simple example

A fund has €100 million of investors' money. If it borrows another €50 million and invests the full €150 million in shares, a 10% rise in share prices makes €15 million, a 15% return on investors' capital. A 10% fall loses €15 million, a 15% loss. The fund also has to pay interest on the borrowing, and lenders may demand repayment at the worst time.

How funds create leverage

  • Borrowing cash to buy more assets.
  • Derivatives, such as futures, forwards, options and swaps, which give exposure to an underlying asset for a fraction of its value. A futures contract on €10 million of an index might require only a small margin deposit.
  • Securities financing, such as repurchase agreements (repos), where the fund sells securities with an agreement to buy them back and reinvests the cash.
  • Short selling, which creates exposure to falling prices, usually using borrowed securities or derivatives.
  • Embedded leverage in some instruments, such as leveraged structured products.

Not all derivative use increases risk. Derivatives used to hedge currency or interest rate risk can reduce it.

How leverage is measured in EU funds

UCITS must measure global exposure to derivatives either:

  • by the commitment approach, converting derivatives into the equivalent position in the underlying asset, with netting and hedging allowed, and limiting exposure to 100% of net assets (so total exposure no more than 200%); or
  • by value at risk (VaR), limiting the potential loss over a set period and confidence level, either in absolute terms or relative to a reference portfolio.

UCITS may borrow only up to 10% of net assets, on a temporary basis.

AIFs must calculate leverage using two methods and report both:

  • the gross method, which adds up the absolute value of all positions, with no netting or hedging; and
  • the commitment method, which allows netting and hedging.

Leverage is expressed as a ratio of exposure to NAV. An unleveraged fund has a ratio of 100%. AIFMs must set a maximum level of leverage for each AIF, and regulators can impose limits where leverage creates systemic risk. Loan-originating AIFs face fixed limits under AIFMD II.

The risks

  • Magnified losses, which can wipe out investors' capital.
  • Margin calls and forced selling, where falling prices trigger demands for more collateral, forcing the fund to sell assets in a falling market.
  • Counterparty risk, if a lender or derivative counterparty fails.
  • Liquidity risk, as leverage increases the fund's need for cash at short notice.
  • Systemic risk, where many leveraged funds sell the same assets at once.

Questions to ask

  • How much leverage does the fund use, measured both ways, and what is it for?
  • What is the maximum level, and has it been approached?
  • How much collateral could be called in a stress scenario, and could the fund meet it?

explainers.title: What is liquidity? Liquidity risk in funds
explainers.summary: A plain-English explanation of liquidity, the different kinds of liquidity risk in funds, how liquidity mismatches arise and how managers measure and manage them.
explainers.bodyHtml:
Liquidity is the ability to turn an asset into cash quickly without significantly affecting its price. Cash is perfectly liquid. Large-company shares are highly liquid in normal markets. Small-company shares, high-yield bonds, private loans and property are less liquid: selling quickly may mean accepting a lower price, or may not be possible at all.

Two sides of liquidity

For a fund, liquidity has two sides:

  • Asset liquidity: how quickly the fund can sell its investments, and at what cost.
  • Funding liquidity: how much cash the fund may need, and how quickly, to pay redeeming investors, meet margin calls on derivatives, repay borrowings or meet commitments.

Liquidity risk is the risk that the fund cannot meet its obligations when they fall due without selling assets at a significant loss, or cannot meet them at all.

The liquidity mismatch

An open-ended fund that offers daily dealing but holds assets that take weeks or months to sell has a liquidity mismatch. In normal times, daily inflows and outflows largely offset, and the fund holds cash and liquid assets to meet net redemptions. In stress, many investors may want to leave at once:

  • The fund sells its most liquid assets first, leaving remaining investors with a less liquid, riskier portfolio.
  • Selling under pressure lowers prices, so remaining investors bear the cost.
  • Investors who see this coming have an incentive to leave early, which can turn into a run.

This is the main reason for liquidity rules, liquidity stress tests and liquidity management tools.

How managers measure liquidity

  • Asset liquidity profile: what share of the portfolio could be sold within one day, one week, one month and so on, without a significant price impact. Estimates use trading volumes, bid-ask spreads and market depth.
  • Liability profile: who the investors are, how concentrated they are, how they have behaved in the past and how they might behave in stress.
  • Stress testing: combining severe but plausible market and redemption scenarios to see whether the fund could meet redemptions and what it would cost.
  • Liquidity buckets and limits: for example, a minimum share of assets that can be sold within a week.

How managers manage liquidity

  • Matching dealing terms to the portfolio, for example monthly dealing or notice periods for less liquid strategies.
  • Holding a liquidity buffer.
  • Limits on illiquid assets.
  • Liquidity management tools, such as swing pricing, anti-dilution levies, redemption gates, notice periods, redemptions in kind, side pockets and, as a last resort, suspension. EU rules require open-ended funds to have at least two such tools available.

Questions to ask

  • Could the fund meet a redemption of its largest investors, or of 10% or 20% of its assets in a week, without harming those who stay?
  • What happens to the liquidity profile when markets are stressed, not just in normal times?
  • Which liquidity tools are ready to use, and who decides to use them?

explainers.title: What is regulated? The crypto perimeter
explainers.summary: How regulators decide which crypto-assets and activities fall within regulation, under MiCA, securities law, payments law and AML rules, and where the grey areas are.
explainers.bodyHtml:
The regulatory perimeter is the boundary between activities that need authorisation and those that do not. For crypto, it is shaped by several overlapping regimes.

Is the token a financial instrument?

The first question is whether a token is a financial instrument, such as a transferable security, a fund unit or a derivative. If so, securities law applies (in the EU, MiFID II, the Prospectus Regulation, the Market Abuse Regulation and, for funds, UCITS or AIFMD), even if the instrument is issued on a blockchain. Tokenised shares, bonds and fund units fall here.

ESMA has published guidelines on when crypto-assets qualify as financial instruments. The test is the substance of the rights, not the label or technology.

Is it covered by MiCA?

If the token is not a financial instrument (or another excluded product, such as a deposit or insurance), MiCA applies to:

  • offering crypto-assets to the public or seeking their admission to trading, with a white paper;
  • issuing asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens;
  • providing crypto-asset services, such as custody, trading platforms, exchange, execution, placing, advice, portfolio management and transfer services.

MiCA excludes crypto-assets that are unique and not fungible, and services provided in a fully decentralised manner without any intermediary.

Is it payments or e-money?

E-money tokens are also electronic money, and services involving them may be payment services. PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation will clarify how payments law applies to them.

AML/CFT

Crypto-asset service providers are obliged entities under EU AML law and must apply the travel rule. Outside the EU, the FATF standards require countries to license or register virtual asset service providers.

The grey areas

  • DeFi. Whether a protocol is "fully decentralised" is a matter of fact. Where a person or group controls or has significant influence over it, for example through admin keys, a foundation or a front-end, regulators may treat them as service providers.
  • Staking. Staking services, lending and borrowing of crypto-assets are not fully covered by MiCA, though custody of staked assets usually is. The Commission is reviewing these gaps.
  • NFTs. Large collections or fractionalised NFTs may be treated as fungible crypto-assets.
  • Hybrid tokens that combine utility, investment and payment features.

The UK approach

The UK is bringing cryptoasset activities into its main financial services law from October 2027, with new regulated activities for stablecoin issuance, custody, trading platforms, dealing, arranging and staking. Its perimeter guidance explains how it applies to DeFi.

Why it matters

Operating without authorisation where it is required can be a criminal offence, and contracts may be unenforceable. Firms need a documented legal analysis of each token and service, reviewed as the business changes.

explainers.title: Where DeFi yield comes from
explainers.summary: The real sources of return in decentralised finance, from lending interest and trading fees to token incentives and leverage, and how to tell sustainable yield from risky or illusory yield.
explainers.bodyHtml:
DeFi often advertises attractive yields. Understanding where they come from is the key to judging the risk.

Main sources

Lending interest. Borrowers pay interest to lenders in lending protocols. Demand usually comes from traders who want leverage or short positions. Rates rise when borrowing demand is high.

Trading fees. Liquidity providers in automated market makers earn a share of trading fees, offset by impermanent loss when prices move.

Staking rewards. Proof-of-stake networks pay rewards for securing the network, partly from new token issuance (which dilutes holders) and partly from transaction fees.

Token incentives. Protocols distribute their own tokens to attract users (liquidity mining or yield farming). This yield depends on the market price of the reward token and often falls as incentives end.

Basis and funding trades. Some products earn the difference between spot and futures prices or funding rates on perpetual futures. These can turn negative.

Real-world assets. Tokenised government bonds and private credit bring off-chain interest on-chain.

Layering and leverage

Yield can be stacked: staking tokens, using the liquid staking token as collateral, borrowing against it, and staking again. This multiplies returns and risks, and can unwind quickly in falling markets.

Warning signs

  • Yields far above traditional or on-chain benchmarks with no clear source.
  • Yields paid mainly in a protocol's own token.
  • Fixed high yields on volatile assets.
  • Complex strategies that are hard to explain.
  • Reliance on new deposits.

A simple test

For any yield, ask: who is paying it, why are they willing to, and what happens if they stop? If the answer is unclear, the risk is probably being underestimated.

explainers.title: Who does what in a fund: the parties and their roles
explainers.summary: A map of the parties involved in running an investment fund, from the board and management company to the depositary, administrator, transfer agent, auditor and distributors.
explainers.bodyHtml:
An investment fund is a network of specialist firms, each with a defined role and contract. The separation of roles is one of the main protections for investors.

The fund and its governing body

  • Fund board (for corporate funds): sets the strategy within the fund documents and oversees the management company and service providers on behalf of investors.
  • Trustee (for unit trusts): holds the assets and oversees the manager.
  • For contractual funds, the management company's board is responsible.

The manager

  • UCITS management company or AIFM: the authorised firm legally responsible for managing the fund. Its core functions are portfolio management and risk management, plus administration and marketing. It may carry these out itself or delegate them.
  • Investment manager: often a separate firm, to which the management company delegates portfolio management. It decides what to buy and sell within the fund's objective and limits.
  • Promoter or sponsor: the firm that originated the fund, often an asset management group whose brand the fund carries.

Asset safety and oversight

  • Depositary: holds the fund's financial instruments in custody, keeps records of other assets, monitors cash flows, and oversees the fund's compliance with its rules on subscriptions, redemptions, valuation, income and investment limits. It is liable for losses of assets in custody.
  • Sub-custodians and prime brokers: hold assets in particular markets or provide financing and securities lending, under the depositary's oversight.

Operations

  • Administrator: keeps the fund's books, values the portfolio, calculates the NAV and prepares financial statements.
  • Transfer agent: keeps the register of investors, processes subscriptions and redemptions, carries out investor AML/CFT checks and deals with investor queries.

Distribution

  • Global distributor and sub-distributors, including platforms, banks, wealth managers and financial advisers, which sell the fund to investors.
  • Paying agents or facilities agents in some markets.

Independent checks

  • Auditor: audits the annual financial statements.
  • Legal advisers and tax advisers.
  • Regulator: authorises the fund and its manager and supervises them.

Why it matters

Each relationship carries risks: poor service, conflicts of interest, concentration on a single group, or failure of a provider. The board and management company must oversee them all, with clear contracts, regular reporting and the ability to change provider if needed.
explainers.sortKey: who does what in a fund: the parties and their roles

explainers.title: Wind-down planning for payment firms
explainers.summary: Why payment, e-money and crypto firms need wind-down plans, what a good plan contains, how it links to safeguarding and resolution packs, and how to test it.
explainers.bodyHtml:
When payment and e-money firms fail, the biggest harm is usually to customers waiting for their money. Regulators therefore expect firms to plan how they would close in an orderly way, returning customer funds quickly. Similar expectations apply to crypto firms, where MiCA requires custody and other service providers to have wind-down plans.

What a wind-down plan contains

  • Triggers and indicators: financial and operational metrics that would prompt the board to consider wind-down, and who decides.
  • Scenarios: severe but plausible events, such as loss of a banking partner, a large fraud loss, regulatory action or loss of key clients.
  • Resources: the capital and liquidity needed to wind down in an orderly way, and how long it would take.
  • Steps and timeline: stopping new business, communicating with customers, returning funds, ending contracts, transferring or closing accounts.
  • Customer funds: how safeguarded funds would be identified and returned, linked to the resolution pack.
  • Critical services and staff: what must keep running, and how key staff would be retained.
  • Third parties: dependencies on banks, processors, card schemes and group companies.
  • Communication: with customers, regulators, banks, partners and staff.

Resolution packs

In the UK, payment and e-money firms must keep a resolution pack: documents that let an insolvency practitioner quickly identify customer funds and return them. It should be accurate, up to date and retrievable within a short time.

Testing

  • Desk-based exercises with management and the board.
  • Checking that data, such as customer balances, can be produced quickly.
  • Reviewing the plan after major business changes.

Common weaknesses

  • Plans that assume an orderly sale rather than a stressed closure.
  • Underestimated costs and timelines.
  • Customer data that cannot be reconciled quickly.
  • No clear triggers or ownership.

explainers.title: Zero-knowledge proofs
explainers.summary: What zero-knowledge proofs are, how they are used in blockchains for scaling and privacy, their potential for compliance, and their limits.
explainers.bodyHtml:
A zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) lets one party prove to another that a statement is true without revealing anything beyond the fact that it is true. For example, proving you are over 18 without revealing your date of birth, or proving a batch of transactions was processed correctly without re-running them.

Main types

  • SNARKs (succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge): short proofs that are quick to verify. Many require a one-off trusted setup.
  • STARKs (scalable transparent arguments of knowledge): no trusted setup and believed to resist quantum attacks, but larger proofs.

Uses in blockchains

  • Scaling: zero-knowledge rollups prove that thousands of transactions were executed correctly, so the main chain need only check the proof.
  • Privacy: privacy coins and protocols hide transaction details while proving validity.
  • Identity and credentials: proving attributes, such as being verified by a regulated firm or not being on a sanctions list, without sharing personal data.
  • Proof of reserves: proving solvency without revealing individual client balances.
  • Bridges: proving the state of one blockchain to another.

Potential for compliance

ZKPs could let firms meet regulatory requirements while protecting privacy, for example:

  • reusable KYC credentials that prove a customer has been verified;
  • selective disclosure to regulators;
  • confidential transactions on public networks for institutions.

Limits

  • Complexity: bugs in proof systems or circuits can be catastrophic and hard to detect.
  • Computation: generating proofs can be expensive.
  • Trusted setups for some systems must be done securely.
  • Regulatory acceptance: authorities need confidence that privacy features do not prevent effective AML and sanctions controls. The EU AML Regulation bars CASPs from handling anonymity-enhancing coins.

resources.title: Anti-Money Laundering Authority
resources.summary: AMLA is the EU's new authority for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism, based in Frankfurt. It will directly supervise a group of the riskiest cross-border financial firms and coordinate national supervisors and financial intelligence units.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

AMLA was set up by Regulation (EU) 2024/1620 as part of the EU AML package, alongside the AML Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and the Sixth AML Directive (EU) 2024/1640. It took over the AML/CFT mandates previously held by the EBA.

What it does

  • Will directly supervise selected credit and financial institutions, including crypto-asset service providers, that operate across borders and present high risk.
  • Oversees and coordinates national AML/CFT supervisors in the financial and non-financial sectors.
  • Supports and coordinates the EU's financial intelligence units, including joint analyses.
  • Drafts technical standards and guidelines under the AML Regulation.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The EU AML package (AMLR, AMLD6 and the AMLA Regulation) and the Transfer of Funds Regulation.

resources.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC)
resources.summary: ASIC is Australia's corporate, markets and financial services regulator, responsible for fund managers, financial advisers and market conduct.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

ASIC operates under the Australian Securities and Investments Commission Act 2001 and enforces company and financial services laws.

What it does

  • Issues Australian financial services and credit licences.
  • Regulates managed investment schemes and their responsible entities.
  • Supervises markets and market integrity.
  • Enforces consumer protection in financial services, including design and distribution obligations and product intervention.
  • Applies financial services law to crypto-assets that are financial products. Australia is legislating a licensing framework for digital asset platforms.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Corporations Act 2001, the National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 and the ASIC Act 2001.

resources.title: Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC)
resources.summary: AUSTRAC is Australia's AML/CTF regulator and financial intelligence unit. It registers digital currency exchanges and has taken high-profile enforcement action against major banks.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

AUSTRAC operates under the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006, combining regulatory and intelligence functions.

What it does

  • Supervises reporting entities' compliance with AML/CTF obligations.
  • Registers and supervises digital currency exchange providers and remittance providers.
  • Receives and analyses suspicious matter reports and other transaction reports.
  • Is implementing 2024 reforms that extend the regime to more virtual asset services and, from July 2026, to lawyers, accountants, real estate agents and other professions.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006, as amended in 2024.

resources.title: Autoriteit Financiële Markten
resources.summary: The AFM is the Dutch conduct regulator. It supervises financial markets, investment firms, fund managers and crypto-asset service providers in the Netherlands.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Under the Dutch 'twin peaks' model, the AFM supervises conduct and De Nederlandsche Bank supervises prudential soundness.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises fund managers and investment firms.
  • Supervises market conduct, financial reporting and market abuse.
  • Supervises the conduct of banks, insurers and pension providers towards customers.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

MiFID II, UCITS, AIFMD, MAR, the Prospectus Regulation and MiCA.

resources.title: Autorité de contrôle prudentiel et de résolution
resources.summary: The ACPR is France's prudential supervisor for banks, insurers, payment institutions and e-money institutions. It is attached to the Banque de France and is also France's resolution authority.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The ACPR safeguards the stability of the financial system and protects customers, policyholders and members of the banking and insurance sectors.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions), insurers, investment firms (prudential), payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance in the banking and insurance sectors.
  • Oversees the business conduct of banks and insurers towards customers.
  • Acts as France's resolution authority.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, PSD2, EMD2, the AML package and BRRD.

resources.title: Autorité des marchés financiers (France)
resources.summary: The AMF is France's financial markets regulator. It supervises asset management companies and French funds, oversees market conduct and authorises crypto-asset service providers in France.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The AMF protects savings invested in financial products, ensures investors are properly informed and keeps markets orderly. Prudential supervision of banks and insurers sits with the ACPR.

What it does

  • Authorises asset management companies and approves French UCITS and AIFs.
  • Supervises listed companies' disclosures and market conduct, and investigates market abuse.
  • Supervises investment services conduct, together with the ACPR.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA; it previously ran France's PSAN registration regime.
  • Has a dedicated enforcement committee.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, MAR, the Prospectus Regulation, SFDR and MiCA.

resources.title: Banca d'Italia
resources.summary: The Banca d'Italia is Italy's central bank and prudential supervisor. It supervises banks, asset management companies, payment institutions and e-money institutions.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Banca d'Italia is part of the Eurosystem and is responsible for prudential supervision and financial stability in Italy.

What it does

  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions).
  • Supervises asset management companies (SGRs) and investment firms on prudential matters, with CONSOB covering conduct.
  • Authorises payment institutions and e-money institutions and oversees payment systems.
  • Hosts Italy's financial intelligence unit (UIF).
  • Shares MiCA responsibilities with CONSOB.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, UCITS and AIFMD (prudential aspects), PSD2, EMD2 and MiCA.

resources.title: Banco de España
resources.summary: The Banco de España is Spain's central bank and banking supervisor. It supervises banks and payment and e-money institutions.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Banco de España is part of the Eurosystem and supervises the solvency and conduct of Spanish credit institutions.

What it does

  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions).
  • Authorises and supervises payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Oversees payment systems and monitors financial stability.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, PSD2 and EMD2.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Banco de España: official website

resources.title: Bank for International Settlements
resources.summary: The BIS is the bank for central banks, based in Basel. It hosts the Basel Committee, the CPMI, the IAIS and the FSB secretariat, and its Innovation Hub runs experiments on tokenisation and central bank digital currencies.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The BIS supports central banks in pursuing monetary and financial stability through international cooperation.

What it does

  • Provides banking services to central banks and hosts international standard-setting committees.
  • Publishes research on monetary policy, financial stability, payments and crypto-assets.
  • Runs the BIS Innovation Hub, whose projects include Project Agorá on tokenised deposits and wholesale central bank money.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

It does not set standards itself. The committees it hosts do (BCBS, CPMI, IAIS) and the FSB.

resources.sourcesHtml: • Bank for International Settlements: official website

resources.title: Bank of England
resources.summary: The Bank of England is the UK's central bank. It sets monetary policy, protects financial stability, supervises financial market infrastructure and, through the PRA, supervises banks and insurers. It will regulate systemic sterling stablecoins.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Bank's mission is to maintain monetary and financial stability. Its Financial Policy Committee identifies and acts on systemic risks.

What it does

  • Sets monetary policy through the Monetary Policy Committee.
  • Identifies and acts on systemic risks through the Financial Policy Committee.
  • Supervises systemically important payment systems, central counterparties and central securities depositories.
  • Operates the RTGS system for sterling settlement.
  • Will regulate systemic stablecoins and service providers, and has worked on the design of a possible digital pound with HM Treasury.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Financial market infrastructure supervision under the Banking Act 2009 and FSMA 2000, the systemic stablecoin regime, and prudential regulation through the PRA.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Bank of England: official website

resources.title: Bank of Lithuania
resources.summary: The Bank of Lithuania is Lithuania's central bank and integrated financial supervisor. Lithuania is one of the EU's leading hubs for licensed e-money and payment institutions.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Bank of Lithuania is part of the Eurosystem and supervises Lithuania's banks, insurers, investment firms, payment and e-money institutions and crypto-asset service providers.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises payment institutions and e-money institutions, many of which passport services across the EU.
  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions), insurers and investment firms.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA.
  • Operates CENTROlink, which gives licensed payment firms access to euro payment systems.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

PSD2, EMD2, CRR/CRD, Solvency II, MiFID II, MiCA and the AML package.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Bank of Lithuania: official website

resources.title: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
resources.summary: The Basel Committee is the global standard setter for the prudential regulation of banks. It is hosted by the BIS and sets the Basel Framework, including the standard for banks' exposures to cryptoassets.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Basel Committee brings together banking supervisors and central banks to strengthen the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide. Its standards apply to internationally active banks and are implemented in national law.

What it does

  • Sets the Basel Framework, including Basel III capital, liquidity and leverage standards.
  • Sets the prudential standard for banks' cryptoasset exposures, implemented from 1 January 2026, which treats tokenised assets, stablecoins and unbacked cryptoassets differently.
  • Monitors how members implement its standards.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Basel Framework, including the cryptoasset standard (SCO60).

resources.title: Bermuda Monetary Authority (BMA)
resources.summary: The BMA is Bermuda's integrated financial regulator, supervising one of the world's largest reinsurance markets and an early, comprehensive regime for digital asset businesses.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The BMA was established in 1969. It issues Bermuda's currency, supervises financial institutions and promotes the stability and integrity of Bermuda's financial system.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises insurers and reinsurers, banks, investment businesses, fund administrators, investment funds and trust companies.
  • Licenses and supervises digital asset businesses under the Digital Asset Business Act 2018.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by regulated firms.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Insurance Act 1978, Banks and Deposit Companies Act, Investment Business Act, Investment Funds Act, Digital Asset Business Act 2018 and Digital Asset Issuance Act 2020.

resources.title: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
resources.summary: The Federal Reserve is the US central bank. It sets monetary policy, supervises many banks and bank holding companies, and operates key payment systems.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Federal Reserve System was created in 1913. Its Board of Governors in Washington works with twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks.

What it does

  • Sets US monetary policy.
  • Supervises bank holding companies, state-chartered banks that are members of the system, and the US operations of foreign banks.
  • Operates payment services, including Fedwire and the FedNow instant payment service, and decides on access to Federal Reserve accounts.
  • Has a role under the GENIUS Act for stablecoin issuers that are subsidiaries of the banks it supervises.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Federal Reserve Act, the Bank Holding Company Act and, for relevant issuers, the GENIUS Act.

resources.title: Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht
resources.summary: BaFin is Germany's integrated financial regulator. It supervises banks, insurers, asset managers and funds, investment firms, payment and e-money institutions, and crypto businesses.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

BaFin supervises the German financial sector to ensure it functions properly, remains stable and treats customers fairly. It works with the Deutsche Bundesbank on banking supervision.

What it does

  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions and the Bundesbank for day-to-day supervision), insurers and pension funds.
  • Authorises German asset management companies (KVGs) and supervises investment funds.
  • Authorises payment and e-money institutions.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA; it previously licensed crypto custody under German banking law.
  • Supervises securities markets, market abuse and AML/CFT compliance.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, UCITS, AIFMD (through the German Investment Code, KAGB), MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2, MiCA and the AML package.

resources.title: Capital Market Authority (Saudi Arabia)
resources.summary: The Saudi CMA regulates Saudi Arabia's capital markets, including the Saudi Exchange, listed companies, capital market institutions and investment funds.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CMA was established in 2003 under the Capital Market Law. It regulates and develops the Saudi capital market and protects investors.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises capital market institutions, such as brokers and fund managers.
  • Regulates offerings and listings and the disclosure of listed companies.
  • Regulates public and private investment funds.
  • Runs a fintech lab and sandbox for new business models.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Capital Market Law and CMA implementing regulations, including the Investment Funds Regulations.

resources.title: Capital Market Authority (UAE)
resources.summary: The CMA, formerly the Securities and Commodities Authority, is the UAE's federal capital markets regulator. It was reconstituted with broader powers from 1 January 2026.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CMA was established in 2000 as the Securities and Commodities Authority. Federal Decree-Laws No. 32 and No. 33 of 2025 renamed it and replaced its framework, effective 1 January 2026.

What it does

  • Regulates and supervises onshore UAE securities and commodities markets, issuers and intermediaries.
  • Regulates investment funds and their managers onshore.
  • Regulates virtual assets in the UAE mainland, outside the emirate-level regime in Dubai and the financial free zones. Trading virtual assets onshore requires the asset to be listed on a CMA-licensed platform and registered with the CMA.
  • Enforces against market misconduct.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Federal Decree-Law No. 32 of 2025 on the Capital Market Authority and Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2025 on the Regulation of the Capital Market.

resources.title: Cayman Islands Monetary Authority (CIMA)
resources.summary: CIMA is the financial regulator and monetary authority of the Cayman Islands, home to one of the world's largest investment fund industries, particularly hedge funds and private funds.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

CIMA was established in 1997 under the Monetary Authority Act. It manages the currency, regulates and supervises financial services and cooperates with overseas regulators.

What it does

  • Registers and supervises mutual funds and private funds, which together number in the tens of thousands.
  • Licenses and supervises banks, insurers, securities investment businesses, fund administrators and trust and corporate service providers.
  • Registers and licenses virtual asset service providers, including custodians and trading platforms.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by regulated firms.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Mutual Funds Act, Private Funds Act, Securities Investment Business Act, Banks and Trust Companies Act, Insurance Act and Virtual Asset (Service Providers) Act.

resources.title: Central Bank of Ireland
resources.summary: The Central Bank of Ireland is Ireland's central bank and its single financial regulator. It authorises and supervises Irish funds, fund management companies, banks, insurers, investment firms, payment and e-money institutions and crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Central Bank is part of the Eurosystem and is the national competent authority for financial services in Ireland, a major domicile for UCITS, AIFs and ETFs.

What it does

  • Authorises Irish UCITS and AIFs (including ICAVs) and their management companies and AIFMs, and sets fund rules through its UCITS Regulations and AIF Rulebook.
  • Sets governance and substance expectations for fund management companies (CP86 guidance).
  • Runs the Fitness and Probity regime and the Individual Accountability Framework, including the Senior Executive Accountability Regime (SEAR).
  • Authorises payment and e-money institutions and, under MiCA, crypto-asset service providers.
  • Supervises firms' AML/CFT compliance.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UCITS, AIFMD, MMFR, ELTIF, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2, MiCA, the AML package and the Individual Accountability Framework.

resources.title: Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE)
resources.summary: The CBUAE is the UAE's central bank and the regulator of banking, insurance and payments in the UAE outside the financial free zones.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CBUAE was established in 1980. Since 2020 it has also been the insurance regulator.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises banks, finance companies, exchange houses, insurers and payment service providers.
  • Regulates payment token services, under which only dirham-backed payment tokens issued by licensed firms may be used for payments in the UAE mainland, with limited exceptions.
  • Oversees payment systems and runs the Digital Dirham CBDC project.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by the firms it licenses.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Central Bank Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 14 of 2018, as amended), the Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation, the Stored Value Facilities Regulation and the Payment Token Services Regulation.

resources.summary: The CNMV is Spain's securities markets regulator. It supervises investment firms, collective investment schemes and their managers, market conduct and crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CNMV ensures the transparency of Spanish securities markets and protects investors.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises investment firms, collective investment schemes and their management companies (SGIICs).
  • Supervises listed issuers and market conduct.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

MiFID II, UCITS, AIFMD, MAR, the Prospectus Regulation and MiCA.

resources.summary: The CMVM is Portugal's securities markets regulator. It supervises investment firms, collective investment undertakings and their managers, listed issuers and market conduct.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CMVM protects investors and ensures the efficiency and transparency of Portuguese securities markets.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises collective investment undertakings and their management companies.
  • Supervises investment services conduct and listed issuers.
  • Investigates market abuse.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, MAR and the Prospectus Regulation.

resources.title: Commissariat aux Assurances
resources.summary: The Commissariat aux Assurances is Luxembourg's insurance supervisor. It matters to asset managers because Luxembourg life insurers distribute unit-linked policies that invest in funds across Europe.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CAA supervises insurance and reinsurance undertakings and insurance intermediaries established in Luxembourg.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises insurers, reinsurers and intermediaries.
  • Applies Solvency II and the Insurance Distribution Directive.
  • Supervises the investment rules for unit-linked life insurance products.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Solvency II, the Insurance Distribution Directive and PRIIPs for insurance-based investment products.

resources.title: Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier
resources.summary: The CSSF is Luxembourg's financial regulator. It supervises Europe's largest fund domicile, along with banks, investment firms, payment and e-money institutions and crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CSSF is the national competent authority for most of Luxembourg's financial sector, apart from insurance (supervised by the Commissariat aux Assurances).

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises UCITS, Part II funds and SIFs, together with their management companies and AIFMs, and supervises RAIFs indirectly through their AIFMs.
  • Sets governance and substance expectations for fund managers, notably in Circular CSSF 18/698.
  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions), investment firms, payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance and the audit profession.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UCITS, AIFMD, MMFR, ELTIF, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2, MiCA, DORA and the AML package.

resources.title: Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa
resources.summary: CONSOB is Italy's securities markets regulator. It supervises market conduct, listed issuers and the provision of investment services, and shares responsibilities with the Banca d'Italia for asset managers and crypto-assets.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

CONSOB protects investors and ensures the transparency and proper functioning of Italian securities markets.

What it does

  • Supervises the conduct of investment firms, banks providing investment services and asset managers, with the Banca d'Italia covering prudential matters.
  • Supervises listed companies' disclosures and approves prospectuses.
  • Investigates and sanctions market abuse.
  • Shares MiCA responsibilities with the Banca d'Italia.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

MiFID II, MAR, the Prospectus Regulation, UCITS and AIFMD (conduct aspects) and MiCA.

resources.title: Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures
resources.summary: The CPMI is the global standard setter for payment, clearing and settlement systems. It is hosted by the BIS and sets the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures with IOSCO.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CPMI promotes the safety and efficiency of payment, clearing, settlement and related arrangements.

What it does

  • Sets, with IOSCO, the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI), and has confirmed that they apply to systemically important stablecoin arrangements.
  • Leads the G20 programme to enhance cross-border payments, with the FSB.
  • Works on fast payments, central bank digital currencies and tokenisation.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The PFMI and the G20 cross-border payments targets.

resources.title: Council of Europe (CoE)
resources.summary: An international organisation of 46 European states, separate from the EU, that promotes human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Its MONEYVAL committee assesses AML/CFT regimes.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Council of Europe is based in Strasbourg and is not part of the EU, although all EU member states belong to it. It runs the European Convention on Human Rights and the European Court of Human Rights, and sets conventions on issues including money laundering, corruption, cybercrime and data protection.

What it does

  • Hosts MONEYVAL, which evaluates member states' AML/CFT systems against the FATF standards.
  • Sets conventions such as the Warsaw Convention on money laundering and terrorist financing, the Budapest Convention on cybercrime and Convention 108 on data protection.
  • Through GRECO, monitors states' compliance with anti-corruption standards.
  • Adopted the first binding international treaty on artificial intelligence and human rights in 2024.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

AML/CFT evaluations through MONEYVAL, and conventions on money laundering, cybercrime, data protection and AI.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Council of Europe: official website

resources.title: Council of the European Union
resources.summary: The EU institution in which ministers of the member state governments meet to adopt EU law jointly with the European Parliament.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Council of the EU is the EU's other co-legislator, representing national governments. Financial services files go through the Economic and Financial Affairs Council (ECOFIN), made up of finance ministers, and are prepared by national officials in Council working parties. The presidency rotates between member states every six months.

What it does

  • Agrees the Council's position ('general approach') on Commission proposals and negotiates the final text with the Parliament.
  • Adopts legislation, usually by qualified majority, and can object to delegated acts.
  • Adopts EU sanctions (restrictive measures) by unanimity, including the packages against Russia that cover crypto-asset services.
  • Adopts legislation in some areas alone, such as the SSM Regulation.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

All EU financial services legislation, plus EU sanctions regimes and the EU list of high-risk third countries for AML purposes (through its role on delegated acts).

resources.title: Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission
resources.summary: CySEC is Cyprus's securities regulator. It supervises a large population of investment firms serving clients across the EU, along with fund managers, funds and crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

CySEC supervises the Cyprus investment services and capital markets sector.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises investment firms, many of which passport services across the EU.
  • Authorises UCITS management companies, AIFMs and Cyprus funds.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by the firms it regulates.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

MiFID II, UCITS, AIFMD, MAR, MiCA and the AML package.

resources.title: De Nederlandsche Bank
resources.summary: De Nederlandsche Bank is the Dutch central bank and prudential supervisor. It supervises banks, insurers, pension funds and payment and e-money institutions, and checks integrity and AML/CFT compliance.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Under the Dutch 'twin peaks' model, DNB is responsible for prudential and integrity supervision; the AFM is responsible for conduct.

What it does

  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions), insurers and pension funds.
  • Authorises payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Supervises integrity and AML/CFT compliance, and before MiCA registered crypto service providers.
  • Is part of the Eurosystem.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, IORP II, PSD2, EMD2 and the AML package.

resources.title: Deutsche Bundesbank
resources.summary: The Deutsche Bundesbank is Germany's central bank and part of the Eurosystem. It carries out much of the day-to-day supervision of German banks with BaFin and operates key payment infrastructure.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Bundesbank contributes to euro area monetary policy, financial stability and payment systems, and shares banking supervision with BaFin.

What it does

  • Carries out ongoing supervision of German banks, including audits and analysis, alongside BaFin.
  • Operates payment and settlement services as part of the Eurosystem.
  • Monitors financial stability in Germany.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD (with BaFin and the ECB) and Eurosystem payment infrastructure.

resources.title: Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA)
resources.summary: The DFSA is the independent regulator of the Dubai International Financial Centre, a financial free zone with its own legal system based on English common law.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The DFSA was established in 2004. It regulates financial and certain non-financial activities in and from the DIFC.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, asset managers, investment firms, insurers and market infrastructure in the DIFC.
  • Regulates funds domiciled in or marketed from the DIFC.
  • Regulates crypto tokens, approving which tokens firms may use in the DIFC, and tokenised securities.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance in the DIFC.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The DIFC Regulatory Law, Markets Law, Collective Investment Law and the DFSA Rulebook, including its crypto token regime.

resources.title: Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units
resources.summary: The Egmont Group is the global network of financial intelligence units. It enables FIUs to exchange information securely to fight money laundering and terrorist financing.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Egmont Group was founded in 1995 and brings together the FIUs of its member jurisdictions.

What it does

  • Provides a secure channel for FIUs to exchange financial intelligence across borders.
  • Sets principles for information exchange between FIUs.
  • Supports training and the development of FIUs.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

It works within the FATF standards, in particular Recommendation 29 on FIUs and Recommendation 40 on international cooperation.

resources.sourcesHtml: • Egmont Group of Financial Intelligence Units: official website

resources.title: European Banking Authority
resources.summary: The EBA writes the single rulebook for banking and payments in the EU and promotes consistent supervision of banks, payment institutions and e-money institutions. Under MiCA it directly supervises significant asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The EBA was set up in 2011 under Regulation (EU) No 1093/2010 and is based in Paris. It works to ensure effective and consistent prudential regulation and supervision across the EU banking sector.

What it does

  • Drafts technical standards and guidelines under the Capital Requirements Regulation and Directive, PSD2 (including strong customer authentication) and the E-Money Directive.
  • Runs the EU-wide bank stress tests.
  • Under MiCA, directly supervises significant asset-referenced tokens and significant e-money tokens and writes rules on reserves, liquidity and own funds.
  • With ESMA and EIOPA, oversees critical ICT third-party providers under DORA.
  • Its AML/CFT mandates have passed to the new Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA).

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive, PSD2 (and in future PSD3/PSR), EMD2, MiCA Titles III and IV (tokens), DORA and the Transfer of Funds Regulation guidelines.
resources.sourcesHtml: • European Banking Authority: official website

resources.title: European Central Bank
resources.summary: The ECB is the central bank of the euro area, based in Frankfurt. It sets monetary policy, runs the Eurosystem's payment and settlement services, is developing the digital euro and leads banking supervision through the Single Supervisory Mechanism.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The ECB's primary objective is price stability in the euro area. It also oversees payment systems and, through ECB Banking Supervision, supervises the euro area's significant banks.

What it does

  • Sets monetary policy for the euro area.
  • Operates, with the national central banks, the Eurosystem's market infrastructure: T2 (real-time gross settlement), T2S (securities settlement) and TIPS (instant payments).
  • Oversees systemically important payment systems and payment schemes.
  • Leads the digital euro project and the Eurosystem's work on settling DLT transactions in central bank money.
  • Gives opinions on draft EU legislation within its competence, such as MiCA's rules on stablecoins.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Eurosystem payment infrastructure, the oversight framework for electronic payments, the digital euro proposal and, through the SSM, prudential banking rules.
resources.sourcesHtml: • European Central Bank: official website

resources.title: European Commission (DG FISMA)
resources.summary: The European Commission proposes EU financial services law and adopts the detailed rules that implement it. Its Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union (DG FISMA) leads this work.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Commission has the sole right to propose EU legislation. In financial services, DG FISMA drafts the proposals that the European Parliament and the Council then negotiate and adopt, such as MiCA, the AML package, AIFMD II and the Retail Investment Strategy. It also adopts delegated and implementing acts (Level 2), often based on draft technical standards from the European Supervisory Authorities.

What it does

  • Proposes Level 1 legislation and adopts Level 2 delegated and implementing acts.
  • Makes equivalence decisions for third countries.
  • Monitors how member states transpose and apply EU law, and can open infringement proceedings.
  • Leads policy on the Savings and Investments Union (formerly Capital Markets Union), sustainable finance and digital finance.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Every EU financial services framework starts with a Commission proposal, including UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, MiCA, PSD2/PSD3, DORA, SFDR and the AML package.
resources.sourcesHtml: • European Commission (DG FISMA): official website

resources.title: European Council
resources.summary: The EU institution made up of the heads of state or government of the member states, which sets the EU's overall political direction and priorities.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The European Council does not make laws. It is chaired by a permanent President and brings together national leaders with the President of the Commission. It should not be confused with the Council of the European Union, where ministers legislate, or with the Council of Europe, which is not an EU body.

What it does

  • Sets the EU's strategic agenda, which shapes the Commission's legislative programme.
  • Agrees major political initiatives, such as the Savings and Investments Union and banking union.
  • Nominates the President of the Commission and appoints the President of the ECB and members of its Executive Board.
  • Agrees the political direction on sanctions, which the Council of the EU then adopts.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

No framework directly. Its conclusions set the priorities for financial services policy, including capital markets integration and the completion of banking union.
resources.sourcesHtml: • European Council: official website

resources.title: European Data Protection Board
resources.summary: The EDPB is the EU body that ensures the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is applied consistently. Its guidelines matter to financial firms using personal data in AI, blockchain and payments.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The EDPB was established by the GDPR. It brings together the national data protection authorities and the European Data Protection Supervisor.

What it does

  • Issues guidelines, recommendations and opinions on applying the GDPR.
  • Settles disputes between national data protection authorities in cross-border cases.
  • Has published guidance relevant to financial services, including on processing personal data with blockchain technologies and on AI models.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive.

sources.title: European Data Protection Board: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • European Data Protection Board: official website

resources.title: European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority
resources.summary: EIOPA is the EU's supervisory authority for insurance and occupational pensions, based in Frankfurt. It matters to asset managers because insurers and pension funds are major fund investors and because insurance-based investment products fall under PRIIPs.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

EIOPA was set up in 2011 under Regulation (EU) No 1094/2010 as one of the three European Supervisory Authorities. Its aims are policyholder and pension scheme member protection and the stability of the insurance and pensions sectors.

What it does

  • Drafts technical standards and guidelines under Solvency II, the Insurance Distribution Directive and the IORP II Directive.
  • Runs insurance stress tests and monitors risks in the sector.
  • Works with ESMA and the EBA on cross-sector rules such as the PRIIPs key information document and SFDR disclosures.
  • Supervises the Pan-European Personal Pension Product (PEPP) framework.
  • With ESMA and the EBA, oversees critical ICT third-party providers under DORA.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Solvency II, the Insurance Distribution Directive, IORP II, PEPP, PRIIPs (jointly), SFDR (jointly) and DORA (jointly).

sources.title: European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority: official website
resources.sortKey: european insurance and occupational pensions authority

resources.title: European Parliament (EP)
resources.summary: The directly elected chamber of the EU, which adopts EU financial services law jointly with the Council of the EU.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Parliament is one of the EU's two co-legislators. Its 720 members are elected every five years. Financial services files are handled mainly by the Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs (ECON), sometimes jointly with other committees.

What it does

  • Amends and adopts Commission proposals under the ordinary legislative procedure, negotiating the final text with the Council in 'trilogues' facilitated by the Commission.
  • Can object to delegated acts adopted by the Commission.
  • Confirms the chairs of the European Supervisory Authorities and holds hearings with the ECB President and the chairs of the ESAs and the SSM.
  • Approves the EU budget and the appointment of the Commission.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Every EU financial services regulation and directive adopted under the ordinary legislative procedure, including MiCA, DORA, the AML package, AIFMD II, PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation.
resources.sourcesHtml: • European Parliament: official website

resources.title: European Securities and Markets Authority
resources.summary: ESMA is the EU's securities markets supervisor, based in Paris. It writes much of the single rulebook for markets, investment firms, funds and crypto-assets, drives supervisory convergence among national authorities and directly supervises certain market entities.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

ESMA was set up in 2011 under Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010 as one of the three European Supervisory Authorities. Its aims are investor protection, orderly markets and financial stability.

What it does

  • Drafts regulatory and implementing technical standards and issues guidelines and Q&As.
  • Promotes consistent supervision through peer reviews, common supervisory actions and supervisory briefings.
  • Directly supervises credit rating agencies, trade repositories, securitisation repositories, certain benchmark administrators and data reporting service providers.
  • Under MiCA, keeps the register of crypto-asset service providers and white papers, and can use product intervention powers.
  • With the EBA and EIOPA, oversees critical ICT third-party providers under DORA.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UCITS, AIFMD, MMFR, ELTIF, cross-border distribution of funds, MiFID II/MiFIR, MAR, EMIR, CSDR, the Prospectus Regulation, MiCA, the DLT Pilot Regime, SFDR (with the other ESAs) and DORA.

sources.title: European Securities and Markets Authority: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • European Securities and Markets Authority: official website

resources.title: European Systemic Risk Board
resources.summary: The ESRB oversees the EU financial system as a whole to prevent and reduce systemic risk. It is chaired by the President of the ECB and works through warnings and recommendations rather than direct supervision.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The ESRB was set up in 2010 under Regulation (EU) No 1092/2010 after the global financial crisis. It is responsible for macroprudential oversight of the EU financial system, covering banks, insurers, funds, market infrastructure and crypto-assets.

What it does

  • Monitors and assesses systemic risks across the EU.
  • Issues warnings and recommendations to EU and national authorities, which must act on them or explain why not.
  • Has focused on liquidity and leverage in investment funds, money market funds, and crypto-assets and stablecoins, including multi-issuance stablecoin schemes.
  • Its secretariat is hosted by the ECB in Frankfurt.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

It does not run a framework itself. Its recommendations shape the macroprudential parts of AIFMD, UCITS, MMFR and MiCA.

sources.title: European Systemic Risk Board: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • European Systemic Risk Board: official website

resources.title: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
resources.summary: The FDIC insures deposits at US banks, supervises many state-chartered banks and resolves failed banks.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FDIC was created in 1933 in response to bank failures during the Great Depression. Its mission is to maintain stability and public confidence in the US financial system.

What it does

  • Insures deposits, up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category.
  • Supervises state-chartered banks that are not members of the Federal Reserve System.
  • Resolves failed banks.
  • Has a role under the GENIUS Act for stablecoin issuers that are subsidiaries of the banks it supervises, Under the GENIUS Act, payment stablecoins are not insured deposits.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Federal Deposit Insurance Act and, for relevant issuers, the GENIUS Act.

sources.title: Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation: official website

resources.title: Financial Action Task Force
resources.summary: The FATF is the global standard setter for anti-money laundering, countering terrorist financing and countering proliferation financing. Its 40 Recommendations, including the standards for virtual assets, shape national AML/CFT laws worldwide.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FATF was set up in 1989 by the G7. Its secretariat is in Paris, at the OECD.

What it does

  • Sets the FATF Recommendations and interpretive notes. Recommendation 15 and its interpretive note cover virtual assets and virtual asset service providers, and Recommendation 16 is the 'travel rule' for transfers.
  • Assesses countries through mutual evaluations, with FATF-style regional bodies such as MONEYVAL.
  • Publishes lists of jurisdictions under increased monitoring ('grey list') and high-risk jurisdictions subject to a call for action ('black list').
  • Publishes typologies, red-flag indicators and targeted updates on virtual assets.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The FATF Recommendations and the methodology for assessing technical compliance and effectiveness.

sources.title: Financial Action Task Force: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • Financial Action Task Force: official website

resources.title: Financial Conduct Authority
resources.summary: The FCA is the UK's conduct regulator for financial services and the prudential regulator for firms not supervised by the PRA. It supervises asset managers, investment firms, payment and e-money institutions and cryptoasset businesses.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FCA's objectives under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 are to protect consumers, protect and enhance market integrity, and promote competition. It also has a secondary objective on the UK's international competitiveness and growth.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises investment firms, asset managers and fund managers, and authorises UK funds (UK UCITS, NURS, QIS and LTAFs).
  • Recognises overseas funds for UK retail marketing under the Overseas Funds Regime.
  • Authorises payment institutions and e-money institutions and enforces the safeguarding rules.
  • Registers cryptoasset businesses for AML purposes, and will authorise cryptoasset firms under the new regime from 25 October 2027.
  • Runs the Senior Managers and Certification Regime and the Consumer Duty, and is the UK Listing Authority.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

FSMA 2000 and the FCA Handbook, UK MiFID, UK UCITS and AIFM rules, the Payment Services and E-Money Regulations, the Money Laundering Regulations 2017, the Cryptoassets Regulations 2026, SM&CR and the Consumer Duty.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Financial Conduct Authority: official website

resources.title: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)
resources.summary: FinCEN is the US financial intelligence unit and administrator of the Bank Secrecy Act, the main US anti-money laundering law. It sets AML rules for banks, money services businesses and crypto businesses.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

FinCEN is a bureau of the US Treasury. It collects and analyses financial intelligence and issues regulations under the Bank Secrecy Act.

What it does

  • Issues AML/CFT regulations and guidance, including for money services businesses that deal in convertible virtual currency.
  • Receives suspicious activity reports and currency transaction reports.
  • Can designate foreign institutions or jurisdictions as of primary money laundering concern, including crypto exchanges and mixers.
  • Runs the beneficial ownership reporting regime under the Corporate Transparency Act.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act and the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020.

sources.title: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • Financial Crimes Enforcement Network: official website

resources.title: Financial Intelligence Analysis Unit (Malta)
resources.summary: The FIAU is Malta's financial intelligence unit and its AML/CFT supervisor. It receives suspicious transaction reports and supervises all firms subject to Malta's AML/CFT rules.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FIAU is responsible both for financial intelligence and for supervising AML/CFT compliance, working with the MFSA and other supervisors.

What it does

  • Receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports and shares intelligence with law enforcement and foreign FIUs.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by banks, financial institutions, crypto-asset service providers and other subject persons, often jointly with the MFSA.
  • Issues implementing procedures and guidance, and imposes administrative penalties.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Malta's AML/CFT legislation implementing the EU AML package and the FATF Recommendations.

sources.title: Financial Intelligence Analysis Unit (Malta): official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • Financial Intelligence Analysis Unit (Malta): official website

resources.title: Financial Services Agency (Japan) (JFSA)
resources.summary: The JFSA is Japan's integrated financial regulator. Japan was one of the first countries to register crypto-asset exchanges and to legislate for stablecoins.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The JFSA was established in 2000. Its objectives include ensuring the stability of Japan's financial system, protecting users of financial services and facilitating financial functions.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises banks, insurers, securities firms and asset managers.
  • Registers and supervises crypto-asset exchange service providers under the Payment Services Act, a regime in place since 2017.
  • Regulates stablecoins as electronic payment instruments, which may be issued only by banks, fund transfer service providers and trust companies, under rules in force since 2023.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Banking Act, Financial Instruments and Exchange Act, Insurance Business Act and Payment Services Act.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Financial Services Agency (Japan): official website

resources.title: Financial Services and Markets Authority (Belgium)
resources.summary: The FSMA is Belgium's conduct and markets regulator. It supervises financial markets, listed companies, collective investment undertakings and their managers, and the conduct of financial firms towards customers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Under Belgium's 'twin peaks' model, the FSMA supervises conduct and markets and the National Bank of Belgium supervises prudential soundness.

What it does

  • Supervises Belgian collective investment undertakings and their management companies.
  • Supervises market conduct, listed issuers and prospectuses.
  • Supervises the conduct of financial firms and the distribution of financial products.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II (conduct), MAR and the Prospectus Regulation.

sources.title: Financial Services and Markets Authority (Belgium): official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • Financial Services and Markets Authority (Belgium): official website

resources.title: Financial Services Regulatory Authority (Abu Dhabi Global Market) (FSRA)
resources.summary: The FSRA regulates financial services in Abu Dhabi Global Market, an international financial centre with a common-law framework and an early regime for virtual assets.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FSRA is the financial regulator of ADGM, established in 2015.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, asset managers, funds, brokers, insurers and market infrastructure in ADGM.
  • Regulates virtual asset activities under a framework introduced in 2018, and fiat-referenced tokens.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance in ADGM.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The ADGM Financial Services and Markets Regulations 2015 and FSRA rulebooks, including the virtual asset framework.

resources.sourcesHtml: • Financial Services Regulatory Authority (Abu Dhabi Global Market): official website
