resources.title: Financial Stability Board
resources.summary: The FSB coordinates international financial regulation for the G20. It monitors global financial stability and sets high-level frameworks, including for crypto-assets, stablecoins and non-bank financial intermediation.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FSB was set up in 2009, succeeding the Financial Stability Forum. It brings together finance ministries, central banks, regulators and the international standard setters, and is hosted by the BIS in Basel.

What it does

  • Coordinates the G20 financial regulatory reform agenda.
  • Published a global regulatory framework for crypto-asset activities and recommendations for global stablecoin arrangements (2023), and monitors their implementation.
  • Leads work on non-bank financial intermediation, including liquidity mismatch in open-ended funds and leverage.
  • Coordinates work on cross-border payments with the CPMI.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The FSB crypto-asset framework, its high-level recommendations on global stablecoin arrangements and its recommendations on liquidity mismatch in open-ended funds.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Financial Stability Board: official website

resources.title: Finansinspektionen (Sweden)
resources.summary: Finansinspektionen is Sweden's integrated financial supervisor. It supervises banks, insurers, investment firms, fund managers, payment institutions and crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Finansinspektionen promotes financial stability, well-functioning markets and consumer protection in Sweden.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, insurers, investment firms and fund management companies.
  • Authorises payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA.
  • Supervises market conduct and AML/CFT compliance.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2, MiCA and the AML package.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Finansinspektionen (Sweden): official website

resources.title: Finanssivalvonta (Finnish Financial Supervisory Authority)
resources.summary: The FIN-FSA is Finland's integrated financial supervisor, operating in connection with the Bank of Finland. It supervises banks, insurers, investment firms, fund managers, payment institutions and crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FIN-FSA promotes financial stability and confidence in Finnish financial markets and protects customers and investors.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, insurers, investment firms and fund management companies.
  • Authorises payment institutions and crypto-asset service providers.
  • Supervises market conduct and AML/CFT compliance.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2, MiCA and the AML package.

sources.title: Finanssivalvonta (Finnish Financial Supervisory Authority): official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • Finanssivalvonta (Finnish Financial Supervisory Authority): official website

resources.title: Finanstilsynet (Denmark)
resources.summary: Finanstilsynet is Denmark's integrated financial supervisor. It supervises banks, mortgage credit institutions, insurers, investment firms, investment funds and payment institutions.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Finanstilsynet supervises the Danish financial sector and contributes to financial stability and consumer protection.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, mortgage credit institutions, insurers and pension companies.
  • Supervises investment firms, investment associations and fund managers.
  • Authorises payment and e-money institutions and supervises crypto-asset service providers.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2, MiCA and the AML package.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Finanstilsynet (Denmark): official website

resources.title: Finanstilsynet (Norway)
resources.summary: Finanstilsynet is Norway's integrated financial supervisor. Norway is in the European Economic Area, so EU financial services law applies there through the EEA Agreement.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Finanstilsynet supervises banks, insurers, pension funds, investment firms, fund managers, payment institutions and markets in Norway.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, insurers, investment firms and fund management companies.
  • Supervises payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Supervises market conduct and AML/CFT compliance.
  • Applies EU rules once they are incorporated into the EEA Agreement.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

EU frameworks as incorporated into the EEA Agreement, including CRR/CRD, Solvency II, UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2 and MiCA.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Finanstilsynet (Norway): official website

resources.title: Finantsinspektsioon (Estonia)
resources.summary: Finantsinspektsioon is Estonia's integrated financial supervisor. It supervises banks, insurers, investment firms, fund managers, payment institutions and, under MiCA, crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Finantsinspektsioon works independently alongside the Bank of Estonia to supervise the Estonian financial sector.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, insurers, investment firms and fund managers.
  • Authorises payment and e-money institutions.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA; before MiCA, Estonia licensed virtual asset service providers through its financial intelligence unit.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2 and MiCA.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Finantsinspektsioon (Estonia): official website

resources.title: Finanzmarktaufsicht (Austria)
resources.summary: The FMA is Austria's integrated financial regulator. It supervises banks, insurers, pension funds, investment firms, investment funds and their managers, payment and e-money institutions, and crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FMA is the single national competent authority for financial services in Austria and works with the Oesterreichische Nationalbank on banking supervision.

What it does

  • Supervises banks (with the ECB and the national bank), insurers and pension funds.
  • Authorises investment firms, fund managers and investment funds.
  • Authorises payment and e-money institutions and, under MiCA, crypto-asset service providers.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance and market conduct.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2, MiCA and the AML package.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Finanzmarktaufsicht (Austria): official website

resources.title: Finanzmarktaufsicht Liechtenstein
resources.summary: The FMA Liechtenstein is Liechtenstein's integrated financial supervisor. Liechtenstein is in the EEA and was an early mover on blockchain with its 2020 Token and TT Service Provider Act.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FMA supervises banks, insurers, asset managers, funds, payment institutions and token service providers in Liechtenstein. EU financial services law applies through the EEA Agreement.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, insurers, asset management companies and funds, many of which are distributed in Switzerland and the EEA.
  • Authorises payment and e-money institutions.
  • Registers service providers under the Token and TT Service Provider Act (TVTG) and applies MiCA through the EEA Agreement.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2, MiCA (through the EEA) and the TVTG.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Finanzmarktaufsicht Liechtenstein: official website

resources.title: Guernsey Financial Services Commission (GFSC)
resources.summary: The GFSC regulates financial services in the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a Crown Dependency and international finance centre with significant funds, insurance, banking and fiduciary sectors.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The GFSC is an independent statutory body established in 1987. Its objectives include protecting the public, maintaining the Bailiwick's reputation as a finance centre and countering financial crime.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises banks, insurers and insurance intermediaries, investment businesses, fiduciaries, and lenders.
  • Authorises and registers collective investment schemes and supervises their managers and administrators.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by financial services businesses and prescribed non-financial businesses, including virtual asset service providers.
  • Cooperates with overseas regulators on cross-border supervision.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Guernsey's regulatory laws for banking, insurance, investment business and collective investment schemes, fiduciaries and lending, and its AML/CFT framework, assessed by MONEYVAL.

sources.title: Guernsey Financial Services Commission: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • Guernsey Financial Services Commission: official website

resources.title: HM Treasury
resources.summary: HM Treasury is the UK's finance ministry. It sets the legislative framework for financial services, including the regulatory perimeter, and makes the statutory instruments that bring new activities such as cryptoassets into regulation.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

HM Treasury is responsible for financial services policy and legislation, while the FCA, PRA and Bank of England write and apply the detailed rules.

What it does

  • Sets the regulatory perimeter under FSMA 2000 through statutory instruments, such as the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026.
  • Leads UK financial services policy, including on payments, stablecoins and the digital pound.
  • Makes equivalence decisions for overseas regimes and sets the regulators' remit letters.
  • Oversees UK financial sanctions through OFSI.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

FSMA 2000 and the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, which repealed retained EU law and replaced it with UK rules.
resources.sourcesHtml: • HM Treasury: official website

resources.title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA)
resources.summary: The HKMA is Hong Kong's central banking institution. It supervises banks and stored value facilities, licenses issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins and runs tokenisation projects.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The HKMA was established in 1993. Its main functions are maintaining currency stability, promoting the stability of the banking system and developing Hong Kong as a financial centre.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks and stored value facility licensees.
  • Licenses issuers of fiat-referenced stablecoins under the Stablecoins Ordinance, in force since August 2025.
  • Runs projects on tokenised deposits, tokenisation and wholesale CBDC settlement, such as Project Ensemble.
  • Oversees payment systems.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Banking Ordinance, the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance and the Stablecoins Ordinance.

sources.title: Hong Kong Monetary Authority: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • Hong Kong Monetary Authority: official website

resources.title: International Association of Insurance Supervisors
resources.summary: The IAIS is the global standard setter for insurance supervision. Its standards shape how insurers, major investors in funds, manage investment and liquidity risk.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The IAIS develops principles and standards for the supervision of the insurance sector, and is hosted by the BIS.

What it does

  • Sets the Insurance Core Principles and the Common Framework for internationally active insurance groups.
  • Developed the Insurance Capital Standard.
  • Monitors systemic risk in the insurance sector.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Insurance Core Principles, ComFrame and the Insurance Capital Standard.

sources.title: International Association of Insurance Supervisors: official website

resources.sourcesHtml: • International Association of Insurance Supervisors: official website

resources.title: International Monetary Fund
resources.summary: The IMF promotes global monetary cooperation and financial stability. It assesses countries' financial sectors and AML/CFT regimes and has set out policy elements for crypto-assets.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The IMF, based in Washington DC, carries out economic surveillance of its member countries and provides financial support and technical assistance.

What it does

  • Carries out Financial Sector Assessment Programs (FSAPs), with the World Bank, reviewing countries' financial stability and supervision.
  • Conducts AML/CFT assessments using the FATF methodology.
  • Published Elements of Effective Policies for Crypto Assets (2023) and advises on stablecoins and CBDCs.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

It does not run a regulatory framework. Its assessments test countries against international standards.
resources.sourcesHtml: • International Monetary Fund: official website

resources.title: International Organization of Securities Commissions
resources.summary: IOSCO is the global body of securities regulators, based in Madrid. Its standards set the international baseline for securities markets, investment funds and, more recently, crypto-asset markets and DeFi.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

IOSCO's members regulate the world's securities and futures markets. Its Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation are the recognised international standard.

What it does

  • Sets the Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation and standards for collective investment schemes, including on liquidity risk management and anti-dilution tools.
  • Published policy recommendations for crypto and digital asset markets (2023) and for decentralised finance (2023).
  • Runs the Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding for cross-border enforcement cooperation.
  • Sets, with the CPMI, the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The IOSCO Objectives and Principles, CIS liquidity recommendations, crypto-asset and DeFi recommendations, and the PFMI (with the CPMI).

resources.title: International Sustainability Standards Board
resources.summary: The ISSB sets the global baseline for sustainability-related financial disclosures. It is part of the IFRS Foundation, alongside the body that sets IFRS accounting standards.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The ISSB was created by the IFRS Foundation in 2021 to develop sustainability disclosure standards for capital markets.

What it does

  • Issued IFRS S1 (general sustainability-related disclosures) and IFRS S2 (climate-related disclosures) in June 2023.
  • Supports jurisdictions that adopt or build on its standards in their own reporting rules.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

IFRS S1 and IFRS S2.

resources.title: Isle of Man Financial Services Authority (IOMFSA)
resources.summary: The Isle of Man FSA regulates financial services in the Isle of Man, a Crown Dependency with a significant insurance, banking and funds sector.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The FSA was created in 2015 by merging the Financial Supervision Commission and the Insurance and Pensions Authority. Its objectives include protecting consumers, reducing financial crime and maintaining confidence in the island's financial services.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises banks, investment businesses, fund services providers, insurers, pension schemes, and corporate and trust service providers.
  • Registers and supervises collective investment schemes.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by designated non-financial businesses, including convertible virtual currency businesses.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Financial Services Act 2008, the Insurance Act 2008, the Collective Investment Schemes Act 2008 and the island's AML/CFT framework, assessed by MONEYVAL.

resources.title: Jersey Financial Services Commission (JFSC)
resources.summary: The JFSC regulates financial services in Jersey, a Crown Dependency and international finance centre with a significant funds, trust and private wealth industry.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The JFSC is an independent statutory body. Its guiding principles include reducing risk to the public, protecting Jersey's reputation, and countering financial crime.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises banks, fund services businesses, funds, investment businesses, trust and company service providers, insurers and money service businesses.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by financial and certain non-financial businesses, including virtual asset service providers.
  • Maintains the island's registry of companies and other entities, including beneficial ownership information.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

Jersey's financial services laws, including the Collective Investment Funds Law and Financial Services Law, and its AML/CFT framework assessed by MONEYVAL.

resources.title: Joint Committee of the European Supervisory Authorities
resources.summary: The Joint Committee is the forum through which ESMA, the EBA and EIOPA work together on rules and supervision that cut across banking, insurance and securities.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The Joint Committee was set up under the founding regulations of the three European Supervisory Authorities to ensure consistency across sectors.

What it does

  • Produces joint technical standards, guidelines and Q&As where rules apply across sectors.
  • Leads cross-sector work on consumer protection, financial conglomerates, cyber risk and digital operational resilience.
  • Runs the oversight framework for critical ICT third-party providers under DORA.
  • Coordinates joint risk reports on the EU financial system.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

PRIIPs (the key information document), SFDR technical standards, DORA, the Financial Conglomerates Directive and the joint ESMA/EBA guidelines on the suitability of management body members under MiCA.

resources.title: Komisja Nadzoru Finansowego (Polish Financial Supervision Authority)
resources.summary: The KNF is Poland's integrated financial supervisor. It supervises banks, insurers, capital markets, investment funds and their managers, and payment institutions.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The KNF ensures the proper functioning, stability, security and transparency of the Polish financial market and protects market participants.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, insurers, pension funds and investment firms.
  • Supervises investment fund companies (TFIs) and investment funds.
  • Authorises payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Supervises market conduct and listed issuers.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2 and EMD2.

resources.title: Latvijas Banka
resources.summary: Latvijas Banka is Latvia's central bank and, since 2023, its integrated financial supervisor, having absorbed the former Financial and Capital Market Commission.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Latvijas Banka is part of the Eurosystem and supervises Latvia's banks, insurers, investment firms, payment institutions and crypto-asset service providers.

What it does

  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions), insurers and investment firms.
  • Authorises payment and e-money institutions.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2 and MiCA.

resources.title: Malta Financial Services Authority
resources.summary: The MFSA is Malta's single regulator for financial services. It supervises banks, insurers, investment services firms, funds, payment and e-money institutions and crypto-asset service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The MFSA is the national competent authority for financial services in Malta and also acts as the listing authority.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises investment services firms, fund managers, UCITS, AIFs and notified AIFs.
  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions), insurers and pension schemes.
  • Authorises payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Authorises crypto-asset service providers under MiCA, which replaced Malta's earlier Virtual Financial Assets regime.
  • Supervises trustees and company service providers.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UCITS, AIFMD, MiFID II, PSD2, EMD2, MiCA, Solvency II, DORA and the AML package (with the FIAU).

resources.title: Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS)
resources.summary: MAS is Singapore's central bank and integrated financial regulator. It supervises banks, insurers, capital markets, fund managers and payment and digital token service providers, and leads major tokenisation projects.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

MAS was established in 1971 and acts as central bank and as regulator of the whole financial sector.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises banks, insurers, capital markets intermediaries, fund managers and payment service providers.
  • Licenses digital payment token service providers under the Payment Services Act, and since June 2025 requires Singapore firms providing digital token services only to overseas customers to be licensed or stop.
  • Has a regulatory framework for single-currency stablecoins issued in Singapore.
  • Leads tokenisation work with the industry, including Project Guardian.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Banking Act, Securities and Futures Act, Payment Services Act, Financial Services and Markets Act 2022 and Variable Capital Companies Act.

resources.title: MONEYVAL
resources.summary: MONEYVAL is the Council of Europe's committee that assesses member states' compliance with international AML/CFT standards. It is a FATF-style regional body covering many European jurisdictions that are not FATF members.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

MONEYVAL assesses its members against the FATF Recommendations, using the FATF methodology.

What it does

  • Carries out mutual evaluations and follow-up reviews of its members, which include Malta, Cyprus, the Baltic states, Liechtenstein and the Crown Dependencies, among others.
  • Publishes evaluation reports with technical compliance and effectiveness ratings.
  • Its findings feed into FATF listing decisions.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The FATF Recommendations, applied through the FATF assessment methodology.

resources.title: National Bank of Belgium
resources.summary: The National Bank of Belgium is Belgium's central bank and prudential supervisor. It supervises banks, insurers, payment and e-money institutions and systemically important market infrastructure based in Belgium.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

Under Belgium's 'twin peaks' model, the NBB is responsible for prudential supervision and the FSMA for conduct.

What it does

  • Supervises banks (with the ECB for significant institutions) and insurers.
  • Authorises payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • Oversees market infrastructure based in Belgium, including the international central securities depository Euroclear and the SWIFT network (with other central banks).

Frameworks it runs or shapes

CRR/CRD, Solvency II, PSD2, EMD2 and the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures.

resources.title: Network for Greening the Financial System
resources.summary: The NGFS is a network of central banks and supervisors working on climate and environmental risk in the financial system. Its climate scenarios are widely used in stress testing.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The NGFS was launched in 2017. It shares best practice and develops tools for managing climate risk, with its secretariat at the Banque de France.

What it does

  • Publishes climate scenarios used by supervisors and firms for scenario analysis and stress testing.
  • Issues guides for supervisors on integrating climate and environmental risks.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

It does not set binding standards. Its scenarios and guides inform supervisory expectations.

resources.title: New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS)
resources.summary: NYDFS regulates banks, insurers and financial services in New York State and runs one of the oldest licensing regimes for virtual currency businesses, the BitLicense.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

NYDFS was formed in 2011 by merging New York's banking and insurance departments.

What it does

  • Charters and supervises state banks, trust companies, insurers and money transmitters in New York.
  • Licenses virtual currency businesses under the BitLicense regime (since 2015) and charters limited purpose trust companies that provide crypto custody and issue stablecoins.
  • Has issued guidance on US dollar-backed stablecoins, covering reserves, redemption and attestations.
  • Enforces its cybersecurity regulation, which applies to all regulated firms.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

New York Banking Law, Insurance Law, Financial Services Law, the virtual currency regulation (23 NYCRR 200) and the cybersecurity regulation (23 NYCRR 500).

resources.title: Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation
resources.summary: OFSI, part of HM Treasury, implements and enforces UK financial sanctions. It issues guidance and licences, receives reports of frozen assets and imposes civil monetary penalties for breaches.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

OFSI helps ensure that financial sanctions are understood, implemented and enforced in the UK, including for cryptoasset firms.

What it does

  • Publishes guidance on the asset-freeze regime and the obligations it creates.
  • Grants licences for activities that would otherwise breach sanctions.
  • Receives reports of frozen assets and suspected breaches, including from cryptoasset firms.
  • Imposes civil monetary penalties and refers serious cases for criminal prosecution.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 and the regulations made under it.

resources.title: Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
resources.summary: OFAC administers and enforces US economic and trade sanctions. Its sanctions lists, including crypto wallet addresses, matter to financial firms worldwide because of the reach of US sanctions and the dollar.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

OFAC is part of the US Treasury. It administers sanctions programmes based on US foreign policy and national security goals.

What it does

  • Maintains the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list and other sanctions lists, which can include digital currency addresses.
  • Issues licences permitting otherwise prohibited activities.
  • Enforces sanctions through civil penalties, including against crypto businesses.
  • Publishes guidance, including sanctions compliance guidance for the virtual currency industry.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the Trading with the Enemy Act and country- and theme-specific sanctions programmes.

resources.title: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
resources.summary: The OCC charters and supervises US national banks and federal savings associations. It is also the main federal licensing authority for non-bank payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The OCC is an independent bureau of the US Treasury, established in 1863. It ensures that national banks operate safely and soundly and treat customers fairly.

What it does

  • Charters, regulates and supervises national banks, federal savings associations and federal branches of foreign banks.
  • Has confirmed that national banks may provide crypto custody, hold stablecoin reserves and take part in blockchain networks, and has granted conditional national trust bank charters to some digital asset firms.
  • Licenses and supervises federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The National Bank Act, the Home Owners' Loan Act and the GENIUS Act.

resources.summary: The OECD sets international standards on corporate governance and tax transparency. These include the G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance and the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The OECD, based in Paris, develops policy standards for its member countries and partners.

What it does

  • Sets the G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance (revised in 2023), a benchmark for board responsibilities and shareholder rights.
  • Developed the Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF) for automatic exchange of tax information on crypto-assets, implemented in the EU through DAC8.
  • Runs the Common Reporting Standard for financial account information.
  • Hosts the FATF secretariat.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The G20/OECD Principles of Corporate Governance, CARF and the Common Reporting Standard.

resources.summary: The Payment Systems Regulator is the UK's economic regulator for payment systems. It introduced mandatory reimbursement for authorised push payment fraud. The UK government has announced that the PSR will be merged into the FCA.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The PSR was set up in 2015 to promote competition and innovation in payment systems and ensure they work in users' interests.

What it does

  • Regulates designated payment systems, such as Faster Payments, Bacs and the card schemes.
  • Introduced mandatory reimbursement of authorised push payment (APP) fraud victims for Faster Payments from October 2024.
  • Works on access to payment systems for payment and e-money institutions.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Financial Services (Banking Reform) Act 2013 and the APP fraud reimbursement requirement.

resources.title: Prudential Regulation Authority
resources.summary: The PRA is part of the Bank of England. It supervises the safety and soundness of banks, building societies, credit unions, insurers and major investment firms in the UK.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The PRA's general objective is to promote the safety and soundness of the firms it regulates; for insurers it also aims to protect policyholders.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, building societies, credit unions, insurers and designated investment firms.
  • Sets prudential rules on capital, liquidity and operational resilience.
  • Approves senior managers at the firms it regulates under SM&CR, jointly with the FCA.
  • Sets expectations on banks' cryptoasset exposures and tokenised deposits.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

UK CRR and the PRA Rulebook, Solvency UK, SM&CR and the UK operational resilience rules (with the FCA).

resources.summary: The QFCRA regulates financial services in the Qatar Financial Centre, a business and financial centre with its own common-law based framework.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The QFCRA was established in 2005 under the QFC Law as an independent regulator of firms conducting financial services in or from the QFC.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, insurers, asset managers, funds and advisers in the QFC.
  • Regulates tokenisation of assets and related services under digital assets rules introduced in 2024.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by QFC firms.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The QFC Financial Services Regulations, QFCRA rulebooks and the QFC Digital Assets Regulations 2024.

resources.summary: The RBI is India's central bank. It regulates banks, non-bank financial companies and payment systems, overseeing one of the world's largest instant payment networks.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The RBI was established in 1935. It conducts monetary policy, issues currency, regulates and supervises the financial system and oversees payment and settlement systems.

What it does

  • Licenses and supervises banks and non-bank financial companies.
  • Regulates and supervises payment systems, including authorising payment system operators and prepaid payment instruments, and oversees the Unified Payments Interface (UPI).
  • Runs pilots of the digital rupee, a central bank digital currency.
  • Manages foreign exchange regulation.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Reserve Bank of India Act 1934, Banking Regulation Act 1949, Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007 and Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999.

resources.summary: The Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) is Saudi Arabia's central bank and the regulator of banks, insurers, finance companies and payment providers.

Remit

SAMA was established in 1952 as the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority and renamed the Saudi Central Bank in 2020, keeping its acronym.

What it does

  • Sets monetary policy and manages reserves.
  • Licenses and supervises banks, insurers, finance companies and payment service providers.
  • Oversees payment systems, including the instant payment system, and runs a regulatory sandbox.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance by the firms it regulates.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Saudi Central Bank Law, Banking Control Law, Cooperative Insurance Companies Control Law, Finance Companies Control Law and Payments and Payment Services Law.

resources.summary: SEBI regulates India's securities markets, including a fast-growing mutual fund industry, alternative investment funds and foreign portfolio investors.

SEBI was established in 1988 and given statutory powers in 1992. Its objectives are protecting investors and developing and regulating securities markets.

What it does

  • Regulates stock exchanges, brokers and other intermediaries.
  • Registers and supervises mutual funds, alternative investment funds and portfolio managers.
  • Registers foreign portfolio investors.
  • Enforces against market abuse and misconduct.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The SEBI Act 1992, Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act 1956, Depositories Act 1996 and SEBI regulations on mutual funds and alternative investment funds.

resources.summary: The SFC regulates Hong Kong's securities and futures markets, including fund managers, public funds and virtual asset trading platforms.

Remit

The SFC was established in 1989 and operates under the Securities and Futures Ordinance.

  • Licenses and supervises brokers, fund managers, advisers and other intermediaries.
  • Authorises investment funds offered to the Hong Kong public, including spot crypto exchange-traded funds since 2024.
  • Licenses virtual asset trading platforms under a regime that took effect in June 2023.
  • Supervises market conduct and enforces against misconduct.

The Securities and Futures Ordinance and the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance (for virtual asset trading platforms).

resources.title: Single Resolution Board
resources.summary: The Single Resolution Board is the resolution authority for significant banks in the banking union, based in Brussels. It plans for bank failures and manages the Single Resolution Fund.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The SRB is the central authority of the Single Resolution Mechanism, the second pillar of the banking union, established under Regulation (EU) No 806/2014.

What it does

  • Draws up resolution plans for significant banks and cross-border groups, and sets their minimum requirement for own funds and eligible liabilities (MREL).
  • Decides on resolution when a bank is failing or likely to fail and resolution is in the public interest.
  • Manages the Single Resolution Fund, financed by contributions from banks.

The Single Resolution Mechanism Regulation and the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive.

resources.title: Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM)
resources.summary: The Single Supervisory Mechanism, run by the ECB with national supervisors, has supervised banks in the euro area and other participating countries since November 2014. It directly supervises significant banks and oversees national supervisors' supervision of the rest.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The SSM is the first pillar of the EU banking union. The ECB works with national competent authorities in each participating country.

What it does

  • Directly supervises significant banks.
  • Grants and withdraws banking licences for all banks in the participating countries and approves acquisitions of qualifying holdings.
  • Sets the supervisory approach for less significant banks, which national authorities supervise day to day.
  • Supervises banks' crypto-asset activities and exposures, including e-money tokens issued by banks.

CRR/CRD and the SSM Regulation (Council Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013).

resources.title: Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA)
resources.summary: FINMA is Switzerland's independent, integrated financial regulator, based in Bern. It authorises and supervises banks, insurers, asset managers, funds and market infrastructures, and has a long-established approach to crypto-assets and DLT.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

FINMA was created in 2009 under the Financial Market Supervision Act, merging three earlier supervisors. Its objectives are protecting creditors, investors and policyholders and ensuring the proper functioning of financial markets.

What it does

  • Authorises and supervises banks, insurers, securities firms, fund management companies, managers of collective assets and Swiss collective investment schemes.
  • Supervises financial market infrastructures, including DLT trading facilities created by the 2021 DLT Act.
  • Supervises AML/CFT compliance, including for crypto service providers.
  • Publishes guidance on how financial market law applies to tokens, stablecoins and staking.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Banking Act, Financial Institutions Act, Collective Investment Schemes Act, Financial Market Infrastructure Act (including DLT trading facilities), Anti-Money Laundering Act and Insurance Supervision Act.

resources.title: US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)
resources.summary: The CFTC regulates US derivatives markets: futures, options and swaps. It treats bitcoin and other crypto-assets as commodities and polices fraud and manipulation in crypto markets.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The CFTC was established in 1974 under the Commodity Exchange Act. It aims to promote the integrity, resilience and vibrancy of US derivatives markets.

What it does

  • Registers and oversees derivatives exchanges, clearing houses, swap dealers and futures commission merchants.
  • Has enforcement authority against fraud and manipulation in commodity spot markets, including crypto-assets.
  • Oversees crypto futures and other derivatives on registered exchanges.
  • Is developing its own rules for crypto-asset markets. Proposed federal legislation (the CLARITY Act) would give it primary authority over spot markets in digital commodities, but the bill stalled in the Senate in September 2026.

The Commodity Exchange Act and the Dodd-Frank Act's swaps provisions.

resources.title: US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
resources.summary: The SEC is the US federal regulator of securities markets, investment advisers, investment companies (mutual funds and ETFs) and broker-dealers. It regulates crypto-assets that are securities and has reshaped its approach to crypto since 2025.
resources.bodyHtml:
Remit

The SEC was created by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Its mission is to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation.

What it does

  • Registers and oversees investment advisers, investment companies, broker-dealers, exchanges and clearing agencies.
  • Oversees disclosure by public companies and offerings of securities.
  • Enforces federal securities laws.
  • Regulates crypto-assets that are securities. Since 2025 it has set up a crypto task force, approved listing standards for crypto exchange-traded products, proposed new rules for crypto-assets and launched an exemption for tokenised securities trading venues.

Frameworks it runs or shapes

The Securities Act of 1933, Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Investment Company Act of 1940 and Investment Advisers Act of 1940.

resources.summary: VARA licenses and supervises virtual asset service providers in Dubai, outside the Dubai International Financial Centre. It was the world's first dedicated regulator for virtual assets.

VARA was established by Dubai Law No. 4 of 2022. It regulates virtual asset activities in Dubai's mainland and free zones, except the DIFC.

What it does

  • Licenses virtual asset service providers for activities such as exchange, broker-dealer, custody, lending and borrowing, management and investment, and advisory services.
  • Issues rulebooks on company, compliance, technology, market conduct and marketing.
  • Regulates virtual asset issuance and marketing.
  • Works with federal authorities on AML/CFT.

Dubai Law No. 4 of 2022 and the Virtual Assets and Related Activities Regulations 2023.

resources.title: AIFMD (including AIFMD II)
resources.summary: The EU framework that regulates managers of alternative investment funds, such as hedge funds, private equity, real estate and private credit funds. This guide covers who is caught, the core obligations, the AIFMD II changes on loan origination, liquidity and delegation, and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

AIFMD regulates the manager (the AIFM), not the fund directly. An AIF is any collective investment undertaking that is not a UCITS. Caught are:

  • EU AIFMs managing one or more AIFs. Managers below the thresholds (assets under management of €100 million including leverage, or €500 million for unleveraged funds with no redemption rights for five years) need only register, unless they opt in for the passport.
  • Non-EU AIFMs marketing AIFs in the EU, which do so under each member state's national private placement regime.
  • Depositaries of AIFs.

Key obligations

Authorisation and capital. Initial capital of €125,000 for an external AIFM, plus 0.02% of assets under management above €250 million (capped at €10 million), plus additional own funds or professional indemnity insurance to cover professional liability.

Organisation. Risk management must be functionally and hierarchically separate from portfolio management. AIFMs need conflicts of interest arrangements, a remuneration policy, and policies on valuation and liquidity.

Valuation. Assets must be valued properly and independently, either by the AIFM with functional independence or by an external valuer.

Liquidity. For each open-ended AIF, the AIFM must align the investment strategy, liquidity profile and redemption policy, and carry out regular liquidity stress tests.

Depositary. Each AIF needs a single depositary for safekeeping, cash monitoring and oversight.

Delegation. The AIFM may delegate functions but must not become a letter-box entity, and remains liable.

Transparency. Annual reports, disclosures to investors before they invest, and regular reporting to the regulator (Annex IV), including on leverage.

Marketing. An authorised EU AIFM can market EU AIFs to professional investors across the EU with a passport. Marketing to retail investors is a matter for national law.

AIFMD II: the 2024 changes

Directive (EU) 2024/927 made targeted changes, including:

  • Loan origination. Funds that originate loans face leverage limits (175% for open-ended and 300% for closed-ended funds), a 20% limit on lending to a single financial borrower, a 5% risk retention requirement on loans sold, and must be closed-ended unless the AIFM can show its liquidity management is compatible with open-ended dealing.
  • Liquidity management tools. AIFMs of open-ended AIFs must select at least two tools from a harmonised list.
  • Delegation and substance. More information on delegation at authorisation and in reporting, and at least two people resident in the EU conducting the AIFM's business.
  • Costs and reporting. Disclosure of all fees and costs charged to the fund, and expanded supervisory reporting.
  • Depositaries. Member states may allow a depositary in another member state, subject to conditions.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • AIFMD II entered into force on 15 April 2024 and had to be transposed by 16 April 2026. Transposition across member states has been uneven.
  • Level 2 rules on liquidity management tools apply from 16 April 2026, with existing funds given until 16 April 2027.
  • New supervisory reporting applies from 16 April 2027.
  • Loan-originating AIFs constituted before 15 April 2024 benefit from grandfathering of some rules until 16 April 2029.

Main supervisors

The AIFM's home member state authority, with host authorities overseeing marketing in their territory. ESMA issues technical standards, guidelines and Q&As.

What boards should watch

  • Whether the liquidity management tools chosen fit each fund's assets and investors.
  • For loan-originating funds: credit risk policies, concentration and whether an open-ended structure is justified.
  • Delegation and substance, especially where portfolio management is delegated outside the EU.
  • Valuation of private and illiquid assets.
  • Cost disclosures and whether every charge to the fund is justified.

  • AIFMD II (Directive (EU) 2024/927)

resources.title: Basel cryptoasset standard for banks
resources.summary: The Basel Committee's global standard for how banks hold capital against cryptoasset exposures: the groups of cryptoassets, their treatment, the exposure limit, how jurisdictions are applying it, and the 2025 to 2026 review.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Internationally active banks, through national implementation of the Basel Framework (chapter SCO60). The standard was published in December 2022, amended in July 2024, and was due to be implemented by 1 January 2026.

The groups of cryptoassets

Group 1 (treated broadly like traditional exposures): - 1a: tokenised traditional assets, such as tokenised bonds, which confer the same rights as the traditional asset. - 1b: cryptoassets with effective stabilisation mechanisms, such as stablecoins that pass tests on reserve quality, redemption and supervision of the issuer.

To qualify for Group 1, cryptoassets must meet classification conditions, including on legal certainty and the risks of the underlying network. Assets on permissionless blockchains were excluded from Group 1, pending further review. An add-on can apply for infrastructure risk.

Group 2 (all other cryptoassets, such as bitcoin and unbacked tokens): - 2a: assets meeting hedging recognition criteria, with a modified market risk treatment. - 2b: all others, with a 1,250% risk weight, meaning capital equal to the exposure.

Exposure limit

A bank's total Group 2 exposures should generally not exceed 1% of Tier 1 capital, and must not exceed 2%.

How jurisdictions are applying it

  • EU: CRR3 introduced transitional rules for banks' cryptoasset exposures from 2025, pending a full implementation, and did not adopt all elements, including those on permissionless blockchains.
  • UK and US: neither has applied the standard in its current form.

Status (as at November 2026)

The Basel Committee agreed in November 2025 to expedite a targeted review of elements of the standard, in light of market developments, especially the growth of stablecoins and tokenisation on public blockchains. The review is in progress.

What boards should watch

  • How the firm's crypto and tokenisation activities would be treated under the final rules.
  • Divergence between jurisdictions where the group operates.
  • Capital implications of holding stablecoins and tokenised assets, and of issuing tokenised deposits.

resources.title: Cross-border distribution of funds
resources.summary: The EU rules on marketing investment funds in other member states, including pre-marketing, de-notification, local facilities and marketing communications. This guide covers who is caught, the main obligations and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • UCITS management companies marketing UCITS in other member states.
  • EU AIFMs marketing AIFs to professional investors across the EU under the AIFMD passport, and their pre-marketing activities.
  • EuVECA and EuSEF managers.

The rules come from Directive (EU) 2019/1160, which amended the UCITS Directive and AIFMD, and Regulation (EU) 2019/1156. Both have applied since August 2021.

Key obligations

Pre-marketing (AIFMs). An EU AIFM may test investor appetite for a fund that is not yet established, or not yet notified for marketing, without triggering the marketing rules, provided no subscription documents are offered. It must notify its home regulator within two weeks of starting. A subscription by a pre-marketed investor within 18 months is treated as resulting from marketing.

Reverse solicitation. Where an investor approaches the manager on its own initiative, marketing rules do not apply. Regulators interpret this narrowly, and it cannot be relied on as a business model.

De-notification. A manager can stop marketing a fund in a member state, after making a blanket offer, publicly available for at least 30 working days, to repurchase investors' holdings free of charge. It may not pre-market the same or a similar strategy there for 36 months.

Facilities. Managers must provide facilities for retail investors in each host member state, such as processing orders and giving information, but need not have a physical presence there. They may be provided electronically.

Marketing communications. Marketing must be identifiable as such, describe risks and rewards equally prominently, and be fair, clear and not misleading. ESMA guidelines set out detailed expectations, including on sustainability claims.

Transparency. National authorities must publish their marketing rules and fees, and ESMA keeps a central database of cross-border funds.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

The rules are in force. The Commission's Market Integration and Supervision Package (December 2025) proposes further simplification, such as notifying cross-border marketing at authorisation and limiting national additions to EU rules. It is being negotiated.

Main supervisors

The home regulator handles notifications. Host regulators supervise marketing communications and local facilities. ESMA keeps the central database and issues guidelines.

What boards should watch

  • A register of where each fund is notified, and where it is actually sold.
  • Controls over pre-marketing and reverse solicitation, with records.
  • Approval of marketing materials, especially claims about sustainability.
  • Costs of maintaining notifications in markets with little or no sales.
