resources.title: Digital euro
resources.summary: The proposed digital euro: what it would be, how it would be distributed, the safeguards for banks and privacy, and where the legislation stands.
resources.bodyHtml:
What it would be

A digital euro would be a retail central bank digital currency issued by the Eurosystem: a digital form of cash, a direct claim on the central bank, usable online and offline across the euro area. It would complement, not replace, banknotes and coins.

How it would work

  • Distribution: through payment service providers, including banks, payment and e-money institutions, which would open digital euro accounts or wallets for customers.
  • Basic services free of charge for individuals.
  • Holding limits for individuals, to avoid large outflows of bank deposits. The Parliament's position would have the Commission set the limit based on an ECB recommendation and review it regularly.
  • No interest paid on holdings.
  • Legal tender: merchants would generally have to accept it, with exceptions.
  • Privacy: offline payments with cash-like privacy; online, the ECB would not see users' identities.
  • Interoperability with private payment solutions, and a single European rulebook.

Why the EU is pursuing it

  • To keep central bank money available as cash use declines.
  • To reduce reliance on non-European card schemes and payment providers.
  • To provide a resilient, pan-European means of payment.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The Commission proposed the legislation in June 2023, as part of a single currency package alongside a regulation on the legal tender of cash.
  • The Council adopted its negotiating mandate on 19 December 2025 and the Parliament on 9 July 2026. Trilogues are under way, with the institutions aiming for agreement by the end of 2026.
  • The ECB has indicated a possible pilot in 2027 and first issuance around 2029, subject to the law being adopted.

What boards should watch

  • For banks and payment firms: the operational and commercial impact of distributing the digital euro, including the scheme rules and compensation model.
  • The holding limit and its effect on deposits.
  • How the digital euro will sit alongside euro stablecoins and instant payments.
resources.sourcesHtml: • ECB: digital euro

resources.title: DLT Pilot Regime
resources.summary: The EU legal sandbox that lets market infrastructures trade and settle tokenised securities on distributed ledgers with some exemptions. This guide covers the three licence types, the limits, take-up and proposed changes.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Operators of market infrastructures that want to use distributed ledger technology to trade or settle DLT financial instruments (financial instruments issued, recorded, transferred and stored using DLT). Regulation (EU) 2022/858 has applied since 23 March 2023.

The three licences

  • DLT multilateral trading facility (DLT MTF): trading only.
  • DLT settlement system (DLT SS): settlement only.
  • DLT trading and settlement system (DLT TSS): trading and settlement combined, which is not normally allowed under EU law.

Operators can be existing investment firms, market operators and central securities depositories, or new entrants, which receive a specific permission.

Exemptions and conditions

Operators can request exemptions from specific requirements of MiFID II, MiFIR and CSDR, such as the need for intermediaries, or for settlement in central bank money, if they meet conditions and compensating measures. They must have a business plan, rules on the operation of the DLT, IT and cyber arrangements, safekeeping of clients' assets and an exit strategy.

Limits

  • Shares of issuers with market capitalisation below €500 million.
  • Bonds with issue size below €1 billion (excluding complex structures).
  • UCITS units with assets under management below €500 million.
  • Total market value of DLT instruments on an infrastructure up to €6 billion.

Status (as at November 2026)

Take-up has been modest, with a small number of authorised infrastructures. ESMA has reported on its experience. The Commission's Market Integration and Supervision Package (December 2025) proposes to make the regime more flexible and proportionate, including raising thresholds and widening eligible instruments. Separately, the Eurosystem is developing services to settle DLT transactions in central bank money.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities grant permissions and exemptions, with ESMA's involvement.

What boards should watch

  • Whether the regime's limits fit the planned business.
  • The settlement asset and how finality is achieved.
  • Interoperability with existing market infrastructure and liquidity.
  • Exit strategy if the regime changes or ends.
resources.sourcesHtml: • DLT Pilot Regime (Regulation (EU) 2022/858)

resources.title: DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act)
resources.summary: The EU regulation on ICT risk and digital operational resilience in the financial sector. This guide covers who is caught, the five pillars of requirements, the oversight of critical ICT providers and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

About 20 types of financial entities, including credit institutions, payment and e-money institutions, investment firms, crypto-asset service providers and token issuers, central securities depositories and counterparties, trading venues, UCITS management companies, AIFMs, insurers and reinsurers, and pension funds. Simplified requirements apply to microenterprises and some smaller entities.

ICT third-party service providers are affected through contracts, and those designated as critical are directly overseen by the ESAs.

The five pillars

1. ICT risk management. A comprehensive framework, approved by the management body, which is ultimately responsible for ICT risk. It covers identification, protection, detection, response and recovery, backups, and communication, with an independent control function.

2. Incident management and reporting. Firms must classify ICT-related incidents and report major incidents to their regulator: an initial notification (within 4 hours of classification and no later than 24 hours after detection), an intermediate report within 72 hours and a final report within one month. Significant cyber threats may be reported voluntarily.

3. Digital operational resilience testing. Regular testing, including vulnerability assessments and scenario-based tests. Firms identified by their supervisor must carry out threat-led penetration testing at least every three years.

4. ICT third-party risk. A strategy and policy for ICT third-party risk, a register of information on all ICT contracts reported to regulators, mandatory contract terms, due diligence, concentration risk assessment and exit strategies.

5. Information sharing. Firms may share cyber threat information within trusted communities.

Oversight of critical ICT third-party providers

The ESAs designate critical ICT third-party providers, such as major cloud providers, based on their importance to the financial sector. A Lead Overseer (EBA, ESMA or EIOPA) can request information, carry out inspections and issue recommendations.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • DORA has applied since 17 January 2025.
  • Firms submitted their first registers of information in 2025.
  • The ESAs designated the first critical ICT third-party providers in November 2025, and oversight is under way.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities for financial entities; the ESAs as Lead Overseers of critical providers.

What boards should watch

  • Board approval and understanding of the ICT risk framework and resilience strategy, and directors' own ICT training.
  • Quality of the register of information and concentration on a few providers.
  • Major incidents, near misses and lessons learned.
  • Testing results and remediation.
  • Exit plans for critical ICT providers.
resources.sourcesHtml: • DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554)

resources.title: E-Money Directive (EMD2)
resources.summary: The EU rules for issuing electronic money and for e-money institutions, and how they will be replaced by PSD3. This guide covers who is caught, the main requirements, the link with e-money tokens and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • E-money issuers: credit institutions, e-money institutions and a few public bodies that issue electronic money.
  • E-money institutions (EMIs): firms authorised to issue e-money and, usually, provide payment services. Member states may allow small EMIs with a lighter regime.
  • Distributors and agents that distribute or redeem e-money on an EMI's behalf.

Key requirements

  • Authorisation and passport. EMIs must be authorised and can passport across the EEA.
  • Capital. Initial capital of at least €350,000, and ongoing own funds of at least 2% of average outstanding e-money (with a separate calculation for payment services not linked to e-money).
  • Safeguarding. Funds received for e-money must be safeguarded, either in a segregated account or secure liquid assets, or covered by insurance or a guarantee.
  • Issuance at par and redemption. E-money must be issued at par on receipt of funds. Holders may redeem at any time at par, and fees for redemption are restricted.
  • No interest. Issuers may not pay interest or any benefit linked to the length of time e-money is held.
  • Restrictions. EMIs may not take deposits, and credit linked to payment services is restricted.

The link with e-money tokens

Under MiCA, e-money tokens are treated as electronic money. Only credit institutions and EMIs may issue them, and they must comply with the e-money rules as well as MiCA.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The current directive (2009/110/EC) has applied since 2011.
  • PSD3 will repeal it. E-money institutions will become a category of payment institution, with e-money rules integrated into PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation. Formal adoption of PSD3 is expected shortly, followed by a transition period.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities. The EBA issues guidelines.

What boards should watch

  • Safeguarding arrangements, reconciliations and audit findings.
  • Own funds against growth in outstanding e-money.
  • Oversight of distributors and agents.
  • Planning for re-authorisation under PSD3.
  • If issuing e-money tokens: MiCA requirements and the EBA's supervision of significant tokens.
resources.sourcesHtml: • E-Money Directive (Directive 2009/110/EC)

resources.title: ELTIF 2.0
resources.summary: The EU label for long-term investment funds that can be sold to retail investors across the EU, as revised in 2024. This guide covers who uses it, the main rules on assets, diversification, borrowing and redemptions, and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

The European Long-Term Investment Fund (ELTIF) is an optional EU product label for AIFs that invest in long-term assets such as infrastructure, private companies, real estate and private loans. An ELTIF must be managed by an EU AIFM authorised to manage ELTIFs. Unlike most AIFs, ELTIFs have a marketing passport to retail investors across the EU.

Key rules (as revised by ELTIF 2.0)

  • Eligible investments: at least 55% of capital in eligible long-term assets, such as equity or debt of unlisted (and some smaller listed) companies, real assets, other ELTIFs and EU long-term funds, and simple securitisations.
  • Diversification: for ELTIFs sold to retail investors, generally no more than 20% in a single undertaking. Funds sold only to professional investors have no diversification limits.
  • Borrowing: up to 50% of net asset value for retail ELTIFs and 100% for professional-only ELTIFs.
  • Structure: ELTIFs can be closed-ended or, since 2024, offer limited redemptions during their life, subject to a minimum holding period, liquidity management tools and a cap linked to liquid assets. A matching mechanism can let exiting investors sell to new ones.
  • Retail investors: the earlier €10,000 minimum investment and 10% portfolio limit for smaller investors were removed. Distributors must assess suitability.
  • Disclosure: a prospectus and a PRIIPs key information document.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • ELTIF 2.0 (Regulation (EU) 2023/606) has applied since 10 January 2024.
  • Level 2 rules on redemptions, matching and liquidity were adopted in 2025.
  • Use has grown strongly, particularly for semi-liquid private markets strategies aimed at wealth managers' clients.

Main supervisors

The AIFM's home regulator authorises the ELTIF. ESMA keeps a register and issues technical standards.

What boards should watch

  • Whether redemption terms are realistic for the assets held, and the liquidity tools are ready.
  • Valuation of private assets, especially where retail investors deal regularly.
  • Suitability of distribution to retail investors and the clarity of disclosure on illiquidity and costs.
  • Conflicts where the manager co-invests or transfers assets from other funds it manages.
resources.sourcesHtml: • ELTIF 2.0 (Regulation (EU) 2023/606)

resources.title: ESAs' outsourcing and cloud guidelines
resources.summary: The European Supervisory Authorities' guidelines on outsourcing and cloud outsourcing, who they apply to, the key requirements, and how they fit with DORA.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • EBA Guidelines on outsourcing arrangements (2019): banks, investment firms, payment institutions and e-money institutions.
  • ESMA Guidelines on outsourcing to cloud service providers (2021): UCITS management companies, AIFMs, depositaries, investment firms, trading venues, CSDs, CCPs and other ESMA-supervised entities.
  • EIOPA Guidelines on outsourcing to cloud service providers: insurers and reinsurers.

National regulators apply them through comply-or-explain, and many have their own guidance on top.

Key requirements

  • Governance: an outsourcing policy approved by the management body, which keeps responsibility for outsourced functions.
  • Critical or important functions: identifying when a function is critical or important, which triggers stricter requirements.
  • Pre-outsourcing analysis: risk assessment, including concentration and step-in risks, and due diligence on the provider.
  • Contracts: mandatory terms, including service levels, data location and security, audit and access rights for the firm and the regulator, subcontracting conditions and termination rights.
  • Register: a register of all outsourcing arrangements.
  • Monitoring and oversight throughout the arrangement.
  • Exit strategies, documented and tested for critical functions.
  • Notification to the regulator of planned outsourcing of critical or important functions.

How they fit with DORA

Since January 2025, DORA sets binding rules for ICT third-party risk, including cloud. For ICT services, DORA's requirements take precedence over the guidelines. The guidelines continue to apply to non-ICT outsourcing. The ESAs are updating their guidance to align with DORA and to cover third-party risk more broadly.

Status (as at November 2026)

The guidelines remain in force alongside DORA. Several national regulators are consulting on broader third-party risk guidance. For example, the Central Bank of Ireland consulted until December 2026 on guidance on the sound management of third-party risks.

What boards should watch

  • A single, consistent register covering outsourcing and ICT arrangements.
  • Concentration on a few cloud and technology providers.
  • Group outsourcing arrangements, which are subject to the same rules.
  • Exit plans for critical providers.

resources.title: ESMA fund names guidelines
resources.summary: ESMA's guidelines on funds that use ESG or sustainability-related terms in their names: the thresholds, the exclusions, who they apply to and when.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Managers of UCITS and AIFs (including EuVECA, EuSEF and ELTIFs) marketed in the EU that use ESG or sustainability-related terms in their names. The guidelines were published in May 2024.

The main rules

80% threshold. A fund using any ESG, environmental, social, governance, impact, sustainability or transition-related term in its name must invest at least 80% of its assets to meet the environmental or social characteristics or sustainable investment objectives in its binding investment strategy.

Exclusions. Depending on the terms used:

Terms used Exclusions applied
Transition, social and governance-related terms Climate Transition Benchmark exclusions (such as controversial weapons, tobacco and companies breaching global norms)
Environmental, impact and sustainability-related terms Paris-aligned Benchmark exclusions, which add exclusions for fossil fuel activity above set revenue thresholds

Sustainability terms. Funds using "sustainable" or similar terms must also invest meaningfully in sustainable investments as defined in SFDR.

Transition and impact terms. Funds using "transition" terms should ensure investments are on a clear and measurable path to transition, and "impact" terms should be used with investments made to generate a positive, measurable social or environmental impact alongside a financial return.

Combinations of terms trigger the combined requirements.

Temporary deviations should be corrected in investors' best interests, and passive breaches may be tolerated for a short period.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The guidelines have applied to new funds since 21 November 2024 and to existing funds since 21 May 2025.
  • Many funds changed their names or investment policies.
  • SFDR 2.0 would set naming and marketing rules in legislation, linked to its new product categories.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities, which apply the guidelines on a comply-or-explain basis. ESMA coordinates.

What boards should watch

  • That every fund with an ESG term in its name meets the 80% threshold and the exclusions, monitored continuously.
  • The data used to assess exclusions.
  • Consistency between names, documents and marketing.

resources.title: EU AI Act
resources.summary: The EU's law on artificial intelligence, as amended by the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI. This guide covers who is caught, the risk-based obligations, which financial services uses are high-risk, the revised timetable and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Providers: those who develop an AI system or general-purpose AI model and place it on the EU market or put it into service under their own name.
  • Deployers: those who use an AI system in a professional capacity. Most financial firms are deployers, and some are also providers of their own systems.
  • Importers and distributors.

The Act applies to providers and deployers outside the EU where the AI system's output is used in the EU.

The risk-based approach

  • Prohibited practices, such as manipulative or exploitative AI, social scoring and some uses of biometric identification.
  • High-risk AI systems, which must meet requirements on risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record keeping, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Deployers must use them according to instructions, assign human oversight, monitor them and, in some cases, carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment.
  • Transparency obligations for systems that interact with people or generate content, such as chatbots and deepfakes.
  • General-purpose AI models, which have documentation, copyright and, for models with systemic risk, risk assessment duties.
  • AI literacy: providers and deployers must take measures to ensure sufficient AI literacy of their staff.

Financial services

High-risk uses listed in the Act include AI used to assess the creditworthiness or establish the credit score of individuals (except for detecting fraud) and AI used for risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance. For regulated financial institutions, financial supervisors oversee compliance, and some requirements can be met through existing governance rules.

Most other uses in financial services, such as investment research, customer service or AML monitoring, are not high-risk under the Act, but remain subject to financial regulation, data protection and the firm's own model risk management.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The Act entered into force on 1 August 2024.
  • Prohibitions and AI literacy have applied since 2 February 2025; general-purpose AI obligations since 2 August 2025.
  • The Digital Omnibus on AI, adopted in July 2026, postponed the high-risk obligations: to 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk systems (including credit scoring) and to 2 August 2028 for AI embedded in regulated products. It also adjusted transparency deadlines and allowed limited processing of special category data to detect bias.

Main supervisors

National market surveillance authorities and, for financial institutions, financial supervisors. The Commission's AI Office oversees general-purpose AI models.

What boards should watch

  • An inventory of AI systems, classified by risk, including those in third-party tools.
  • Whether any use is high-risk, and readiness for December 2027.
  • AI literacy across the firm, including the board.
  • Governance of AI agents and generative AI.
resources.sourcesHtml: • EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)

resources.title: EU AML package: AMLR, AMLD6 and AMLA
resources.summary: The EU's overhaul of anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing rules: a single rulebook for firms, a revised directive for national authorities and a new EU authority. This guide covers who is caught, the main changes, the timetable and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Obliged entities, including credit and financial institutions (banks, payment and e-money institutions, investment firms, fund managers and collective investment undertakings, insurers), crypto-asset service providers, auditors, lawyers, trust and company service providers, estate agents and dealers in high-value goods. The AML Regulation adds some new sectors, such as crowdfunding platforms and, from 2029, professional football clubs and agents.

The package

  • AML Regulation (AMLR) (Regulation (EU) 2024/1624): a directly applicable single rulebook for obliged entities.
  • Sixth AML Directive (AMLD6) (Directive (EU) 2024/1640): rules for national supervisors, financial intelligence units and beneficial ownership registers.
  • AMLA Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1620): creates the Anti-Money Laundering Authority in Frankfurt.
  • The recast Transfer of Funds Regulation (2023/1113), which applies the travel rule to crypto-asset transfers.

Key changes for firms

  • Harmonised customer due diligence: detailed EU-wide rules, replacing national variations, with more prescriptive requirements on identifying beneficial owners (25% ownership threshold, with lower thresholds for higher-risk sectors possible).
  • Group-wide policies, internal controls and a compliance manager at management body level.
  • Enhanced due diligence for high-risk third countries, PEPs and certain cross-border correspondent relationships, including with crypto-asset service providers.
  • Crypto: CASPs may not keep anonymous accounts or accounts allowing anonymity-enhancing coins, and must apply enhanced measures to some transfers involving self-hosted wallets.
  • Cash limit: an EU-wide limit of €10,000 on cash payments for goods and services.
  • Information sharing within partnerships between obliged entities, with safeguards.

AMLA

AMLA coordinates national supervisors and FIUs, sets technical standards and guidelines, and will directly supervise around 40 of the highest-risk cross-border financial institutions, including CASPs. It will select them in 2027 and begin direct supervision in 2028.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • AMLA began operating in 2025.
  • The AMLR applies from 10 July 2027. Most of AMLD6 must be transposed by the same date.
  • AMLA is consulting on, and adopting, the technical standards that will fill in the detail of the AMLR.

Main supervisors

National AML/CFT supervisors, AMLA, and financial intelligence units.

What boards should watch

  • A gap analysis between current procedures and the AMLR's detailed requirements.
  • The designation of a management body member responsible for AML/CFT.
  • Whether the firm may be selected for direct supervision by AMLA.
  • Data and systems for customer due diligence and beneficial ownership.
resources.sourcesHtml:
• AML Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1624)
  • Sixth AML Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/1640)
  • AMLA Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1620)
resources.sortKey: eu aml package: amlr, amld6 and amla

resources.title: EU Retail Investment Strategy
resources.summary: The EU package that reforms how investment products are sold to retail investors: inducements, value for money, suitability, client categorisation, marketing and the PRIIPs KID. This guide covers what it changes and when.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Manufacturers of retail investment products: UCITS management companies, AIFMs, investment firms and insurers.
  • Distributors: investment firms, banks and insurance distributors that advise on or sell products to retail investors.

The package comprises an omnibus directive amending MiFID II, the Insurance Distribution Directive, UCITS, AIFMD and Solvency II, and a regulation amending the PRIIPs Regulation.

Key changes

  • Value for money: manufacturers and distributors must identify and quantify all costs and assess whether they are justified and proportionate. ESMA and EIOPA will develop benchmarks based on peer groups of comparable products. Products that do not offer value should not be offered to retail investors.
  • Inducements: no outright ban on commissions, but a stricter test that payments must not harm the client's best interest, with clearer disclosure.
  • Suitability and appropriateness: simpler, more client-focused assessments, including for independent advice and execution-only services.
  • Client categorisation: more retail clients can opt up to professional status if they meet set criteria, such as wealth and experience.
  • Marketing communications: firms are responsible for marketing, including by finfluencers and on social media.
  • Financial literacy: member states are encouraged to promote it.
  • PRIIPs KID: a revised, machine-readable document with more meaningful performance and cost information.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The Parliament and Council reached political agreement on 18 December 2025. The final texts were approved in committee in 2026 and are in the last stages of formal adoption. Check the latest position before relying on dates.
  • The PRIIPs changes are expected to apply around 18 months after publication, and most other changes later, implying implementation over 2027 to 2029.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities. ESMA and EIOPA draft value-for-money benchmarks and technical standards.

What boards should watch

  • How each fund will compare against value-for-money benchmarks, and what to do about outliers.
  • Distribution agreements and inducements.
  • Data and processes to calculate and evidence costs.
  • Readiness for the revised KID.

resources.title: EU sanctions framework
resources.summary: How EU sanctions (restrictive measures) are made and applied, the main types of measure, the obligations on firms, the crypto-specific measures against Russia, and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
How EU sanctions are made

  • The Council of the EU adopts a decision under the Common Foreign and Security Policy, by unanimity.
  • Economic measures are then implemented by a Council regulation, which applies directly in all member states.
  • Member states enforce them and set penalties. Since 2024, an EU directive harmonises criminal offences and penalties for sanctions violations.

Who must comply

  • Anyone within EU territory, including in its airspace.
  • EU nationals and companies incorporated in the EU, wherever they are.
  • Any business done wholly or partly in the EU.

EU parent companies must use their best efforts to ensure non-EU subsidiaries do not undermine sanctions.

Main types of measure

  • Asset freezes and a ban on making funds or economic resources available to listed persons, directly or indirectly, including to entities they own or control.
  • Sectoral measures, such as restrictions on financial services, securities, loans, deposits, trade, technology and services.
  • Travel bans.
  • Anti-circumvention measures, including a tool to restrict trade with third countries that help circumvent sanctions.

Crypto-assets and Russia

The EU's Russia sanctions include measures aimed at crypto:

  • a ban on providing crypto-asset wallet, account or custody services to Russian nationals and residents;
  • bans on transactions in specific crypto-assets used to evade sanctions, such as the A7A5 rouble stablecoin (19th package, October 2025), and RUBx and the digital rouble (20th package);
  • from 24 May 2026, a sector-wide ban on transactions with Russian crypto-asset service providers and platforms (20th package, adopted on 23 April 2026).

Obligations on firms

  • Screen customers, counterparties, payments and, for crypto, wallet addresses against EU sanctions lists, and apply ownership and control tests.
  • Freeze assets and report to the national competent authority.
  • Apply for licences where exemptions are available.
  • Report information that would facilitate compliance.
  • Not participate knowingly in activities that circumvent sanctions.

What boards should watch

  • The firm's sanctions risk assessment and exposure to high-risk jurisdictions, sectors and intermediaries.
  • The speed with which new designations are applied.
  • Circumvention red flags, especially in trade finance, payments and crypto.
  • Coordination with UK, US and other regimes that may apply to the group.

resources.title: EU Taxonomy Regulation
resources.summary: The EU's classification system for environmentally sustainable economic activities, how it works, how funds and companies disclose against it, and the 2026 simplification.
resources.bodyHtml:
What it is

The EU Taxonomy (Regulation (EU) 2020/852) is a classification system that defines which economic activities are environmentally sustainable. It is a reference for disclosures by companies and financial products, not a list of mandatory investments.

Six environmental objectives

  1. Climate change mitigation.
  2. Climate change adaptation.
  3. Sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources.
  4. Transition to a circular economy.
  5. Pollution prevention and control.
  6. Protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.

When an activity is taxonomy-aligned

An activity is aligned if it:

  • substantially contributes to at least one objective, meeting the technical screening criteria in the delegated acts;
  • does no significant harm to any of the other objectives;
  • is carried out in compliance with minimum safeguards on human rights and governance.

Disclosures

  • Companies in scope report the share of their turnover, capital expenditure and operating expenditure that is taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned.
  • Financial institutions report key performance indicators, such as a bank's green asset ratio.
  • Financial products that promote environmental characteristics or have sustainable investment objectives under SFDR disclose the share of their investments that are taxonomy-aligned.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • A simplification delegated act (Regulation (EU) 2026/73), part of the EU's omnibus simplification, entered into force on 28 January 2026. It introduces a materiality threshold so that companies need not assess activities that are not financially material (generally below 10% of turnover, capex or opex), simplifies reporting templates and the "do no significant harm" criteria, and applies from financial year 2026, with an option to use it for 2025.
  • ESMA has consulted on simplifying taxonomy disclosures for financial products.
  • SFDR 2.0 would change how product disclosures refer to the taxonomy.

What boards should watch

  • Data quality and availability for taxonomy alignment figures.
  • Consistency between taxonomy disclosures and fund marketing.
  • The impact of the simplification and SFDR 2.0 on product disclosures.

resources.title: FATF Recommendations: the core standards
resources.summary: The FATF's 40 Recommendations, the global standard for anti-money laundering and countering terrorist and proliferation financing. This guide summarises what they cover, how countries are assessed and what it means for firms and their boards.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

The Recommendations are addressed to countries, which implement them in national law and regulation. They then apply to financial institutions, virtual asset service providers and designated non-financial businesses and professions (such as lawyers, accountants, trust and company service providers, real estate agents and dealers in precious metals).

What the 40 Recommendations cover

  • Policies and coordination (R1–2). A national risk assessment and a risk-based approach to applying measures.
  • Money laundering and confiscation (R3–4). Criminalising money laundering and confiscating criminal proceeds.
  • Terrorist and proliferation financing (R5–8). Criminalising terrorist financing, targeted financial sanctions and protecting non-profit organisations from abuse.
  • Preventive measures (R9–23). Customer due diligence (R10), record keeping (R11), politically exposed persons (R12), correspondent banking (R13), money or value transfer services (R14), new technologies and virtual assets (R15), payment transparency, or the travel rule (R16), reliance on third parties (R17), internal controls (R18), higher-risk countries (R19), suspicious transaction reporting and tipping off (R20–21), and non-financial businesses (R22–23).
  • Transparency of legal persons and arrangements (R24–25). Beneficial ownership information on companies and trusts.
  • Powers of authorities (R26–35). Regulation and supervision, financial intelligence units, law enforcement and sanctions for non-compliance.
  • International cooperation (R36–40).

How countries are assessed

FATF and its regional bodies, such as MONEYVAL, carry out mutual evaluations that rate technical compliance with each Recommendation and the effectiveness of the system. Countries with strategic deficiencies are placed under increased monitoring (the "grey list") or are subject to a call for action (the "black list"). Firms must apply enhanced due diligence to higher-risk countries.

Status (as at November 2026)

  • The FATF's current round of evaluations places greater emphasis on effectiveness and on risk-based, proportionate measures, after changes in 2025 to promote financial inclusion.
  • Recommendation 16 was revised in June 2025, with implementation due by the end of 2030.
  • Beneficial ownership standards (R24 and R25) were strengthened in 2022 and 2023.

Main bodies

The FATF, the FATF-style regional bodies (such as MONEYVAL for many European jurisdictions), and national authorities.

What boards should watch

  • Whether the firm's risk assessment reflects its national risk assessment and the latest FATF lists.
  • Changes in the status of countries the firm deals with.
  • How the results of the country's mutual evaluation are likely to change supervisory expectations.
resources.sourcesHtml: • FATF Recommendations

resources.title: FATF standards for virtual assets
resources.summary: How the FATF's global AML/CFT standards apply to virtual assets and virtual asset service providers, including Recommendation 15 and the travel rule. This guide covers who is caught, the key requirements, implementation status and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

The FATF standards are addressed to countries, which implement them in national law. Under Recommendation 15 and its Interpretive Note, countries must apply AML/CFT requirements to virtual asset service providers (VASPs): businesses that exchange virtual assets for fiat or other virtual assets, transfer them, provide custody, or take part in issuance, for or on behalf of others.

FATF guidance explains that creators, owners and operators of DeFi arrangements who keep control or sufficient influence may be VASPs, even if the arrangement is described as decentralised.

Key requirements

  • Risk assessment. Countries and VASPs must identify and assess the money laundering and terrorist financing risks of virtual assets.
  • Licensing or registration. VASPs must be licensed or registered where they are created, and countries must act against unlicensed VASPs.
  • Supervision. VASPs must be supervised for AML/CFT by a competent authority.
  • Preventive measures. VASPs must apply the same measures as other financial institutions: customer due diligence (with a threshold of USD/EUR 1,000 for occasional transactions), record keeping, suspicious transaction reporting and sanctions screening.
  • Travel rule. Under Recommendation 16, VASPs must obtain, hold and transmit required originator and beneficiary information with virtual asset transfers, and screen it. They must also manage risks of transfers to and from self-hosted wallets.

Status (as at November 2026)

  • The standards for virtual assets were adopted in 2018 and 2019. The FATF publishes an annual targeted update showing that implementation remains uneven, particularly of the travel rule.
  • The FATF revised Recommendation 16 in June 2025 to cover all payment types more consistently, with implementation expected by the end of 2030.
  • Key risks the FATF highlights include stablecoin misuse, theft and laundering by state-linked hackers, scams and the use of unhosted wallets.

Main supervisors

The FATF sets standards and assesses countries through mutual evaluations. National supervisors license and supervise VASPs.

What boards should watch

  • The firm's AML/CFT risk assessment for each product, network and customer type.
  • Travel rule compliance, including with counterparties in countries that have not implemented it.
  • Exposure to self-hosted wallets, mixers, privacy coins and high-risk jurisdictions.
  • Use of blockchain analytics, and how alerts are handled.
resources.sourcesHtml: • FATF: virtual assets

resources.title: Fit and proper and suitability of management bodies (EU)
resources.summary: How EU financial regulators assess whether directors and key function holders are suitable for their roles, across banks, investment firms, fund managers, payment firms and crypto-asset firms. This guide covers who is caught, the assessment criteria and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Members of the management body (executive and non-executive directors) and, in many regimes, key function holders such as the heads of risk, compliance and internal audit, and the MLRO. The requirements appear across EU frameworks:

  • Banks and investment firms: CRD and MiFID II, with joint ESMA and EBA guidelines on suitability and, for significant banks, the ECB's fit and proper guide. CRD VI strengthens the rules, including assessment before some appointments take effect.
  • UCITS management companies and AIFMs: persons who conduct the business must be of sufficiently good repute and sufficiently experienced.
  • Payment and e-money institutions: managers must be of good repute and have appropriate knowledge and experience.
  • Crypto-asset service providers and token issuers under MiCA: management body members must be of sufficiently good repute and possess appropriate knowledge, skills and experience, with joint EBA and ESMA guidelines setting out how this is assessed.
  • Qualifying shareholders are also assessed for reputation and financial soundness under most regimes.

Assessment criteria

Common criteria across the guidelines:

  • Reputation, honesty and integrity: criminal, regulatory and civil proceedings, past conduct and transparency with the regulator.
  • Knowledge, skills and experience: relevant to the role, the firm's business and its risks, including theoretical knowledge and practical experience.
  • Independence of mind: ability to challenge, and absence of conflicts of interest that cannot be managed.
  • Time commitment: enough time for the role, considering other directorships.
  • Collective suitability: the board as a whole must have the range of knowledge and experience to understand the business and its main risks.

Firms are responsible for assessing suitability first, before applying to the regulator, and must reassess when circumstances change. Many regulators interview candidates for senior roles.

Status (as at November 2026)

The frameworks are in force. CRD VI applies from January 2026 for most provisions, with transition for some rules. The MiCA suitability guidelines have applied since the regime began.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities, and the ECB for significant banks in the euro area. The ESAs set the guidelines.

What boards should watch

  • A documented suitability policy, covering both individual and collective suitability.
  • A current skills matrix and succession plan.
  • Induction and ongoing training, including on new risks such as crypto-assets, ICT and AI.
  • Time commitment and the number of other roles held by directors.
  • Prompt notification to the regulator of changes and of matters that affect a person's fitness.

resources.title: Instant Payments Regulation
resources.summary: The EU regulation requiring payment providers to offer instant euro credit transfers at no extra cost, with a verification of payee service, and opening payment systems to non-bank providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Payment service providers (banks, payment institutions and e-money institutions) that offer euro credit transfers to their customers in the EU. Regulation (EU) 2024/886 amends the SEPA Regulation and the Settlement Finality Directive.

Key requirements

  • Offer instant transfers: providers that offer standard euro credit transfers must also offer instant credit transfers, sending and receiving, through all the same channels, at any time.
  • Price parity: charges for instant transfers must not be higher than for standard transfers.
  • Verification of payee: before a payer authorises a transfer, the provider must check that the payee's name matches the account identifier and tell the payer if it does not.
  • Sanctions screening: instead of screening each instant payment, providers screen their customers against EU sanctions lists at least daily and when lists change.
  • Access to payment systems: payment and e-money institutions can now participate directly in designated payment systems, subject to safeguards.

Timeline

  • Euro area providers had to receive instant transfers from January 2025 and send them, with verification of payee, from 9 October 2025.
  • Providers in non-euro member states must meet the requirements for euro transfers in 2027.
  • Payment and e-money institutions have later deadlines, also in 2027.

Status (as at November 2026)

The euro area requirements are in force. Verification of payee has been widely implemented. Supervisors are monitoring pricing and fraud outcomes.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities, with the EBA and the ECB (for payment systems).

What boards should watch

  • Fraud risk from faster payments, and the effectiveness of verification of payee and transaction monitoring.
  • Sanctions screening under the new approach.
  • Liquidity and operations for 24/7 payments.
  • Access to payment systems for payment and e-money institutions.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Instant Payments Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/886)

resources.title: Investment firms prudential regime (IFR and IFD)
resources.summary: The EU prudential regime for MiFID investment firms, based on the risks a firm poses to clients, markets and itself. This guide covers the classes of firm, the K-factors, liquidity and governance requirements.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Investment firms authorised under MiFID II, and UCITS management companies and AIFMs with MiFID top-up permissions for the capital requirements on those services. The regime (Regulation (EU) 2019/2033 and Directive (EU) 2019/2034) has applied since June 2021.

Three classes

  • Class 1: the largest, systemic firms (assets over €30 billion, or dealing on own account or underwriting at scale), which must be authorised as credit institutions and follow the bank rules.
  • Class 2: most investment firms, subject to the full IFR/IFD regime.
  • Class 3: small, non-interconnected firms below set thresholds (for example, assets under management below €1.2 billion and no client money held), with simpler requirements.

Capital requirements

A firm's own funds requirement is the highest of:

  • its permanent minimum capital, from €75,000 to €750,000 depending on its activities;
  • a quarter of its fixed overheads for the previous year; and
  • for Class 2 firms, the K-factor requirement.

K-factors measure risk to clients (assets under management, client money held, assets safeguarded and administered, client orders handled), to markets (net position risk, clearing margin) and to the firm (trading counterparty default, daily trading flow, concentration).

Other requirements

  • Liquidity: liquid assets of at least one-third of the fixed overheads requirement.
  • Concentration risk monitoring and limits for firms dealing on own account.
  • Internal capital adequacy and risk assessment (ICARA) under IFD.
  • Governance and remuneration, including variable pay rules for Class 2 firms above thresholds.
  • Reporting and disclosure.

Status (as at November 2026)

The regime is in force. The Commission is reviewing it. The UK applies its own version, the Investment Firms Prudential Regime (IFPR), under the FCA's MIFIDPRU rules.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities, with the EBA drafting technical standards.

What boards should watch

  • The adequacy of capital and liquid assets against business plans and stress scenarios.
  • The ICARA process and whether it reflects real risks, including wind-down.
  • Remuneration policy compliance.

resources.title: IOSCO recommendations for crypto and DeFi
resources.summary: The international securities regulators' policy recommendations for crypto-asset markets and decentralised finance, adopted in 2023, which shape how national regulators approach crypto trading, custody and DeFi.
resources.bodyHtml:
What they are

IOSCO, the global body of securities regulators, published two sets of policy recommendations in late 2023:

  • Policy Recommendations for Crypto and Digital Asset Markets (November 2023): 18 recommendations.
  • Policy Recommendations for Decentralized Finance (December 2023): 9 recommendations.

They are not binding law, but IOSCO members have committed to apply them, and they are used to assess national regimes.

Crypto and digital asset markets

The recommendations follow the principle of "same activities, same risks, same regulatory outcomes". They cover:

  • Conflicts of interest from vertically integrated businesses that combine trading platform, brokerage, market making, custody, lending and token issuance.
  • Market manipulation, insider dealing and fraud, with surveillance and enforcement.
  • Cross-border cooperation between regulators.
  • Custody and client assets: segregation, reconciliation and disclosure of custody arrangements.
  • Operational and technology risk, including cyber.
  • Retail access, suitability and disclosure.
  • Listing and delisting standards for crypto-assets.

Decentralised finance

The DeFi recommendations call on regulators to:

  • analyse DeFi products and services to see whether they fall within existing rules;
  • identify responsible persons, such as those who control or have sufficient influence over an arrangement or its activities, regardless of claims of decentralisation;
  • apply the same outcomes as for equivalent traditional activities;
  • address conflicts, operational and technology risks, disclosure, and interconnections with centralised crypto and traditional finance.

Status (as at November 2026)

IOSCO has monitored implementation, including thematic reviews of how members have applied the crypto recommendations, and continues work on tokenisation and stablecoins with the FSB.

Why they matter

They underpin MiCA's approach to conflicts and custody, the UK's new regime and other national frameworks, and they set expectations for how regulators will treat DeFi arrangements with identifiable controllers.

resources.title: Ireland: Individual Accountability Framework and fund management company guidance (CP86)
resources.summary: Ireland's Individual Accountability Framework, including the Senior Executive Accountability Regime, and the Central Bank's guidance for fund management companies, and the 2026 reviews that may change both.
resources.bodyHtml:
The Individual Accountability Framework (IAF)

The Central Bank (Individual Accountability Framework) Act 2023 introduced:

  • Senior Executive Accountability Regime (SEAR): applies from July 2024 to banks, insurers, certain investment firms and third-country branches. Firms must set out the responsibilities of senior executives in statements of responsibilities and a management responsibilities map.
  • Conduct standards: common standards for all staff in controlled functions, and additional standards for senior staff.
  • Enhancements to the fitness and probity regime, including certification by firms.
  • Changes to enforcement, allowing action directly against individuals for their own breaches.

SEAR does not yet apply to fund management companies.

Fund management company guidance (CP86)

The Central Bank's Fund Management Companies Guidance (2016, known as CP86) applies to UCITS management companies and AIFMs authorised in Ireland. Its main elements are:

  • Delegate oversight: how the fund management company oversees delegates, especially investment managers.
  • Managerial functions: six managerial functions (investment management, fund risk management, operational risk management, distribution, capital and financial management, and regulatory compliance), each allocated to a designated person with time commitment expectations.
  • Organisational effectiveness: a director with responsibility for reviewing the company's organisational effectiveness.
  • Location: requirements on where directors and designated persons are based, calibrated to the firm's risk rating.
  • Operating and board procedures, including a business plan and procedures for escalation.

Directors and designated persons hold pre-approval controlled functions (PCFs).

Status (as at November 2026)

  • The Central Bank published a review of delegation in the Irish funds sector in July 2026, finding generally good practice but areas to strengthen, such as risk management resourcing and outsourcing governance.
  • It is reviewing governance arrangements for fund management companies, including simplifying CP86, reinforcing the PCF framework and considering how to apply the IAF and SEAR proportionately to the funds sector.
  • It consulted until 3 December 2026 on new cross-sector guidance on managing third-party risks.

What boards should watch

  • Gaps against the delegation review findings, with a board-approved plan.
  • Designated persons' time commitment and resources.
  • Readiness for a possible extension of SEAR to fund management companies.

resources.title: Market Abuse Regulation
resources.summary: The EU rules against insider dealing, unlawful disclosure of inside information and market manipulation, and the obligations on issuers, firms and managers. This guide also covers the crypto-asset market abuse rules in MiCA.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

The Market Abuse Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 596/2014) applies to financial instruments traded on EU trading venues, and to related instruments, including OTC derivatives. It applies to everyone who trades, including asset managers and their staff. Issuers, persons discharging managerial responsibilities (PDMRs), trading venues and firms that arrange or execute transactions have specific obligations.

Title VI of MiCA sets equivalent rules for crypto-assets admitted to trading on EU crypto-asset trading platforms.

The prohibitions

  • Insider dealing: trading, or recommending or inducing others to trade, on the basis of inside information (precise, non-public, price-sensitive information).
  • Unlawful disclosure of inside information, except in the normal exercise of employment or under the market soundings regime.
  • Market manipulation: transactions or orders that give false or misleading signals or secure an artificial price, using fictitious devices, or disseminating false or misleading information.

Key obligations

  • Issuers: disclose inside information as soon as possible, unless delay is permitted; keep insider lists; notify PDMR transactions.
  • PDMRs: notify their transactions above a threshold (€20,000 a year) and observe closed periods.
  • Firms that arrange or execute transactions: have systems to detect and report suspicious orders and transactions (STORs) to regulators.
  • Investment recommendations: fair presentation and disclosure of conflicts.
  • Market soundings: procedures for disclosing information to gauge investor interest before a transaction.

Status (as at November 2026)

  • MAR has applied since July 2016.
  • The EU Listing Act (2024) amended MAR, including raising the PDMR threshold and changing disclosure of inside information in protracted processes, with changes applying in stages up to June 2026.
  • Crypto market abuse rules under MiCA have applied since 30 December 2024.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities, coordinated by ESMA.

What boards should watch

  • Controls over inside information and wall-crossing, including for private markets deals.
  • Personal account dealing rules and monitoring.
  • The effectiveness of trade surveillance and STOR reporting.
  • For crypto firms: surveillance systems and suspicious order reporting under MiCA.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Market Abuse Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 596/2014)

resources.title: MiCA: asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens
resources.summary: The MiCA rules for issuers of stablecoins: asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens. This guide covers who can issue them, reserve and redemption requirements, the extra rules for significant tokens and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Issuers of asset-referenced tokens (ARTs): crypto-assets that aim to keep a stable value by referencing another value or right, or a combination, such as a basket of currencies or commodities. Issuers must be authorised under MiCA, unless they are credit institutions that follow a notification process.
  • Issuers of e-money tokens (EMTs): crypto-assets that aim to keep a stable value by referencing one official currency. Only credit institutions and e-money institutions may issue them, and EMTs are treated as electronic money.
  • Persons seeking admission of ARTs and EMTs to trading, and CASPs that offer them.

Key obligations

White paper. Issuers must publish a crypto-asset white paper. For ARTs it must be approved by the regulator; for EMTs it must be notified.

Reserve of assets (ARTs). A reserve, legally segregated from the issuer's assets, held with approved custodians, invested only in highly liquid instruments with minimal risk, valued regularly and independently audited every six months.

EMT funds. Funds received in exchange for EMTs must be safeguarded under the e-money rules, with at least 30% held in deposits with credit institutions (60% for significant EMTs) and the rest in high-quality liquid assets.

Redemption. Holders have a right of redemption at any time: at par value for EMTs, and at market value of the reserve or delivery of the reference assets for ARTs. No fees for EMT redemption.

No interest. Issuers and CASPs may not grant interest or any benefit related to the length of time a holder holds an ART or EMT.

Own funds. ART issuers must hold at least €350,000 or 2% of the average reserve, whichever is higher, rising to 3% for significant ARTs.

Recovery and redemption plans. Issuers must have plans to restore compliance and to redeem holders in an orderly way if they cannot.

Limits on use. Where an ART, or an EMT in a non-EU currency, is widely used as a means of exchange (more than about one million transactions or €200 million a day in a single currency area), the issuer must stop issuing and reduce its use.

Significant tokens

The EBA classifies ARTs and EMTs as significant based on criteria such as number of holders, market value and transaction volumes. Issuers of significant ARTs, and of significant EMTs issued by e-money institutions, are supervised by the EBA, with higher own funds, liquidity and interoperability requirements.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The rules on ARTs and EMTs have applied since 30 June 2024.
  • The Commission is reviewing MiCA, including how multi-issuance stablecoins issued jointly in the EU and other jurisdictions should be treated.
  • PSD3 will bring EMT-related payment services more clearly within payments law once it applies.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities, and the EBA for significant tokens. The ECB and national central banks have a say on monetary policy and payment system risks.

What boards should watch

  • Composition, custody and liquidity of the reserve, and independent assurance.
  • Redemption capacity in a run, and tested recovery and redemption plans.
  • Concentration on a few banks for reserve deposits.
  • Use of the token as a means of exchange, and the limits that could apply.
  • For firms using stablecoins: whether the tokens they hold or offer are MiCA-compliant.
resources.sourcesHtml: • MiCA (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114)

resources.title: MiCA: crypto-asset service providers
resources.summary: The EU authorisation and conduct regime for firms that provide services in crypto-assets, under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA). This guide covers who is caught, the main obligations, the end of the transitional period, the proposed shift to ESMA supervision and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Any legal person providing one or more crypto-asset services to clients in the EU on a professional basis. The services are:

  • custody and administration of crypto-assets for clients;
  • operating a trading platform;
  • exchanging crypto-assets for funds or for other crypto-assets;
  • executing orders;
  • placing crypto-assets;
  • receiving and transmitting orders;
  • giving advice;
  • portfolio management;
  • transfer services.

MiCA does not cover crypto-assets that are already financial instruments (MiFID II applies), deposits, or unique and non-fungible crypto-assets. Services provided in a fully decentralised manner, with no intermediary, are outside its scope. Banks, investment firms, UCITS management companies, AIFMs and other already-authorised firms can provide some services after notifying their regulator rather than applying for a new authorisation.

Key obligations

  • Authorisation and passporting. Authorisation by the home regulator gives a passport to provide services across the EU.
  • Prudential safeguards. Minimum capital of €50,000, €125,000 or €150,000 depending on the services, or a quarter of fixed overheads if higher.
  • Governance. Management body members of good repute with appropriate knowledge, skills and experience; suitable shareholders; sound governance, business continuity and ICT systems (DORA applies).
  • Conduct. Act honestly, fairly and professionally in the best interests of clients; fair, clear and not misleading information, including on the environmental impact of consensus mechanisms; complaints handling; conflicts of interest policies.
  • Client assets. Client crypto-assets and funds must be segregated from the firm's own. Custodians are liable for loss of crypto-assets resulting from incidents they could have prevented.
  • Outsourcing and wind-down. Firms remain responsible for outsourced functions and must have a wind-down plan, at least for certain services.
  • Service-specific rules. For example, operating rules for trading platforms, best execution, suitability assessments for advice and portfolio management.
  • Market abuse. MiCA bans insider dealing and market manipulation in crypto-assets and requires firms to detect and report suspicious orders and transactions.
  • AML/CFT and the travel rule. CASPs are obliged entities under EU AML law and must comply with the Transfer of Funds Regulation.

Firms with at least 15 million active users in the EU are significant CASPs, subject to additional reporting and supervisory cooperation.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The CASP regime has applied since 30 December 2024.
  • Transitional arrangements for firms already operating under national regimes ended on 1 July 2026 at the latest. Firms without MiCA authorisation can no longer provide services.
  • In December 2025 the Commission proposed, in its Market Integration and Supervision Package, to move the authorisation and supervision of CASPs from national authorities to ESMA. The Parliament's draft report suggests limiting this to significant CASPs. Negotiations continue.
  • The Commission is also reviewing MiCA, including how it should treat DeFi, staking and lending.

Main supervisors

The national competent authority of the CASP's home member state, with ESMA promoting consistent supervision and, if the proposal is adopted, becoming the direct supervisor.

What boards should watch

  • Segregation, reconciliation and protection of client crypto-assets.
  • Quality of the authorisation application and ongoing compliance with conditions.
  • Outsourcing to group entities and technology providers outside the EU.
  • Readiness for a possible change of supervisor.
  • Marketing and the information given to clients.
resources.sourcesHtml: • MiCA (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114)

resources.title: MiFID II and MiFIR
resources.summary: The EU framework for investment services and trading venues. This guide covers who is caught, the main conduct and organisational rules, how it applies to asset managers and crypto, and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Investment firms providing investment services, such as reception and transmission of orders, execution, dealing on own account, portfolio management, investment advice, underwriting and operating trading venues, in relation to financial instruments.
  • Banks providing investment services.
  • UCITS management companies and AIFMs authorised to provide discretionary portfolio management or investment advice (the "MiFID top-up" services), which apply many MiFID rules to those services.
  • Trading venues: regulated markets, multilateral trading facilities and organised trading facilities.

MiFID II is Directive 2014/65/EU. MiFIR (Regulation (EU) No 600/2014) applies directly and covers transparency, transaction reporting and trading obligations.

Key obligations

  • Authorisation and passporting. Authorised firms can provide services across the EU.
  • Organisation and governance. Management body responsibility, compliance, risk management and internal audit functions, conflicts of interest, record keeping including recording of calls.
  • Client categorisation. Retail, professional and eligible counterparty, with different levels of protection.
  • Suitability and appropriateness. Advice and portfolio management must be suitable; for other services, firms check appropriateness for complex products.
  • Inducements. Limits on payments from third parties, and a ban for independent advice and portfolio management.
  • Product governance. Manufacturers define a target market; distributors check products reach it.
  • Costs and charges. Disclosure before and after the service.
  • Best execution. Obtaining the best possible result for clients.
  • Transparency and reporting (MiFIR). Pre- and post-trade transparency and transaction reporting to regulators.

Crypto-assets

Crypto-assets that qualify as financial instruments, such as tokenised shares or bonds, fall under MiFID II rather than MiCA. MiFID-authorised firms can also provide crypto-asset services under MiCA after notifying their regulator.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • MiFID II and MiFIR have applied since January 2018.
  • The 2024 MiFIR review introduces consolidated tapes and bans payment for order flow, with transitional arrangements.
  • The Retail Investment Strategy (politically agreed December 2025) will change inducements, value for money, suitability and client categorisation once adopted.
  • The Market Integration and Supervision Package proposes further changes, including ESMA supervision of significant trading venues.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities authorise and supervise firms. ESMA issues technical standards, guidelines and Q&As, and runs product intervention powers alongside national authorities.

What boards should watch

  • Product governance and target market, especially for complex products sold to retail clients.
  • Inducements and conflicts arising from distribution arrangements.
  • Quality of suitability assessments.
  • Readiness for the Retail Investment Strategy's value-for-money and cost rules.
resources.sourcesHtml:
• MiFID II (Directive 2014/65/EU)
  • MiFIR (Regulation (EU) No 600/2014)

resources.title: Money Market Funds Regulation
resources.summary: The EU rules for money market funds: the three types of fund, liquidity and diversification requirements, stress testing, and the outcome of the 2026 review in the EU and the UK.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Any UCITS or AIF that invests in short-term assets and aims to offer returns in line with money market rates or preserve the value of the investment must be authorised as a money market fund (MMF) under Regulation (EU) 2017/1131, which has applied since 2018.

The three types

  • Variable net asset value (VNAV) MMFs: price moves with the market value of assets. Can be short-term or standard.
  • Public debt constant net asset value (CNAV) MMFs: keep a stable price, investing at least 99.5% in public debt, cash and related repos.
  • Low volatility net asset value (LVNAV) MMFs: can keep a stable price as long as it stays within 0.2% of the market-value NAV.

Key requirements

  • Eligible assets: money market instruments, eligible securitisations, deposits, reverse repos, derivatives for hedging and other MMFs. No short selling or borrowing.
  • Diversification and concentration limits by issuer.
  • Maturity limits: weighted average maturity and weighted average life limits.
  • Liquidity: short-term MMFs must hold minimum daily and weekly liquid assets (for example, at least 10% daily and 30% weekly for CNAV and LVNAV funds).
  • Liquidity fees and gates for CNAV and LVNAV funds if weekly liquid assets fall below thresholds.
  • Credit quality assessment procedures.
  • Stress testing, using ESMA's annually updated scenarios, and reporting to regulators.
  • No external support from sponsors.

Status (as at November 2026)

  • EU: after reviewing the framework, the Commission concluded in May 2026 that it works well overall. Instead of new legislation, it published a Notice clarifying how liquidity buffers should be maintained and used, especially in stress.
  • UK: the government and FCA plan to replace the onshored UK MMFR with FCA rules, with legislation expected by the end of 2026, increasing liquidity requirements. EEA money market funds are excluded from the UK's Overseas Funds Regime equivalence decision.

Main supervisors

The fund's home regulator. ESMA sets stress test scenarios and reporting.

What boards should watch

  • Liquidity buffers against investor concentration and behaviour in stress.
  • Stress test results and actions taken.
  • The stable NAV mechanism for LVNAV funds and readiness for fees or gates.
  • Tokenised MMF share classes and their use as collateral.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Money Market Funds Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2017/1131)

resources.title: PRIIPs Regulation and the key information document
resources.summary: The EU rules requiring a short, standard key information document (KID) for investment products sold to retail investors. This guide covers who is caught, what the KID must contain, the changes agreed under the Retail Investment Strategy and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Manufacturers of packaged retail and insurance-based investment products (PRIIPs) made available to retail investors in the EU: investment funds (including UCITS since 2023), structured products, derivatives and insurance-based investment products.
  • Persons advising on or selling PRIIPs, who must give the KID to retail investors in good time before they invest.

Products exempt from the KID include pension products, deposits other than structured deposits, and simple shares and bonds.

Key obligations

The KID is a standardised document of no more than three A4 pages. It must cover:

  • What is this product? Type, objectives and the intended retail investor.
  • What are the risks and what could I get in return? A summary risk indicator on a scale of 1 to 7 and performance scenarios.
  • What happens if the manufacturer is unable to pay out?
  • What are the costs? Total costs over time and their breakdown, including entry, exit, ongoing and performance-related costs.
  • How long should I hold it and can I take money out early?
  • How can I complain?

The KID must be accurate, fair, clear and not misleading, consistent with the contract documents, reviewed regularly and updated when needed.

Changes under the Retail Investment Strategy

The Parliament and Council reached political agreement on the Retail Investment Strategy in December 2025. For PRIIPs, it includes:

  • a revised KID with more meaningful performance information and clearer presentation of costs;
  • a machine-readable KID;
  • tools to help investors compare products.

The PRIIPs changes are expected to apply around 18 months after publication in the Official Journal.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The PRIIPs Regulation has applied since 2018. UCITS moved from the KIID to the PRIIPs KID on 1 January 2023.
  • The Retail Investment Strategy amendments were politically agreed in December 2025 and are in the final stages of adoption. Check the latest status before relying on dates.
  • The UK no longer applies the EU PRIIPs regime and is moving to its own disclosure rules for consumer composite investments.

Main supervisors

National authorities enforce the rules. The ESAs (EBA, ESMA and EIOPA, through the Joint Committee) draft the detailed technical standards on content and methodology.

What boards should watch

  • Whether the risk indicator, scenarios and cost figures are calculated correctly and reviewed.
  • Consistency between the KID, prospectus and marketing.
  • Readiness for the revised KID, including data and systems.
  • How the KID fits with value-for-money assessments under the Retail Investment Strategy.
resources.sourcesHtml: • PRIIPs Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014)
resources.sortKey: priips regulation and the key information document

resources.title: PSD2 to PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation
resources.summary: The EU framework for payment services, and its replacement by PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation. This guide covers who is caught, the main obligations, what changes and the timetable.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Payment service providers: banks, payment institutions, e-money institutions and post office giro institutions providing payment services such as payment accounts, credit transfers, direct debits, card issuing and acquiring, money remittance, payment initiation and account information services.
  • Payment institutions need authorisation (or registration for account information services and small institutions).

PSD2: the current regime

PSD2 (Directive (EU) 2015/2366) sets:

  • authorisation, capital and safeguarding requirements for payment institutions;
  • information requirements and rights and obligations of users and providers;
  • liability rules for unauthorised and incorrectly executed payments;
  • strong customer authentication;
  • access to payment accounts for account information and payment initiation services (open banking);
  • incident reporting and security requirements.

What PSD3 and the PSR change

The package splits the framework:

  • PSD3 (a directive) covers authorisation and supervision of payment institutions. It repeals the E-Money Directive, so e-money institutions become a type of payment institution. Existing institutions must be re-authorised within a set period, which may be streamlined where they already meet the new requirements.
  • The PSR (a regulation) sets conduct rules that apply directly, with less room for national variation.

Main changes include:

  • Fraud. Payee name verification for all credit transfers; refunds for victims of fraud where a criminal impersonates the provider's staff; obligations on online platforms to remove fraudulent content; sharing of fraud information between providers.
  • Open banking. Better-performing dedicated interfaces and a permissions dashboard for customers.
  • Safeguarding. Clearer rules, more options and requirements to avoid concentration on one bank.
  • Access. Better access for payment institutions to bank accounts and payment systems.
  • Transparency. Clearer information on currency conversion and ATM charges.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • Political agreement was reached on 27 November 2025, and final texts were published in April 2026.
  • The Council adopted its first-reading position on 28 October 2026, and the Commission has accepted it. Formal approval by the Parliament and publication in the Official Journal are expected shortly.
  • The PSR is expected to apply about 18 months after entry into force, with a similar transposition period for PSD3.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities authorise and supervise. The EBA drafts technical standards and guidelines.

What boards should watch

  • Re-authorisation planning, especially for e-money institutions.
  • Fraud prevention and liability exposure under the new rules.
  • Safeguarding arrangements and bank concentration.
  • Open banking interface performance and the customer dashboard.
resources.sourcesHtml: • PSD2 (Directive (EU) 2015/2366)
