resources.title: SFDR (including the SFDR 2.0 proposal)
resources.summary: The EU rules on sustainability disclosures by asset managers and financial advisers, and the proposed overhaul known as SFDR 2.0. This guide covers who is caught, the current Article 6, 8 and 9 regime, what is proposed and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Financial market participants: asset managers (UCITS management companies and AIFMs), portfolio managers, insurers offering investment products, pension providers and others that make financial products.
  • Financial advisers giving investment or insurance advice.

The Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2019/2088) has applied since March 2021, with detailed templates under Level 2 rules since January 2023.

Key obligations (current regime)

Entity level. - Policies on how sustainability risks are integrated into investment decisions or advice. - A statement on principal adverse impacts of investment decisions on sustainability factors, mandatory for firms with more than 500 employees and otherwise on a comply-or-explain basis. - Disclosure of how remuneration policies are consistent with integrating sustainability risks.

Product level. - Article 6: all products disclose how sustainability risks are integrated, or why they are not relevant. - Article 8: products that promote environmental or social characteristics disclose how those characteristics are met, using prescribed templates before investment and in periodic reports. - Article 9: products with sustainable investment as their objective disclose how the objective is achieved.

Fund names. ESMA guidelines (applying to all funds since May 2025) set minimum thresholds and exclusions for funds that use ESG or sustainability-related terms in their names.

SFDR 2.0: what is proposed

The Commission published its proposal on 20 November 2025. It would:

  • replace the Article 8 and 9 designations with three voluntary product categories (Sustainable, Transition and ESG Basics), each requiring at least 70% of investments to meet the category's objective, with exclusions;
  • simplify and reduce disclosures, including removing the entity-level principal adverse impacts statement;
  • restrict the use of sustainability-related terms in names and marketing for products outside the categories.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The Council agreed its negotiating mandate on 24 June 2026 and the Parliament on 5 October 2026. Trilogue negotiations are under way, with political agreement targeted by the end of 2026.
  • The new rules are not expected to apply before about 2029. The current regime continues to apply in the meantime.

Main supervisors

National competent authorities supervise compliance and greenwashing. The ESAs draft technical standards and have published reports and guidance on greenwashing.

What boards should watch

  • Whether each fund's classification and claims are consistent across documents and marketing.
  • Data quality and reliance on ESG data providers.
  • Compliance with the fund names guidelines.
  • Planning for SFDR 2.0 categories: which funds will qualify, and the cost of changing documents and portfolios.
resources.sourcesHtml: • SFDR (Regulation (EU) 2019/2088)

resources.title: Transfer of Funds Regulation (the travel rule)
resources.summary: The EU rules requiring information about the payer and payee to travel with transfers of funds and crypto-assets. This guide covers who is caught, what information is required, how it applies to self-hosted wallets and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Payment service providers and intermediaries making transfers of funds in any currency, where at least one provider is in the EU.
  • Crypto-asset service providers making or receiving transfers of crypto-assets, including intermediary CASPs.

Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 recast the earlier rules on transfers of funds and extended them to crypto-assets, implementing the FATF's Recommendation 16.

Key requirements

Information that must accompany a transfer

  • For funds: the payer's name, account number and address (or an alternative such as an official ID number or date and place of birth), and the payee's name and account number. Simplified requirements apply to some transfers within the EU.
  • For crypto-assets: the originator's name, distributed ledger address or account number, and address or alternative identifier, and the beneficiary's name and address or account number. There is no minimum threshold for crypto-asset transfers between CASPs.

Verification and checks

  • The originator's information must be verified before the transfer.
  • The beneficiary's provider must check that required information is present and have risk-based procedures for missing or incomplete information: rejecting, suspending or returning the transfer, and reporting repeated failures.

Self-hosted wallets

  • For transfers above €1,000 to or from a self-hosted wallet, CASPs must assess whether the wallet is owned or controlled by their customer.
  • CASPs must apply risk-mitigating measures to transfers involving self-hosted wallets.

Counterparty due diligence

CASPs must assess other CASPs they transact with, especially those outside the EU, before transmitting information.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The recast regulation has applied since 30 December 2024, alongside MiCA. EBA guidelines set out how firms should handle missing information and self-hosted wallets.
  • The FATF's June 2025 revision of Recommendation 16 will require further changes to payment messages by the end of 2030.

Main supervisors

National AML/CFT supervisors, with the EBA (and in future AMLA) issuing guidelines.

What boards should watch

  • Travel rule data completeness rates and the handling of transfers with missing information.
  • Coverage of counterparties outside the EU, where the rule may not be implemented.
  • Controls on self-hosted wallets.
  • Choice and oversight of travel rule technology providers.
resources.sourcesHtml: • Transfer of Funds Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1113)
resources.sortKey: transfer of funds regulation (the travel rule)

resources.title: UCITS Directive (including UCITS VI)
resources.summary: The EU framework for retail investment funds that can be sold across the EU with a single authorisation. This guide covers who is caught, the main product rules, the 2024 amendments known as UCITS VI and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • UCITS funds: open-ended funds that invest in liquid financial assets and are authorised in an EU or EEA member state. They can take the form of an investment company, a unit trust or a common contractual fund.
  • UCITS management companies, which manage UCITS and must be authorised in their home member state. A UCITS investment company that does not appoint a management company is self-managed and must meet the same requirements itself.
  • Depositaries, which hold the fund's assets and oversee its operations.

Once authorised, a UCITS can be marketed to retail investors in any other member state through a notification procedure (the marketing passport), and a management company can manage UCITS in other member states (the management passport).

Key obligations

Eligible assets and diversification. A UCITS may invest only in eligible assets: transferable securities, money market instruments, units of other UCITS and similar funds, bank deposits and financial derivatives. Spreading rules apply, most famously the "5/10/40" rule: no more than 10% of assets in securities of a single issuer, and holdings above 5% may not together exceed 40%. There are separate limits on deposits, derivative counterparties and investment in other funds.

Global exposure and leverage. A UCITS must measure its exposure to derivatives using either the commitment approach (exposure no more than 100% of net assets) or value at risk. Borrowing is limited to 10% of net assets on a temporary basis.

Liquidity and dealing. UCITS must redeem at investors' request, at least twice a month. Following the 2024 amendments, managers must select at least two liquidity management tools from a harmonised list (money market funds need only one), set out in the prospectus and governed by policies.

Depositary. Each UCITS must appoint a single depositary to safekeep assets, monitor cash flows and oversee subscriptions, redemptions, valuation and compliance with the fund rules. The depositary is liable for the loss of financial instruments held in custody.

Governance and conduct. Management companies must have sound organisation, risk management separate from portfolio management, conflicts of interest arrangements, a remuneration policy and rules on delegation that prevent letter-box entities.

Investor information. A prospectus, annual and half-yearly reports and, since 2023, a PRIIPs key information document for retail investors.

UCITS VI: the 2024 amendments

Directive (EU) 2024/927 amended both the UCITS Directive and AIFMD. For UCITS it:

  • introduced the harmonised list of liquidity management tools (suspension, redemption gates, notice periods, redemption fees, swing pricing, dual pricing, anti-dilution levies, redemptions in kind and side pockets) and the requirement to choose at least two;
  • tightened rules and reporting on delegation;
  • strengthened the prohibition on charging undue costs to investors;
  • added new supervisory reporting.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • UCITS VI had to be transposed into national law by 16 April 2026.
  • The Level 2 rules on liquidity management tools apply from 16 April 2026, with existing funds given until 16 April 2027 to comply.
  • New supervisory reporting applies from 16 April 2027.
  • Further change is in negotiation through the Retail Investment Strategy (value for money and costs) and the Market Integration and Supervision Package (cross-border marketing and supervision).

Main supervisors

The fund's home member state authority authorises and supervises the UCITS and its management company. ESMA promotes consistent supervision and issues guidelines and Q&As.

What boards should watch

  • Whether the liquidity management tools chosen are realistic for the fund's assets and investors, and could be activated quickly.
  • Whether delegation leaves enough substance in the management company.
  • Undue costs: whether every cost charged to the fund is justified and disclosed.
  • Liquidity mismatches in funds that hold less liquid eligible assets.
  • How changes from the Retail Investment Strategy will affect costs, distribution and value-for-money assessments.
resources.sourcesHtml:
• UCITS Directive (2009/65/EC)
  • Directive (EU) 2024/927 (AIFMD II and UCITS VI)

resources.title: UK Consumer Duty
resources.summary: The FCA's Consumer Duty: the higher standard of care firms must give retail customers, its four outcomes, the board's role and how it is evolving.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

FCA-authorised firms whose products and services are offered to retail customers, including manufacturers and distributors along the chain. It applies to payment and e-money institutions and, from October 2027, to authorised cryptoasset firms.

It applied from 31 July 2023 for open products and from 31 July 2024 for closed products.

The three parts

The Consumer Principle: a firm must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers.

Cross-cutting rules: firms must: - act in good faith; - avoid causing foreseeable harm; - enable and support customers to pursue their financial objectives.

Four outcomes: 1. Products and services: designed to meet the needs of a target market and distributed appropriately. 2. Price and value: the price is reasonable relative to the benefits (fair value). 3. Consumer understanding: communications are clear and tested. 4. Consumer support: customers can use the product as expected and easily switch, complain or exit.

Firms must monitor outcomes, including for customers with characteristics of vulnerability, and act where outcomes are poor.

The board's role

The board (or equivalent) must review and approve an annual report assessing whether the firm is delivering good outcomes, and agree any actions. A board champion is expected.

Status (as at November 2026)

  • The Duty is in force. The FCA has published reviews of firms' fair value assessments, communications and treatment of vulnerable customers.
  • As part of its simplification agenda, the FCA has consulted on changes, including on how the Duty applies in distribution chains and to wholesale firms.
  • It underpins the UK's new Consumer Composite Investments disclosure regime and the cryptoasset regime.

What boards should watch

  • The quality of outcome data and management information, not just processes.
  • Fair value assessments, including for legacy products.
  • Outcomes for vulnerable customers.
  • The annual board report: specific, evidenced and with actions.

resources.title: UK cryptoasset regime
resources.summary: The UK's new framework for regulating cryptoasset activities under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. This guide covers who will be caught, the new regulated activities, the FCA's rules and the timetable to October 2027.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Firms carrying on new regulated activities in relation to qualifying cryptoassets, created by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026. The activities include:

  • issuing qualifying stablecoins in the UK;
  • safeguarding qualifying cryptoassets (custody);
  • operating a qualifying cryptoasset trading platform;
  • dealing in qualifying cryptoassets as principal or agent;
  • arranging deals in qualifying cryptoassets;
  • arranging qualifying cryptoasset staking.

The regime applies to firms providing services to UK consumers, including some overseas firms. The FCA's perimeter guidance explains when activities, such as some DeFi arrangements, need authorisation.

Key obligations

Authorised firms will be subject to the FCA Handbook, adapted for cryptoassets, including:

  • Threshold conditions, senior managers and certification regime, and the Consumer Duty.
  • Stablecoin issuance: backing assets, redemption at par and disclosures.
  • Custody: client asset rules, segregation and reconciliation.
  • Trading platforms and intermediaries: conduct, conflicts, order handling and best execution.
  • Prudential rules: capital and liquidity.
  • Admissions and disclosures, and market abuse: a new regime for admitting cryptoassets to trading platforms, disclosure documents, and a market abuse regime for cryptoassets.
  • Financial promotions: in place since October 2023.

Systemic stablecoins, used widely for payments, will be supervised by the Bank of England.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • The Cryptoassets Regulations were made in February 2026.
  • The FCA published its final rules on 30 June 2026 and final perimeter guidance on 16 September 2026.
  • The FCA's authorisation gateway opened on 30 September 2026 and closes on 28 February 2027 for firms that want to rely on transitional arrangements.
  • The regime comes into force on 25 October 2027. Until then, cryptoasset firms remain subject to the money laundering registration regime and the financial promotions rules.

Main supervisors

The FCA, with the Bank of England for systemic stablecoins and HM Treasury setting the legislative framework.

What boards should watch

  • Whether the firm's activities are within scope, and the deadline for applying.
  • Readiness of governance, senior manager responsibilities and the Consumer Duty.
  • Custody and client asset arrangements.
  • How the UK regime interacts with MiCA for firms operating in both.

resources.title: UK fund regime and the Overseas Funds Regime
resources.summary: The main types of UK authorised fund, the rules for marketing overseas funds to UK investors, the Overseas Funds Regime and the end of temporary permissions, and the new disclosure regime.
resources.bodyHtml:
UK authorised funds

  • UK UCITS: the onshored version of the EU UCITS regime, now governed by FCA rules (COLL). They no longer have an EU passport.
  • Non-UCITS retail schemes (NURS): retail funds with wider investment powers, for example for property.
  • Qualified investor schemes (QIS): for professional and sophisticated investors.
  • Long-term asset funds (LTAFs): for long-term, illiquid assets, with dealing no more often than monthly and at least 90 days' notice.

Legal forms include open-ended investment companies (OEICs or ICVCs), authorised unit trusts and authorised contractual schemes. Each is run by an authorised fund manager and has a depositary.

Marketing overseas funds in the UK

Overseas funds can be marketed to UK retail investors only if recognised:

  • Overseas Funds Regime (OFR): a streamlined route for funds from jurisdictions HM Treasury has found equivalent. The first decision, in 2024, covers EEA UCITS, except money market funds.
  • Section 272 recognition: an individual, more demanding route for other funds.

EEA UCITS have relied on the temporary marketing permissions regime (TMPR) since Brexit. The FCA has been moving them into the OFR, and the TMPR closes at the end of 2026.

Marketing AIFs to professional investors uses the UK national private placement regime.

Disclosure: the CCI regime

The Consumer Composite Investments (CCI) regime replaced UK PRIIPs and UCITS KIID disclosure from 6 April 2026. Manufacturers produce a more flexible product summary, with an optional transition until 8 June 2027, when the CCI regime applies in full.

Other developments (as at November 2026)

  • UK money market fund rules are being replaced by FCA rules.
  • The FCA has worked on rules to support fund tokenisation and is reviewing the UK UCITS and AIF rulebooks.
  • SDR labels and disclosures apply to UK funds but not yet to OFR funds.

What boards should watch

  • For EEA managers: OFR recognition before the TMPR ends.
  • Readiness for CCI product summaries by June 2027.
  • Consumer Duty value assessments and annual assessments of value for UK funds.
resources.sourcesHtml: • FCA: Overseas Funds Regime

resources.title: UK Money Laundering Regulations 2017
resources.summary: The main UK AML/CFT rules for firms, who they apply to, the key obligations, the 2026 amendments and how they apply to cryptoasset businesses.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (the MLRs) apply to the "regulated sector", including:

  • credit and financial institutions (banks, investment firms, fund managers, payment and e-money institutions, insurers);
  • cryptoasset exchange providers and custodian wallet providers, which must register with the FCA;
  • auditors, accountants, tax advisers, lawyers, trust and company service providers, estate agents, high-value dealers, casinos and art market participants.

Key obligations

  • Risk assessment: a documented firm-wide assessment of money laundering and terrorist financing risks.
  • Policies, controls and procedures, including a nominated officer (MLRO) and, for some firms, a board member responsible for compliance.
  • Customer due diligence, including identifying beneficial owners, with simplified and enhanced measures according to risk.
  • Enhanced due diligence for PEPs, correspondent relationships, high-risk third countries and complex or unusual transactions.
  • Ongoing monitoring, record keeping and training.
  • Reporting discrepancies in beneficial ownership information to Companies House.
  • The travel rule for cryptoasset transfers, applied since September 2023.

Suspicious activity reporting obligations sit in the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and the Terrorism Act 2000.

The 2026 amendments

The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026 came largely into force on 30 June 2026. Among other changes they:

  • limit mandatory enhanced due diligence on high-risk countries to those on the FATF's call for action list, with other higher-risk countries handled on a risk basis;
  • convert euro thresholds into sterling;
  • clarify customer due diligence requirements and reduce unnecessary over-compliance;
  • tighten controls on cryptoasset businesses, including change of control rules, with some provisions from 1 February 2027.

Supervision

The FCA supervises financial firms and cryptoasset businesses; HMRC and professional body supervisors cover other sectors. The government has announced plans to make the FCA the single professional services AML supervisor.

What boards should watch

  • Whether the firm-wide risk assessment reflects the 2026 changes.
  • EDD policies for high-risk countries.
  • For cryptoasset firms: the transition to FCA authorisation under the new regime from October 2027.

sources.title: The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/621)

resources.title: UK operational resilience (FCA and PRA rules)
resources.summary: The UK operational resilience framework for financial firms: important business services, impact tolerances, mapping and testing, the new incident and third-party reporting rules, and the critical third parties regime.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Banks, building societies, PRA-designated investment firms and insurers (PRA and FCA rules).
  • Enhanced firms under the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, recognised investment exchanges, and payment and e-money institutions (FCA rules).

Other FCA-regulated firms are subject to general systems and controls and business continuity requirements, and to the new incident reporting rules.

Key requirements

  • Identify important business services: services whose disruption could cause intolerable harm to clients or risk to market integrity (FCA), or threaten the firm's safety and soundness or financial stability (PRA).
  • Set impact tolerances: the maximum tolerable disruption for each service, usually expressed as a time limit.
  • Map the people, processes, technology, facilities and information that support each service.
  • Test the ability to remain within tolerances in severe but plausible scenarios.
  • Self-assessment: a written assessment, approved by the board, kept up to date.
  • Communications plans for disruption.
  • Lessons learned and remediation.

Firms had to be able to remain within impact tolerances by 31 March 2025.

New incident and third-party reporting rules

The FCA (PS26/2) and PRA (PS7/26) published final rules in March 2026, which come into force on 18 March 2027. They require:

  • reporting of operational incidents that meet set thresholds, using a single form with initial, intermediate and final stages;
  • notifying regulators of material third-party arrangements and keeping a register of them.

Critical third parties

Under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023, HM Treasury can designate third parties, such as major cloud providers, as critical third parties, bringing them under direct oversight by the Bank of England, PRA and FCA.

What boards should watch

  • That the important business services and tolerances reflect harm to clients, not just current capability.
  • Results of scenario testing and remediation.
  • Readiness for the March 2027 reporting rules.
  • Dependence on third parties, including group entities.

resources.title: UK payments and e-money: PSRs, EMRs and safeguarding
resources.summary: The UK framework for payment and e-money firms: the Payment Services Regulations 2017, the Electronic Money Regulations 2011, the FCA's safeguarding rules and the planned reforms. This guide covers who is caught, the main obligations and what boards should watch.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • Authorised and small payment institutions under the Payment Services Regulations 2017 (PSRs).
  • Authorised and small e-money institutions under the Electronic Money Regulations 2011 (EMRs).
  • Account information and payment initiation service providers, agents and distributors.
  • Banks, for the conduct of payment services.

Key obligations

  • Authorisation or registration with the FCA, including capital, governance and fit and proper management.
  • Conduct of business: information requirements, rights and obligations, liability for unauthorised payments, strong customer authentication and open banking access.
  • Safeguarding: relevant funds must be protected from the day they are received.
  • Consumer Duty: payment and e-money firms must deliver good outcomes for retail customers.
  • AML/CFT: the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 apply.
  • APP fraud reimbursement: since October 2024, payment providers in Faster Payments must reimburse most victims of authorised push payment fraud, up to a set limit, under rules set by the Payment Systems Regulator.

The safeguarding regime

The FCA's new safeguarding rules (CASS 15 and related rules), which took effect on 7 May 2026, add to the PSRs and EMRs. They require:

  • a resolution pack to help return funds quickly if the firm fails;
  • daily reconciliations and better records;
  • a monthly safeguarding return to the FCA;
  • an annual safeguarding audit for firms holding relevant funds above a threshold;
  • a named senior manager responsible for safeguarding.

A second stage, replacing the legislative requirements with a trust-based regime, depends on the government's wider reforms.

Status and key dates (as at November 2026)

  • HM Treasury consulted from July to October 2026 on modernising payment services regulation. It proposes moving most detailed requirements from the PSRs and EMRs into FCA rules, strengthening senior accountability and adapting the framework for new technologies, including stablecoins and agentic AI.
  • The government has announced that the Payment Systems Regulator will be merged into the FCA.

Main supervisors

The FCA, the Payment Systems Regulator for payment systems (until it is merged into the FCA), and the Bank of England for systemic payment systems.

What boards should watch

  • Safeguarding compliance under the new rules, including reconciliation breaks and audit findings.
  • The quality of the resolution pack and wind-down plan.
  • Fraud losses and reimbursement costs.
  • Consumer Duty outcomes and annual board report.
  • The direction of HM Treasury's reforms.

resources.title: UK Senior Managers and Certification Regime
resources.summary: The UK's individual accountability regime for financial services: senior managers, certification and conduct rules, and the 2026 reforms including the planned removal of the Certification Regime.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

Almost all firms authorised under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, including banks, insurers, investment firms, asset managers and consumer credit firms. Cryptoasset firms authorised under the new regime from October 2027 will also be covered. Payment and e-money institutions are not currently in scope.

The three parts

1. Senior Managers Regime - Individuals in senior management functions (SMFs), such as chief executive, chair, compliance oversight and the MLRO, must be approved by the regulator. - Each has a statement of responsibilities, and firms allocate prescribed responsibilities. - Larger firms keep a management responsibilities map. - The duty of responsibility means a senior manager can be held accountable if the firm breaches requirements in their area and they did not take reasonable steps to prevent it.

2. Certification Regime - Firms must assess as fit and proper, at least annually, staff who are not senior managers but whose roles could cause significant harm.

3. Conduct Rules - Basic standards of behaviour that apply to almost all staff, with extra rules for senior managers.

The 2026 reforms

  • Phase 1 (FCA PS26/6 and PRA PS12/26, effective 24 April 2026): firms have 12 weeks to submit an SMF application, rather than to obtain approval, and other changes reduce the administrative burden, including fewer overlapping certification roles.
  • Phase 2 (consultations published 22 October 2026): proposals, dependent on new legislation, to remove the Certification Regime from statute and to replace pre-approval with notification for some SMF roles. Firms would still need to ensure staff are fit and proper.

What boards should watch

  • Clear allocation of responsibilities with no gaps, especially for new activities such as crypto and AI.
  • Evidence of reasonable steps by senior managers.
  • How the firm will maintain fitness and propriety checks if the Certification Regime is removed.

resources.title: UK Sustainability Disclosure Requirements (SDR) and labels
resources.summary: The UK's regime for sustainability claims, product labels, naming and marketing, and disclosures for asset managers, and where its extension stands.
resources.bodyHtml:
Who is caught

  • All FCA-authorised firms for the anti-greenwashing rule.
  • UK asset managers of UK funds for labels, naming and marketing, and disclosures.
  • Distributors of in-scope products to UK retail investors, who must pass on labels and disclosures.

The rules were set in FCA policy statement PS23/16 (November 2023).

The main elements

Anti-greenwashing rule. Since 31 May 2024, any reference to the sustainability characteristics of a product or service must be consistent with those characteristics and be fair, clear and not misleading.

Labels. Since 31 July 2024, managers can use one of four voluntary labels if a product meets the criteria, including a sustainability objective, at least 70% of assets invested in line with it, and robust evidence and stewardship:

  • Sustainability Focus: assets that are environmentally or socially sustainable.
  • Sustainability Improvers: assets with the potential to improve their sustainability over time.
  • Sustainability Impact: assets that achieve a positive, measurable impact.
  • Sustainability Mixed Goals: a combination of the above.

Naming and marketing. Since December 2024 (with a temporary extension to April 2025 for some firms), products without a label may use sustainability-related terms in their names and marketing only if they meet conditions, including a statement that they do not have a label.

Disclosures. Consumer-facing disclosures, pre-contractual and ongoing product-level disclosures, and entity-level disclosures for larger managers: from December 2025 for those with more than £50 billion of assets under management and from 2 December 2026 for those with more than £5 billion.

Status (as at November 2026)

  • The regime is in force for UK funds.
  • The FCA paused its plan to extend SDR to portfolio management in 2025 and still intends to extend it to portfolio management and overseas funds, with timing not confirmed.
  • UK SDR labels and EU SFDR categories differ, which matters for firms operating in both.

What boards should watch

  • Evidence for any label and its ongoing criteria.
  • Compliance with the anti-greenwashing rule in all communications.
  • Readiness for entity-level disclosures.

resources.title: US stablecoins (GENIUS Act) and crypto market structure
resources.summary: The US federal framework for payment stablecoins under the GENIUS Act, its implementation timetable, and the state of US crypto market structure legislation and agency rule-making.
resources.bodyHtml:
The GENIUS Act

The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins Act, signed on 18 July 2025, creates a federal framework for payment stablecoins: digital assets designed to be used for payment and redeemable for a fixed amount of money.

Who may issue: only permitted payment stablecoin issuers: - subsidiaries of insured banks, supervised by their federal regulator; - federal qualified issuers, licensed by the OCC; - state qualified issuers, under state regimes certified as substantially similar, for issuers with up to $10 billion in issue.

Foreign issuers can access the US market if their home regime is comparable and they meet conditions.

Key requirements: - Reserves at least one-to-one in cash, deposits, short-term US Treasuries, repos and money market funds investing in these. - Monthly public reserve reports, examined by an accountant and certified by senior management. - Redemption at par, with published procedures and timely payment. - No interest or yield paid by the issuer to holders. - AML/CFT and sanctions: issuers are financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act and must be able to freeze and seize tokens. - Priority for holders if the issuer becomes insolvent. - Payment stablecoins are not securities or commodities, and are not insured deposits.

Implementation: the OCC adopted its final rule on 21 October 2026. The Act and the rule take effect on 18 January 2027. AML and sanctions rules are being set separately with the Treasury.

Market structure

  • The CLARITY Act, which would divide jurisdiction over crypto-asset markets between the SEC (digital securities) and the CFTC (digital commodities), passed the House in July 2025. It failed a procedural vote in the Senate in September 2026, and passage in the current Congress is uncertain.
  • Meanwhile, the SEC has proposed rules for crypto-assets (August 2026) and launched an exemption for tokenised securities trading venues, and the CFTC is developing its own crypto market rules.
  • States continue to license crypto businesses, for example New York's BitLicense.

Main supervisors

The OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, state regulators and the Treasury (including FinCEN and OFAC) for stablecoins; the SEC and CFTC for markets.

What boards should watch (non-US firms too)

  • Whether stablecoins the firm uses or offers will be permitted in the US from January 2027.
  • Comparability of the firm's home regime for foreign issuers.
  • Interaction with MiCA and UK rules for firms operating in several markets.
resources.sourcesHtml: • OCC: GENIUS Act final rule (October 2026)

resources.title: AML/CFT oversight and the MLRO's report
resources.summary: Questions to test whether the firm's anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing controls work, and how the board should use the MLRO's report.
resources.bodyHtml:
Senior management and the board are accountable for the firm's AML/CFT framework. The MLRO's report is the board's main window on it and should be read critically, not just noted.

The risk assessment

  • Has the board approved a business-wide risk assessment, and does it reflect our actual clients, products, channels and geographies?
  • How has our risk changed in the last year: new products, new markets, new types of clients or new typologies?
  • Is our risk appetite for high-risk clients, countries and activities clear, and is it followed?

The controls

  • How many customers are high risk, PEPs or from high-risk countries, and are their reviews up to date?
  • What is the backlog of customer due diligence reviews, periodic reviews and alerts, and is it growing?
  • How well does transaction monitoring work? How many alerts lead to suspicious activity reports?
  • How are sanctions screened, and how quickly are new designations applied?
  • What did the last independent review or internal audit of AML/CFT find, and are the actions closed?

A good answer combines data and trends with the MLRO's own judgment, including where the MLRO is not satisfied.

The MLRO

  • Does the MLRO have enough seniority, independence, resources and access to the board?
  • Does the MLRO's report set out problems and what is needed to fix them, or only activity?
  • When did the board last meet the MLRO without management present?

Red flags: an MLRO's report that is the same every year; alert or review backlogs that keep growing; no suspicious activity reports, or many reports filed late; the MLRO role combined with heavy commercial duties.
resources.sourcesHtml: • EU AML Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1624)

resources.title: Annual board calendar and standing agenda
resources.summary: A model annual calendar and standing agenda for a financial services board, so that every key matter gets attention at the right time.
resources.bodyHtml:
Every meeting

  • Declarations of interest.
  • Minutes and action log.
  • CEO report and key performance indicators.
  • Risk report against risk appetite, and key risk indicators.
  • Compliance report, including breaches and regulatory matters.
  • Committee reports.
  • Any decisions required.

Through the year (example)

Quarter Main items
Q1 Annual financial statements and audit findings; MLRO annual report; annual compliance plan review
Q2 Strategy review; risk appetite review; operational resilience self-assessment; Consumer Duty annual report (UK)
Q3 Board effectiveness review; skills matrix and succession; policy reviews; ICT and cyber review
Q4 Business plan and budget; internal audit plan; remuneration policy review; service provider and delegate reviews

Funds also cover, during the year, half-yearly accounts, valuation and liquidity reviews, fund-level performance and costs, depositary reports and distribution reviews.

Tips

  • Leave space on each agenda for strategic discussion, not only reporting.
  • Put the most important items early, when attention is highest.
  • Track that every item on the calendar was actually covered.
  • Review the calendar each year as regulation and the business change.
resources.sortKey: annual board calendar and standing agenda

resources.title: Asking good questions: techniques for directors
resources.summary: Practical techniques for asking questions in the boardroom that get useful answers, with examples of open, probing and closing questions.
resources.bodyHtml:
The questions a director asks shape what the board learns. Good questions are short, specific and open, and are followed up until they get a real answer.

Types of question

Type Purpose Example
Open Gets the full picture "Talk us through how this risk arose."
Probing Tests depth and evidence "How do you know? What data supports that?"
Hypothetical Tests the downside "What happens if the largest client leaves?"
Comparative Gives context "How does this compare with last year, or with our peers?"
Reflective Checks understanding "So what you are saying is... Is that right?"
Closing Pins down action "Who will do what, by when, and when will we hear back?"

Techniques

  • Start broad, then narrow. Open questions first, then specific ones.
  • One question at a time. Multiple questions let the answer choose the easiest.
  • Listen for what is not said. Note what the answer avoids, and ask again.
  • Ask for evidence. "Can we see the data?" or "Has anyone independent looked at this?"
  • Use silence. After an answer, a pause often brings out more.
  • Ask what keeps people awake. "What worries you most about this that is not in the paper?"
  • Ask the control functions directly. "Is the risk function comfortable with this?" Ask them, not the business.

Questions worth asking regularly

  • "What would you cut from this pack if you had to halve it?"
  • "What has gone wrong since we last met that is not in the papers?"
  • "What did the board decide not to get involved in, and why?"
  • "What would make us change our minds?"
resources.sortKey: asking good questions: techniques for directors

resources.title: Audit committee terms of reference
resources.summary: Model terms of reference for an audit committee of a financial services firm, to adapt to its size and structure.
resources.bodyHtml:
Membership

  • At least three members, all non-executive and a majority independent, including the chair.
  • At least one member with recent and relevant financial experience.
  • Members appointed by the board for a set term.

Meetings

  • At least four times a year, aligned with the financial reporting cycle.
  • The external auditor and head of internal audit attend as needed and meet the committee privately at least once a year.
  • Quorum of two members.

Responsibilities

Financial reporting - Review the financial statements and significant judgments. - Review accounting policies and changes.

Internal controls and risk - Review the effectiveness of internal controls over financial reporting, where no separate risk committee does so.

Internal audit - Approve the internal audit charter and plan. - Review reports and the implementation of actions. - Review the effectiveness and resources of internal audit.

External audit - Recommend the appointment, reappointment or removal of the auditor. - Approve audit fees and the policy on non-audit services. - Assess independence, objectivity and audit quality.

Whistleblowing - Review arrangements for staff to raise concerns, where not covered by the board.

Reporting

  • Report to the board after each meeting.
  • Review its own effectiveness and terms of reference annually.

resources.title: Board chair
resources.summary: What the chair of a financial services board is for, the main responsibilities, what good looks like and the red flags.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

The chair leads the board and is responsible for its effectiveness. A good chair makes sure the board focuses on the right issues, gets the right information and reaches sound decisions with real challenge.

Main responsibilities

  • Set the board agenda with the CEO and company secretary, keeping strategy, risk and culture in view.
  • Make sure directors receive accurate, timely and clear information.
  • Lead meetings so that all directors contribute and challenge is encouraged.
  • Build a constructive relationship between the board and management, and between executive and non-executive directors.
  • Lead board effectiveness reviews, succession planning and the induction and development of directors.
  • Act as the main contact for the regulator and, where relevant, shareholders on governance matters.
  • Hold the CEO to account on behalf of the board.

What good looks like

  • Curates the agenda rather than just approving it.
  • Draws out quieter directors and limits those who dominate.
  • Brings discussion to a clear decision and makes sure the rationale is minuted.
  • Deals with underperforming directors and conflict directly.
  • Is independent of management, ideally on appointment.
  • Has the time to do the job, including in a crisis.

Red flags

  • Dominates discussion or answers on behalf of the CEO.
  • Is too close to the CEO or major shareholder.
  • Meetings regularly overrun or leave items unaddressed.
  • Board effectiveness reviews are skipped or produce no change.
  • The chair has many other demanding roles.

resources.title: Board effectiveness review: self-assessment or external?
resources.summary: How to choose between an internal and an externally facilitated board effectiveness review, what a good review covers and how to make sure it leads to change.
resources.bodyHtml:
A board effectiveness review asks whether the board is doing its job well and what would make it better. Most governance codes expect an annual review, with an external review every few years.

Choosing the approach

Internal review External review
How Questionnaire or interviews led by the chair or company secretary An independent facilitator interviews directors, observes meetings and reviews papers
Strengths Cheaper, quicker, directors know the context More candid answers, fresh perspective, benchmarking against other boards
Weaknesses Directors may hold back; the chair is reviewing their own leadership Cost; the facilitator needs time to understand the business
When Most years Every two to three years, or when the board has changed a lot or has problems

Check that an external facilitator has no other links to the firm or its directors.

What a good review covers

  • Composition: skills, experience, independence, diversity and succession.
  • Information: the quality and timeliness of papers and management information.
  • Meetings: the agenda, use of time, quality of discussion and challenge.
  • Committees: whether their roles are clear and they report back effectively.
  • The chair: leadership, how they draw out views and manage conflict.
  • Individual directors: contribution, time commitment and development needs.
  • Relationships: with management, control functions, auditors and the regulator.

Making it count

  • Agree a short list of actions with owners and dates, and track them at board meetings.
  • Feed findings into the skills matrix, succession plan and director training.
  • Report briefly on the review and its outcome where governance codes or the regulator expect it.

A useful question: "When was your last review, what did it find, and what changed as a result?"
resources.sortKey: board effectiveness review: self-assessment or external?

resources.title: Board of a crypto-asset service provider
resources.summary: The role, responsibilities and particular challenges of the board of a crypto-asset service provider.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

The board of a CASP is responsible for the firm's strategy, governance and compliance with crypto regulation such as MiCA or the UK regime, and for protecting clients' assets in a fast-moving, high-risk market.

Main responsibilities

  • Approve the strategy, business plan and risk appetite, including which crypto-assets and services to offer.
  • Oversee custody and protection of client assets, including key management, segregation and reconciliation.
  • Oversee conflicts of interest, especially where the firm combines trading platform, brokerage, market making, lending or staking.
  • Oversee AML/CFT, the travel rule and sanctions.
  • Oversee ICT and cyber risk, under DORA where it applies.
  • Oversee market abuse surveillance and the listing of crypto-assets.
  • Approve key policies and the wind-down plan.

What good looks like

  • Directors with real crypto, technology, financial crime and regulatory expertise.
  • Strong independent challenge, not a board dominated by founders or the group.
  • Clear oversight of group entities and outsourcing outside the jurisdiction.
  • Regular deep dives on custody, financial crime and incidents.

Red flags

  • Founders control the board and key decisions.
  • Treasury, client assets and group assets are mixed.
  • Rapid launch of new tokens or services without risk review.
  • Heavy dependence on a parent outside the regulated jurisdiction.
resources.sortKey: board of a crypto-asset service provider

resources.title: Board of a payment or e-money institution
resources.summary: The role, responsibilities and particular challenges of the board of a payment or e-money institution.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

The board of a payment or e-money institution is responsible for the firm's strategy, governance and compliance, and above all for protecting customers' money, which is not covered by deposit guarantee schemes.

Main responsibilities

  • Approve the strategy, business plan and risk appetite.
  • Oversee safeguarding: arrangements, reconciliations, audits and the resolution pack.
  • Oversee financial crime controls, including AML/CFT, sanctions and fraud.
  • Oversee capital and liquidity.
  • Oversee operational resilience, cyber and third parties, including banking partners and agents.
  • Oversee agents and distributors.
  • Oversee consumer outcomes, complaints and fraud reimbursement.
  • Maintain an up-to-date wind-down plan.

What good looks like

  • Independent directors with payments, financial crime and operational expertise.
  • Regular, detailed safeguarding reporting with breaks explained.
  • Clear oversight of growth through partners and embedded finance arrangements.

Red flags

  • Safeguarding treated as an operational detail.
  • Rapid growth outpacing financial crime controls.
  • Dependence on a single bank that could close accounts.
  • Weak oversight of agents and programme partners.
resources.sortKey: board of a payment or e-money institution

resources.title: Board skills matrix
resources.summary: How to build and use a board skills matrix to identify gaps and guide appointments and training.
resources.bodyHtml:
Step 1: decide what skills the board needs

Start from the strategy and main risks. A financial services board typically needs:

  • sector and business model knowledge;
  • financial reporting and audit;
  • risk management;
  • legal and regulatory, including AML/CFT;
  • investment management or markets (for funds and investment firms);
  • technology, cyber and data;
  • digital assets, payments or other specialist areas relevant to the business;
  • governance and leadership;
  • customer and conduct;
  • sustainability.

Step 2: assess each director

For each skill, rate each director, for example as expert, experienced or basic. Ask directors to self-assess, then calibrate with the chair.

Step 3: identify gaps

  • Skills where no one is expert.
  • Skills held by only one director (key-person risk).
  • Skills that will matter more as strategy changes.

Step 4: act

  • Use gaps to define the profile for new appointments.
  • Arrange training for existing directors.
  • Use external advisers or committee co-optees where appropriate.

Step 5: keep it current

Review annually, as part of the board evaluation and whenever strategy or membership changes. Some regulators expect to see the matrix and how it is used.

resources.title: Breaches, errors and escalation
resources.summary: Questions for a board on how breaches, errors and incidents are identified, escalated, fixed and reported.
resources.bodyHtml:
Identification

  • How are breaches and errors identified, and by whom?
  • Do we have a breaches and errors register, and does the board see it?
  • What proportion are found by us, rather than by clients, auditors or regulators?

Escalation and reporting

  • What are the thresholds for escalating to senior management, the board and the regulator?
  • Were any reportable breaches reported late, or not at all?
  • How are investors or clients compensated, and how is that calculated and checked?

Root causes

  • What are the main causes, and are we fixing them, not just the individual cases?
  • Are the same types of breach recurring?
  • Are breaches linked to particular delegates, systems or teams?

A good answer shows a trend analysis, root-cause actions and timely reporting.

Red flags: very few breaches recorded (suggesting under-reporting); repeated breaches of the same kind; compensation decided by the business without independent check.

resources.title: Chief risk officer
resources.summary: The role of the chief risk officer: purpose, responsibilities, independence, what good looks like and red flags.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

The CRO leads the independent risk management function, ensuring the firm identifies, measures, monitors and manages its risks within the board's risk appetite.

Main responsibilities

  • Develop and maintain the risk management framework and risk appetite.
  • Provide an independent view of risks in strategy, business plans and major decisions.
  • Monitor risk exposures and limits, and escalate breaches.
  • Oversee stress testing and capital and liquidity assessments.
  • Report to the board and risk committee.
  • For fund managers: oversee investment, liquidity, counterparty and operational risk for each fund, independently of portfolio management.

Independence

The CRO should report to the board or risk committee, be able to veto or escalate decisions, and not have pay tied to business results.

What good looks like

  • Involved early in strategy and new products.
  • Willing to challenge senior management.
  • Clear, forward-looking risk reporting.

Red flags

  • The CRO is brought in after decisions are made.
  • Risk reporting is backward-looking and descriptive.
  • The CRO reports through the business they oversee.

resources.title: Conflicts of interest
resources.summary: Questions to test whether the firm identifies, manages and records conflicts of interest, including those of directors, the group and key service providers.
resources.bodyHtml:
Conflicts are unavoidable in financial services. What matters is whether they are identified, managed fairly and disclosed where they cannot be managed. Directors must also manage their own.

Identifying conflicts

  • Is there a conflicts of interest policy and a register, and when was the register last reviewed by the board?
  • Does the register cover conflicts between the firm and clients, between clients, within the group and with service providers?
  • How are new conflicts identified when the firm launches a product, enters a market or takes on a service provider?

A good answer shows a register that changes over time, not one that has looked the same for years.

Managing them

  • For each significant conflict, what controls manage it, and how do we know they work?
  • How are related-party transactions, such as use of group service providers or cross-trades between funds, approved and priced?
  • How are gifts, hospitality, personal account dealing and outside interests of staff controlled?
  • Which conflicts cannot be managed, and how are they disclosed to clients or investors?

Directors' own conflicts

  • Are directors' interests declared at the start of every meeting and recorded in the minutes?
  • How does the board deal with a director who has a conflict on an item: do they leave the discussion?
  • Does any director have links to the promoter, investment manager or a major service provider that affect their independence?

Red flags: a register with no entries for the group; related-party fees never benchmarked; directors who never declare an interest; disclosure used as the default answer to every conflict.

resources.title: Conflicts register
resources.summary: What a conflicts of interest register should contain and how to keep it useful.
resources.bodyHtml:
What to record for each conflict

  • A description of the conflict and who it involves.
  • Its type: firm and client, between clients, group, service provider, personal (staff or directors).
  • Where it arises: product, service, activity or relationship.
  • The potential harm and its likelihood.
  • The controls in place: separation, information barriers, independent review, pricing checks, disclosure.
  • The owner responsible.
  • Whether it is managed or, if it cannot be managed, disclosed to clients.
  • Review date.

Typical entries for asset managers

  • Allocation of trades and investment opportunities between funds.
  • Cross trades between funds.
  • Use of group service providers and their fees.
  • Personal account dealing and outside interests.
  • Gifts, hospitality and inducements.
  • Remuneration linked to sales of particular products.
  • Valuation of assets where fees depend on value.

Keeping it useful

  • Review it at least annually, and when the business changes.
  • Link it to the conflicts policy and the risk register.
  • Report material changes and new conflicts to the board.
  • Test whether controls actually work.

resources.title: Crypto custody and key management
resources.summary: Questions for the board of a crypto-asset firm on how client assets and private keys are held, segregated and protected, and what would happen if keys were lost or stolen.
resources.bodyHtml:
Whoever controls the private keys controls the crypto-assets. Losses through hacks, insider theft, lost keys and commingled client assets have been among the largest harms in the sector. Under MiCA, custodians are liable to clients for losses of crypto-assets they hold.

Ownership and segregation

  • Are client crypto-assets legally and operationally separate from the firm's own assets, and would they be protected if the firm became insolvent?
  • Do we hold client assets in individual or omnibus wallets, and how do we reconcile our records with what is on-chain?
  • How often are reconciliations done, who checks them, and how are differences resolved?
  • Is there an independent proof of reserves or assurance report, and what does it cover, including liabilities?

A good answer shows daily on-chain reconciliations and a clear legal analysis of how client assets are protected on insolvency.

Keys

  • What share of assets is held in cold, warm and hot wallets, and how are the limits set?
  • How are keys generated, stored, backed up and recovered? Do we use hardware security modules, multi-signature or MPC?
  • How many people are needed to move assets, and can any single person or small group do it alone?
  • How are key holders vetted, and what happens when they leave?

Third parties and incidents

  • If we use a sub-custodian or technology provider, what due diligence have we done and what are our rights if it fails?
  • What is our plan if keys are compromised or a wallet is drained, and has it been rehearsed?
  • Do we have insurance, what does it actually cover, and how do the limits compare with assets held?

Red flags: reconciliations done weekly or less; a few staff able to move large amounts; insurance limits far below client assets; client and firm assets in the same wallets.
resources.sourcesHtml: • MiCA (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114)

resources.title: Culture, conduct and speaking up
resources.summary: Questions for a board on whether the firm's culture supports good conduct and whether staff feel able to speak up.
resources.bodyHtml:
The culture we want

  • Have we defined the culture and behaviours we expect, and do staff recognise them?
  • How do our purpose, strategy, incentives and leadership behaviours reinforce them?

Evidence

  • What do staff surveys, exit interviews, complaints, conduct breaches and disciplinary cases tell us?
  • Are there pockets of the business with different results?
  • How do customers and investors experience us?

Speaking up

  • How many concerns are raised through whistleblowing and other channels, and what happens to them?
  • Do staff believe they can raise concerns without detriment? How do we know?
  • Who on the board oversees whistleblowing, and do they see the cases?
  • Have we acted on concerns raised, and told staff what changed?

Consequences

  • Are poor behaviours addressed regardless of seniority or performance?
  • Does remuneration reflect conduct as well as results?

A good answer draws on several sources of evidence and shows action where culture falls short.

Red flags: very few concerns raised; the same issues recurring; high performers exempt from consequences; culture discussed only once a year.

resources.title: Cyber security and incident response
resources.summary: Questions to test the firm's cyber defences, how it detects and responds to attacks, and whether the board is ready to lead through a serious cyber incident.
resources.bodyHtml:
Cyber risk is one of the most likely ways a financial firm will suffer a severe disruption or loss. Boards do not need to be technical, but they need to know the firm's main exposures and how a crisis would be handled.

Exposure

  • What are our most valuable assets to an attacker: client data, money, private keys, trading systems or access to other firms?
  • What are the main threats to firms like ours, such as ransomware, phishing, insider threats, supply chain attacks or social engineering of payment staff?
  • How do we know our defences work? When were they last tested by someone independent?

A good answer sets out a short list of priority risks, tested controls and an improvement plan with dates.

Basics

  • Is multi-factor authentication used for all remote and privileged access?
  • How quickly are critical security patches applied?
  • Are backups kept offline and has restoring them been tested?
  • How are staff trained to spot phishing and social engineering, and how often do they fail tests?

When it happens

  • Is there an incident response plan with clear roles, including who decides on shutting systems down, contacting law enforcement and paying ransoms?
  • Has the board taken part in a cyber crisis exercise?
  • Do we know our regulatory and contractual notification deadlines and who makes the calls?
  • Do we have specialist incident response support and, if relevant, cyber insurance in place before we need it?

Red flags: cyber reports full of technical metrics with no assessment; critical patches outstanding for months; a board that has never rehearsed a cyber incident; no agreed position on ransom payments.

resources.title: Data quality and management information
resources.summary: Questions for a board on whether the data and management information it relies on are accurate, complete and useful for decisions.
resources.bodyHtml:
The information we get

  • Does our management information tell us what we need to know to oversee the business and its risks?
  • Is it concise, focused on trends and exceptions, and clear about what we are asked to decide?
  • What do we receive too much of, and what is missing?

Where it comes from

  • Do we know the main sources of the data in our reports, and the manual steps involved?
  • Who owns each key data set, and who checks its quality?
  • How much depends on spreadsheets and individuals?
  • How much of our information is produced or summarised by AI tools, and how is it validated?

Trust in the numbers

  • When was the accuracy of our key reports last independently checked?
  • Have we found significant data errors in the last year? What caused them?
  • Do regulatory reports and board reports reconcile?

Investment

  • Is there a plan and budget to improve data quality where it matters most?

Red flags: different numbers for the same thing in different reports; heavy reliance on manual workarounds; data issues discovered by regulators or auditors before management.

resources.title: DeFi, smart-contract and bridge exposure
resources.summary: Questions for the board of a firm that uses, holds or provides access to DeFi protocols, smart contracts or bridges, on the risks and controls involved.
resources.bodyHtml:
Where are we exposed?

  • Which protocols, smart contracts and bridges do we use, directly or through clients, and how much value is at stake in each?
  • Do we hold wrapped tokens or liquid staking tokens whose value depends on a bridge or protocol?
  • Do we provide access to DeFi for clients, and under what regulatory permissions?

Due diligence

  • How do we assess a protocol before using it: audits, track record, value locked, governance, admin keys, oracles?
  • Who controls the protocol's upgrades, and is there a timelock?
  • How do we monitor for exploits, governance changes or de-pegging after we start?

Limits and response

  • What limits do we set on exposure to any one protocol or bridge?
  • Could we exit quickly if a protocol were exploited, and what would we lose?
  • Do we have an incident plan for a protocol failure, including client communications?

Regulation and financial crime

  • How do we screen counterparties and flows in DeFi for sanctions and AML risk?
  • Have we analysed whether our DeFi activity needs authorisation?

Red flags: exposure to unaudited or recently deployed protocols; reliance on a single bridge; no monitoring after entry; no legal analysis of the activity.

resources.title: Delegation framework
resources.summary: How to design a framework that sets out what the board delegates, to whom, with what limits, and how it is held to account.
resources.bodyHtml:
A delegation framework makes clear who can take which decisions. It protects the board's role on key matters and lets management run the business efficiently.

Components

  • Matters reserved for the board.
  • Committee terms of reference, setting out what each committee decides or recommends.
  • Delegated authorities to the CEO and onward to executives, with financial and other limits.
  • External delegation, such as portfolio management or administration delegated to other firms, with contracts and oversight.

Design principles

  • Every important decision has a clear owner.
  • Limits are specific: amounts, types of transaction, risk levels.
  • Decisions outside limits go back up the chain.
  • Delegation is consistent with the risk appetite and regulatory responsibilities, such as senior manager responsibilities.

Accountability

  • Regular reporting on decisions made under delegation.
  • Periodic review of whether limits are respected.
  • Internal audit coverage of the framework.

Review

Review at least annually, and when the business, people or regulation change.

resources.title: Depositary, administrator and transfer agent oversight
resources.summary: Questions for a fund board on how it oversees the depositary, administrator and transfer agent.
resources.bodyHtml:
The depositary

  • What exceptions has the depositary raised this period, and how were they resolved?
  • How does it oversee sub-custodians, especially in higher-risk markets?
  • How does it verify assets that cannot be held in custody?
  • Do we meet the depositary directly, without management?

The administrator

  • How many NAV errors and pricing exceptions were there, and what caused them?
  • Is the NAV delivered on time?
  • What did the administrator's latest controls report (such as an ISAE 3402 or SOC 1) say?

The transfer agent

  • How many dealing errors and complaints were there?
  • What is the backlog of investor due diligence reviews?
  • How are nominee and distributor relationships assessed for AML?

Across all three

  • Are service levels being met, and how is that measured?
  • Have there been changes in their staffing, systems or ownership?
  • When did we last carry out a full review or visit?
  • Are any of them in the same group as the manager, and how are conflicts managed?

Red flags: reports from providers simply passed to the board; findings that stay open; no direct contact with the depositary.
resources.sortKey: depositary, administrator and transfer agent oversight

resources.title: Director induction pack
resources.summary: What a new director should receive and do in their first months, so they can contribute fully and quickly.
resources.bodyHtml:
Documents to provide

  • Constitutional documents, the schedule of matters reserved and committee terms of reference.
  • The strategy, business plan and budget.
  • The risk appetite statement, latest risk register and key risk reports.
  • The last year of board and committee packs and minutes, including the action log.
  • Recent internal audit, compliance, MLRO and external audit reports.
  • Regulatory correspondence, open findings and any remediation programmes.
  • Organisation chart, key people and responsibilities map.
  • Key policies, such as conflicts of interest, valuation, AML/CFT and outsourcing.
  • For funds: prospectus, latest financial statements, service provider agreements and reports.
  • Directors' and officers' insurance and indemnity details.

Meetings to arrange

  • The chair, the CEO and the company secretary.
  • Heads of risk, compliance, internal audit, finance and the MLRO.
  • The external auditor and, for funds, the depositary.
  • Key business heads and, where useful, major delegates.

In the first months

  • Site visits to key operations and service providers.
  • Training on the firm's regulatory regime and any specialist areas.
  • An early conversation with the chair on how the board works and what the new director is expected to contribute.
  • A check-in after six months on what the induction missed.

resources.title: Distribution, product governance and target market
resources.summary: Questions for a fund or management company board on whether funds reach the investors they were designed for, how distributors are overseen and whether investors get fair outcomes.
resources.bodyHtml:
A fund can be well managed and still cause harm if it is sold to the wrong investors. Product governance rules require manufacturers to define a target market, test the product and check that it reaches the investors it was designed for.

Designing the product

  • For each fund, who is the target market, and who should not buy it?
  • Was the fund tested before launch, including its costs, liquidity and how it would perform in stress?
  • How often is each fund reviewed to confirm it still meets the needs of its target market?

A good answer describes a product approval and review process with clear outputs that reach the board.

Distribution

  • Through which channels and in which countries are the funds sold, and who are the largest distributors?
  • What information do we receive from distributors about who actually buys the funds?
  • How are distributors selected, monitored and, if necessary, terminated?
  • Is any marketing aimed at retail investors in a fund designed for professionals?

A good answer compares sales data with the target market and investigates sales outside it.

Investor outcomes

  • Do investors get value from the fund after all costs, compared with similar products?
  • What complaints have we received, and what do they tell us about the product or how it is sold?
  • Are marketing materials fair, clear and not misleading, and who approves them?

Red flags: no data on end investors; distributors chosen only on the volume they bring in; marketing approved only by the sales team; target market definitions so broad they exclude nobody.
resources.sourcesHtml: • MiFID II (2014/65/EU)
resources.sortKey: distribution, product governance and target market

resources.title: Due diligence before accepting a directorship
resources.summary: A checklist for anyone considering a board appointment: what to find out about the firm, the board, the role and your own exposure before you say yes.
resources.bodyHtml:
Directors take on personal legal and regulatory responsibility. Accepting a board seat without proper due diligence is one of the commonest regrets of directors whose firms later run into trouble.

The firm

  • What does the firm do, how does it make money, and what is its financial position? Read the last two or three sets of accounts and the business plan.
  • Who owns and controls it? Are there shareholders, promoters or group companies whose interests might conflict with those of clients or investors?
  • What is its regulatory history: authorisations, conditions, enforcement action, open investigations, recent inspections and findings?
  • What do the press, litigation searches and online sources say about the firm and its key people?

The board and governance

  • Read the last year of board packs and minutes. Does the board challenge, and are actions followed through?
  • Who are the other directors and the chair? Is there enough independence and relevant expertise?
  • Are there committees, and do they work? What do the latest internal audit, compliance and MLRO reports say?
  • Has there been a recent board effectiveness review, and what did it find?

The role

  • What is expected: committee roles, time commitment, specific responsibilities, regulatory approval?
  • Why is the seat vacant? If possible, speak to the person you are replacing.
  • How much time will it take in a normal year, and in a crisis?

Your protection

  • Is there directors' and officers' insurance, with adequate limits and cover for regulatory investigations?
  • Is there a deed of indemnity, and is it backed by assets?
  • Can you get independent advice at the firm's expense if needed?

Yourself

  • Do you have the skills and time, considering your other roles?
  • Do you have any conflicts of interest?
  • Would you be comfortable explaining the firm's business and risks to a regulator in an interview?

If the firm will not let you see board minutes or key reports before you join, treat that as a warning sign.
resources.sortKey: due diligence before accepting a directorship

resources.title: Effective challenge without confrontation
resources.summary: How directors can challenge management and each other in a way that is evidence-based, persistent and productive, rather than personal or combative.
resources.bodyHtml:
Challenge is the core of a non-executive director's job. Done well, it improves decisions and builds trust. Done badly, it makes management defensive and the board less effective. Avoiding challenge to keep the peace is as much a risk as making every disagreement personal.

Challenge or confrontation?

Effective challenge Confrontation
Based on evidence Based on opinion or suspicion
Focused on the issue Focused on the person
Persistent until there is a real answer Repetitive, raising the temperature
Open to being persuaded Out to win
Seeks to improve the decision Seeks to show who is right

Techniques

  • Prepare. Read the papers early, identify the two or three issues that matter and, where appropriate, give the executive notice of difficult questions.
  • Ask, don't tell. Open questions ("What would have to be true for this to work?") get further than statements ("This won't work").
  • Separate the person from the problem. Talk about the proposal, the assumptions and the evidence.
  • Follow up. If an answer does not address the question, say so calmly and ask again, or ask for a follow-up paper.
  • Use the record. Ask for concerns, and the answers, to be minuted.
  • Escalate proportionately. Move from questions in the meeting, to a conversation with the chair, to a request for independent advice, to a formal dissent minuted, and, as a last resort, resignation.

When challenge is not welcome

If challenge is regularly met with irritation, or management goes around the board, raise it privately with the chair or senior independent director. If that fails, the issue may belong in the board effectiveness review or, in serious cases, with the regulator.

A useful question: "What is the most robust challenge you have seen on this board, and how was it raised and received?"

resources.title: ESG claims and greenwashing
resources.summary: Questions for a fund or management company board on whether sustainability claims are accurate, supported by the investment process and consistent across documents and marketing.
resources.bodyHtml:
Sustainability claims must match what the fund actually does. Regulators across Europe have made clear that misleading claims about ESG characteristics are a conduct and enforcement priority.

The claim

  • What exactly do we say about sustainability for each fund: in the name, the prospectus, the disclosures and the marketing?
  • Under SFDR, how is each fund classified (Article 6, 8 or 9), and can we justify that classification?
  • Does the fund's name use ESG or sustainability-related terms, and does the fund meet the requirements that apply to such names?

A good answer shows that claims are consistent across documents and backed by evidence.

The process

  • How are ESG factors actually used in the investment process: exclusions, screening, integration, engagement or impact targets?
  • What data do we rely on, from which providers, and how do we deal with gaps and inconsistencies?
  • How are binding commitments monitored, and what happens if the fund breaches them?

Oversight

  • Who reviews marketing materials for sustainability claims before they are published?
  • Has internal audit or compliance reviewed our sustainability disclosures and processes?
  • How do we report to investors on whether the fund met its sustainability objectives?

Red flags: marketing that is more ambitious than the prospectus; binding commitments that are not monitored; reliance on a single data provider without challenge; fund names with ESG terms that the portfolio does not support.
resources.sourcesHtml: • SFDR (Regulation (EU) 2019/2088)

resources.title: Fees, costs and value for money
resources.summary: Questions for a fund or management company board on whether the fees and costs charged to investors are justified and whether funds offer value for money.
resources.bodyHtml:
The costs

  • What is the total cost to an investor in each fund and share class, including ongoing charges, transaction costs and performance fees?
  • How do our costs compare with similar funds, and why are any of ours more expensive?
  • Is every cost charged to the fund justified, disclosed and in the investors' interest? Are any costs charged that should be borne by the manager?
  • Have economies of scale been passed on as funds have grown?

The value

  • Has each fund delivered against its objective after costs, over a meaningful period?
  • Are investors in the most appropriate share class, or are some paying more than they need to?
  • For actively managed funds: is the management genuinely active, or is the fund a closet tracker?
  • What does our value assessment conclude, and what did we change as a result?

Performance fees

  • Do performance fees reward genuine outperformance against an appropriate benchmark, with a high-water mark?
  • Have performance fees been paid in years when investors lost money?

A good answer compares each fund with peers, explains outliers and shows actions taken, such as fee cuts, share class conversions, mergers or closures.

Red flags: value assessments that find every fund offers value; costs rising faster than assets; legacy share classes left in place; performance fees on easy benchmarks.
resources.sortKey: fees, costs and value for money

resources.title: Financial statements and the external audit
resources.summary: Questions for a board or audit committee on the financial statements and the relationship with the external auditor.
resources.bodyHtml:
The financial statements

  • What are the key judgments and estimates, such as valuations, provisions and going concern, and how were they reached?
  • Have accounting policies changed, and why?
  • Are disclosures clear and consistent with what we say elsewhere?

The audit

  • What did the auditor identify as the key risks, and what did it find?
  • Were there any disagreements with management, unadjusted errors or control weaknesses?
  • Did the auditor get all the information and access it needed?

The auditor

  • How independent is the auditor? What non-audit services does it provide?
  • How long has it been in place, and when was it last tendered?
  • How do we assess the quality of the audit?

A good answer includes private time between the auditor and the audit committee or board, without management present.

Red flags: late or qualified audit opinions; repeated control findings; significant non-audit fees; reluctance to meet the auditor without management.
resources.sortKey: financial statements and the external audit

resources.title: Five tests of a good board pack
resources.summary: Five quick tests a director can apply to any board pack and set of minutes to see whether the board is getting what it needs and using it.
resources.bodyHtml:
A board pack shows what management thinks the board needs to know. Minutes show what the board did with it. Five tests cut through the volume.

1. Time

Where does the agenda spend the board's time? Count the minutes or pages given to growth and commercial updates against those given to risk, control and compliance. A board that spends most of its time on sales and very little on risk is likely to be surprised.

2. Challenge

Do the minutes record questions, challenge and decisions, or only that items were "noted"? A long run of "the board noted the report" with no questions suggests a board that receives information but does not test it.

3. Follow-through
