Are actions closed, or do they roll over meeting after meeting? Look at the action log. Items that stay open for many meetings, or are closed without evidence, show a board that does not hold management to account.

4. Information

Is the management information honest and complete? Does a red indicator lead to a discussion and a decision, or does it stay red for months? Good information is concise, focused on exceptions and trends, and clear about what it is asking the board to do.

5. Absence

What would you expect to see that is not there? Common gaps include: no downside case in a business plan; no mention of a known incident; no report from internal audit or the MLRO; a major decision taken by written resolution with no paper; no discussion of a regulatory change that clearly affects the firm.

Using the tests

  • Apply them to the last three or four packs, not just one.
  • Compare the pack with what you know from other sources: audit reports, regulatory correspondence, complaints and the press.
  • Raise gaps with the chair and the company secretary, and agree changes to the pack template.

A useful question: "What in this pack would you cut if you had to halve it?"
resources.sortKey: five tests of a good board pack

resources.title: Fund board director (UCITS and AIF)
resources.summary: The role of a director of an investment fund company, such as a UCITS or AIF structured as a company, including responsibilities, what good looks like and red flags.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

Where a fund is set up as a company, it has its own board of directors. The fund board's job is to protect the interests of investors, by making sure the fund is managed in line with its documents and the rules, and by overseeing the management company or AIFM and other service providers.

Main responsibilities

  • Approve the fund's prospectus and constitutional documents and changes to them.
  • Appoint and oversee the management company or AIFM (or, for a self-managed fund, carry out its functions directly), the depositary, the auditor and other key providers.
  • Oversee investment performance, compliance with investment restrictions, liquidity, valuation and risk.
  • Approve the annual and half-yearly financial statements.
  • Oversee conflicts of interest, fees and costs, and fair treatment of investors.
  • Decide on matters such as suspension of dealing, use of liquidity tools, fund mergers, closures and liquidation.
  • Make sure the fund deals openly with its regulator.

What good looks like

  • An independent majority, or at least a strong independent presence, with a mix of investment, operational, legal and risk skills.
  • Clear reporting from each service provider, with exceptions highlighted.
  • Regular meetings with the depositary, auditor and the management company's risk and compliance functions.
  • A clear view on value for money and investor outcomes, not just compliance.

Red flags

  • A board made up of employees of the promoter and its service providers.
  • Board meetings that last minutes and approve everything on the agenda.
  • No direct contact with the depositary or auditor.
  • Directors with dozens of other fund boards.

resources.title: Fund liquidity and redemption risk
resources.summary: Questions for a fund board on whether the fund's assets can be sold fast enough to meet redemptions in normal and stressed markets, and which liquidity tools are available and ready to use.
resources.bodyHtml:
An open-ended fund promises to return investors' money on a set dealing frequency. If the assets cannot be sold that quickly without a big discount, the investors who leave first are paid at the expense of those who stay. Liquidity mismatch is one of the most important risks a fund board oversees.

Matching assets to dealing terms

  • Is the fund's dealing frequency consistent with how quickly its assets can be sold in normal markets and in stress?
  • What share of the portfolio could be sold within one day, one week and one month without a significant price impact?
  • How concentrated is the investor base? What happens if the largest investors, or a platform, redeem at once?
  • Does the fund hold unlisted, thinly traded or hard-to-value assets, and are there limits on them?

A good answer shows a liquidity profile of both assets and investors, with the assumptions behind it.

Stress testing

  • How often are liquidity stress tests run, and do they include severe but plausible scenarios, both market-wide and fund-specific?
  • What did the last stress test show, and what action did the manager or board take?
  • Are the stress test assumptions about how fast assets can be sold reviewed against what happened in real market stress?

Liquidity management tools

  • Which tools are available under the fund documents: notice periods, redemption gates, swing pricing, anti-dilution levies, redemptions in kind, side pockets or suspension?
  • Who decides to use them, how quickly can they be activated, and have they been tested operationally?
  • How would investors and the regulator be told, and is there a communications plan ready?

A good answer shows the tools are set out in the prospectus, governed by a policy, and could be used within a day.

Red flags: liquidity reports that look at the assets but not the investors; holdings in unlisted securities creeping towards the limit; tools that exist in the prospectus but have never been operationally tested; a board that has never discussed when it would suspend dealing.
resources.sourcesHtml: • AIFMD II (Directive (EU) 2024/927)

resources.title: Groupthink: warning signs and counters
resources.summary: How to spot groupthink on a board, which boards are most exposed, and practical steps to counter it.
resources.bodyHtml:
Groupthink is consensus at the expense of a realistic appraisal. A board can be friendly, efficient and unanimous, and still make poor decisions because nobody wants to break the consensus.

Who is most exposed

  • Long-tenured boards with little turnover.
  • Directors who are socially close or come from similar backgrounds.
  • A dominant chair or CEO.
  • A strong track record that breeds confidence.
  • Time pressure or a crisis.

Warning signs

  • Quick, unanimous decisions on topics that are genuinely contested.
  • An illusion of unanimity, with quiet dissenters keeping their doubts to themselves.
  • Independent directors who hold private doubts they have not raised in the meeting.
  • Contrary information dismissed or explained away.
  • Outsiders who challenge the board's view treated as not understanding the business.

Counters

  • Designated devil's advocate. Ask a director, in rotation, to argue against the proposal.
  • Anonymous polling. Collect views before the meeting so that the board sees the real spread of opinion.
  • Speak in reverse order. Ask the most junior or newest directors for their view first, and the chair last.
  • Pre-mortem. Assume the decision has failed in two years and ask why.
  • "What would change our mind?" Agree in advance what evidence would cause the board to reconsider.
  • Outside views. Bring in independent advisers, and refresh the board's membership over time.
  • Diversity. Different backgrounds, experience and thinking styles reduce the risk.

resources.title: Head of compliance
resources.summary: The role of the head of compliance: purpose, responsibilities, independence, what good looks like and red flags.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

The head of compliance leads the second-line function that helps the firm comply with regulatory requirements and manage compliance risk.

Main responsibilities

  • Identify applicable rules and track regulatory change.
  • Advise the business and the board on compliance.
  • Design and run a risk-based compliance monitoring programme.
  • Oversee policies, training and regulatory reporting.
  • Manage breaches, regulatory notifications and the relationship with regulators.
  • Report to the board on compliance risk and the effectiveness of controls.

Independence

The head of compliance should have direct access to the board, enough resources and authority, and pay that does not depend on the performance of the areas they oversee. They should not be responsible for business activities they monitor.

What good looks like

  • Candid reporting, including where the firm falls short.
  • Early involvement in new products and changes.
  • A monitoring programme that tests outcomes, not just processes.

Red flags

  • Compliance seen as a box-ticking function.
  • Under-resourced team with a growing backlog.
  • Monitoring that never finds issues.

resources.title: Independent non-executive director
resources.summary: What an independent non-executive director is for, their main responsibilities, what good looks like and the red flags.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

An independent non-executive director (INED) brings an objective view to the board, free from relationships with management, shareholders or service providers that could affect their judgment. Their main job is constructive challenge and oversight, in the interests of the firm and its clients or investors.

Independence

Independence is judged in substance, not just form. Common tests include: no recent employment with the firm or group; no material business relationship; no close family ties with directors or senior staff; not representing a major shareholder; no significant fees beyond the director's fee; and not having served so long that independence is in doubt.

Main responsibilities

  • Challenge and help develop strategy.
  • Scrutinise management's performance against agreed goals.
  • Satisfy themselves that financial information is accurate and that risk management and internal controls are robust.
  • Oversee conflicts of interest and fair treatment of clients or investors.
  • Often chair or sit on the audit, risk, remuneration or nomination committees.
  • Be available to staff, auditors and control functions who need to raise concerns.

What good looks like

  • Reads and understands the papers, and asks focused questions.
  • Gives time beyond board meetings: committee work, site visits, meeting control functions.
  • Builds relationships with the heads of risk, compliance and internal audit.
  • Keeps their own knowledge up to date.
  • Is willing to dissent, and to have that minuted.

Red flags

  • Rarely speaks or never challenges.
  • Too many other roles to give the time needed.
  • Relationships with the promoter, manager or major service providers.
  • Long tenure with no refreshment.

resources.title: Management company or AIFM director
resources.summary: The role of a director of a UCITS management company or an AIFM: responsibilities, the designated persons model, what good looks like and red flags.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

A UCITS management company or AIFM is the authorised firm responsible for managing funds: portfolio management, risk management, administration, distribution and the oversight of anything delegated. Its board is responsible for running that firm soundly and for the outcomes it delivers for the funds and their investors.

Main responsibilities

  • Set the firm's strategy, risk appetite and business plan, and make sure it has the capital, people and systems to deliver them.
  • Make sure the firm keeps substance: enough senior staff, with the right expertise, actually doing the managerial functions, and not acting as a letter-box entity.
  • Oversee the managerial functions, often through designated persons or conducting officers, such as investment management, risk management, operational risk, distribution, fund administration, capital and financial management, and regulatory compliance.
  • Approve and oversee delegation, including due diligence and ongoing monitoring of delegates.
  • Oversee the risk management, compliance, internal audit and AML/CFT functions.
  • Approve key policies, including valuation, liquidity, conflicts of interest, remuneration and best execution.

What good looks like

  • An organisational plan that shows who does what, where, and how much time they spend.
  • Designated persons who are senior, knowledgeable and actively challenging delegates.
  • A risk function that is independent of portfolio management.
  • Management information that covers every fund and every delegate, with exceptions escalated.

Red flags

  • Designated persons who spend little time on the role or rely entirely on delegates' reports.
  • The same individuals acting as directors and designated persons with no independent challenge.
  • Delegation chains that the board cannot describe.
  • Under-resourced risk and compliance functions.

resources.title: Managing a crisis: suspension, gating and communication
resources.summary: How a fund board should prepare for and manage a liquidity or valuation crisis, including decisions to gate or suspend and how to communicate.
resources.bodyHtml:
Before a crisis

  • Know which liquidity tools the fund can use, who decides, and how quickly they can be activated.
  • Agree the triggers that would lead the board to consider each tool.
  • Test the operational steps with administrators, transfer agents, distributors and the depositary.
  • Prepare template communications for investors, distributors and regulators.
  • Make sure board members can meet at short notice.

When stress emerges

  • Get the facts: size and source of redemptions, liquidity of assets, valuation reliability.
  • Consider fairness between investors leaving and those staying.
  • Use the least drastic effective tool first: anti-dilution measures, then gates, then suspension.
  • Take advice from the manager, risk function, depositary and lawyers.
  • Record the reasons for every decision.

Suspension

Suspension is a last resort, used when it is in investors' interests, such as when assets cannot be valued or sold without serious harm. Notify the regulator and investors immediately. Plan how and when the fund will reopen or be wound down, and review regularly.

Communication

  • Be prompt, clear and consistent across all audiences.
  • Explain what has happened, why, what investors can expect and when they will hear more.
  • Coordinate with distributors and platforms, which hold many investors' accounts.

After the crisis

  • Review what happened, what worked and what did not.
  • Update liquidity management, tools and documents.
resources.sortKey: managing a crisis: suspension, gating and communication

resources.title: Matters reserved: crypto-asset service provider
resources.summary: A model list of decisions the board of a crypto-asset service provider should reserve to itself.
resources.bodyHtml:
Adapt this model list to the firm's services, structure and the regulatory regime.

Strategy and business

  • Strategy, business plan and budget.
  • New crypto-asset services, markets or client types.
  • Material partnerships, acquisitions and disposals.

Assets and listings

  • The listing and delisting policy, and admission of significant crypto-assets to the platform.
  • Use of client crypto-assets for staking, lending or other purposes, and the related client terms.

Risk and capital

  • Risk appetite, including limits on proprietary exposures and treasury.
  • Capital and liquidity plans, and the wind-down plan.

Custody

  • The custody and key management policy, including the split between cold, warm and hot wallets.
  • Appointment of sub-custodians and critical technology providers.

Financial crime

  • AML/CFT risk assessment and policy, sanctions policy and the travel rule approach.

Organisation and people

  • Appointment of directors, senior managers, heads of control functions and the MLRO.
  • The remuneration policy.
  • Outsourcing of critical functions, especially to group entities.

Reporting and the regulator

  • Financial statements and regulatory submissions requiring board approval.
  • Material communications with regulators.
  • Responses to major incidents, hacks or losses of client assets.

resources.title: Matters reserved: fund board
resources.summary: A model list of decisions a fund board (for a fund set up as a company) should reserve to itself rather than delegate.
resources.bodyHtml:
A schedule of matters reserved makes clear which decisions only the board can take. Everything else can be delegated, with reporting back. Adapt this model list to the fund's structure, documents and local law.

Structure and documents

  • Approving the prospectus, supplements and key investor information, and material changes to them.
  • Amending the constitutional documents (subject to shareholder approval where required).
  • Launching new sub-funds or share classes.
  • Merging, closing, converting or liquidating the fund or a sub-fund.
  • Changing the fund's investment objective or policy.

Appointments

  • Appointing, reviewing and removing the management company or AIFM (or, if self-managed, the key officers), the depositary, the auditor, the administrator, the investment manager and other key service providers.
  • Approving the terms of those appointments and material changes to fees.
  • Appointing the chair and company secretary, and recommending director appointments.

Oversight and policies

  • Approving the valuation policy and any significant changes to valuation methods.
  • Approving the conflicts of interest policy and related-party transactions.
  • Approving liquidity risk management arrangements and the use of liquidity management tools.
  • Approving the business-wide AML/CFT risk assessment, where the fund is responsible for it.

Financial

  • Approving annual and half-yearly financial statements.
  • Declaring dividends and distributions.
  • Approving borrowing beyond agreed limits.

Investors and the regulator

  • Suspending the calculation of NAV or dealing.
  • Approving material communications to investors and responses to the regulator on significant matters.
  • Approving material errors and breaches remediation, including investor compensation.

Governance

  • Approving this schedule, committee terms of reference and the board's own effectiveness review.

resources.title: Matters reserved: management company or AIFM
resources.summary: A model list of decisions the board of a UCITS management company or AIFM should reserve to itself rather than delegate.
resources.bodyHtml:
Adapt this model list to the firm's size, structure, group arrangements and local law.

Strategy and business

  • Approving the strategy, business plan and budget.
  • Entering new business lines, fund types, markets or distribution channels.
  • Acquisitions, disposals, joint ventures and material contracts outside the business plan.

Risk and capital

  • Approving the risk appetite statement and risk management policy.
  • Approving the capital plan, including any capital injections or distributions to shareholders.
  • Approving the internal capital and liquidity assessment where required.
  • Approving the professional liability arrangements (additional own funds or insurance) for an AIFM.

Organisation and people

  • Approving the organisational structure and programme of operations, including how managerial functions are allocated.
  • Appointing and removing directors, designated persons or conducting officers, and the heads of risk, compliance, internal audit and the MLRO.
  • Approving the remuneration policy and its annual review.

Delegation

  • Approving any delegation of portfolio management, risk management or other critical functions, and the due diligence behind it.
  • Approving changes to, or termination of, material delegations.

Policies

  • Approving key policies: conflicts of interest, valuation, liquidity, best execution, voting, AML/CFT, outsourcing, business continuity, ICT risk and sustainability.

Funds

  • Approving new funds and material changes to existing funds managed by the firm.
  • Using liquidity management tools or suspending dealing, where the firm has this power.

Reporting and the regulator

  • Approving annual financial statements and regulatory returns that require board approval.
  • Approving material communications with the regulator.
  • Reviewing reports from risk, compliance, internal audit and the MLRO.
resources.sortKey: matters reserved: management company or aifm

resources.title: Matters reserved: payment or e-money institution
resources.summary: A model list of decisions the board of a payment or e-money institution should reserve to itself.
resources.bodyHtml:
Adapt this model list to the firm's services, structure and the regulatory regime.

Strategy and business

  • Strategy, business plan and budget.
  • New payment services, markets or programmes, including embedded finance partnerships.
  • Acquisitions, disposals and material contracts.

Safeguarding and capital

  • The safeguarding policy and method, including choice of safeguarding banks and insurers.
  • The capital and liquidity plan.
  • The wind-down plan and resolution pack.

Risk and financial crime

  • Risk appetite.
  • AML/CFT risk assessment and policy, sanctions policy and fraud strategy.

Partners, agents and outsourcing

  • Appointment of agents, distributors and programme managers above set thresholds.
  • Outsourcing of critical functions and key technology providers.

Organisation and people

  • Appointment of directors, senior managers, heads of control functions and the MLRO.
  • The remuneration policy.

Reporting and the regulator

  • Financial statements and safeguarding audit reports.
  • Material regulatory communications and incident notifications.
resources.sortKey: matters reserved: payment or e-money institution

resources.title: Money laundering reporting officer (MLRO)
resources.summary: The role of the money laundering reporting officer: responsibilities, seniority and independence, what good looks like and red flags.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

The MLRO is responsible for overseeing the firm's AML/CFT compliance and for deciding whether suspicions of money laundering or terrorist financing should be reported to the financial intelligence unit. The MLRO is a key control function and, in most jurisdictions, an approved role.

Main responsibilities

  • Receive internal reports of suspicion, investigate them and decide whether to file a suspicious activity report.
  • Act as the main contact with the financial intelligence unit and the regulator on AML/CFT matters.
  • Oversee the business-wide risk assessment, AML/CFT policies and procedures, and staff training.
  • Monitor customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, sanctions screening and record keeping.
  • Report to the board, at least annually, on the effectiveness of AML/CFT controls, with recommendations.

Seniority and independence

The MLRO should be senior enough to challenge the business, have direct access to the board, and have the resources and authority to do the job. Combining the MLRO role with heavy commercial duties creates a conflict. In some firms a separate money laundering compliance officer runs the day-to-day programme.

What good looks like

  • Reports to the board that are candid about weaknesses and backlogs.
  • Decisions on suspicion recorded with reasons, whether or not a report is made.
  • A strong grasp of the firm's business and the typologies relevant to it.
  • Willing to say no to clients, products or markets.

Red flags

  • An MLRO who is part-time, junior or over-stretched.
  • Reports that list activity but draw no conclusions.
  • Business teams able to override the MLRO's decisions.
  • Persistent backlogs in reviews and alerts.

resources.title: New products and new markets
resources.summary: Questions for a board before approving a new product, service, market or business line.
resources.bodyHtml:
The case

  • What is the opportunity, and how does it fit our strategy and risk appetite?
  • Who are the target customers, and what need does it meet?
  • What are the realistic revenue, costs and timeline, and what if they are wrong?

Risks

  • What new risks does it bring: regulatory, conduct, financial crime, operational, technology, reputational?
  • Do we need new permissions or approvals, and have we engaged regulators?
  • Does it rely on new third parties, technology or jurisdictions?

Readiness

  • Have risk, compliance, legal, operations and finance reviewed it and signed off?
  • Are systems, controls, staff and training ready before launch?
  • How will we monitor it after launch, and what would make us pull back?

Fairness

  • Does the product offer fair value and good outcomes for customers?
  • How will it be marketed and distributed?

A good answer comes through a documented approval process with clear conditions and a post-launch review date.

Red flags: products launched under commercial pressure before controls are ready; no post-launch review; risk functions consulted after the decision.

resources.title: Operational resilience and DORA
resources.summary: Questions to test whether the firm can keep delivering its important services through disruption, and how it meets the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA).
resources.bodyHtml:
Operational resilience is about assuming disruption will happen and making sure the firm can keep delivering its most important services. In the EU, DORA sets detailed requirements for how financial firms manage ICT risk, and makes the management body responsible for it.

Important services

  • Which business services matter most to clients and markets, and how much disruption could each tolerate?
  • Have we mapped the people, processes, technology, data and third parties behind each of those services?
  • Have we tested severe but plausible scenarios, and could we stay within our tolerances?

A good answer names the services, shows the mapping and explains what scenario testing revealed and what was fixed.

DORA and ICT risk

  • Has the board approved the ICT risk management framework and digital operational resilience strategy, as DORA requires?
  • Is there an independent control function for ICT risk, and does it report to the board?
  • Do we keep a register of information on all ICT third-party arrangements, and is it complete?
  • How are major ICT incidents classified and reported to the regulator within the required deadlines?
  • What testing do we carry out (vulnerability scans, scenario tests, and, if required, threat-led penetration testing)?

Board capability

  • Have directors had training on ICT risk, as DORA requires, and does the board have enough expertise to challenge management?
  • When did the board last discuss a real incident and the lessons learned?

Red flags: resilience treated as an IT matter only; no board-level discussion of incidents; ICT third-party register incomplete; tests that are always passed.
resources.sourcesHtml: • DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554)

resources.title: Outsourcing and third-party risk
resources.summary: Questions to test whether the firm knows which functions it relies on others for, has assessed the risks and can keep operating if a key provider fails.
resources.bodyHtml:
Firms rely more and more on third parties: group companies, technology and cloud providers, administrators, custodians and specialist vendors. The firm stays responsible for everything it outsources.

What do we rely on?

  • Do we have a register of all outsourcing and third-party arrangements, showing which are critical or important?
  • Which functions would stop if a single provider failed? Are several critical services concentrated in one provider or group?
  • Do our providers subcontract critical work, and do we know to whom?

A good answer shows a current register, with criticality assessed and approved, and visibility of key subcontractors.

Before we sign

  • What due diligence was carried out on the provider's financial strength, controls, security and resilience?
  • Does the contract give us audit and access rights, service levels, data protection, incident reporting, and exit and termination rights?
  • Was the regulator notified where rules require it?

While it runs

  • What management information do we receive on the provider's performance, incidents and audit findings?
  • Who owns each relationship in the firm, and do they have the expertise to challenge the provider?
  • When were the most critical providers last reviewed or visited?

If it fails

  • Is there a documented, tested exit plan for each critical provider?
  • How long would it take to move the service to another provider or bring it in-house?

Red flags: a register maintained by procurement but not used by risk; group providers exempt from oversight; exit plans that have never been tested; critical providers whose contracts lack audit rights.
resources.sourcesHtml: • DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554)

resources.title: Oversight of the investment manager and performance
resources.summary: Questions for a fund or management company board on how it oversees the investment manager: whether the fund is managed in line with its objective and limits, and whether performance and risk are understood.
resources.bodyHtml:
Directors are not expected to second-guess individual investment decisions. They are expected to check that the fund is managed as investors were told it would be, within its limits, and that underperformance or style drift is spotted and acted on.

Mandate and limits

  • Is the fund being managed in line with its stated objective, policy and investment restrictions?
  • Who monitors limits before and after trading, and how are breaches reported to the board?
  • How are passive breaches (for example, caused by market moves or redemptions) corrected, and within what timeframe?

A good answer distinguishes active from passive breaches and shows how each was corrected and whether investors were compensated.

Performance

  • How has the fund performed against its benchmark and peers, over one, three and five years, after fees?
  • Can the investment manager explain where performance came from (attribution) and whether it matches the stated style?
  • Is there evidence of style drift: rising risk, more illiquid assets, more concentration, or a different type of holding from that described?
  • At what point would the board escalate persistent underperformance, and what options does it have?

A good answer is candid about weak performance and explains what the manager is doing about it.

Risk

  • How does the risk function, independent of portfolio management, monitor market, liquidity, credit and counterparty risk?
  • Are stress tests run, and do the results reach the board in a form it can use?
  • How are the use of derivatives, leverage and securities lending controlled and reported?

Red flags: performance reported only gross of fees or against a flattering benchmark; a risk function that reports through the portfolio managers; repeated limit breaches described as technical.
resources.sortKey: oversight of the investment manager and performance

resources.title: Oversight of the management company and delegates
resources.summary: Questions for a fund board on how it oversees its management company or AIFM and the firms to which functions such as portfolio management, administration and distribution are delegated.
resources.bodyHtml:
A fund board can delegate functions but not its responsibility. Where the fund has a management company or AIFM, the fund board's job is to oversee how that firm carries out its role and how it oversees its own delegates.

The overall arrangement

  • Do we have a clear map of who does what: the management company or AIFM, the investment manager, the administrator, the transfer agent, the depositary and the distributors?
  • Is each arrangement covered by a written agreement with service levels, reporting, termination rights and the right to audit?
  • Does the management company have the people, expertise and systems to oversee its delegates, or is it a letter-box entity?

A good answer comes with a one-page map and a schedule of agreements, reviews and key performance indicators.

Ongoing oversight

  • What reports do we receive from each delegate, how often, and who checks them?
  • When did the management company last carry out a due diligence visit or review of each delegate, and what did it find?
  • How are service failures, errors and breaches reported to the board, and how quickly?
  • How would we know if a delegate's own financial position, staffing or control environment was weakening?

A good answer describes a risk-based programme: closer review of critical delegates, with follow-up of findings to closure.

Change and exit

  • If we had to replace a delegate, how long would it take and what would it cost?
  • Are there conflicts of interest because delegates are in the same group as the management company or promoter?
  • When were the fees for each delegate last tested against the market?

Red flags: oversight reports that are copied from the delegate's own reporting; findings that stay open for many quarters; no one able to say what would happen if a key delegate failed.
resources.sourcesHtml:
• UCITS Directive (2009/65/EC)
  • AIFMD (2011/61/EU)
resources.sortKey: oversight of the management company and delegates

resources.title: Preparing for a regulator's interview (a director's view)
resources.summary: How directors and senior managers can prepare for an interview with a regulator, whether for approval, a supervisory review or a thematic visit.
resources.bodyHtml:
Regulators interview directors and senior managers when assessing applications for authorisation or approval, during supervisory reviews and after incidents. The aim is to find out whether you understand the firm, its risks and your own responsibilities. Preparation is about knowing your business, not memorising answers.

What the regulator is testing

  • Do you understand the firm's business model, strategy and main risks?
  • Do you know your own responsibilities and how you discharge them?
  • Does the board challenge management, and can you give examples?
  • Do you understand the regulatory requirements that apply to the firm?
  • Are you honest and open about weaknesses?

Before the interview

  • Re-read the business plan, risk appetite, latest risk register, board and committee minutes, and the last internal audit, compliance and MLRO reports.
  • Know the key numbers: revenue, capital and liquidity, client assets, number of complaints and breaches.
  • Know your own role: statement of responsibilities, committee roles, and the areas you oversee.
  • Prepare two or three examples of challenge you have made, and what changed as a result.
  • Know the open issues: regulatory findings, incidents, remediation programmes and their status.
  • Check with the firm's compliance function what the regulator has asked for and why.

In the interview

  • Answer the question asked, briefly and directly.
  • Use examples and evidence rather than general statements.
  • If you do not know, say so and offer to follow up. Do not guess.
  • Be candid about problems and explain what is being done.
  • Do not read from scripts or defer every answer to the CEO.

Afterwards

  • Note what was asked and any commitments you made, and follow them up promptly.
  • Share the lessons with the board.

Red flags for regulators: directors who cannot describe the firm's main risks; answers that are identical across interviewees; no examples of challenge; problems minimised or blamed on others.
resources.sortKey: preparing for a regulator's interview (a director's view)

resources.title: Reading a board's culture
resources.summary: Observable signs of a board's real culture, in meetings, minutes and conversations, and what a director can do to improve it.
resources.bodyHtml:
A board can have the right structure, committees and policies and still not work. Culture shows in behaviour: who speaks, who is heard and what happens when someone disagrees.

What to watch

  • Who speaks. Is airtime spread across the table, or dominated by one or two voices?
  • Who stays silent. Silence can mean deference, disengagement or simply not being asked. Each means something different.
  • Interruptions. A pattern of interrupting certain people shows whose views carry weight.
  • Response to challenge. Is disagreement explored, or does the conversation simply move on?
  • Where decisions are made. If the real discussion happens in pre-meetings, the board meeting becomes a ratification exercise.
  • Executives in the room. Do they present openly, including bad news, or defend and minimise?

Psychological safety

Challenge depends on directors feeling able to voice concerns or admit uncertainty without being seen as disloyal. Its absence shows up as silence, dissent raised late or only in private, and challenge that appears only once a decision is safely made.

The chair's role

An effective chair An ineffective chair
Invites views from directors who have not spoken Dominates discussion or answers for the CEO
Asks follow-up questions to test an argument Lets the same few voices dominate
Brings circular discussion to a conclusion Treats disagreement as something to manage away
Deals with conflict directly Has no way to draw out quieter directors
Curates the agenda Avoids difficult conversations with underperforming directors

Evidence beyond the meeting

Culture in the boardroom shapes culture in the firm. Look at staff surveys, whistleblowing reports, complaints, staff turnover in control functions and how quickly bad news reaches the board.

A useful question: "Give me an example of a time a director disagreed with the CEO or chair. What happened?"

resources.title: Recognising board personalities
resources.summary: Common behaviour patterns on boards, how they help or hinder, and how a chair or director can work with each.
resources.bodyHtml:
Recognising common patterns helps a chair run better meetings and helps directors understand the dynamics. These are tendencies, not labels, and anyone can show them at times.

Pattern How it shows How to work with it
The dominator Speaks first and most; may answer for others The chair invites others first and limits airtime
The silent director Rarely volunteers a view Ask directly, in advance or in the meeting, for a specific view
The absentee Often missing or disengaged The chair addresses it privately; it may affect fitness for the role
The box-ticker Procedurally correct but adds little challenge Ask what they would change; assign specific topics
The permanent devil's advocate Challenges everything, whatever its merit Recognise valuable challenge; ask what would satisfy them
The specialist Contributes only on their area Encourage broader engagement; use their expertise in committees
The executive in disguise A non-executive who micromanages Clarify the line between oversight and management

Using this well

  • Focus on behaviour and its effect, not personality.
  • Address patterns early and privately, before they become entrenched.
  • Use board evaluations to surface them.
  • Remember that a balance of styles can strengthen a board.

resources.title: Risk appetite: is it real and used?
resources.summary: Questions to test whether the firm's risk appetite statement actually shapes decisions, with measurable limits, clear reporting and consequences when limits are breached.
resources.bodyHtml:
A risk appetite statement is only useful if it changes what the firm does. Many are written once, approved and filed. These questions help a board find out whether its own statement is real.

Is it specific?

  • Does each main risk have a statement of appetite and at least one measurable limit or indicator?
  • Are the limits set at levels that would actually be reached in a bad year, or only in a catastrophe?
  • Is there a qualitative appetite for conduct, compliance and reputational risk, and how is it measured?

A good answer points to metrics with green, amber and red thresholds that management reports against every quarter.

Is it used?

  • Name a decision in the last year that was changed or stopped because of the risk appetite.
  • When a new product, market or major supplier is proposed, does the board paper show how it fits the appetite?
  • Is the risk appetite cascaded into business limits, delegated authorities and remuneration?

A good answer can give examples. If nobody can, the appetite is decoration.

What happens on a breach?

  • How quickly is the board told when a limit is breached, and by whom?
  • What has to happen next: a plan to return within appetite, a decision to accept the breach, or a change to the limit?
  • How often have limits been raised just after they were breached?

Red flags: no breaches ever reported; limits quietly raised to fit what happened; risk appetite reviewed only as a formality once a year; metrics that management cannot explain.
resources.sortKey: risk appetite: is it real and used?

resources.title: Risk committee terms of reference
resources.summary: Model terms of reference for a board risk committee of a financial services firm, to adapt to its size and structure.
resources.bodyHtml:
Membership

  • At least three members, mainly non-executive and independent, including the chair.
  • Members with risk management and relevant sector expertise.

Meetings

  • At least four times a year.
  • The CRO attends and has direct access to the committee chair, and meets the committee privately at least annually.

Responsibilities

  • Advise the board on risk appetite and strategy, and recommend the risk appetite statement.
  • Oversee the risk management framework and its effectiveness.
  • Review risk exposures against appetite, and breaches.
  • Review stress testing, capital and liquidity assessments, such as the ICARA.
  • Review emerging risks, including technology, cyber, AI and climate.
  • Oversee the risk function's independence, resources and effectiveness.
  • Review the risk aspects of major decisions, such as new products, acquisitions and outsourcing.
  • Advise the remuneration committee on risk adjustment of pay.
  • Oversee operational resilience, where not covered elsewhere.

Reporting

  • Report to the board after each meeting.
  • Review its own effectiveness and terms of reference annually.

resources.title: Safeguarding client funds (payment and e-money firms)
resources.summary: Questions for the board of a payment or e-money institution on how customer money is safeguarded and reconciled, and whether customers would get their money back if the firm failed.
resources.bodyHtml:
Payment and e-money firms must safeguard the money they receive from customers so that it can be returned if the firm fails. Weak safeguarding has led to long delays and losses for customers when firms have gone into administration.

The arrangements

  • Which safeguarding method do we use: a segregated account at a bank, investment in secure liquid assets, or an insurance policy or guarantee?
  • Which funds are relevant funds that must be safeguarded, and from when?
  • Are safeguarding accounts correctly named and acknowledged by the bank so that they are protected from our creditors?
  • How concentrated are we on one safeguarding bank, and what is our plan if it closes our account?

A good answer comes with a clear safeguarding policy, a map of funds flows and bank acknowledgement letters on file.

Reconciliation

  • How often are internal and external reconciliations done, and who reviews them?
  • How are shortfalls identified and corrected, and how quickly is the board told?
  • What were the findings of the last safeguarding audit, and are they closed?

If we fail

  • Do we have a resolution pack or wind-down plan showing how customer funds would be identified and returned quickly?
  • Would an insolvency practitioner be able to rely on our records?

Red flags: reconciliations that regularly show unexplained differences; customer money passing through operating accounts; safeguarding audit findings repeated year after year; no up-to-date wind-down plan.
resources.sourcesHtml:
• PSD2 (Directive (EU) 2015/2366)
  • E-Money Directive (2009/110/EC)
resources.sortKey: safeguarding client funds (payment and e-money firms)

resources.title: Sanctions exposure
resources.summary: Questions for a board on how exposed the firm is to sanctions risk and whether its controls can keep pace with new designations and circumvention schemes.
resources.bodyHtml:
Exposure

  • Which sanctions regimes apply to us and our group (EU, UK, US, UN and others), and do they conflict?
  • Where is our exposure: customers, investors, counterparties, investments, payments, suppliers, staff?
  • What share of our business involves high-risk jurisdictions, sectors or intermediaries?
  • For crypto: how do we screen wallet addresses and detect exposure to sanctioned services or tokens?

Controls

  • How quickly are new designations applied to screening, and how is that tested?
  • Do we identify entities owned or controlled by designated persons, not just those named?
  • How are alerts handled, and how many are cleared, escalated or frozen?
  • What circumvention red flags do we look for, such as trade-based schemes, front companies or third-country intermediaries?

Response

  • Who decides on freezing and reporting, and how fast?
  • Have we had any breaches or near misses, and did we report them?
  • Do we have specialist advice on licences and conflicting regimes?

A good answer shows a sanctions risk assessment, tested screening with measured speed and quality, and clear escalation.

Red flags: screening lists updated weekly; no ownership and control analysis; crypto activity screened only at onboarding; no record of licences or reports.

resources.title: Stablecoin reserves and redemption
resources.summary: Questions for the board of a stablecoin issuer, or a firm that relies on stablecoins, on reserve assets, redemption rights and what happens in a run.
resources.bodyHtml:
A stablecoin is only as stable as the assets behind it and the holder's ability to redeem at par. Under MiCA, issuers of e-money tokens and asset-referenced tokens must hold reserves, give holders redemption rights and meet governance and liquidity requirements. Firms that hold or use stablecoins need to understand the same risks.

For issuers

  • What assets make up the reserve, where are they held, and are they segregated and protected from our creditors?
  • How much could be paid out in one day, one week and one month in a run? What is the largest daily redemption we have handled?
  • Are redemptions at par, free of charge and within the time our terms and the rules require?
  • How often is the reserve independently verified or audited, and is the report published?
  • How concentrated are reserves in a few banks, and what happens if one fails?
  • What is our recovery and redemption plan, and has it been tested?

A good answer shows a daily reserve report, liquidity stress tests and a tested plan for orderly redemption.

For firms that use stablecoins

  • Which stablecoins do we hold or accept, who issues them, and are they authorised where our clients are?
  • How would a loss of peg affect us, our clients and our liquidity?
  • Can we redeem directly with the issuer, or only by selling on the market?
  • What limits do we set on exposure to any one stablecoin?

Red flags: reserves held in assets that are hard to sell quickly; attestations that are infrequent or narrow; no direct redemption route; heavy reliance on a single stablecoin or banking partner.
resources.sourcesHtml: • MiCA (Regulation (EU) 2023/1114)

resources.title: Strategy and business model: where the risk sits
resources.summary: Questions a board can ask to test whether the strategy is realistic, where the business model makes and could lose money, and whether the risks that come with the strategy are understood and owned.
resources.bodyHtml:
Strategy is the board's job, and so are the risks that come with it. Most failures can be traced back to a business model that relied on something the board did not test: one client, one product, one counterparty, or a market that stayed benign.

The business model

  • How does the firm make money, and which three products, clients or channels matter most to revenue?
  • What would have to happen for the business model to stop working?
  • Where are we concentrated: clients, distributors, counterparties, banks, technology suppliers or key people?
  • Which parts of the business are growing fastest, and are controls keeping up?

A good answer is short, specific and quantified, and the same answer comes from the CEO, the CFO and the risk function.

The plan

  • What has to be true for the plan to succeed, and how confident are we in each assumption?
  • What is the downside case, and could the firm survive it with capital and liquidity to spare?
  • How does this plan compare with last year's, and why did any of last year's targets slip?
  • What is the plan for the regulatory changes that are coming, and who owns it?

A good answer sets out the key assumptions, a realistic downside and the actions the firm would take if it happened.

Risk and strategy together

  • Was the risk function involved in shaping the strategy, or only shown it afterwards?
  • Does the strategy fit within the risk appetite the board has approved? If not, which has to change?
  • Which new risks does the strategy create (new markets, products, technology or partners)?
  • What would make the board change course, and how would it find out in time?

Red flags: a plan that is all upside; growth targets with no matching investment in controls; a risk function that cannot describe the strategy; the same targets missed year after year with no change in approach.

resources.title: Testing the quality of a board decision
resources.summary: Seven questions to test whether a significant board decision was well made, judged by the process rather than by how it turned out.
resources.bodyHtml:
Judge how a decision was made, not whether it turned out well. A good outcome can follow a poor process, and a sound decision can still go wrong. Use these questions before a significant decision, and again when looking back at one.

Question What good looks like
Why? The board was clear what problem or opportunity the decision addressed.
Why now? There was a reason this was the right time, rather than earlier or later.
Alternatives Genuine options were weighed, and the paper explains why the others were rejected.
Assumptions The board identified what had to be true for the decision to succeed, and challenged it.
Downside The worst case was set out, and the board was comfortable it could live with it.
Success measures The board knows how it will judge, in twelve months, whether the decision was right.
Recorded rationale The minutes capture why the board decided as it did, not just what it decided.

Before the decision

  • Does the paper state the decision required at the top?
  • Has the proposal been challenged before it reached the board (by risk, compliance, finance or an independent adviser)?
  • Was the decision effectively made in pre-meetings, leaving the board meeting to ratify it?
  • Does any director have a conflict of interest?

Looking back

Good boards revisit major decisions 12 to 18 months later as a standing item, not only after a failure. They ask whether the assumptions held, whether the success measures were met and what they would do differently, and feed the lessons into future papers, risk appetite and training.

Warning sign: the same kinds of problem recurring across different decisions, which suggests the board is not learning from its own history.

resources.title: Tokenising a fund
resources.summary: Questions for a fund or management company board considering issuing fund shares or units as tokens on a distributed ledger.
resources.bodyHtml:
Purpose

  • What problem does tokenisation solve for our investors or distribution: faster settlement, new channels, collateral use?
  • Which share classes or funds, and for which investors?

Legal and regulatory

  • Will the ledger be the legal register (native) or mirror a traditional register? Is that recognised in our domicile?
  • Which regulatory approvals or notifications are needed, and has the regulator been engaged?
  • How do investor protections, including on insolvency, apply to tokenised holdings?

Operations and technology

  • Which network will be used (public or permissioned), and who controls the smart contract?
  • How are investors identified and transfers restricted to eligible holders?
  • How are subscriptions and redemptions settled, and with what cash leg?
  • How are reconciliations between the ledger and the transfer agent's records done?
  • What happens if the network fails, forks or is attacked?

Oversight

  • What does the depositary do differently, and is it comfortable?
  • How are smart-contract risks audited and monitored?
  • Have the transfer agent and administrator the capability to operate the model?

Red flags: technology-led projects without a clear investor benefit; unclear legal status of the register; no plan for failure of the network or provider.

resources.title: Use of AI, including agentic AI
resources.summary: Questions for a board on how the firm uses artificial intelligence, including AI agents that take actions, and how it controls the risks to clients, data and decisions.
resources.bodyHtml:
AI is moving quickly from experiments to tools that draft, decide and act. Agentic AI systems can take steps on their own, such as sending messages, moving data or placing instructions. Accountability stays with the firm and its management, whatever the tool.

Where we use it

  • Do we have an inventory of AI systems in use, including tools built into third-party software and those staff use on their own?
  • Which uses affect clients, investment decisions, compliance, financial reporting or the board's own information?
  • Which AI tools can take actions without a human approving each one, and what are they allowed to do?

A good answer shows a current inventory with each use classified by risk and an owner for each.

Controls

  • Is there an AI policy approved by the board, setting out acceptable uses and approval steps?
  • How are AI outputs tested for accuracy, bias and drift, and how often?
  • What data do the tools see, and could client or confidential data leave the firm?
  • For agents: what limits, permissions and kill switches apply, and are their actions logged and reviewed?
  • How do we meet the EU AI Act and data protection rules where they apply?

Board use

  • Is any information in the board pack produced or summarised by AI, and how is it validated?
  • Does the board have enough understanding to challenge AI-based proposals?

Red flags: no inventory; staff using public tools with client data; AI-generated outputs reaching clients without review; agents with broad permissions and no logging.

resources.title: Valuation and hard-to-value assets
resources.summary: Questions for a fund board on how assets are valued, how independent and robust the process is, and how hard-to-value and illiquid assets are priced.
resources.bodyHtml:
Every subscription and redemption happens at the net asset value, so a wrong valuation transfers money between investors and can mislead them about performance. The board owns the valuation policy even when it delegates the work.

The framework

  • Is there a written valuation policy approved by the board, covering every asset type the fund holds?
  • Is the valuation function independent of portfolio management, and who has the final say?
  • Is there a valuation committee, who sits on it, and how does it report to the board?

A good answer shows a clear chain from policy to daily practice, with portfolio managers able to give input but not decide prices.

Hard-to-value assets

  • What share of the portfolio is priced using models or broker quotes rather than observable market prices?
  • How are stale prices, suspended securities and price overrides identified and approved?
  • For private assets, how often are valuations updated, who provides them, and how are the key inputs challenged?
  • How do our valuations compare with the prices achieved when assets are actually sold?

A good answer tracks price overrides and stale prices and back-tests valuations against sale prices.

Errors and challenge

  • What is the threshold for a NAV error, and how are errors corrected and investors compensated?
  • When did the board last challenge a valuation, and what happened?
  • Does the auditor or an independent valuer review the valuation of the hardest-to-value assets?

Red flags: portfolio managers pricing their own positions; many manual price overrides; private asset valuations that never fall; NAV errors explained away as immaterial without a documented threshold.

resources.title: What a good policy contains
resources.summary: A checklist for writing or reviewing a policy in a regulated firm, so that it is clear, owned and used.
resources.bodyHtml:
Contents

  • Purpose and scope: what the policy covers, which entities and activities.
  • Regulatory basis: the rules and guidance it implements.
  • Principles and standards: what the firm will and will not do.
  • Roles and responsibilities: board, committees, senior managers, control functions and business teams.
  • Key processes at a high level, with links to detailed procedures.
  • Limits and thresholds, linked to risk appetite.
  • Escalation and exceptions: how breaches or exceptions are handled and approved.
  • Monitoring and reporting: how compliance is measured and reported.
  • Training requirements.
  • Ownership, approval and review: who owns it, who approves it, review frequency and version history.

Qualities

  • Clear, concise and written for the people who use it.
  • Consistent with other policies and with what actually happens.
  • Specific to the firm, not a template.

Common failings

  • Copied from templates and never used.
  • Out of date after regulatory or business changes.
  • Procedures that contradict the policy.
  • No evidence of monitoring.

resources.title: Writing good minutes
resources.summary: How to write board minutes that record the board's discussion, challenge, decisions and reasons, and stand up to regulatory scrutiny.
resources.bodyHtml:
Minutes are the formal record of what the board did. Regulators, auditors, courts and future directors read them to judge whether the board did its job.

What good minutes contain

  • Attendees, apologies and quorum.
  • Declarations of interest and how conflicts were managed.
  • For each item: the paper considered, the main points discussed, the questions and challenges raised, the answers given and the decision, with the reasons.
  • Dissenting views, where a director asks for them to be recorded.
  • Actions, owners and deadlines.

Style

  • Concise but substantive: not a transcript, but more than "the board noted the report".
  • Neutral and factual.
  • Attribute challenge where it matters, for example a director's specific concern.
  • Record when the board asked for more information before deciding.

Process

  • Draft promptly, ideally within a few days.
  • Circulate to the chair, then to all directors for comment.
  • Approve at the next meeting and sign.
  • Keep an action log and review it at every meeting.

Common weaknesses

  • "Noted" with no record of discussion.
  • Decisions recorded without reasons.
  • Minutes that read as if the decision was made elsewhere.
  • Challenge omitted because it was uncomfortable.
